[The Sūcīpatra is completed.
Oṃ, salutations to the Guru; salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Oṃ, that which is the seed of the Veda-tree, possessing complete and infinite branches.

I bow to that Bhairava-Āgama which they say yields the fruit of that very [practice]. Having purified the ground— whether it be white, red, yellow, or black— and having endowed it with fragrant scents and flowers...
Having thus made the ground beautiful— adorned with canopies, abundant with the fragrance of excellent incense, and treated with various ointments—
a person should perform the initiation, beginning first with Gaṇeśa.

By performing the worship of Gaṇeśa at the beginning of rites such as worship, a person becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done; likewise, Vāgīśī should be worshipped with great effort for the sake of long life. Through such worship—
One certainly attains success in all undertakings;
first, there is the worship of Pustakavāgīśvarī, who is seated upon a lotus, very white, three-eyed, and holding a trident and a rosary.
I bow to Sarasvatī, the bestower of success, who constantly holds a garland and a sword in her four hands;
[this is] the offering of unguent and fragrance to Śrī Pustakavāgīśvarī.

Maḥ, obeisance to Arghya; namaḥ, obeisance to Puṣpa; namaḥ, aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ, obeisance to Sarasvatī, the speaker of speech, Vāgvādinī; oṃ hsauḥ aṃ āṃ, and so on, ending with haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ, hsauḥ, obeisance to Sarasvatī.

Having offered honey, ghee, and sugar as the *naivedya* (food offering), and having made the *mudrā* of the offering substance, one should dismiss [the deity] with these words: "O four-armed one, seated upon a great lotus,
holder of the lotus, abode of the garland of phonemes, eternal one, wielder of the trident..."

O Goddess Sarasvatī, whatever has been done by me that is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in procedure, though joined with garlands and head-ornaments—may that be forgiven by you; O Goddess, show mercy. Now, for the pacification of obstacles:
For the worship of Gaṇapati, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus outside the maṇḍala on one's left, one should place fruits and other offerings upon the pericarp,
along with a rosary, a goad, and a vessel containing oil and sweets.

Gaṇeśvara, with four arms, holding a noose and a goad, having two tusks, and riding upon a lion—come, come, O Lord Gaṇapati, accept this worship! Thus is the invocation. Om, to the remover of obstacles.

"Obeisance to the one who wears the moon as his crest-jewel; O Hara, grant me wealth for the sake of my purpose, svāhā! Having offered the sacrificial food (*naivedya*) consisting of honey, clarified butter, and sugar, he should dismiss [the deity]. [If] the ritual is deficient in materials...
Whatever was deficient, whatever was lacking in mantras, or whatever has gone astray—all that may be forgiven by you, O Lord;
O Vighneśvara, show your grace. Now, therefore, for the pacification of obstacles, one should recite the *Bahurūpagarbha-stotra*.
Om, salutations with my head to the true Guru, who is peaceful, the manifest form of Śiva,
seated upon the Yogapīṭha for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha— to him whose unbroken, circular form pervades all that is moving and stationary.

Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that supreme state has been revealed; salutation to that venerable Guru by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge.

*Obeisance to the Guru! The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is Maheśvara himself; the Guru alone is the entire universe—obeisance to that glorious Guru.* Having thus prostrated before the True Guru, [one recites]: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sarva...*

Salutation to Janapriyāyamukhāya. Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ, salutation as I offer this purifying [substance]. You are the single form of the universe, the soul of the universe, the cause of the creation and other processes of the universe, and whose body is supreme light.
We praise Svacchandabhairava; salutations to Him, the non-terrible one whose nature is more terrible than the terrible,
the cause of creation, maintenance, dissolution,
concealment, and grace, who is established in the central breath.

He who, as Svacchanda-nātha, reverses those [energies]— which have the supreme haṃsa as their source of hair-pores, whose nature consists of subtle discernment, and which comprise three and a half crores—
in the form of mantras, is the Lord.

He who is the roaring, fierce-bodied one, whose form is supreme and eternal splendor— having bathed there, having performed his daily rites, and having adorned his body with the twelve-fold ornaments beginning with the turban and including the finger-rings;

With his hair tied up, having first sat upon an auspicious seat such as a svastika, seated on a skin or similar seat with the hair facing upward and the head toward the east, his face smeared with fragrant perfumes, he is well-pleased.
Adorned with fine incense, well-chewed betel, and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum, his body marked by necklaces, bracelets, and armlets—
to him, Sadyojāta, I go for refuge; obeisance indeed to Sadyojāta.

"O Bhava, O Bhava, O Atibhava, protect me; O Bhavodbhava!"—with this mantra, [the disciple] is smeared with fragrant scents; he is well-incensed with incense by means of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra; and excellent betel-leaf is offered. 1 2 3. [I offer] Amṛteśvara Bhairava to me.
With the mantra "rakṣa 2ṃ3ṃ2ṃ1ṃ," his body adorned with necklaces, bracelets, and armlets,
he knelt upon the ground and, having constructed a pitcher-altar (kalaśavedi) thirty-six finger-breadths in height, [he placed] twelve [fingers] on his left side therein.

Having established two *kalaśas* [filled with] *aṅgula* [water] and having fashioned the protective mandala of the Lokapālas and other deities in front of them, one should place the vessel for the *astra-argha* offering in the southwest (nairṛtya) corner; with that, one performs the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of all the ritual substances with the syllable *phaṭ*.

*Straḥ phaṭ phaṭ! May there be purification through all ritual offerings, phaṭ svāhā!* Having displayed the *astra-mudrā*, one should meditate upon the Weapon [deity] stationed at the door— three-eyed, blazing, revolving, and bringing about the destruction of all sins and the host of obstructors.
Facing the Vashya [deity], one should sprinkle oneself and the ritual materials with that water, saying: "Welcome, welcome to Śiva together with his retinue, O sir!
Then follows the worship of the messenger (dūtī), who is gentle, four-armed, and sweet-sounding.
We praise her who utters the sound of mantras, holding a rosary, a book, and a garland as her excellent attributes in her hands.
Oṃ huṃ, homage to the messenger Maṃtramātṛ, the embodiment of pure knowledge (Śuddhavidyā). Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, homage to the messenger Jagaddhvani-maṃtramātṛ.

Thus, one should sound the *dūtī* with the left hand; right there, for the sake of preventing confusion, one should perform the offering of incense: *oṃ tanmaheśāya vidmahe vāgviśuddhāya dhīmahi tannaḥ śivaḥ pracodayāt*.
May [He] grant [it]. (3) Oṃ, we know the Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us.
(3) Oṃ, we know the Bahurūpa; we meditate upon Koṭarākṣa; may Ghorasiva impel us.
Out of compassion: "All this is of the nature of Śiva; from Śiva alone does it proceed. For the sake of Śiva, for Him who contains Śiva within, may Śiva impel everything.
(3) Then, before the deity, there is worship of the circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*). [The form] has one face.

One should meditate upon him who has four arms, who destroys all obstacles, who is radiant with a halo of light, and who is resplendent; [reciting] "Oṃ, homage to the Halo of Light. He is white, three-eyed, mounted on a bull, and blazing with a trident.
[He who is] thus the remover of all sins, with hands marked by the boon-granting and fear-dispelling gestures;
*oṃ* obeisance to Vṛṣabha; *oṃ* obeisance to Bhṛṅgīśa; *oṃ* obeisance to Ambikā; *oṃ* obeisance to Dvāraśrī; *oṃ* obeisance to Lakṣmī.
Maḥ! Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; oṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī; oṃ, obeisance to the Trident-bearer;
oṃ, obeisance to Viśvakarman. Then, one should worship the ten Mothers of the Directions in order, beginning from the east. [The visualization of them...]
Just as they are beautiful, holding jars of nectar and garlands of fine flowers in their hands, with faces turned toward the single-faced deity in the sky, [one should worship]:
*Oṃ, obeisance to Umā* in the east; *Oṃ, obeisance to Durgā* in the southeast.
Oṃ, salutation to Bhadrakālī in the south; Oṃ, salutation to Svasti in the southwest (nairṛtya);
Oṃ, salutation to Svāhā in the west; Oṃ, salutation to Śubhaṃkārī in the northwest (vāyu); Oṃ, salutation to Śrī in the north; Oṃ, salutation to Gaurī in the northeast (īśāna). Oṃ.
*Oṃ namo bhūtadhātryai* above; *Oṃ namo vāgīśvaryai* below. Then, the worship of the elements (*bhūta-pūjā*) in order starting from the east: *Oṃ lāṃ namaḥ pṛthivyai* in the east;
*Oṃ rauṃ namo 'gnaye* in the southeast; *Oṃ śauṃ namo yajamānāya*.
Homage to the South: Oṃ ṣāṃ, homage to Āditya; to the Southwest: Oṃ vauṃ, homage to Jala; to the West: Oṃ yauṃ, homage to Vāyu; to the Northwest:
Oṃ sauṃ, homage to Candramas; to the North: Oṃ hauṃ, homage to Ākāśa; to the Northeast.
Thus, inside the sacrificial hall, on the left and right doorposts:
*Oṃ nandinena namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ caṇḍāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ śaṅkhanidhaye namaḥ*, *Oṃ*.
Oṃ, salutations to the treasure Mahāśaṅkha; Oṃ, salutations to Diṇḍin—on one's own right and left branches; Oṃ, salutations to Mahākāla;
Oṃ, salutations to Yamunā; Oṃ, salutations to Chāgalāsya.
Oṃ, obeisance to Upacaṇḍa; Oṃ, obeisance to Padmanidhi;
Oṃ, obeisance to Mahāpadmanidhi; Oṃ, obeisance to Mahodara. Above, obeisance to Dvāraśrī; below, obeisance to Dehalī; in the center, Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā.
Oṃ namaḥ; Oṃ vāstupuruṣāya namaḥ; Oṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ;
Maṇibhadrāya namaḥ; to the west of oneself, namaḥ to all beings (sarvebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ); then, to the left of oneself, the worship of Gaṇeśa: Oṃ gho...
*Oṃ namaḥ radadaṃṣṭrāya*, *namaḥ virūpākṣāya*, *namaḥ kākatuṇḍāya*, *namaḥ cillavaktrāya*. Thus ends the worship of the gatekeepers of Gaṇeśa.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is: "Holding [the tusk] in the right hand... *Gaṃ tatpuruṣāya viṣṇave...* (The mantra for the Tatpuruṣa face).
Kratuṇḍāyadhīṣṭannodantīpra... Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to Mahāpadmāsana; obeisance to Siṃha—thus [is] the seat. Oṃ Galūṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; Glūṃ Saḥ.
"Salutation to Gaṇapativallabhā. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with "Gāṅgī" and so forth, one says:
"O, O Lord of the Gaṇas! Make this place free from obstacles now; I shall perform the worship of Hara for the sake of protection in the hereafter. Thus [it is said].

Then follows the worship of Neshana; next, the worship of Surya on one's right: "Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ, piṅgalāya namaḥ"—thus is the worship. "Oṃ hāṃ padmāsanāya namaḥ, aṃ arkāsanāya namaḥ, hāṃ khaśo... [The text continues].

Salutations to the form of the Sun of the Body. Oṃ, salutations to the one seated on a vast throne; thus [is] the seat. Oṃ, [I salute him] who is seated upon a white lotus, possessing the luster of a pomegranate flower, situated in the center of a circular mandala of shimmering, great red radiance.
One should meditate upon the Sun as having two arms, wearing red garments, and holding in his two hands white lotus stalks with throbbing buds resting upon his shoulders. Thus is the meditation.
We know that which belongs to the form of the Sun; we meditate upon the wisdom of the Sun; may He inspire us.
May the Sun impel [me]. (3) Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to the Sun.
Aṃ at the heart; *arka* at the head; Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, obeisance to Jvālinī at the crest-lock;
Hrāṃ at the armor; Bhāṃ at the eyes; Raḥ at the weapon; obeisance to the eight-petaled lotus seat.
"Salutations to the seven-leaved ones; salutations to the seven-horsed ones;
salutations to the one seated upon the twelve-petaled lotus. Thus is the worship of the Sun. In the center is the worship of Kumāra. [One should offer] a beautiful bell fashioned of gold...

May that Prince Kumāra— who possesses such power, who has a beautiful crest of peacock feathers, whose face is ever-gracious, and whose state is one of increasing prosperity— be for your well-being, even though he remains in the age of childhood. Thus is the meditation (dhyāna).
*Ṛtikeyāvidmahe senādhipataye dhīmahi, tannaḥ kumāraḥ pracodayāt.* (3) *Oṃ klūṃ kāṃ kumārāya namaḥ, kāṃ kīṃ,* etc., is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). *Oṃ namaḥ kumārāya śakti...*

"Obeisance to him who has a cock in his hand, who has a peacock as his vehicle, who has six faces, who is accompanied by the Yoginī, who is the Great Minister, the Lord, and the Commander of the Army;
obeisance, svāhā! Thus is the worship of Kumāra. Then, on one's own right, upwards...
The worship of the planets in the order of the *ṛṣi-paṅkti*: Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to Agni and Āditya;
Oṃ Kaṃ, salutation to Varuṇa and Candramas; Oṃ Caṃ, salutation to Kumāra and Bhauma;
Oṃ Ṭaṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu and Budha.
Maḥ Oṃ, salutation to Indra and Bṛhaspati; Oṃ Yaṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī and Śukra; Oṃ Yaṃ, salutation to Prajāpati and Śanaiścara;
Oṃ Śaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati and Rāhu.
Maḥ Oṃ, salutations to Rudra and Ketu; Oṃ, salutations to Brahmā and Dhruva; Oṃ, salutations to Ananta and Agasti; Oṃ, all you venerable planets and whatever other secondary planets there may be.
May they all assemble here for the pacification of obstacles;
having consecrated the *yuṣya* with the *astra-mantra* and the *nārāca-mudrā* using the middle fingers and thumbs,
and having meditated upon it as having a blazing, radiant form, [one should ward off] the obstacle.
For the purpose of driving away [obstacles], one should cast [the mantra] into the interior of the *vedi* with "Phaṭ Astrāya Phaṭ. Then:
"Oṃ, may those beings depart who are established in this place;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva."
May those who have become heretics, whether they dwell on the earth, in the intermediate space, or in the heavenly world— may they perish by the command of Śiva;
likewise may the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *caras*, *rākṣasas*, and *sarīsṛpas* [perish].
"O you all, depart! Struck by the divine weapon:
*oṃ hrīṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya huṃ phaṭ*. Then, with three claps of the hand using the weapon-mantra (*astra*), [he should strike] those situated in the intermediate space with kicks of the heels.

Having warded off the terrestrial obstacles with ten snaps of the fingers and those of the cardinal and intermediate directions by clearing the throat, having veiled [the self] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), having covered the body with the trident-gesture (*triśūlamudrā*), and [having performed] the withdrawal-gesture (*saṃhāramudrā*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Having warded off obstacles, one should contemplate a rampart of fire. With the mantra "Oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ," one should worship Brahmā with flowers and other offerings in the center in front of the deity. [One should worship] with "Oṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ" and "Padmāsanāya..."
Saying "Nāya namaḥ," having offered flowers upon a soft skin on one's own seat and having assumed a posture such as the svastika, one should begin the karanyāsa.
Therein, having smeared the two hands with perfume and sprinkled them with water while reciting the Astra-mantra;
Having enveloped [the two] with the Kavaca mantra, one should flood them with nectar.
Having meditated on the Śakti arisen from the seat of the root (kanda) and having contemplated her as she has reached the twelve [finger-breadths], one should take the nectar from that place.

Having meditated on [the breath] as having emerged through the nostrils and the twelve [finger-breadths], one should contemplate that both hands have been bathed. Immediately thereafter, having formed the lotus-mudrā (*padmamudrā*),
one should meditate upon the Support-Power (*ādhāraśakti*) at the base of the thumbs and the lotus at its tip.
There, one should place the thirty-two-syllable deity in the form of the *rimūrti*; the five limbs from the thumb to the little finger; the weapon (*astra*) on the nails;
and the eight Bhairavas on the left side, beginning from the right index finger and ending with the left index finger.
Beginning with the left index finger and ending with the right index finger, one should assign the eight Bhairavas;

thereafter, one should assign the partless (niṣkala) form along with its limbs (sāṅga) upon the two thumbs. This is the ritual assignment on the hands (karanyāsa). Now, the breath control (prāṇāyāma): "Laṃ, I perform exhalation (recaka); obeisance."
One should expel that impure prāṇa-vāyu through the right nostril for the duration of twelve recitations of the praṇava with the mantra: *vaṃ pūrakaṃ karomi namaḥ*.
Then, one should draw in the pure, heard prāṇa-vāyu for four [recitations].

One should cause that very vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) to enter within through the left nostril for as long as it takes to recite twenty *praṇavas*, like a water-filled jar; [this is] the *kuṃbhaka* (retention), and I pay homage to it.
One should restrain [the breath] internally for as long as it takes to utter thirty-six *praṇavas* with a steady duration; having thus performed three such *prāṇāyāmas*,
one should [hold] that very vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) in the state of *kumbhaka* at the heart, throat, and palate.
Because it is impossible to pierce the middle *brahmarandhra* all at once, one should gradually expel [the breath] through the left nostril;
this is the upward *recaka*. In this manner, the Self residing in the heart-lotus...

Having focused the mind and ego-sense upon the subtle [point], resembling a firefly, shimmering like a star, by means of the piercing through the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā, one should project it upward through the sequence of the upper *recaka* to the *dvādaśānta*.
Having dissolved the intellect (*buddhi*) into the Supreme Reality, one should meditate upon the body as empty;

this is the purification of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*). Then, one should effect the purification of the gross body (*sthūla-deha*) through the concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) of withering and so forth, as follows: *Oṃ kṣyūṃ*.
Thinking "I shall dry up my body," one should contemplate the *praṇava* (Oṃ) in the form of the sun and visualize one's own body as resembling a withered tree;
this is the earth-element concentration (*pārthivī dhāraṇā*). Oṃ, for the sake of protection.

Saying "Māṃ tanuṃ dāhayāmi namaḥ," one should assume the svastika or another posture with the right foot [extended] and begin the *karanyāsa*. Therein, having smeared the two hands with sandalwood paste and sprinkled them with water using the *astra-mantra*, one should perform the *kavaca-nyāsa*.

If they are not veiled, one should flood them with nectar; having visualized the Śakti risen from the location of the *kanda* and having contemplated her as she has reached the *dvādaśānta*, one should take the nectar from that place and [inhale it] through the nose.
Having visualized [the water] emerging from the end of the twelve [fingers], one should bathe both hands and meditate. Immediately thereafter, having formed the lotus mudrā,
one should meditate on the *ādhāra-śakti* at the base of the thumbs, the lotus at the tips, and the *mūrti* (the deity's form) upon that.
One should place the thirty-two-syllable deity on the five fingers from the thumb to the little finger; the weapon-mantra (*astra*) on the nails;
and the eight Bhairavas starting from the right index finger and ending with the left index finger.
Beginning from the right index finger and ending with the little finger, one should assign the eight Bhairavas;
then, one should assign the Niṣkala [mantra] along with its limbs (the Aṅgas) to the two thumbs. This is the Karanyāsa.
Now, the Prāṇāyāma: "Laṃ, I perform exhalation (recaka), obeisance"—thus [one expels] the impure.

One should expel the *prāṇa* breath through the right nostril for the duration of twelve recitations of the *praṇava*; then, [performing] the inhalation (*pūraka*) with "vaṃ," one should draw in the pure,
white *prāṇa* breath with "karaṃ namaḥ."
One should contemplate the dissolution [of the breath] through the left nostril for as long as it takes to utter twenty *praṇavas*.
Just as the poisonous nature of poison is neutralized by the power of a mantra without its essential nature being changed, so too is the identification with the body [neutralized].

The meaning of "vasya-lopa" is the destruction of one's own individual form. Thus, when the body has ceased to exist within the *kośika* (the subtle sheath), one should contemplate the Self as consisting of supreme bliss (*paramānandamaya*), with the thought: "I am indeed Śiva, free from desire. Om.
"Hāṃ! I enliven the divine body; obeisance. Having meditated upon the seat (āsana) starting from the root (kanda), [one offers]: "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti at the kanda;
obeisance to Dhātrī at the kanda; obeisance to the Ocean of Milk extending up to the navel."

Having meditated upon the Yoga-pīṭha seat, which extends from the heart down to the heart and is accompanied by the [four] quarters beginning with Dharma, one should visualize in its center, upon that,
a white lotus seat with eight petals, filaments, and a pericarp.

"Salutation to the petals; salutation to the solar disc. One should meditate on the white petals. "Salutation to Brahmā, the lord thereof. One should meditate on Brahmā as four-faced and four-armed. [Salutation] to the filaments.
Salutation to the lunar disc; salutation to the filaments, which one should meditate upon as yellow and white. Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord thereof;
one should meditate on Viṣṇu as being black in color. Salutation to the pericarp; [salutation] to Vahni.
One should meditate on the pericarp as golden, saying "Salutation to Maṇḍalāya";
one should meditate on Rudra as white, saying "Salutation to Pataye Rudrāya";
then one should meditate on Īśvara as white, saying "Salutation to Īśvarāya."
Thereafter, one should place the Great Preta, who is laughing, conscious, red in color, possessing great splendor, and adorned with three eyes.
Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to the seat of Sadāśiva, the Great Preta. Oṃ.

Salutation to the *ātmatattva* (principle of the self) on the petals; salutation to the *vidyātattva* (principle of knowledge) on the filaments; salutation to the *śivatattva* (principle of Śiva) on the pericarp.
Having thus worshipped the four Vedas upon the seat, [one should proceed].

From the *dvādaśānta* at the crown of the head, one should [visualize] the Blessed One in the form of a shimmering star; by means of the upward *recaka* breath, [the deity is brought] through the sequence of the *brahmarandhra*, the space between the eyebrows, and the palate,
into the form of the Blessed One situated in the heart-lotus at the *dvādaśānta*.
The meaning is that one should gradually unite [the elements] in this manner and thus make the self itself Śiva. *Oṃ oṃ oṃ*, I make [this] immortal, *namaḥ*—
by means of the water of the Śākta nectar fallen from the *dvādaśānta*.
I immerse the body, including its exterior and interior;
obeisance! Obeisance to the lower covering; obeisance to the upper covering; obeisance to the middle covering.
Oṃ, obeisance to Sattva; obeisance to Rajas. Raṃ, obeisance to Rajas.
Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord with the visualization "Oṃ Śiva" at that center, [specifically] upon the deity in the pericarp (karṇikā) there, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa):
"Oṃ, salutation to the Śiva-tattva in the aperture of the heart. Always.

Oṃ, salutation to the Śiva-tattva on the forehead; salutation to the Vidyā-tattva at the palate; salutation to the Māyā-tattva at the throat; salutation to the Kāla-tattva at the heart; salutation to the Niyati-tattva...

At the navel: *Namaḥ puruṣatattvāya* (Salutation to the principle of Puruṣa). At the penis: *Namaḥ prakṛtitattvāya* (Salutation to the principle of Prakṛti). At the feet: [Salutation to the principle of Māyā]. Now follows the Nyāsa of the three principles: At the aperture of the crown: *Saḥ śivatattvāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the principle of Śiva). *Juṃ vidyātattvāya* (Salutation to the principle of Vidyā). [At the heart: *Haṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the principle of Ātman)].
*Oṃ* *namas* to the *Ātmatattva* (Principle of the Self) between the eyebrows;

*oṃ juṃ saḥ namas* to the form of Amṛteśa in the heart; [and *namas*] to the entire body. Then, perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs (*kara-aṅga-nyāsa*) by means of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

One should again perform the root [mantra] and place it upon the entire body with "Oṃ mūrtyai namaḥ" and "Oṃ śuddhadehāya namaḥ. One should worship the deity with the five mental offerings (mānasa-pañcopacāra), and then perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
One should perform the external sacrifice on the sacrificial ground;

having worshipped the vessel for the *arghya* water with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) in one's own right hand, [one visualizes] the three-eyed [deity], who is blazing like fire, who destroys the multitude of obstacles and brings about the destruction of great sins.
One should meditate on the Weapon-mantra (astra) facing the deity at the doorway;
then, by means of a seat made of two blades of darbha grass, the purification of the ritual substances (dravya-saṃskāra) is performed.
Next follows the worship of the vessel for the Śiva-water (śivāmbu) and the vessel for the sacrificial offering (arghapātra) according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having sprinkled the four vessels with the Astra mantra,
encircled them with the Varma mantra, veiled them with the Kavaca mantra,
and worshipped them with the Praṇava, [one says]: "Oṃ, I veil these four vessels."

Having performed the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*) with "HŪṂ NAMAH," and having worshipped with "NAMAH TO THE VIDHI, NIRODHA, ŚIVA, AMBU, AND PAŚVARGHA VESSELS," [he should place them] upon two stalks of *darbha* grass serving as a seat, together with the eight limbs.

Without having performed worship, water, milk, kuśa grass, ghee, curd, rice, barley, and white mustard seeds are proclaimed as the components of the *arghya* offering; [the mantra is] "Lāṃ, obeisance to Jagaddhātrī, the Earth."
Maḥ! To Rudra with three matted locks and tawny hair above, salutation—rice grains;
Oṃ! To Brahmā, the eldest of the gods, salutation—barley;
Oṃ! Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods—beans.
Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Sāvitrī, the devourer of sins; *Sāvitryai huṃ phaṭ*—[offer] flowers and darbha grass. Oṃ Svāṃ Svāṃ Svāṃ, obeisance to Soma; [offer] water. Oṃ Tat Sad Om.

*Oṃ namaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ tilān* (To the ancestors, salutation: sesame seeds). *Oṃ huṃ vāgīśvaryai vāk-pade sarasvatyai namaḥ kṣīram* (Oṃ huṃ, to the Mistress of Speech, at the place of speech, to Sarasvatī, salutation: milk). *Oṃ phaṭ astrāya namaḥ ghṛtam* (Oṃ phaṭ, to the Weapon [mantra], salutation: ghee). *Oṃ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ sarvottama* (Oṃ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ, O Supreme One).

"Salutation to the substances; these substances should be cast into the vessel according to the rule"—thus is the eightfold nature of the *arghya* (offering water), intended for the presentation of the eightfold group (*puryaṣṭaka*).
Therein, from the perspective of the Supreme, first [is the offering] to the All-pervasive Lord (*vibhu*).
One should perform the worship with water for the feet and other offerings, saying: *oṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ*.
One should worship with the principles of *vidyā*, *śiva*, *prakṛti*, and *puruṣa*, and with the digits (*kalā*) of the sun, moon, and fire; first, in that regard:
The digits of the Sun: *Oṃ marīcyai namaḥ*; likewise to Jvālinī, Dhūmrā, Tāpanī, Tāpinī, Pācanī, Havyavāhā, Tejovatī, Śatadhāmā, and Sudhāmā.
To Durgāgarbhā, to Tamopahāriṇī—thus are the digits of the Sun (Sūryakalās).
Om, now the digits of the Moon (Candrakalās): Om, salutation to Pūṣā;
likewise to Yaśasī, Sumanasī, Prīti, Prītikarī, Dhṛti, and Dhṛti...
Salutations to Tika, Somyā, Marīci, Aṃśumālinī, Śaśinī, Hṛdutā, Lakṣmī, Chāyā, Saṃpūrṇamaṇḍalā, and Amṛtā—thus [are] the lunar digits (somakalāḥ). Now, the fire-digits (vahnikalāḥ):
*oṃ* salutations to Dhūmrā; likewise to Nīlā, Raktā, and Kapilā.
One should worship the ten fire-kalās— Visphuliṅginī, Jvālā, Tejovatī, Havyavāhā,
Kavyavāhā, Raudrī, and Saṃhāriṇī—
with the root mantra and the five ancillaries (aṅgas).
Thus is the worship with the vidyā-argha; therein,

the observation of the implements as perceived by the Supreme [Consciousness], which is unobscured, perfectly real, and free from conceptual construction— that, O Goddess, is declared to be the Supreme.

The final destination is the Kāṣṭhāsā. Then, one should sprinkle all the ritual substances from the arghya vessel. Next, in the center, one should worship the Nirodha-arghya with the root mantra alone, and there one should display the Niṣṭhura-mudrā.

Near that [liṅga], one should perform the worship of Śiva’s water with "Oṃ huṃ śivāya namaḥ. Near that, on one's right, one should worship the Pāśupata weapon with the root mantra accompanied by its ancillaries (aṅgas) and the goddess, using the Pāśupata-weapon mantra.
Oṃ ślīṃ paśu huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya phaṭ | Oṃ hṛdayāya phaṭ namaḥ ślīṃ śirase phaṭ svāhā | Yaḥ śikhāyai phaṭ vaṣaṭ | Śuk kavacāya phaṭ huṃ hūṃ paśu ||
"HŪṂ, PHAṬ VAṢAṬ PHAṬ from each and every eye; PHAṬ PHAṬ to the weapon (astra),
PHAṬ PHAṬ"— with this [mantra], one performs the worship of the water for the peaceful *arghya* vessel according to the procedure of the cessation of Śiva,
and effects the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the sheep-and-nectar mudrā (*meṣamṛtamudrā*).
One should perform self-prokṣaṇa from the *argha* vessel with the mantra "naumi svātmā.

Having performed the worship of one's own self (*svātmapūjā*) seven times with the root mantra, one should perform the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*) ritual by sprinkling the palms with the water of Śiva, the water of the weapon (*astra*), and the water of the *viḍya*.

Having sprinkled [the deity] with water, veiled [him], and washed [his] hand with scented water, one should worship the Lord— who is joined with Śiva, endowed with five faces, and accompanied by all his limbs— with one hand smeared with fragrance, while remaining seated upon a seat.

Śiva, standing firm, the cutter of bonds, the bringer of security, is proclaimed as Śivahasta. It is as follows: the ritual for the fragrant water consists of saffron, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, tagara, and priyaṅgu.

Having prepared the scented water (*gandhodaka*) according to the sequence in the ritual for the worship of Śaṅkara, one should smear the hands with it. [Reciting] *oṃ somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*, [one places it] on the left hand; [reciting] *oṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*, on the right.

Having worshipped the root mantra along with its limbs (aṅgas) and all its faces, using fragrant substances on the tip of the index finger of the right hand while holding flowers with the middle finger and thumb of that same hand, and placing them upon the other hand, one should perform the union of mantras (mantrasandhāna), the union of channels (nāḍīsandhāna), and the supreme unification.
One should perform the battle; therein, first, the application of mantras:
the armor of weapons, the armor of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the armor of Bhairava, the armor of Śakti, and the limbs [of Śakti] as the limbs [of the deity].
The "joining of mantras" (*mantrasandhāna*) consists in the joining of the faces of the Lord within the *kṣetras*;
this is done after meditating upon the Power (*śakti*) that has arisen from the location of one's own *kanda*.

Having meditated on [the breath] having reached as far as the *dvādaśānta*, one should take the nectar from that place; it emerges through the left nostril of the practitioner and enters through the right nostril of the deity. From that...
Having reached the location of the *kanda*, having risen from there, having reached the *dvādaśānta*,
and having taken the nectar from there, she has entered through the left nostril,
reached the location of the *kanda*, and risen from there.
Having reached the *dvādaśānta* and taken up the nectar, she emerges through the left [nostril];
in this very manner, having extended through the sequence of the coverings (*āvaraṇa*) along a single channel, she enters the practitioner’s own right nostril— thus one should meditate.

However, the method for joining the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*) is as follows: one should meditate on the power (*śakti*) arising from the *kanda* of the self, having emerged through the *dvādaśānta*, and entering simultaneously into the veils (*āvaraṇas*) themselves. Thus it is said.
Having visualized the hand as being filled with such flaming groups of mantras, one should utter the root mantra and place the right hand [upon it];
having offered a flower from the left hand with the right hand, that [right hand]— the dakṣiṇa...

One should place that hand upon one's own head; by this rite of the Śiva-hand, the worship of the Blessed One becomes complete. The underlying thought is: "I am indeed Śiva. Now follows the procedure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the prescribed rule.
Having prepared nine compartments with powdered *vāśī* stone, and having brought nine vessels ranging from gold to clay, one should recite seven times: "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I purify the vessels, haḥ phaṭ."

One should consecrate the vessels with water from the *jñānakhaḍga* [vessel] made of thirty-six *darbha* grasses that have been empowered by mantra. Then, having veiled them with the *kavaca* [mantra] while reciting: "Oṃ haiṃ, I envelop the vessels, huṃ," one should [proceed] to the central square.
Beginning from the east and proceeding in order: *oṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ*;
likewise for Sadāśiva-tattva, Īśvara-tattva, Vidya-tattva, Māyā-tattva, Kāla-tattva, Niyati-tattva, Puruṣa-tattva, and Prakṛti-tattva.
Having worshipped [the central deity], one should worship without a vessel in the middle, east, south, west, and north, saying:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Supratiṣṭhā; likewise obeisance to Suśāntā, Tejovatī, Amṛtāsvādā, and Śukrodayā."
Having thus worshipped, [one should offer]: *hāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*, with cow dung in the west;
*hrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*, with cow urine in the north; *huṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*, with curd in the east; and *haiṃ* to the armor, [with] curds in the center.

*Huṃ*, [offer] milk in the southwest (*nairṛtye*), *haḥ astrāya phaṭ*. *Hoṃ*, [offer] clarified butter (*ghṛtaṃ*) to the eyes (*netrebhyaḥ*) with *vauṣaṭ*. One should consecrate the water of *kuśa* grass with the *Gāyatrī*.

In the northeast (*īśāne*), the *Gāyatrī* is as follows: *Tat pūruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi | tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt*. (Note: The provided fragment "tatmaheśāyavi" appears to be a corruption of the standard *mahādevāya*.)
We bow to the one of pure speech; we meditate upon him; may Śiva impel us toward that.
(3) Then, placing each preceding substance before the next, one should combine them:
cow dung in cow urine, cow urine in curd, curd in milk, and milk in [cow's] milk.

One should place ghee into ghee and water consecrated with the *kuśa* grass; all of that should then be set down in a vessel upon a lotus in the southeast corner of the mandala atop the separate kalaśa. Then, having stirred it with the six limbs (*aṅga-ṣaṭka*), [one should contemplate it as] nectar.

Having consecrated them with their respective mudrās as nectar, one should worship Ananta beneath the vessel with "Namaḥ," and Aghora— consisting of Aghoreśvarī, the Niṣkala [mantra], along with his limbs (aṅgas), faces (vaktas), and retinues (āvaraṇas)— above the vessel with "Vāme kheṭaka."

Having enveloped oneself with the *kavaca* (armor mantra), one should sprinkle both oneself and the sacrificial ground (*yāgabhūmi*) with that [mixture]. This is the procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Now, standing in the south-eastern direction and facing north on the sacrificial ground, [one should prepare] a seat made of thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass.

One should worship the Sword of Knowledge with: *oṃ haḥ phaṭ namaḥ to the Sword of Knowledge, whose form consists of the thirty-six principles*. Then, by means of that five-fold cow-product (*pañcagavya*) and a seat made of seven *darbha* grasses over which the seven weapons have been recited (*japta*), one should [perform] the command (*ājñā*).

Sprinkling the ground with *nakhaḍgyena*, *phaṭ*; scratching with *ullikhanaṃ ka romi*, *phaṭ*; likewise, removing the earth, clearing away impurities, making it adamantine (*vajrīkaraṇa*), filling it with pearls, pounding, and sprinkling.
Leveling and sweeping—these purifications are performed mentally;
this is the purification of the ground. Then, for the smearing, one uses the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and scented water, reciting:
*Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the smearing, haḥ phaṭ*. *Ta*.

The scattering of *tōvika* flowers, sesame seeds, parched rice, barley, *dūrvā* grass, auspicious white mustard seeds, and abundant white, fragrant flowers; and with the lord [of the mandala] smeared with sandalwood paste—
This auspicious scattering of flowers (*śroyaṃvikira*) is performed by means of the *astra* mantra;

one should meditate upon the scattered flowers as being the weapons of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and with the *cāmara* or a bunch of *kuśa* grass, one should offer them from the southwest (*nairṛta*) to the northeast (*īśāna*).
One should recite *kāye oṃ haḥ phaṭ abhyukṣaṇaṃ karomi phaṭ*.

Having sprinkled the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) with scented water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one performs the worship of Śrī in the western direction in the center of the altar (*vedī*) with the *dhruva* mantra.

She has a lotus in her hand and beautiful eyes; she is scattering white flowers and is endowed with all auspicious marks. She is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, gazing at the heart of the sacrifice, and resides in the Brahma-sthāna.
To those seated facing the auspicious door, [one should offer] "Oṃ śriyai namaḥ" on one's own left;
then follows the worship of the Gurus ending with Īśāna: "O Gaṇanātha, O Ambikā, O Svāminī, O Ādike, O Mother of the World, [I worship] this teacher of the world whom men worship."
Having worshipped the sacrificial altar (yāgavedī) with the root-mantra and the sāṅga [mantra] according to the prescribed procedure,
one should then draw a svastika in the northeast (īśāna) and a lotus near it; thereafter, the disciple...
Having brought the *vakula* branch, having sprinkled it with auspicious water using the *astra-mantra*, having wiped it with a white cloth and smeared it with fragrant water,
and having filled it with that water along with pieces of horse-dung, mustard seeds, and *dūrvā* grass;
Having filled it with gems, grains, medicinal herbs, sahadevī, bilva fruit, jātī fruit, betel nut, and so forth, and having perfumed it with fragrant substances,
one should worship it upon a svastika in the northeast.

One should install the auspicious *kalaśa* (vessel) in the form of Amṛteśvara upon the seat and worship it with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) along with its five ancillaries (*sāṅga-pañcaka*). In the same way,
having worshipped [the vessel] in the form of Amṛtalakṣmī with the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should...

Then the Guru, having placed [the vessel] upon the cloth, should take the mantra-vase and, placing the weapon-vase (*astrakalaśa*) into the hand of the disciple, cause a stream [of water] to fall in the directions starting from the east, saying: "O Indra, come! O Indra, come! (2)

Reciting "O Kuvera! O Bhogi! O Īśāna! O Bho-bho! O Brahmā!
O Ananta!", he should perform the pouring of the stream [of water]. Then the Guru, muttering the *Bhairava* mantra, should place the *Śiva-kalaśa* upon a lotus while muttering the *astra-mantra*.
One should place the *stravārdhānī* (the vessel for the remnants) upon a *svastika* to its right.
With the mantra: "The heart of the *bhaga* is the *liṅga*; the heart of the *liṅga* is the *bhaga*.
To that *bhaga-liṅga*, to the venerable Rudra, obeisance," [one should perform the offering].
One should not perform the special worship of another [deity] there in the Śiva-kumbha with the Bhaga-linga-mudrā or the sword of higher knowledge; rather,
one should worship Aghora along with its limbs and faces, as well as Aghoreśvarī with her limbs, and Niṣphala.

[He worshipped] Mṛtyuñjaya with his limbs (Sāṅga), together with the Goddess (Sadevīka) and his enclosures (Sāvaraṇa); the enclosure of Bhairava; the seven enclosures beginning with Vidyeśa; the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī; the eight forms (Mūrti) beginning with Earth (Kṣiti); the eight names beginning with Bhava; and Gaṇe...
...the mantras beginning with Śaśisūryakumāra, Viṣṇu, Durgā, Kulavāgīśvarī, Mahātripurasundarī, Kubjikā, Śārikā, Śāradā, Śrīmahārājñī, Jvālāmukhī, Siddhalakṣmī, and so forth.
One should worship the six groups [of deities] at the appropriate times according to one's capacity.

With the visualization beginning with "vāme kheṭake," one should meditate upon the Deity residing in the water-pot (kalaśa), together with his limbs (aṅgas) and retinue (parivāra). "Oṃ, salutation to the path of mantras; to the path of words..."
Salutation to the path of phonemes; salutation to the path of worlds; salutation to the path of principles; salutation to the path of kalās. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the kalā of Nivṛtti;
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the kalā of Nivṛtti.
Oṃ Brahmaṇe namaḥ. Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhā-kalā.
Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of Pratiṣṭhā-kalā. Oṃ Huṃ, obeisance to Vidyā-kalā. Oṃ Hūṃ, [obeisance to the lord of] Vidyā-kalā...
Oṃ *pataye rudrāya* namaḥ. Oṃ *hai śāntākalāyai* namaḥ. Oṃ *hai śāntākalādhipataye īśvarāya* namaḥ.
Oṃ *hauṃ śāntyatītākalāyai* namaḥ. Oṃ *hau śāntyatītā...*
"Obeisance to Sadāśiva, the Lord of the past kalpa.
Having thus worshipped the Śiva-kalaśa, one should also worship the Astra-vārdhānī with: "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, obeisance to the Astra, the power of Ananta."
Phaṭ! Oṃ, obeisance to you who possess the forms of Rudra; to the great Pāśupata weapon, which is impenetrable by enemies, Phaṭ! Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, to the weapon, Phaṭ!
Oṃ phaṭ, to the weapon, Phaṭ! Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, to the weapon of knowledge (jñānāstra).
*Phaṭ*. Thus: to the Brahmāstra, to the Brahmāśirostra, to the Agnyastra, to the Lokapālāstra, to the Pāśupatāstra, to the Aghorāstra, to the Divyāstra—*Oṃ haḥ phaṭ*, [to] all!
*Strāyahaḥ phaṭ*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the sword (*khaḍga*),

salutation to the shield (*kheṭaka*), to the noose (*pāśa*), to the goad (*aṅkuśa*), to the arrow (*śara*), to the Pināka bow (*pināka*), to the boon-granting gesture (*vara*), to the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), to the severed head (*muṇḍa*), to the khaṭvāṅga staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), to the lute (*vīṇā*), and to the drum (*ḍamaru*).

One should worship Rava, Ghaṇṭā, Triśūla, Vajra, Daṇḍa, Paraśu, and Mudgara, as well as the weapons of the world-protectors (Lokapālas) beginning with Vajra; thereafter, one should perform the connection of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) within one's own kanda.
Having meditated on the Śakti as she has arisen from her station and reached the dvādaśānta,
one should visualize her exiting through the right nostril of the deity,
entering through the left nostril, and reaching the heart. At the heart—
From the throat, the palate, and the space between the eyebrows, in this sequence up to the *dvādaśānta*,
having reached the *dvādaśānta* and taken the nectar,
[the practitioner] emerges from the right side of the God; in this very same way, [he does so for] the Goddess and Bhairava.
Having performed the entry and exit through the skull-caps, one should enter the heart through the left [nostril]; this is the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*).
Now, the union of the mantras (*mantra-sandhāna*): one should contemplate oneself as merged into Viṣṇu.
[He is] Brahmā in the Śūnya-Brahman, Īśa in Īśa, Kuvera in Kuvera,
Vāyu in Vāyu, Varuṇa in Varuṇa, Nairṛta in Nairṛta, Yama in Yama, Agni in Agni, [and] him in Indra; [he is] him in the King of Knowledge (Vidyārāja) and him in the King of Soma (Somarāja).
To him in Meghanāda, to him in Manmatha, to him in Vikarāla, to him in Krodharāja,
to him in Śikhivāhana, to him in Kapāleśa, to him in Astra, to him in Netra, to him in Kavaca, to him in Śikhā, to her in the head.
One should contemplate that [deity] as dissolved into that Supreme Goddess;

this is the *mantrasandhāna*. Now follows the *paramīkaraṇa*: having uttered the root mantra from one’s own heart, [one proceeds through] the heart, throat, palate, and the space between the eyebrows.
Having established [the sequence] from the heart, forehead, and the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) in order—
consisting of A, U, and M; the lotus, half-moon, nirodhinī, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpinī, samanā, and unmanā— one should [proceed] up to the twelve.

Having experienced peaceful rest, one should again enter one's own heart by way of descending through the stages and contemplate the Lord together with his retinue and his consort; this is the process of supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*). Then, the mantra...

Having performed the specific worship of the weapon (astra), and having performed the worship of the weapon-vessel with the weapon-mantras, one should perform one hundred and eight recitations of the root mantra [with the prayer]: "Come, manifest your presence, protect, fulfill the sacrifice, and purify."
"O Daughter of Dr̥ṣadvatī, you are the power that removes all evil and the universal self of the Supreme Lord"— having received this command, one should perform the worship of the maṇḍala:
*oṃ laṃ indrāya vajrahastāya namaḥ*, *oṃ raṃ a...* [and so forth].
Oṃ gnaṃ, salutation to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand;
Oṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to Nirṛti, who holds a sword in his hand;
Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand; Oṃ yaṃ, [salutation] to Vāyu...

Oṃ yāṃ, salutation to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand; oṃ kuṃ, salutation to Kubera, who holds a mace in his hand; oṃ śūṃ, salutation to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand; oṃ āṃ, salutation to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand; oṃ hlāṃ...
*Oṃ*, salutation to the one with infinite ploughs in hand; *oṃ raṃ*, salutation to Agni;
*oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ*, salutation to Sūrya in the center; *oṃ varuṇāya*, salutation to Varuṇa; *oṃ hsīṃ saḥ*, salutation to Śītāṃśu (the Moon) in the east; *oṃ kuṃ ku*.

Oṃ māraya namaḥ (to Māra) in the southeast; oṃ raḥ arthaṃ aṅgārakāya namaḥ (homage to Aṅgāraka for the sake of wealth) in the southeast; oṃ hūṃ viṣṇave namaḥ (homage to Viṣṇu) in the southeast; oṃ hrīṃ budhāya namaḥ (homage to Budha) in the south; oṃ luṃ indrāya namaḥ (homage to Indra) in the south; oṃ hrīṃ bhogāspadāya (homage to the abode of enjoyment).
Homage to the West: Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ! Speak, speak! Homage to Sarasvatī, the Goddess of Speech.
Oṃ hrīṃ asurottamāya namaḥ in the north; oṃ praṃ prajāpataye namaḥ; oṃ hrīṃ kṛṣṇavarṇāya śanaiścarāya namaḥ in the southwest;
oṃ gluṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ; oṃ hrīṃ amṛ... [in the northwest].
Oṃ namas tasyai priyāyai vāyavyām; oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya īśāne; oṃ hrīṃ jyotiṣke-tave namaḥ īśāne; oṃ hvāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ; oṃ hrīṃ uttānapādātmajāyai dhruvāyai.

Outside the sacrificial area to the north: *Oṃ anantāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ hrīṃ agastyāya namaḥ*. Then, outside the sacrificial area to the south. Thereafter, in the center, the enclosure of Bhairava; first, one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) in the *karṇikā* (pericarp).

Having fully worshipped Bhairava, one performs the worship of the Bhairava-enclosure (bhairavāvaraṇa) in the order starting from the east: Oṃ kṣa ma ra ya rthaṃ, obeisance to Kapāleśa Bhairava in the east;
Oṃ ra ha rthaṃ, obeisance to Śikhivāhana Bhairava in the southeast.

In the southeast: Oṃ kṣaṃ, to Krodharāja; in the south: Oṃ jhā ra thaṃ, to Vikarāla; in the southwest: Oṃ ha va rthaṃ, to Manmatha; in the west: Oṃ ha ra ya rthaṃ, to Meghanāda; in the northwest: Oṃ huṃ, to Somarāja; in the north.
Oṃ 9ṃ, O King of Vidyās, in the northeast; now, the worship of the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapāla).
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Vaṭukanātha, the son of the Goddess, in the south;
to the circle of Vaṭukas in the north; to the Yoginīs in the west; [and] in the place.

To Kṣetrapāla in the east; to the Bhūtas in the center; to Rājarājeśvara in the northeast (īśāna); to Viṣvaksena in the southeast (āgneya); to Vetālabhairava in the southwest (nairṛtya); to Bahukhādaka in the northwest (vāyavya); and to Maṅgala [in the north].
To Rājānaka Ānanda-rājānaka, to Saṃkhābhidhaturuṣka-rājānaka, to Pañcāla-rājānaka,
to Rudragaṇeśvara, and to Athaheruka and the others: Oṃ hrīṃ kṣaṃ.
KṢŪṂ HERUKĀYA NAMAḤ | HRĪṂ HUṂ KṢĪṂ AGNIVETĀLĀYA NAMAḤ | HRĪṂ KṢŪṂ HUṂ AGNIJIHVĀYA NAMAḤ | HRĪṂ HRĪṂ HUṂ KĀLĀKṢĀYA NAMAḤ | KṢĀṂ YŪṂ KṢĪṂ KARĀLINE NAMAḤ | ĀṂ YŪṂ KṢĪṂ E...
*Oṃ* *kapādāya* *namaḥ*; *kṣūṃ yūṃ kṣāṃ* *bhīmarūpiṇe* *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ huṃ hrīṃ* *tārakākhyāya* *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ hrīṃ huṃ* *hāṭakeśvarāya* *namaḥ*;
*hrīṃ hrīṃ* *rājarājeśvarāya* *namaḥ*. Then, *paṃ*...

Having offered the *pañcāmṛta-caru* with the mantra: *oṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ dravyarūpiṇe ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*, and having presented as an offering the five nectars—clarified butter, milk, sugar, honey, and likewise grapes—one should address the All-pervading Lord: "Come! (*āgaccha*).
The request is "one should resort to the presence" (sannidhiṃ bhaja). Thus is the ritual of the vase-installation (kalaśasthāpana).
Then follows the worship of the vase (kalaśapūjana). Thereafter, having brought the disciple and seated him to one's right, one should cause him to perform the worship as prescribed.

Oṃ! I bow to the Great Lord (Maheśa), who is the light of one's own self and who has quelled the arrows of discordant afflictions; and I honor that Goddess of Speech, who indeed constitutes the very root of the creeper of speech. [She is] intent upon devouring obstacles...
I take refuge in the preeminent teacher, the king of obstacles, who has a vast belly like a cloud and whose initiation was first bestowed by him; I take refuge in another, the bestower of knowledge.
We bow to Maheśa, the Lord of the Universe; we bow to the supreme Goddess of Speech.
"I bow to the god whose belly is like a cloud, and to the sandals of the Guru. Thus is the *mukhasnāna* (mouth-bath).
"Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ, I offer the sacred thread (*pavitraka*), obeisance. Thus is the *pavitra* mantra. Having applied the *tilaka* with pure water and speech, [recite] "Oṃ va..."

One whose mind is bound like a golden bracelet should worship with skill that which is immovable, stainless, and leads to the cessation of the fear of worldly existence, for the sake of the eternal state and the end of rebirth—
[the breaths] Prāṇa and Apāna, the eyes, ears, and nose. (1) Ma...
May that very Lord Śiva protect our heads and hands, even though they are in their natural state; may the Blessed Śiva, the remover of sin, take away your misfortune,
and may the hosts of spirits strive with effort for your peace.

May Rāyaṇa protect [me]. (3) To the one whose nature is the auspicious Self, [I offer] the self-anointing; fragrance, obeisance; water for the guest-offering, obeisance; flowers, obeisance. For the cessation of the great delusion in the desert of the ocean of saṃsāra, this indeed is nectar.
O Śiva, please accept this lamp; it has the form of Kālāgnirudra, the destroyer of all sins and the generator of all auspiciousness. O Śiva, please accept this incense; it has two arms and one face.

One should meditate upon the Sun in this manner— as bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation— as being gentle, holding a lotus in his hand, situated within the orb of light, circular, and clad in red garments; he who is the very nature of Śiva unto the self.

May there be success through the resolve for incense and lamps; homage to incense, homage to the lamp. Then, the inquiry: homage to Gāyatrī. Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, that Savitṛ... (3) We know that Puruṣa, the Great God...

May Rudra inspire us for that; may he impel us toward it. (3) For the sake of the one whose form is the Sun, for the sake of the knowledge of the Sun—may Sūrya inspire us for that. (3) For Kārtikeya, the commander of the army—may Kumāra inspire us for that.
May He impel us; that [is] for Maheśa, for the one whose speech is purified—*dhī* for us, *tat* for Śiva, *pra*.
(3) For Amṛteśa, for the one whose body is the void—*naḥ* for Netra, (3) for Bahurūpa, for Koṭarākṣa—*tat* for us, *ghoraḥ* for Parā.

To her whose essence is consciousness and whose nature is pure awareness—*tanno ghorī*. To the Supreme Swan (*paramahaṃsa*) and the Great Swan (*mahāhaṃsa*)—*tanno śivaḥ*. To the Person (*tatpuruṣa*) and the Great God (*mahādeva*)—*tanno rudraḥ*. This [universe] is of the nature of Śiva.

May Śiva, who proceeds from Śivā, who is the womb of Śiva, impel all that is auspicious for us. (3) May Viṣṇu [grant] that to us, [who is] Vāsudeva, whose measure is half of Lakṣmī. (3) [Salutation] to Subhagā, who wears a garland of desire. To her...
nnodurgā (3) aiṃ to the Goddess Tripurā, klīṃ to Kāmeśvarī, sauḥ to her; tannaḥ klinnā (3). Today, [I offer] to the Blessed One Nandinirudra, to Gaṅgā, to Mahākāla, and to Yamunā. Me.
Of Śākhāsya, Chāgalāsya, Caṇḍa, Upacaṇḍa,
Śaṅkhanidhi, Padmanidhi, Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, and Viśvakarman.
To the deities of the door, to Prajāpati Brahmā, to the deities of the water-pot (kalaśa), to Prajāpati Brahmā, to the deities of the water-pot,
and to the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, [in the] four Vedas...
To Śvara with his followers, to Ṛtupati, to Nārāyaṇa,
to the deities of the ancestral hosts beginning with Agniṣvātta, to Svacchandabhairava with his retinue, and to the god Bhava...
The messengers, together with their retinues, of the god Tryambaka, the god Rudra, the god Paśupati, the god Ugra, the god Mahādeva, the god Bhīma, and the god Īśāna, [are here].
To the left of the cause [of the ritual], [one should place] the deities of the injunctions, the cessation, Śiva, the waters, the sacrificial animals, and the offerings;
and to the right, the lineage of gurus: the supreme guru, the ultimate guru, the highest teacher, the great preceptor, and one's own personal guru. At the beginning...

[The worship] of the eleven grahas beginning with Tyadī, of Brahmā together with his retinue, of Viṣṇu together with his retinue, of the deities of the mantra-pitcher, of the deities of the weapon-pitcher, and of Vāsudeva (8).
*Hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ* for Sūrya; (9) *Vināyakasya*; (13) *Amāyā*, etc.; for Indra, the lord of the Asuras, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand;
for Agni, the lord of splendor, who holds a spear in his hand; for Yama, the lord of the Pretas.
To Nirṛti, the lord of the southwest, who holds a staff in his hand;
to Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, who holds a sword in his hand; to Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths, who holds a banner in his hand; and to Kubera, the lord of the Yakṣas...
To the Lord who holds the trident in his hand; to Brahmā, the sovereign of the Vedas, who holds a lotus in his hand; to Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the three worlds, who holds a discus in his hand;
and to Agni, Āditya, and Varuṇa.
Of the Moon and Kuja (Mars), of Viṣṇu and Budha (Mercury),
of Indra and Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), of Sarasvatī and Śukra (Venus), of Prajāpati and Śanaiścara (Saturn), of Gaṇapati and Rāhu, and of Rudra and Ketu.
Of Brahmā and Dhruva, of Ananta and Agastya, of Kapāleśa-Bhairava,
of Śikhivāhana-Bhairava, of Krodharāja-Bhairava, and of Vikarāla-Bhairava.

Of the venerable Svacchandabhairava situated within this maṇḍala, together with the deities of the seven enclosures (saptāvaraṇa), the Lord (bhaṭṭāraka) Sakala, [and his attendants] Manmathabhaī, Meghanādabhaī, Somarājabhaī, and Vidyārājabhaī.

Of Aghora, of Aghoreśvarī, of Niṣkala-Svacchanda-Bhairava, of Amṛteśvara, of Amṛtalakṣyā, of Ānanda-Bhairava with his Goddess, and of the face of Īśāna [represented by] *kṣaṃ*. *Yaṃ* is that which... [is its power].
To Ruṣavaktra, Raṃ Aghoravaktraka,
Laṃ Sadyojātavaktra, Vaṃ Vāmadevavaktra, to the six limbs (aṅga-ṣaṭka), to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and to Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā.
To Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī,
Balapramathanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, Manonmanī, and to Brahmā, the lord of the Nivṛtti-kalā, and [to Viṣṇu], the lord of the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā...
Śāntā belongs to the father Viṣṇu, the Lord of Vidyā-kalā;
Śāntyatītā belongs to Rudra, the Lord of Kalā; [the state] belongs to Īśvara, the Lord of Śānti-kalā;
and [the state] belongs to Sadāśiva, the Lord of Śāntyatīta-kalā. [These are the states] of the Path of Mantra (mantrādhvan), the Path of Word (padādhvan), and the Path of Phoneme (varṇādhvan).
Of the path of sound, the path of the worlds, the path of the principles (tattvas), and the path of the kalās;
[and] of the goddesses beginning with Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, Pratyaṅgirā, Siddhalakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, and the goddess Kubjikā.
Of Mālinī; of the six-armed Durgā; of the eight-armed Durgā;
of the eighteen-armed Durgā; of the Blessed Śrī Śārikā;
of the Blessed Śrī Śāradā; of the Blessed Śrī Rājñī.
Of the Blessed Lady Śrījvālābhagavatī, of the Blessed Lady Śrībhīḍābhagavatī, of the Blessed Lady Śrīśivābhagavatī, of Vajreśvarī, of Kāmeśvarī,
of Bhagamālinī, of Bhuvanamālinī, and of the Goddess Dīkṣā...
The protectors of the mantra-mātṛkā, the mantra-ḍāmarikās,
those of Bhadrakālī, Tārā, and Vāgīśvarī with her attendants,
the blessed Gaṅgā, the blessed Vitastā, and Agni with his retinue—
Of Vāra, the son of Śrīdevī; of Vaṭukanātha, the food of the *vaṭukas*;
of the Lord of the Yoginīs; of Bhūtabali; of Rājarājeśvara;
of Viśvakasena; of Vetālabhairava; [and] of Bahukhā.
Of Dakasya Maṅgalarājānaka, Anandarājānaka, Tuṣkarāja, Maṅgaleśvara, Rudragaṇeśvara,
Pañcālarājānaka, Heruka, and Tri...
Of Purāntaka, Agnivetāla, Agnijihva, and Kārāla.
To Kālākṣa, Ekapāda, the Lord of the Lords of Kings,
to the field-protectors beginning with Ajara, to all the deities who are field-protectors,
to Kūrma, Dhruva, Ananta, and Hari-Vāstu.
For the purpose of warding off the sins accumulated through one's own speech, mind, and body against the deities of the directions, for the purpose of pleasing one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā),
[I shall perform] the worship of the water-pot (kalaśapūjā), the worship of the sacrifice (yāgapūjā), and the worship of the guardian of the field (kṣetrapālapūjā).

I shall perform the *namaścāma* (prostration with offerings); Oṃ, do so! Having scattered sesame and mustard seeds, likewise [prepare] the seat for Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, and the others; I worship you all with water; Oṃ, worship!

"I shall invoke Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, and the others. Saying "Oṃ, invoke! and scattering barley grains, he invokes the Lord of the Gaṇas, who holds a tusk, a rosary, and a bracelet in his right hands.
Upon his two arms shines a lion-throne, and in his left pair of hands he holds an axe and a vessel for the protection of the earth;
I invoke the Lord, the Sovereign, the husband of Pārvatī.
Seated upon his throne and adorned with ornaments of serpents,
may the Lord of the World be pleased and be well-disposed toward that sacrificer; Vali is white in color,
possessed of great splendor, and adorned with white garlands and radiance.
"May this flower, incense, and lamp be accepted. I invoke the god Viṣṇu, who possesses universal forms, four arms, a massive body,
and who bears the conch, discus, and mace, [complexioned] like the *atasī* flower."
I, Bali, invoke the King of the Gods, who is clothed in yellow garments like the *kāśa* flower,
who is infallible (*acyuta*), by whom Govinda is saluted, and before whom no fear exists; I call him who stands amidst his hosts, the wielder of the thunderbolt, for the sake of the sacrifice.
I invoke the Fire-god, who bears a moon-crested crown, who holds a parasol together with a spear,
who possesses three eyes, who is stainless, and who holds the Vedas, the mudrā, and a rosary of beads for the sake of protecting his mouth.
I invoke Yama, who has a parrot upon his left hand and likewise holds a staff and a rosary in his right hand, who is the supreme three-eyed protector of the sacrificial horse,
and who possesses a trident.

I invoke Nirṛti, who is marked with a thunderbolt, mounted upon the back of a buffalo, three-eyed, holding a lute together with a staff, possessing four arms on his left side for the sake of protecting the buffalo,
and wearing a crescent moon.

I invoke Varuṇa, who has a moon-like crest, for the protection of my mouth— he who is intent on worshiping with joined palms, who holds a trident and a sword in his right hands, and who, seated upon a bull, carries a shield and a noose in his left hands.
One should meditate upon him as being intent on the worship of the *ḍa* and *ma* syllables, holding a trident and a sword in his right hands, and in his left hands possessing a shield and a noose,
seated upon a crocodile throne.
For the sake of protecting his mouth, I invoke Vāyu, who holds the wind within himself,
initiated by the Supreme Lord with his own pair of hands;
likewise, he holds a rosary and a water-pot in his left hand, while a shimmering deer [leaps] about him.
For the sake of guarding the mouth of the assembly, I invoke the Giver of Wealth (Kubera),
who is mounted upon his man-vehicle (the elephant), holding in his own hand the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) as well as a rosary (*akṣasūtra*),
and bearing the moon, a book, and the lion-banner.

I invoke [the deity] who wears a crescent moon as a crown, who holds a trident along with the Lord (Śiva) in his right hands, and likewise holds a mirror in his left hand, for the sake of protecting those who have turned their faces away from the Supreme Lord.
I invoke him who has a bull as his vehicle on the left, the three-eyed one, seated upon a lotus throne for the protection of the mouth;
he who carries the Veda, a rosary, a staff, and a water-pot, along with the [appropriate] mudrā.

I invoke for the sake of protection Brahmā, who carries the *mathosa* rosary and whose supreme face is directed toward the Lord (Īśvara), and Viṣṇu, who constantly bears his own portion of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and holds a rosary along with a plow.

Then, for the purpose of protecting my mouth, I shall perform the invocation (āvāhana) of the planets in their proper sequence, [visualizing] myself seated upon a tortoise throne, joined by the embrace of Vālī, and holding a pestle in my left hand. Having thus invoked the planets...
O Ādityas, come forth! I invoke the conscious one;
I invoke the Lord of Day who bears the staff, the cord of Dakṣa, and the banner of smoke, who is mounted upon seven horses, who holds a mass of rays with his two hands, and who is three-eyed.
For the protection of my mouth, I invoke the Three-eyed One,
who wears the moon as a garment, holds a rosary in his right hand, carries a smoke-colored staff and a banner, and is joined by a deer with his two hands, appearing like a mass of rays.
For the sake of protecting the imperishable, I invoke the three-eyed one, the refuge of the three eyes, the son of the Earth, who carries a rosary and a bracelet in his right hand,
who is seated upon the peacock-vehicle, and who holds a discus and a staff in his left.
I invoke the white-complexioned Vighna, who has three eyes, whose refuge is the syllable *akṣa*,
and who wears a crown and a necklace; for the sake of protecting the mouth, he holds a rosary and a bracelet in his right hand, is seated upon Garuḍa, and carries a discus in his left hand.
I invoke the beautiful Three-eyed One, who bears the preceptor of the gods,
who holds a rosary and a ring in his right hand, who is mounted upon the elephant-vehicle,
who carries a water-pot in his left, and who is clad in yellow garments; I invoke the Three-eyed One, O Kavi.

I invoke the fierce one in the form of Śiva, who holds a rosary and a bracelet in his right hand, is mounted upon the monkey-vehicle, carries a discus in his left, possesses three eyes, is white in color, and has the form of the destroyer of Śani. I invoke the fierce one who holds a rosary and a bracelet in his right hand... [and so forth].
I invoke that three-eyed one who is mounted upon a man, who likewise holds a water-pot in his left hand, who wears earrings and a garland,
who has the form of a head, and who has taken the *svadhā* offering— Rāhu.
I invoke him who sits upon a lion-throne, whose face is exceedingly fierce, who has three eyes,
and who is accompanied by ten serpents; he holds a water-pot in his right hand and a banner in his left— salutations to the one who wears a garland of black snakes.
I invoke the slender, tall, three-eyed one who possesses the form of Brahmā,
beginning with the raised hand; I invoke the god Agastya, the lord served by the gods, who resides within the body of a bird, whose limbs are red, and who is immovable and eternal.
I invoke that Lord who eternally assumes the form of Viṣ� who wears a crown of moon-crests, the glorious Kapālin who bears a garland of skulls,
the five-faced one with three eyes.

I invoke that Bhairava whose vehicle is the peacock, who possesses the splendor of blood, who has five faces, who wears a garland of skulls upon his graceful forehead, and who takes refuge in the crescent-moon crest of Śiva for the sake of protecting his mouth— him who is as beautiful as a corpse. I invoke him.
I invoke that King of Wrath, who resembles a fresh cloud, radiant with splendors, stainless, adorned with a garland of skulls, five-faced, terrifying,
the form of the Lord, glowing like fire, and possessing beautiful locks of hair.
I invoke the Lord, the embodiment of the Destroyer of Desire (Manmatha), who wears a garland of skulls, has five faces, and holds smoke-colored [objects]. I invoke that beautiful youth,
the garlanded one with five faces, who bears a smoke-colored form.

I invoke that Meghanāda, whose bodily luster is stainless, who wears a garland of skulls, who is five-faced, who holds a skull-cup, who resembles the moon, and who is the stainless king of the moon-gods, radiant with splendors and adorned with a garland of skulls. Five-faced... [he is] the stainless one.
I invoke Nana, who resembles a white gem, the King of Vidyās, whose head is adorned with a garland of skulls; I invoke the Great Lord Maheśa, who has five faces and beautiful moon-like arms.

I bow to the Lord who is self-willed, pure as a clear gem, the supreme Self, the three-eyed Rudra with matted locks adorned by the crescent moon, the five-faced one, the immeasurable Supreme Cause, the god with fifteen eyes, wearing a crown of matted hair.
Adorned with a crown, resembling ten million moons, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
five-faced, large-eyed, decorated with a serpent for a sacred thread, shining with a necklace of scorpions glowing like the color of fire.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, bearing a sword and a shield, holding a noose and a goad, the god holds a bow in his hand and carries a trident;
he has hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he bears a severed head and a khaṭvāṅga staff. Vī...
Holding a drum and a bell in his hands, bearing a trident, and displaying the majesty of a vajra-staff,
he holds an axe as a weapon in his hand;
he is resplendent with a mallet held in a variegated manner, and [clad in] a lion-skin.

One should meditate upon the Great Lord (Maheśāna), who has eighteen arms, a blue throat, and great splendor; he wears an elephant hide as his lower garment and a silken cloth as his upper garment; he has an upward-facing face, resembles a crystal, and is yellowish-green in the front.

One should know that the face has the luster of a blue lotus petal; the right [face] should be understood as such, and one should likewise contemplate the left as resembling the juice of pomegranate and sugarcane,
similar to saffron water, and like the moon and the planet Mercury.

One should contemplate Kāśa in the west as the god Svacchandabhairava, the cause of all causes. That man who, with a disciplined mind, meditates upon him, shall quickly attain perfection. This which was previously described is called Yāsā.
That supreme, formidable power (Aghorā-śakti) indeed possesses a form exactly like that of Bhairava himself. Having worshipped Bhairava,
one should then contemplate her as being seated upon his lap, with a slightly terrifying face and a deep, piercing gaze.
One should meditate upon Bhairavī, who has a gracious face and is seated upon a corpse; she is momentarily struck with wonder.
O you whose form is the universe, whose self is the universe, the cause of the creation and other processes of the universe, whose body is supreme light—we praise Svacchandabhairava.

I worship that light which transcends the universe yet consists of the universe, joined with the eight Bhairavas; it is profoundly peaceful, partless, pure, all-pervasive, and untainted; it is a dense abyss of consciousness, awakening, and bliss, the refuge of all. Homage to You!

O Goddess Durgā, worshipped by the Asuras, who are of a nature both terrible and more terrible than the most terrible, and who are the cause of creation, preservation, destruction, dissolution, and grace— I invoke you; O bestower of boons, grant me a beautiful woman.

To the goddess Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, who possesses eight arms holding in sequence the conch, discus, mace, sword, noose, goad, bow, and arrow, and who bestows the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha— this is the arghya, the pādya, and the incense.
"May she be accepted! I invoke the goddess Pārvatī, the bestower of boons, the beloved wife of Hara, whose limbs are beautiful and who increases prosperity. Come, O Goddess, O Mistress of the World!
[Mīnākṣī]...

O delighter of the heart, O pure one, O most excellent and gentle one, O beloved of your devoted followers— please accept this water for honoring (arghya), this water for the feet (pādya), and this incense (dhūpa). I invoke you, O Goddess.
He [taught] the Kārikā, the supreme sovereign consisting of twenty verses.
In this enchanting sacrifice named Sarvasiddhi,
I invoke the goddess Śāradā, the bestower of boons, who resides at Śrīśaila, is eternally worshipped by Śāṇḍilya, and possesses six arms— at the very beginning, I invoke her.

I invoke the Goddess Mahātripurasundarī, the Queen, the bestower of sovereignty, who resides upon half the body of Bhūteśvara and is seated upon a lion-throne; I invoke her here in this very [mandala].
I invoke the Goddess, who is endowed with Yajñekāmeśvara,
the blessed one who is fearful, holding a vessel of *śīdhu* wine in her hand,
adorned with ornaments, and having the form of a swan; I invoke Jvālā.
I invoke here the Goddess Lakṣmī, who possesses the splendor of Vaiśvānara, who is endowed with the life-force of Mahādeva, who is seated upon a lion-throne,
and who bestows all prosperity, sitting upon a lotus-seat.
I invoke the goddess Bhadrakālī, the Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī), who rests upon the chest of the Lowly One (Dmanābhava), the bringer of auspiciousness,
whose splendor is like a cloud in this sacrifice of mine. I invoke her.
I bow to the Goddess Dakṣiṇā Kālikā, the supreme one, who has the luster of a dark cloud,
who is formidable, and who is accompanied by Mahākāla; the Lord who possesses fifteen eyes, whose face is like that of a deer, and whose form bears the full moon.
He bears the crescent moon upon his crest; with his left hands he holds a bell,
a terrifying mallet, a noose, an arrow, a staff,
a skull-topped club, a lute, and a hand-drum, and likewise with his right hands he holds an axe and a bow.

The goddesses are seated upon Rudra-thrones in the center of the heart-lotus; they possess a brilliance that surpasses ten million suns, hold tridents and [other weapons], are accompanied by Bhaya on their left, and are adorned with great scorpion-earrings.
Indeed, with this thought I shall invoke the god Kṣetrapāla, the great lord who dwells among worms, insects, and moths,
and within all embodied beings, as well as in houses, fields, forests, and groves.
One should worship the kṣetrapālas, bhūtas, piśācas, the hosts of gandharvas and gods, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) with offerings and flowers.
I invoke the one who shines brilliantly with serpents and whose garment is the sky.

I shall invoke these deities— the three-eyed one, the trident-handed one, the dark-faced one, the remover of sins and suffering, the Lord of the Gods, the Guardian of the Field, and the one with wonderful hips— for the sake of protecting the sacrificial ground: Oṃ Ā.
Drive [the obstacles] away, scattering sesame, mustard seeds, and barley; [perform] breath control (*prāṇāyāma*);
*phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*. [Perform] the ritual for the scented water with saffron, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, tagara, and priyaṅgu.
One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) in due order to Bhagavān, Gaṇapati, Kumāra, and so forth, according to the sequence of the *Vidyā* for the worship of Śaṅkara.
"Namaḥ" for the water for the feet; one should ward off the remainder of the foot-water with "phaṭ astrāya phaṭ.
Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, ghee, curd, honey, barley, and white mustard seeds—this indeed is the eightfold *arghya*.
Having offered a little water from the vessel of the ritual procedure, one recites: "O Blessed One, this is the *arghya* for Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, and the others;
salutations! For Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, and the others... and so forth.

To these deities: salutation for the anointing, salutation for the fragrance, salutation for the water-offering (*arghya*), salutation for the flower, salutation for the incense, salutation for the lamp; to these deities, salutation for the garment. [This is] the offering of the *arghya* to these deities.
May the entire procedure of today’s worship be complete. *Annaṃ namaḥ* (2). *Ājyaṃ* (2). May there be success today according to my resolve.
Whatever is deficient in food, deficient in ritual action, deficient in materials, or deficient in mantra—[may it be made whole].
May all that has gone away depart; *phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*.
To these deities: *arghaṃ namaḥ*, *puṣpaṃ namaḥ*, *apośānaṃ namaḥ*, *ācamanīyaṃ namaḥ*, *phaṭ astrāya*.

*Phaṭ!* To these deities, for the sake of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), I give sesame seeds, gold, silver, and a *niṣka* coin. May these deities, together with the sacrificial fee, be pleased by this; may they be satisfied. *Apa*.

With his left hand, using water mixed with sesame seeds, he should first mention the lineage of Śiva (Śivagotra) and then that of the ancestors, saying, "May Śiva be pleased for the sake of the ancestors' attainment of the state of Śiva. Having given the canopy, the water-pot,
the banner, the parasol, the fly-whisk, and so forth, as well as the jewel-lamps and other offerings.
Having placed a full vessel containing rock-salt balls (*saindhava-vaṭaka*) and other offerings, one should make this request:
"O Lord of the Bhogas, now make this place free from obstacles; I shall perform the vision of Hara."

O Blessed One, for the sake of protection here and in the hereafter, may all the planets and those who are considered secondary planets be present with me for the pacification of obstacles. O Indra, by you in your own direction...
For the sake of pacifying obstacles, one must perform the concluding rites with vigilance by the command of Śiva:
"O Agni! O Yama!
O Nairṛta! O Varuṇa! O Vāyu! O Kuvera! O Īśāna!"
"O Brahman! O Ananta!"—thus the world-protectors (Lokapālas) and the goddesses, having caused the wise to flee, [uttered]: "Oṃ, obeisance to all Yoginīs; obeisance, obeisance to the Siddhas;
obeisance to the Seizer of the Lord of Form and Formless; obeisance to Śakti."
Having performed a half-pradakṣiṇā by moving from left to right and back again, he offers the *nirodhārghya* while saying, "Be present here."
One should go near the *gnivedi*; then, having gone near the fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*), one should perform the purification of the seat, the binding of the directions, and so forth, as before.
*Oṃ haḥ phaṭ*—to the sword, which is the form of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) and the knower.

Having worshipped the sword of knowledge with "Yaṃ Namaḥ," one should worship the vessel for the *arghya* of the weapon on one's right with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*). Having performed the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) of drying, burning, and so forth through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [one should perform] the ritual restraint and the water of Śiva.
Having performed the worship of the animal, the arghya vessel, and the sacrificial ground, I sprinkle [the area] with that;

*phaṭ*. One should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) previously prepared. One should gaze at the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the root mantra, and sprinkle and strike the pit with "Astrāya Phaṭ."
With "Cca Humiti," one should sprinkle the *kuṇḍa*. Thus is the fourfold consecration (*saṃskāra*).

Likewise, [reciting] "I perform the digging, smearing, removal of loose earth, kneading, cleansing, and sprinkling, phaṭ, for the self that is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), O *kuṇḍa*... [one should proceed].

"Oṃ ḍāyanamaḥ"—with this, the worship is performed. With the Astra-mantra, I perform the vajrīkaraṇa (the rite of making [the site] adamantine), Phaṭ. The vajrīkaraṇa is performed with the Astra-mantra: three lines are drawn from east to west, and one from south to north; this is proclaimed as the "Vajra. A.

One should cover the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with *darbha* grass blades pointing eastward; having worshipped it with the mantra "Ādhāraśaktyai namaḥ," one should establish Brahmā to the right of the pit using fifty-four *darbha* blades and place him in the center of a ball of cow dung.
One should worship with: *Oṃ brahmāsanāya namaḥ*. O Blessed One Brahmā, come (2); be present (2); remain near (2); I veil you, *namaḥ*. *Āṃ* to Brahmā, the Lord of all worlds, *namaḥ*. *Pā*.

One should worship with [the mantra] beginning with *dyauḥ* and so forth; then, having placed one blade of *darbha* grass with its tip pointing east in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and another blade of *darbha* grass with its tip pointing north behind it, one should create a crossroads.
Having placed a seat (*viṣṭara*) behind that, [one should worship] with *oṃ vāgīśyai*.

Having worshipped her with "Salutation to the Ancient One," [one should meditate upon] Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses, who resembles a blue lotus, who is endowed with all auspicious marks,
adorned with all ornaments, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, and [present] during the fertile season.

Having meditated upon the Goddess— possessing beautiful eyes, seated in the Brahma-sthāna, facing the door, and of auspicious form— and having visualized her thus with incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should install such a Goddess in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, [reciting] *oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvari āgaccha* (twice), having displayed the mudrās for invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth,
