Homage! To him who is mounted on a ram, whose hand holds a mace, who is yellow, and whose vehicle is a man. One should remember the Lord of Yakṣas with devotion for the attainment of the success of dharma, kāma, and artha—to Kuvera, the wielder of the mace. Homage! To him who has a banner in his hand. Homage! To him who is mounted on a ram, whose hand holds a mace, who is yellow, and whose vehicle is a man. One should remember the Lord of Yakṣas

Maḥ: He who holds a trident in his hand, is mounted upon a bull, adorned with a crown of matted locks, joined by the white Gaurī, possesses three eyes, wears an elephant hide as a garment, and is to be meditated upon—Śūṃ!
Salutation to Īśāna, the wielder of the trident. Brahmā is gentle.

The four-faced one with a large belly, possessing a short beard, holding a lotus stalk, a water-pot, a kusha grass, and a lotus; the creator who is the source of the Vedas and the mind-born [Brahmā], he should be meditated upon as the bearer of obstacles. *Hlāṃ* to Brahmā, the lotus-seated one.
One should meditate upon the one stationed in the direction of Pātāla as the white Lord Ananta, mounted upon a tortoise, holding a plough-weapon, and possessing a thousand hoods;
[reciting] "Hlāṃ, obeisance to Ananta, who holds a plough in his hand. Thus [it is said].

Then follows the *graha-homa* (oblation to the planets). Therein, first, [one worships] Sūrya, who bears a smoke-colored banner (*dhūmradhvaja*) and a garland of rays in his two hands; he moves upon seven horses, is red, three-eyed, and possesses the nature of wind. Of him [is this]: *Śrīsūryama*...
Śatacin Ṛṣi, Triṣṭubh Chanda, Savitṛ Devatā. Oṃ vī śrīṃ śa hsauḥ kīṃ.
In the fire during the homa, [offer] flowers for the invocation, water for the feet, and so forth, to Āditya, to Mārtaṇḍa; may Sūrya inspire our intellect.
Oṃ raṃ agnaye svāhā | Oṃ hrāṃ gnyīṃ saḥ vīreśvara-bhairavāya svāhā (108). Oṃ hrāṃ ghrīṃ saḥ vīra-lakṣmyai svāhā—this is half for the Goddess. Oṃ hsauṃḥ śrīṃ āṃ graharājāya ādityāya svāhā (108).
With clarified butter: *Oṃ namaḥ ādityāya svāhā*. *Oṃ aṃ śivacaryādharāya svāhā*. *Oṃ aṃ dāḍimīkusumavarṇāya svāhā*.
*Oṃ aṃ kaliṅgasthānabhavāya svāhā*. *Oṃ aṃ kā...*
Oṃ śyāpāya svāhā; Oṃ sahasrakiraṇāya svāhā; Oṃ aṃ grahādhipataye svāhā; Oṃ aṃ kamalabāndhavāya svāhā; Oṃ aṃ yajamānavarapradāya svāhā. [Pūrṇā]

I worship the primordial deity Mihira, who shines with thousands of rays as clear as the sun itself, beautifying the region of the earth, whose chariot is drawn by seven horses and who holds a lotus in his hand;
[I worship him] within the lotus of my heart, from the root-mantra to the end, with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
May Nirodhārgha, Tarpaṇa, Udayastu, Mahābhanu, Tejasa, Bhayankara, Sahasraraśmi, Dīpta,
and Āditya be pleased with me. Now, [the offering] for the rays of the Moon:

May the three-eyed Moon, who always carries a mass of rays, a garland, and a smoky banner, and who is as white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, come to protect us. For this Śrī Candramas, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and Soma is the deity (devatā).

The application (*viniyoga*) for the *oṃ vīṃ śrīṃ śa ktrīṃ kīṃ* [mantras] is in the fire. [Offer] flowers, the invocation, water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth. [Recite]: "To the maker of night, to the one with cool rays, let there be meditation; may Soma grant that to us. (3) *Oṃ valūṃ varuṇa*.
*Rājānakāya svāhā; oṃ hsiṃ saḥ śītāṃśave svāhā* (108);
*oṃ śrīṃ krīṃ caṃ candrāya namaḥ svāhā* (108). The oblations are as before, with clarified butter: *oṃ namaḥ kaṃ somāya svāhā*. *Oṃ...*

Kaṃ svāhā to the one who upholds the conduct of the Teacher; Oṃ kaṃ svāhā to the Lord of the sixteen digits; kaṃ svāhā to the one born at the site of Yamunā; kaṃ svāhā to the one of jasmine-white complexion; kaṃ svāhā to the descendant of Atri; kaṃ na...
Svāhā to the sovereign lord of the Kṣatriyas! Svāhā to the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer!
[I praise] that beloved moon-like Lord who resides upon the crown of the head, whose form is worthy of praise, the lord of the night, possessing a pair of lotuses.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the Heart-lotus, the Moon, the ruler of the planets, at the end of the root-mantra, with the syllable *vaṣaṭ*.

The offering for restraint (*nirodhārghaḥ*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) are performed; the King of the Twice-born (the Moon) is of great merit, especially as the Lord of the Stars and the King of medicinal herbs.

May Soma be pleased with me. Now, for Mars: May Kuja, the son of the Earth, who is equipped with a water-pot, an eye, and a garland, who has an excellent peacock as his vehicle, who is red, three-eyed, and adorned with a wreath, protect us. His [mantra] is *Śrībhauma*.
Agni, Ṛgveda, Gāyatrī meter, Bhauma (Mars), Oṃ Vī Śrīṃ Śa Kaṃ Kī.
For the fire-oblation (*homa*), [offer] flowers into the fire; for the invocation, the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth:
*Oṃ hrīṃ raktāṅgāya kumārāya svāhā*; *Oṃ hsauṃḥ śrīṃ drāṃ*.
To Bhauma, the lord of the planet Kaṃ, svāhā! (108) Oṃ raharthaṃ, to Aṅgāraka, svāhā! (108) The oblations are as before, with clarified butter:
Oṃ śrīṃ saḥ, O Maṅgala, king of the planets, remove [my] affliction! (2)
Bestow prosperity! (2) Oṃ śrīṃ saḥ phaṭ svāhā (108). Oṃ namaḥ caṃ aṅgārakāya svāhā. Oṃ caṃ kumāravratadhāriṇe svāhā.
Oṃ caṃ dharāsutāya svāhā. Oṃ caṃ avantījanma.
Nesvāhā! Oṃ bhāradvājāya svāhā! Oṃ caṃ lohitāya svāhā!
Oṃ caṃ aṣṭasahasrakiraṇāya svāhā! Oṃ caṃ ugratejase svāhā! Oṃ caṃ śatrūvimardakāya svāhā!

Oṃ caṃ, svāhā to the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer! [I offer] the full oblation to the Lord of Planets, who resembles molten gold from the Gaṅgā, who is seated upon a lion-throne, who is supported by the goddess Kamalā,
and whose lotus feet are worshipped by gods and asuras.
I remember the compassionate-hearted one, whose heart-mantra is *smara*, with *mūla* at the end and *vaṣaṭ*; by him,
through the offering of water for the restraint of the senses, eternal fame was won throughout the world, and by that son of the Earth, his enemies were sacrificed as oblations.
May Bhauma, by whom enemies were slain together with his own self, be pleased;
may Bhauma always be satisfied with me.
Now, for Budha: seated upon the Garuḍa-throne, holding a rosary...
Maṇḍaluḥ, adorned with a crown, necklace, and ornaments, three-eyed, seated upon a lotus—this is the Śrī-Buddha. Brahmā is the seer, Triṣṭubh is the meter, and Śrī-Buddha is the deity;
he is employed in the fire-ritual, the offering of flowers, the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth. Oṃ Hūṃ.

*Viṣṇave svāhā*. *Oṃ hrāṃ kroṃ ṭaṃ grahanāthāya budhāya svāhā* (108 times). *Oṃ hrīṃ budhāya svāhā* (108 times). Offer oblations with clarified butter as before. *Oṃ namaḥ ṭaṃ budhāya svāhā*. *Oṃ ṭaṃ viṣṇu ca*.
Oṃ ṭaṃ, svāhā to the one who dwells beneath the earth; Oṃ ṭaṃ, svāhā to the Lord of Form;
Oṃ ṭaṃ, svāhā to the one born in the land of Magadha; Oṃ ṭaṃ, svāhā to the one of golden complexion; Oṃ ṭaṃ, svāhā to the descendant of Atri; Oṃ ṭaṃ, svāhā to the one with eight rays.
*Ya-svāhā*. *Oṃ ṭaṃ*, svāhā to the one whose body is great wisdom (*mahābuddhi*).

*Oṃ ṭaṃ ya*, svāhā to the bestower of boons upon those who sacrifice. [I meditate on] the Full Moon, the son of Soma, who has gone to the state of *Haṃsa*, who has two arms, whose form is like the moon and its crescent, and who holds a sword and a noose in his hands.
One should remember the wise one, a treasure-house of compassion, whose limbs are adorned with ornaments, within the lotus of the mind;
*oṃ mūla-ante vaṣaṭ*. This is the offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
He is the wise one, the bestower of intelligence, the son of Soma, and possessed of great luster; he is the primordial...
May the wise one, standing upon his chariot, be pleased with me. Now, may that Jīva—
who is three-eyed, holds a water-pot, is mounted on an elephant, is adorned with a garland of lotuses,
and is endowed with knowledge— approach us with the luster of a white water-lily.

For this [hymn] to Śrī-Bṛhaspati, the seer is Gṛtsamada, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is Bṛhaspati. In the fire, [one offers] flowers, and performs the invocation, the offering of water for the feet (pādya), and so forth. *Laṃ* to Indra, Svāhā! *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ blīṃ aiṃ glauṃ gra*.
To Bṛhaspati, the lord of speech, vīṃ ṭhaḥ śrīṃ ṭhaḥ aiṃ ṭhaḥ svāhā (108).
Oṃ hrīṃ, to the abode of enjoyment, svāhā (108). The oblations are as before with clarified butter: Oṃ namaḥ taṃ bṛhaspataye svāhā.

Hā! To that bearer of the holy life, svāhā! To that protector of progeny, svāhā! To that lord of the Siddhavada region, svāhā! To that descendant of Aṅgiras, svāhā! To that Gaurīcana, svāhā! To that one of incomparable rays...
Svāhā! To that bestower of boons upon the sacrificer, Svāhā!

I shall ever remember the Guru, who is fullness, whose hand holds the trident of power consisting of splendor, whose lotus feet are praised by the foremost of the lords of gods, who is a treasury of wisdom, seated upon a fish, possessing two arms.
*Sapaṃkaje haṃ mūlānte vauṣaṭ*—this is the *nirodhārgha*.
May my preceptor, who has ascended to the summit of Mount Meru, who is the priest of the king of the gods, and who is the knower of all scriptures, be pleased with me. Now, [the mantra] for Śukra:

His [form] is endowed with a book, a bull, and a water-pot; he is yellowish-white in color, and in one instance within the great host (*mahāgaṇa*), he is seen holding a treasure and a book in his hands.
His [mantra] is *Śrī-Śukra-kroṃ*, the seer is Aṅgiras, the meter is Bṛhatī, and the deity is Śukra.

At the domestic fire, [offer] flowers, the water for invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ vāgvādini sarasvatyai namaḥ svāhā*. *oṃ aiṃ jaṃ gīṃ graheśvarāya śukrāya namaḥ svāhā* (108 times). *oṃ hrīṃ*.
*Asurottamāya svāhā* (108). Offerings are made with clarified butter (*ājya*) as before:
*Oṃ namo yaṃ śukrāya svāhā*, *yaṃ inducaryadharāya svāhā*, *yaṃ māyādhipataye svāhā*, *yaṃ bhojakaṭājanma*.
Svāhā to him whose seven rays [are bright]; svāhā to him who is the sovereign lord of the asuras;
svāhā to him who has the color of cow’s milk; svāhā to him who grants boons to the sacrificer. Full [is the vessel] resembling molten gold.

I meditate upon Śukra, the compassionate one with two arms, clad in yellow garments, holding a pair of lotuses and a trident, seated upon a crane, whose lotus feet are served by the Asuras, and who has two eyes; [I place him] within the lotus of my heart. At the end of the root mantra, "Oṃ," and at the end of the *mūla*, "Vauṣaṭ," [is the seal of] *nirodha*.

May that Kāvya, who is long-armed, whose splendor is equal to Soma, who is the preceptor of the Asuras, and the conqueror of all enemies, be pleased with me. Now, for Śanaiścara: he has eyes like a water-jar and is fragrant.

Trilocana is situated in the *rasa* (taste) [element], endowed with the digit (*kalā*) of *daṇḍākṣa*; he is Kṛṣṇa, adorned with a black garland. For this venerable Śanaiścara, the *gāyatrī* meter is used; in the fire-oblation for Śanaiścara, flowers are offered into the fire.

For the vehicle, water for the feet, and so forth: *oṃ prīṃ prajāpataye svāhā*. *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ grahacakravartine śanaiścarāya klīṃ aiṃ saḥ svāhā* (108 times). *oṃ hrīṃ kṛṣṇavarṇāya śanaiścarāya svāhā* (108 times).
To the one who possesses a garland of impure atoms, who moves with speed, who removes all diseases, to Śanaiścara, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā* (108).
*Oṃ hrīṃ mardinyai svāhā*. This is the power (*śakti*); the oblations are as before.
With clarified butter: *Oṃ* to Śanaiścara, svāhā! To Yamayamacara, svāhā! To Saurāṣṭrajanman, svāhā! To Kāsyapa, svāhā! To Rājavartavarṇa, svāhā! To Kṣa... [svāhā!]
Yaṃ karāya svāhā! Yaṃ mahāmṛtyu-adhikāriṇe svāhā!
Yaṃ chāyāsutāya svāhā! Yaṃ yajamāna-varapradāya svāhā! Pūrṇā! To the planet Saturn (Śanaiścara), who is like black collyrium and who granted a son to Iṣṭa.

I meditate upon Śani, who has a serpent as his armlet, who holds a noose in his hand, who causes fear to gods and demons, and who has two arms; [the mantra is] "mūlānte vaṣaṭ" for the offering of water (argha) and libation (tarpaṇa). He is black in color, with emaciated limbs, and... [is] cruel.
May Saturn, the son of the Sun, resembling a dark cloud,
be pleased with me. Furthermore, may Rāhu— whose form is that of a head,
who is adorned with garlands and earrings, and who is seated upon a lion-throne— protect me from the poison.

To him whose beloved is her abduction, the illustrious Rāhu, O Gautama, the deer-marked one (Candramas), the three-eyed one (Śiva), and Rāhu— here in the fire, [perform] the offering of flowers, the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth:
*Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ sarvavighnādhipataye svāhā* (*Oṃ krīṃ*).
KRĪṂ HUṂ HUṂ ṬAṂ ṬAṂKADHĀRIṆE RĀHAVE Ī HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ BHAISVĀHĀ (108).
OṂ AMṚTAPRIYĀYA SVĀHĀ (108). With clarified butter: OṂ NAMAḤ ŚAṂ RĀHAVE SVĀHĀ. ŚAṂ GAṆAPATIVRATADHĀRIṆE SVĀHĀ.

Svāhā to the lord of the Gandharvas! Svāhā to the one born from the heat of the king! Svāhā to the one of the Paiṭhīnasa lineage! Svāhā to the one resembling a hundred thousand flowers! Svāhā to the one with eighteen thousand rays!
Svāhā! To the bestower of boons upon the sacrificer, Svāhā!
To the full moon, the cool-rayed one, the friend, the destroyer of enemies, the worshipful form, the terrible one, and the one resembling lapis lazuli;
to Rāhu, the lord of planets, who has two arms, who grants protection to the three worlds, and who bestows desired objects—svāhā!
I remember [the mantra] *hṛdaye smara mūlānte vauṣaṭ*. This is the offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
May the one who is red-eyed, smoke-colored, the conqueror of enemies, possessed of great strength, situated in the atmosphere with Rāhu at his side, be pleased with me. May he grant satisfaction.
Stationed upon ten serpents, joined by the bull and the pitcher, the banner (Ketu) has a massive body, its lower part possessing the luster of the ocean;
its seer is Aṅgiras, its meter is Gāyatrī, and its deity is Ketu.

Offering flowers into the fire, along with the water for invocation (*āvāhana*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*), etc.: *Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ krūṃ krūra-rūpiṇe ketave aiṃ sauḥ svāhā || (108) Oṃ hrīṃ jyotiṣ-ketave svāhā ||*
Hā! (108) With clarified butter: *oṃ namaḥ kṣaṃ ketave svāhā*; *kṣaṃ agnicaryadharāya svāhā*; *kṣaṃ dhūmravarṇāya svāhā*; *kṣaṃ jaimineyāya svāhā*; *kṣaṃ antarvedisaṃbhavāya svāhā*.

*Oṃ kṣaṃ mahāmṛtyu-adhikāriṇe svāhā! Oṃ kṣaṃ yajamāna-varapradāya svāhā!* [To the one] who possesses a full [hand] joined with a finger, who bestows fear, who has two arms, who utters "huṃ", who resembles a dark rain-cloud, the sole hero, who wears black garments— *śaṃ*.
I worship Ketu, who holds a trident in his hand, with my mind-lotus; *mūlāntaṃ vaṣaṭ*.

This is the offering of water for obstruction (*nirodhārgha*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Ketu, the son of Agni, possessed of great splendor, the ender of all planets—he who agitates all living beings.
May Ketu be pleased with me. Now, Dhruva, who is a form of Viṣṇu, is of great merit;
he is the son of Uttānapāda, seated above all, three-eyed, and always devoted to Śiva. Of him [is this] the Śrī-Dhruva[-mantra].
The Ṛṣi is Nārada, the metre is Jagatī, and the deity is Dhruva for the oblation.
For the fire, flowers, and the offerings of invocation, water for the feet, and so forth: *oṃ hlāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*;
*oṃ hrīṃ uttānapādātmajāya dhruvāya svāhā* (108).
Oṃ! That which is all-pervading, supreme among the supreme, subtle, great, and short;
which stands pervading all, possessing a form more beautiful than a conch shell, praised by the lords of sages, and delighting in circumambulating the circle of stars—the Seven Sages.
May the best of Kinnaras, whose abode is established by the foremost of gods,
who is the Dhruva of Uttānapāda, who is at the root of all things, and who is the offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*),
grant us nourishment; may the highly meritorious Dhruvarāja, established in the northern direction, perform our libation (*tarpaṇa*).
"May Adhruva, the most excellent among the sages, be pleased with me. Then there appeared Agastya, white-complexioned, with eyes like the petals of a lotus,
a face like the full moon, holding a lotus in his two hands.
May the one born from a jar (Agastya)— who dwells perpetually with his consort in that beautiful lotus-posture in the southern quarter,
who is the lord of the yellow-robed one (the Sun), who possesses steady intellect, and who is the enemy of Vātāpi— protect us always.

For the worship of Śrī Agastya: the seer is Brahmā, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Agastya. In the fire-offering (homa), [one offers] flowers into the fire. For the invocation, the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth:
*Oṃ anantāya svāhā*. *Oṃ hrīṃ*, to Agastya, whose feet are of the color of the cloud (*avarṇa*) and who is born from the earth (*pṛthivī*).
*Yasvāhā* (108), with clarified butter: *Oṃ namaḥ agastyāya svāhā*,
*Oṃ kumbhayonaye svāhā*, *Oṃ vātādhiśatrave svāhā*,
*Oṃ pītajalanidhaye svāhā*, *Oṃ dakṣiṇāśādhipa*.

*Taye svāhā | Oṃ viṣṇurūpadharāya svāhā | Oṃ kṛṣṇaśarīrāya svāhā | Oṃ yajamānavarapradāya svāhā | Pūrṇā [is offered] at the end of the root mantra with *vauṣaṭ*. Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with *vātāpiḥ su*.*
May Agastya, who swallowed the great ocean—a source of harm to the world—and thereby dried it up;

he who is born from a water-jar and dwells in the southern direction—may he be pleased with me. May the enemy of Vindhya [be pleased with me]. May Agastya, born from a jar and situated in the southern quarter, [grant me success].
Even while being consumed by digestion, may Vindhyadhara be pleased with me;
through this method of long-duration restraint, whatever oblation is performed for the circle of planets, one attains all desires and enjoys infinite fruit.

(On page 52a, half the page is blank) Therefore, may the ocean-dwelling Vindhya, who stands in the southern direction and swallows the sea, be pleased with me; this is the *nirodhārgha* [offering]. By this...

One should offer oblations to the circle of planets with the *dhināyu* mantra; one obtains all desires and enjoys infinite fruit. Then follows the seven-fold enclosure oblation (*saptāvaraṇa-homa*), after which one should offer three full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) to the Lord seated upon the lotus throne.
[One should meditate on the Lord] resembling the snowy mountain (Himalaya), with one face and three eyes;
holding a full pitcher, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands, and a full moon in his left;
and [one should meditate on] the Goddess with one face, holding a conch and a lotus, and bearing the boon-granting gesture and the gesture of fearlessness.

I bow to the Three-eyed Lord, who bears the crescent moon as his mark, who is saluted by the three worlds, and who is the Master of the Eyes. Oṃ juṃ saḥ! May there be satisfaction for all the circles of mantras; vauṣaṭ. (1) [He is] like a pearl, a yellow cloud, and a pearl.

I bow to the Lord, adorned with five faces possessing three eyes each, wearing a crown of the moon, and radiant as ten million full moons; he who holds in his hands the trident, axe, sword, thunderbolt, fire,
the king of serpents, bell, goad, noose, and the gesture of fearlessness.
I worship him who holds the sacrificial ladle (*rāndadhāna*), whose limbs are radiant with immeasurable ornaments; *Oṃ huṃ bhai*, salutations for nourishment, *svāhā vauṣaṭ*.
I worship him who bears the appearance of a thief (*vandhakābha*), who possesses three eyes, who wears a crescent moon, and who has a smiling face, holding [these] in his hands.

I bow to Him whose body is embraced by the hand of the goddess Vāmorus-tumbhagā, which shines with a beautiful red lotus in its palm; He who holds a trident, a skull-bowl, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, possesses a lovely smile, and is resplendent with jewels.
Oṃ, for my beloved wife Abhūṣaṇā, I fulfill the ritual requirements of deficiency and excess; vauṣaṭ!
(3) By this very oblation of sesame seeds, may all the deities be satisfied and grant their boons. Now, O Goddess...
The procedure for the Nāmānya-homa: therein, first, one should visualize Durgā seated upon a lion,
adorned with a crescent moon on her crest, resembling an emerald, holding a conch, a discus, a bow, and arrows in her four arms, and possessing three eyes.

May the glorious Durgā—the destroyer of misfortune—protect you both; she who is adorned with armlets, necklaces, bracelets, jingling girdles, and tinkling anklets, and who shines with jeweled earrings. (This is in the Triṣṭubh meter.)

At the end of the *Śrī Durgā* mantra—*Hrīṃ Vīṃ Duṃ Śaḥ Oṃ*—one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with flowers in the fire. [One offers] the invocation, water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, saying: "To Subhagā, to Kāmalinī, to that Durgā.
(3) *Oṃ Hrīṃ Duṃ Durgāyai Namaḥ Svāhā*. (108)
Or (54), or (27), or (14), or (7). A tenth part of the limbs:
*oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ svāhā*, *hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *duṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ svāhā*, *duḥ kavacāya huṃ svāhā*, *gāṃ netrebhyo vauṣaṭ svāhā*.
HĀYAI NAMAḤ ASTRĀYA PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. [The deity] holds in her left hands a trident,
a sword, a great arrow, a discus, a conch, a shield, a bow,
and a threatening gesture, and she stands upon the back of the Mahāmahiṣa Dānava.

Having first established [the deity], let that which is desired be attained through the mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*. If the *homa* is for the purpose of protecting the fetus, then there should be a *homa* of sesame, mustard seeds, and clarified butter. Then, [one should worship] Vanadurgā, Suratha, and Suratha.

May that mountain fortress, which possesses a mind delighted by the subduing of worldly existence through meditative absorption equal to my own, and which attains the fulfillment of its desired goals, ever prevail.
Yasena, having attained the splendor of Śrīvanadurgā, [praises] the excellent chariot;
following the *anuṣṭubh* meter, in the *Śrīvanadurgādevī-homa*, [the ritual begins] with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites into the fire with flowers:
*Oṃ uttiṣṭha puruṣi kiṃ svapiṣi yan me...*
If fear has arisen—whether it be possible [to overcome] or impossible—O Blessed One, pacify it for me! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Svāhā! (108) The oblations are as before:
"Arise, O Puruṣa! To the heart, namaḥ svāhā!"

Whatever [is] in the head, svāhā! Whatever fear has approached me, to the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ svāhā! Whether it be possible or impossible, to the armor, huṃ svāhā! That [fear], O Blessed One, from the eyes...
*vauṣaṭ svāhā śamaya ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ astrāya phaṭ svāhā*—ending with *vauṣaṭ* at the root mantra, this is the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). Now, Gaurī:
she who bears a body radiant like molten gold, adorned with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.

May that Durgā— who is Śrī, seated upon a golden lotus-throne, holding in her hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who dwells within the beautiful waist of the auspicious Gaurī— bestow prosperity upon you today. She is the roaring flame and the conch.

For the oblation to the venerable Gaurī, the meter is Uṣṇik. [The mantra for] the invocation, the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, is: *oṃ namo bhagavatyai gauri durge giriduhite svāhā svadhā vaṣaṭ hrīṃ kṣrīṃ phaṭ*. [Offer] flowers into the fire.
Ṭsvāhā, the syllables (28), the oblations according to the detailed procedure: Oṃ hrīṃ saumahiṣāsuraghātinī durgāyai namaḥ (108);
Oṃ hrīṃ raktakāpālinyai svāhā (108); Oṃ hrīṃ durmati... (108).
Nidurgābhagavatyai namaḥ svāhā (108). Oṃ siṃhadurge siṃhasvāmini aṣṭādaśabhuje rudra-raudre ghora-rūpe huṃ phaṭ namaḥ (108). Oṃ namo bhagavati durge.
*Durgottāriṇi huṃ valkuṃ svāhā* (108)—this is the mantra for the thirty-six-armed [form].
*Hāṃ hīṃ huṃ haiṃ hoṃ haḥ*—these are the limb-mantras (*aṅga*).
Then, the full [arrow] is drawn back to the ear.
With the sound of thunder produced by the bow.
With her fierce bell ringing and her trident,
Durgā— Cāmuṇḍā— laughing, struck the Dānava on his broad chest with her hand placed upon her staff, spraying him with the blood and fat that gushed forth.
From the dissolution [of the syllable] *ya*, there arise: *suranutacaraṇa* (praised by the gods), *aśoṇadantacchada* (with lips not red),

*mūla* (the root), *anteva* (the end), *auṣaṭ* (the sacrificial exclamation), *nirodha* (restraint), *argha* (the offering of honor), *tarpaṇa* (satisfaction), *oṃ* (the sacred syllable), *bhūti* (prosperity), *sannati* (humility), *kānti* (beauty), *kṣānti* (patience), *dyauḥ* (the sky/heaven), and *pṛthivī* (the earth).
You alone are indeed fortitude, modesty, nourishment, wrath, nobility, and forgiveness; you whom they call Āryā, Durgā, Vedagarbhā, Māyā, Bhadrā,
Bhadrakālī, Kṣemā, and Kṣemaṅkarī.
And at that very time, in the afternoon, they shall propitiate you with bowed bodies;
by your grace, every desire of theirs shall be fulfilled through this mantra, oblation, and sacrifice for the attainment of their goals, O Many-Durgās.

May she be pleased; may they be pleased. Now, [I worship] Śārikā, who possesses the splendor of the rising sun, whose arms bear the moon-crested Lord, the excellent sword, the discus, and the gesture of fearlessness, seated upon a lion-throne, and merged with the left half of the body of Śiva.
To her whose hair is like a parrot’s crest, to the venerable Śrī Śārikā Bhagavatī, to the venerable Mahādevī, in the Triṣṭubh meter:
O venerable Śrī Śārikā, [grant] peace! Hrāṃ Śrīṃ Āṃ Kīṃ! [This is for] the fire-oblation (homa).
[Perform] the flower offering into the fire, the invocation, the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth. [Recite] *oṃ hrīṃ śārikāyai vi* with the seven-syllable mantra, *dhī tannaḥ śilā pra*.
(3) *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ phrāṃ aṃ śāṃ śārikāyai namaḥ*. (108) *śrāṃ śrīṃ śū*.

The six-limbed [nyāsa] beginning with *mityā* and so forth; now, the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*): *oṃ hrīṃ aṃ amāyai svāhā*, *oṃ hrīṃ kaṃ kāmāyai svāhā*, *oṃ hrīṃ caṃ cārvaṅgyai svāhā*, *oṃ hrīṃ ṭaṃ ṭaṭaṅkadhāriṇyai svāhā*.
Svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ taṃ, svāhā to Tārā; oṃ hrīṃ paṃ, svāhā to Pārvatī; oṃ hrīṃ yaṃ, svāhā to Yakṣiṇī; oṃ hrīṃ śaṃ, svāhā to the Blessed Lady Śārikā—this is the completion with the seven seed-syllables.

[The offering] is complete through the meditation on the ritual procedure: *mūlāntaṃ vaṣaṭ*, the water-offering of restraint (*nirodhārghaḥ*), and the libation (*tarpaṇam*). [One should worship] the Mistress of the Seat (*pīṭheśvarī*), Śilā, who sits upon the peak of Pradyumna and is adorned with the *mātṛcakra*.
I bow to Śārikā, whose form is radiant; by this mantra, may the Blessed Lady Śrī Śārikā, together with her retinue, be pleased; may she be gracious. Now, [salutation to] Śāradā, the illustrious Śrī.
May the Blessed One, who stands firm, whose face is smiling, who is Pārvatī with the trident in hand,
whose eyes are fire, sun, and moon, the mother of the three worlds, six-armed, and possessing all powers— she who was brought forth by Śāṇḍilya— be victorious!
May Sarasvatī, who is accessible through devotion to the Three, who sits upon a lion-throne,
and who grants the heart's desired fruits—
she who possesses three eyes and holds a sword, an arrow, a horn-bow, and a bell— bestow auspiciousness.

May this autumnal goddess Śāradā, who is radiant with the golden hue of refined gold, who bestows all fruits through her splendor, and who is enriched by elephants adorned with golden bells and trappings and equipped with weapons, indeed grant [this] to you.
May the venerable Goddess Śāradā [be present].
Bhairava, Anuṣṭubh meter; Oṃ, Śrī Śāradā Bhagavatī, Oṃ Klīṃ Vīṃ Hrīṃ Śaḥ, Namaḥ. For the fire-oblation (homa), flowers [are offered] into the fire.
Āvāhana, Pādya, and so forth for Śāradā, the seventeen-syllable mantra.
dhī tannaḥ sarasvatī pra (3) oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ namo bhagavatyai śāradāyai hrīṃ svāhā (108). oṃ hrāṃ klāṃ, etc., for the six limbs. oṃ hrīṃ namo bhagavati bhairavi vāgi.
Oṃ śvarimahāprade mahāprabhāve bhagavati śāradāyai hrīṃ svāhā (108). Oṃ hrīṃ namo bhagavati hṛdayāya namaḥ svāhā. Bhairavi vāgīśvari śirase svāhā.
Hā Mahāpradeśikhāyai vaṣaṭ svāhā! Mahāprabhāve kavacāyai huṃ svāhā! Bhagavati Śāradāyai netrebhyo vauṣaṭ svāhā! Hrīṃ svāhā astrāya phaṭ svāhā!
The goddess is always complete, possessing three eyes, seated upon a tiger, and red in hue; she holds a parrot,
the autumnal sun and moon, a bow and arrow, a spear, a sword,
and the gestures of generosity and fearlessness, along with a dagger.
Bearing a face like the orb of the full moon, adorned with garlands and earrings,
the supreme Śāradā, who is always present, [is worshipped] at the beginning and end of the root mantra with *vauṣaṭ*;
this is the offering of water for restraint (*nirodhārgha*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) joined with Vijayeśvara.
I bow to Śāradā, the mistress of the seat of knowledge (Vidyāpīṭheśvarī), who bestows smiles and eloquence, who increases the intellect; I bow to that Bhavānī,
skilled in destroying the afflictions of existence, the autumnal goddess, as pure as an autumnal cloud.
We bow to her who is seated upon a white lion-throne. By this mantra-homa, may the venerable Śāradā, being well-pleased, become a granter of boons.
Now, [the visualization of] Rājñī: she possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns, has three eyes, and is seated upon a lion.
I worship the Queen, who is seated upon a lotus, adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread, holding in her hands a sword, a lotus, a jar, and a vessel of nectar, her lotus-face smiling;

[this is the mantra] of the illustrious Mahārājñī. The Ṛg Veda Gāyatrī for the venerable Mahārājñī: *Hrīṃ vīṃ sauḥ śrīṃ klīṃ kīṃ*, [addressed] to the fifteen-syllabled one who bestows sovereignty upon the king during the fire-oblation (*homa*): *Tanno rājñī pracodayāt*.
(3) *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rāṃ klīṃ sauḥ*.
Bhagavatyairājñaihrīṃ svāhā (108). Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rāṃ rājñī bhagavatyai namaḥ (108). Oṃ halara-rthaṃ mahārājñyai viśvavyāpikāyai svāhā (108). Oṃ hrāṃ śrāṃ, etc., six [syllables].
I bow to that Goddess Bharga, who is the syllable *ḍaṃ*, who is full, whose form is adorned by twelve suns, who is seated upon a single lion-throne, who is surrounded by serpents,
who has attained the state of the Lord beyond the reach of the mind and the senses, and who is the sovereign power itself.
Vapuṣaṃ paramārtharājñīṃ mūlānte auṣaṭ; with this mantra-homa of the long *nirodhā* libation, may the venerable Mahārājñī, residing on the Mountain of Flames, be satisfied and grant boons.

I bow to her who has three eyes, who is established upon the three seats, adorned with a mass of flames, possessed of a beautiful face, eternally visible to people, situated in the midst of the lotuses of the six chakras,
and who, in the form of consciousness, holds a supreme mace, a lotus, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
I bow to Jvālāmukhī, who illuminates the meaning of the *pāṃsakala*.
Of this [mantra] dedicated to the illustrious Jvālāmukhī, the meter is Anuṣṭubh and the deity is the illustrious Jvālāmukhī. The seed-syllables are: Hrīṃ Vī Śrīṃ Śa Huṃ Kī Ho.

O Jvālāmukhī, [I offer] the flower, the invitation, the water for the feet, and so forth, to you whose mouth is flame and who devours the world; may there be wisdom in that, O Jvālāmukhī! (3) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Jvālāmukhi, devour all my enemies! (2) Huṃ phaṭ!

Svāhā (108). Oṃ hrīṃ hṛ śrīṃ śira jvālāmukhi śikhā, devour all my enemies (2), kava huṃ phaṭ netre svāhā, to the weapon (astra), the full oblation; [O Goddess] whose face and head are surrounded by flames.
I meditate upon Jvālāmukhī, who holds a lotus, a conch, a sword, and a mace, with her pair of feet placed upon a lion-throne;
at the end of the root mantra, "Oṃ [Name] Svāhā," I offer the water of obstruction (*nirodhārgha*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Jvā... [mantra].
O Jvālāmukhi, whose mouth is a great flame, whose eyes are tawny with fire,
O you of great splendor and fiery brilliance, salutations and praise to you! And by this mantra and oblation, may Jvālāmukhī be pleased and grant boons.

I bow to Dīkṣā, the Great Goddess of Maheśa, who stands upon Rudra, possesses a body with nine faces, and holds in her right hands a trident, a goad, a severed head, a scythe, and a skull-cup filled with nectar.

With devotion, [one should offer] a flower into the fire; with the *āvāhana*, *pādya*, and other rites held in hand, there is the *tilājya-homa* (oblation of sesame and ghee) with "Oṃ Huṃ Bhuvanamālini Hrīṃ" repeated 108 times.
With the root mantra, the *pūrṇāhuti* and *tarpaṇa* (libation) are performed. This is declared to be the eight-syllabled [mantra].

O Goddess of the gods, the sin of reciting the *Liṅga-pāṭha* and other such acts is destroyed merely by remembering Dyābhuvanamālinī; she utterly consumes the heap of sins of a person, O Goddess, whether she has entered the path of one's ears or been worshipped.
I meditate. By this mantra-homa, may the Goddess Dīkṣā, being satisfied, become a granter of boons.
Now, [I worship] Pāpāntakāriṇī, who holds a noose, a goad, and a rosary.
Meditate upon the Mother, whose lotus-hands are adorned with the *kamala* flower, whose face and three eyes are gentle,
who rests upon a beautiful white lotus, who is red in hue,
who increases the abundant happiness of her devoted followers, and who is intent on the cause of the destruction of all sins.

The *mi agnaupuṣpa* [offering], the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth: *Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ namo bhagavati gauri vāg-viśuddhe śodhaya bodhaya sāṃ sāṃ klīṃ svāhā*. The twenty-six syllables [are recited]. The full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is performed with the root mantra; the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is *ha*.

The entire universe is filled with Brahmins; he is not smeared by sins, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. By this mantra-homa, may she who brings an end to sin become a granter of boons. Now...
To the Goddess Kulavāgīśvarī, who dwells in a grove of Kadamba trees, who resides within a reddish triangular mandala, who stands upon the pericarp of a white and black excellent lotus,
and whose lotus-feet are endowed with a sacred book and a rosary— to that Vāgīśvarī...

Rīṃ, I perpetually bow to the Kulaguru. Of this [mantra]: *Śrī-kulavāgīśvarī-de* (O Goddess of the Speech-Lord of the Kula), *aiṃ vī sauḥ ś klīṃ kī*. For the oblation (*homa*), [offer] a flower into the fire.
[Offer] the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, to Vāgīśāyī and Kāmeśāyī.
Dhī tannaḥ śaktiḥ pra aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ. Salutation to the sandals of Mahātripurabhairavī Kulavāgīśvarī. (108) Oṃ klīṃ hrauṃ śrīṃ huṃ jhaṃ jhaṣahaste kulavāgīśvari aiṃ ṭhaḥ.
JHAṂ ṬHAḤ KHĪṂ ṬHAḤ SVĀHĀ (108). AIṂ HṚ KLĪṂ ŚI SAUḤ ŚIKHĀ. TRIPURABHAIRAVĪ KAVA. KULAVĀGĪŚVARĪ NETRĀ AMBĀ PĀDUKĀBHYO NAMAḤ. ASTRA. PŪRNĀ TRIŚŪLĀSIDHARĀM.

I worship Kulavāgīśvarī, who holds a red lotus in her two hands, resembles fire, possesses three eyes, and is seated upon a lion-throne; [I offer] *vauṣaṭ* at the end of the root-mantra. This triple world is strung upon the great thread of the syllable of libation (*tarpaṇa*).
I bow to that Siddhamātṛkā, beginning with *ha* and ending with *ṅa-ṭha-a-ha*.
By this mantra and fire-oblation (*homam*), may Kulavāgīśvarī grant boons.
Now, Kāmeśvara Bhairava, mounted upon Kālikā, [is] a tree...
Resembling the sun, endowed with great vigor, his face was radiant and he was free from decay; adorned with a garland of skulls, wearing an elephant hide as an upper garment,
and holding a trident and a sword in his hands, he resounded with the ringing of bells and the *ḍamaru* drum.
Adorned with necklaces, bracelets, and earrings, he was accompanied by cobras, scorpions, and thieves,
and joined by the dance of his wife who resembled an evening cloud; upon his lap sat the goddess Mahātripurasundarī, who was like a mass of vermilion.
The goddess, possessing a luster equal to a ruby, radiant as the rising sun, and augmented by divine splendor,
illumines the ten directions with rays of light originating from herself.
Four-armed and single-faced, adorned with bow and arrow,
resplendent with a book consisting of all-encompassing knowledge,
and graced by a crystal rosary held in her hand— [the goddess] red...
Remember her who is clothed in garments, adorned with red flowers, bound with a girdle and anklets,
decorated with necklaces and armlets,
appearing like a sixteen-year-old girl, and graced by jar-like breasts.
One should meditate upon her who is adorned with the bending of the earth as it is split by the bow, whose three eyes possess beautiful faces, who is overflowing with nectar,
standing face-to-face with the God of gods, and smiling. Such is her form.

One should worship the Supreme Goddess, who has descended [to earth], who removes the suffering of those who bow to her, and who is endowed with the four seats (catuṣpīṭha). [One offers] flowers into the fire, the invocation, the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth. Oṃ vāgīśāya vikāmeśā.
If that is so, may Śiva [bestow] upon us with his hand curd, honey, and milk;
[this is] the oblation of parched grain (*lājā-homa*): *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ kāmeśvara-bhairava-nātha-pādukābhyāṃ namaḥ* (108 times). *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ tripura-bhairavī*.
Salutation to Vyomavyāpādukā (108). As for what was stated—that there are no limbs—this is the Goddess Vidyā Tripurabhairavī who has been described;
when conjoined with her own name-words, she is complete even while being devoid of the six limbs.

I bow to Kāmeśvarī, my family preceptor, whose entire body is filled with streams of vermilion, who holds in her two hands a bow fashioned from a conch shell, and whose lotus feet are adorned with a sacred book and a rosary of beads.
"Always, with 'mūla-ante vauṣaṭ', there is the libation (tarpaṇa) and the offering for restraint (nirodhārgha).
Now, Vajreśvarī, exceedingly ruddy like the fire at the end of an aeon,
adorned with golden necklaces and jeweled earrings, [is] in the thunderbolt."

I bow to the auspicious Śvarī, who has three eyes and whose hands are equipped with a goad, a noose, arrows, a bow, and other weapons. [Offer] flowers into the fire; [perform] the invocation (āvāhana), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth. Om, salutation to the highly fortunate one, to the eternally moist one (Nityaklinnā). Dhīḥ.
May that power impel us. (3) Hrīṃ klinne aiṃ krauṃ nityamada drave hrīṃ (108) aiṃ hṛ hrīṃ hrīṃ klinne śira klinne hrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ kroṃ śikhā kroṃ aiṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ nitye kavaca nitye hrīṃ hrīṃ.

Madanetrā, who possesses the weapons of *mada*, *hrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *indra*, *drava*, and *astra*; whose hand shines with the homa-offering of camphor, saffron, musk, and clarified butter; and who holds a full [arrow], a bow, an arrow, a noose, a goad, and a thunderbolt along with *tuluṅga* flowers.
May this Goddess Bhagavatī, who resides on a lotus throne, possesses three eyes, and is free from defeat, grant me my desired objects perpetually;
[may she be worshipped] with the root mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ* for libation (*tarpaṇa*), and with the *nirodha-argha* [offering]. Now, the Great...

The varieties of Tripurasundarī: therein, first, I worship Kāmeśvara, who possesses the splendor of ten million moons, who bears the moon upon his crest, who has three eyes, and who holds a boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, and a sword in his hands. Of this Śrīkā...
To the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is the embodiment of the Pañcākṣara mantra, in the presence of Śrī Kāmeśvara:

*Śrīṃ Vīṃ Hrīṃ Śa Klīṃ Kīṃ*. Having offered flowers into the fire for the oblation (*homa*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, the oblation is performed with the root mantra (*mūla*). At the end of the root mantra, [one says] *Vauṣaṭ*.

Thus ends the *pūrṇā* libation, the *nirodha-argha*, or *alā*. [She is] one who colors the quarters of space with networks of rays, holds a rosary, a book, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, and is enriched by another hand holding a lotus.
May the auspicious Bālā Tripurasundarī, who resides in the heart of Śiva and possesses an eternally beautiful form, [be established].
The seer (ṛṣi) is the venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the meter (chandas) is Paṅkti; the deity is the venerable Bālā Tripura...
The application (*viniyoga*) of *aiṃ vīṃ sauḥ śaklīṃ kīṃ* is for the oblation (*homa*).

[One offers] a flower into the fire; [the mantra for] the invocation, the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth is: *aiṃ tripurādevyai viklīṃ vāgīśvaryai dhīḥ sauḥ tanno muktiḥ pracodayāt*. (3) *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*.

*Vālāyai namaḥ* (108). Having performed the six-limbed *homa* by repeating the three seed-syllables twice, [I offer] the final oblation (*pūrṇā*). I meditate upon you in my heart—you who are adorned with a crescent moon, as white as the autumnal moon, consisting of fifty syllables, holding a book and a rosary.

[One should worship] her who holds a jar rich with nectar and the *Vyākhyā-cakra* (the wheel of exposition) in her lotus-like hands, and who has three eyes; [the mantra is] *mūlāntaṃ vaṣaṭ*, followed by the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, the fifteenth [verse]: [He sees] him seated upon a large red lotus, [resembling] a pomegranate...
One should meditate upon the form of the Goddess, which is of beautiful luster, possessing four hands equipped with a noose, a goad, a bow, and an arrow;
having three eyes and one face, she is most charming with various ornaments, endowed with all auspiciousness. Of this [mantra]:
The venerable *Pañcadaśī* (Fifteen-Syllabled Mantra), the venerable *Dakṣiṇāmūrti-Ṛṣi*, the *Paṅkti* meter,

the venerable *Pañcadaśākṣarī Tripurasundarī Devatā*, *Aiṃ Vī Sauḥ Śaklīṃ Kīṃ*— in the fire-offering (*homa*), [the offering of] flowers, invocation (*āvāhana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, into the fire.
Aiṃ to the Goddess Tripurā; Klīṃ, may the wisdom of Kāmeśvarī enter us; Saut, may Śakti impel us. (3) Keīlahrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ.
(108) The six-limbed fire-oblation with the Vālā-mantra; the final oblation [is performed] with the mantra "udyadbhānusahasrakā" (resembling a thousand rising suns).
She wears a crown of garlands and garments of fresh crimson silk; her breasts are smeared with red pigment;
she holds a rosary, a scripture, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons in her lotus-like hands; and she possesses the beauty of a three-eyed, radiant lotus-face.
I bow to that Goddess who sits upon a lotus, adorned with a crown of jewels like the full moon.
*Mūlānta vaṣaṭ* for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the *nirodhārgha*.
Now, [one should meditate upon] Mahātripurasundarī; then the Goddess who resembles a lotus, reddened by the rays of the rising sun, like the *japā* flower, and like the *dāḍima* fruit.
Resembling the moon, with a complexion like a ruby, appearing as if an opening bud of saffron,
adorned with a network of tinkling bells and rubies from her shimmering crown,
and possessing curved locks resembling a swarm of black bees—
To the Supreme Goddess, whose garment is made of bark, whose lotus-face is like the glow of the rising sun, whose forehead is adorned with a crescent moon slightly curved like a digit,
and whose creeper-like eyebrows are shaped like the bow of Śiva.

Her eyes were playfully swinging with waves of bliss and joy; her golden earrings shone with a mass of flickering rays; and the full expanse of her beautiful cheeks surpassed the orb of the nectar-filled moon. Viśva...
Her nose was clearly defined like a thread of magically emanated karma; her lips were red like rubies, coral, and bimba fruit, resembling nectar;
she surpassed the ocean of the essence of sweetness with the sweetness of her smile. O Lord, [I bow] to her.
Behold her, whose chin is graced by excellent qualities, whose neck is like that of a conch, who has large eyes, and whose arms are as graceful as lotus stalks,
beautifully adorned with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and necklaces.

Her lotus-like hands are delicate, shaped like the petals of a red lotus; the radiance from the moonlight of her fingernails illuminates the expanse of the sky; her full breasts are adorned with strings of pearl necklaces; and she possesses the three folds of skin on her waist.
Her waist was beautifully adorned with a well-proportioned navel that resembled an eddy in a river of loveliness; her hips were graced by a girdle fashioned from priceless jewels.

I bow to the Sovereign Lady, whose lower lip is like a lotus bud, who holds a goad, and whose thighs are as delicate as the graceful trunks of plantain trees; she is adorned with a pair of shanks resembling lovely plantain stems, and she causes the crest-jewels of the prostrating Brahmā to shine.
She whose lotus-feet are rubbed [by devotees], who resembles a hundred moons,
who laughs with three-fold continuity, who surpasses vermilion and the *japā* flower in her redness,
who possesses the hue of the *dāḍima* fruit, who is clothed in red garments, and who wears red ornaments...
Adorned with ornaments, four-armed and three-eyed, holding five arrows and a bow,
her mouth filled with betel-leaf mixed with camphor, her body reddened by great musk and saffron;
Salutations to her who is enriched with every graceful adornment, resplendent with all ornaments,
the one who generates delight for the world, the one who brings joy to the world,
the one who attracts the world, and the one whose form is the cause of the universe.
Having meditated upon the Goddess who consists of all mantras, who is beautiful with all auspiciousness,
who is the eternal embodiment of all Lakṣmī, who is delighted by supreme bliss,
and who is the Great Seal (Mahātripuramudrā), [one should invoke her] with the invocation mudrā.

The best of practitioners, having meditated upon Mahātripurasundarī with the previously mentioned mantra dedicated to salutation— which is auspicious and to be invoked— and having visualized her for the sake of one studying the Krama, should then begin the worship.
Reddish in luster, with three eyes, wearing a jeweled crown and beautiful gem-studded earrings,
she shines with her lotus-like hands holding a noose, a goad, a bow of love, and arrows; her face is full and high-browed.

One should meditate upon the Goddess of the lords, the venerable Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, the queen of mantras, whose limbs are radiant with the pearls rolling on her banks, who stands upon a lotus, and who wears a crimson garment.
For this [mantra], the seer is Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is Paṅkti, the deity is Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, the seed-syllable is Aiṃ, the power-syllable is Sauḥ, and Kīlaka is Śakti;
in the fire-offering (homa), the flower is offered into the fire, and [the sequence begins with] Āvāhana, Pādya, etc., starting with Aiṃ.

To Tripurādevī, svāhā; to Kāmeśvarī, dhīḥ; to Sauḥ-Klīnne, tat naḥ pra [svāhā]. With the root mantra, one hundred and eight oblations (homa) are offered; with five [repetitions] for the heart, three for the head, six for the crest-lock, and four for the armor.
From these two, the weapon-mantra [is offered] five times; this is the ten-fold portion for the limbs.
Now, in another manner, follows the fire-oblation of the root-mantra: the three peaks (kūṭas) within the Great Wheel of the Bindu, which is the Great Tripura, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.

Salutations to the sandals of Nandarya (108). *Sauṃ klīṃ aiṃ* and so forth are the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Now, the meditation on the Fullness (*pūrṇādhyāna*): Her form is established within a triangle of three syllables;
she shines with the three supreme mudrās and bears [the crescent moon].

May the Lord who holds in his four arms a bow with a multitude of arrows, nooses, and goads— accompanied by three goddesses, as well as eight principal goddesses of the cardinal and intermediate directions,
and eight Vasus who are bowed down before him— be victorious over the world.

Having performed the *nirodhārghya* offering with the mantra *nmātṛkā mūlānta vaṣaṭ* and likewise performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the best of practitioners, having first recited [the mantra] according to his capacity, should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with one-tenth the number [of recitations], using *brahmavṛkṣa* wood, O Brāhmaṇa.
Then, by offering *yāmbhu* flowers smeared with the three sweets according to the prescribed rite, this Vidyā becomes effective for the pacification of the flood of great obstacles;
she is the Goddess who grants all desires and bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. [The Yoni-kunda...]
In a *ḍebhaga* (triangular), a circular, a horse-shoe-shaped, a nine-triangle, a moon-shaped, a square, or an eight-petaled lotus-shaped *kuṇḍa*, one becomes eloquent;
in a *yoni*-shaped *kuṇḍa*, there is supreme power of attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*); and in a circular one, there is prosperity (*lakṣmī*). In a semi-circular [shape], [there is]...

In a triangular fire-pit (kuṇḍa), there will be three moons; in a nine-triangular pit, movement through the sky arises; in a square pit, there is peace, fortune, nourishment, and freedom from disease; and in a lotus-shaped pit, all prosperity is attained without delay.
O auspicious one, by offering eight lotuses (*devajāta*) with the desired results,
or by offering *mallikā*, *mālatī*,
and *jātī* flowers drenched in clarified butter and honey, even a mute person becomes a lord of speech (*vāgīśa*).

O Parameśvarī, likewise, O Maheśvarī, by offering parched grain (*lājā*) mixed with curd, honey, and milk, one is not afflicted by diseases, nor by the fear of death resulting from past actions (*karma*). By this mantra-homa, [one attains] Śrī Mahātripura...

May the beautiful Goddess, together with her attendants, her retinue, her limbs, her vehicles, her weapons, and her followers— propitiated by supreme and ever-increasing worship— be the bestower of boons. Now, [the mantra of] Sarasvatī...

The oblation of pure sesame seeds for protection is performed with fifty distinct syllables; she whose face, arms, feet, hips, belly, and chest are adorned with these, who wears the crescent moon upon her matted locks, and who is as white as the moon and jasmine— [to her, I bow].
I bow to that Bhāratī, who speaks beautifully, whose excellent hands hold a rosary,
a water-pot, and a book, whose eyes are like lotuses, who is seated upon a lotus, who is of pure complexion,
and who bears the weight of her full breasts and hips. Of this [work]:

The Ṛṣi is the venerable Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī-Brahmā; the metre is Gāyatrī; the deity is Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī. For the *aiṃ vī hrīṃ śa oṃ* [mantra], during the fire-oblation (*homa*), one offers flowers into the fire, beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, starting with *hrāṃ hrīm*, etc.
The Nyāsa of the Dīnī: Oṃ tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt (108). Pūrṇā: mūlānte vaṣaṭ. Or else, [the mantra] of this Śrīmātṛkā-Sarasvatī.
Brahmā is the Ṛṣi, Gāyatrī is the metre, Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity,
the consonants are the Vījas, the vowels are the Śaktis, and the Brahma-vīja is the Kīlaka. In the fire sacrifice (homa),
one should perform the offering of pure sesame seeds with the *vikaraṇa* mantra, followed by the invocation (āvāhana), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
The fire-oblation of pure sesame seeds: *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svas tatsavitur* (3) *hsauḥ aṃ āṃ i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa*.
Ṭhaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃḥ hsauṃḥ, obeisance to Sarasvatī (108). Aṃ kaṃ (5) āṃ hya iṃ caṃ pīśi.
Ra-uṃṭaṃ (5) rthaṃśikhā eṃtaṃ (5) aiṃkava oṃ paṃ (5) auṃ netre aṃyaṃ ṭha(0) aḥ astrāyaphaṭ ||
Now, the second [form]: *hasavayarthaṃ vidyāvidyeśvaryai namaḥ* (108).
*Oṃ rakṣajharīṃ vāgbhaveśvaryai namaḥ* (108). *Oṃ hrīṃ vadavadavāgvādini svāhā* (108). Now, Vaikharī: *aiṃ*.
*klīṃ sauḥ vāgīśvarī-vāk-prade-sarasvatyai namaḥ* (108).
[The mantra for] the *pūrṇāhuti* with pure sesame seeds for all [the goddesses]:
[I bow to her] who is endowed with four arms and holds a rosary made of crystal beads.
She who holds a lotus, a cup, and a book in one hand,
and in the other [hand] shines with a luster like jasmine, the moon, a conch, crystal, and gems— she is this very goddess of speech, who is peerless.
Having always well-attained the utterance of *vasat*, with *mūla*, *ante*, *vauṣaṭ*,
and the offering of water for cessation (*nirodhārgha*), by this mantra-homa, [one is freed from] misfortune,
disease, poison, untimely death, dullness of intellect, poverty, and so forth.

Those who touch these [seven] are born seven times as virtuous men; Sarasvatī, together with her retinue and her attendants, becomes present for them. May she be pleased; may she be well-pleased. Now, Bhavānī, whose face is like the rising moon—
I worship Bhavānī, who has four arms, whose lotus-eyes are red, and whose smile is radiant;

she is marked by the sword, the spear, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, and she stands upon a corpse—may she grant me constant auspiciousness. Of this [hymn] to Śrī Bhavānī... may there be peace.

The meter is Anuṣṭubh. For the worship of Śrī Bhavānī: *Śrīṃ* is the seed syllable; *Hrīṃ Śa Hūṃ Kī*. In the fire-offering (*homa*), [offer] flowers into the fire. For the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth:
*Oṃ Śrīṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śrīṃ Bhavāni Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā* (108 times).

The six-limbed [mantra] beginning with *śrāṃ hrāṃ* and others, and furthermore: *durgāyai vidmahe, kātyāyanyai dhīmahi, tanno bhavānī pracodayāt* (3). With the hand, there is the *śuddhatila-homa* (oblation of pure sesame): *oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍayogeśvari bhava-bhavāni sarvakā...*

O bestower of boons, O giver of all auspiciousness, *hrīṃ namaḥ* (108). The *pūrṇā* [offering] begins with "to the stainless one whose crest is the half-moon," and so forth, ending with the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*. This is the *nirodhārgha* and the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Now, as for Kuñjikā:

Rising from the peak of the triangle with five hoods from the interior of Meru, Vāgīśvarī— the eternal Śrī Kulanāyikā, the destroyer— [proceeded] with the speed of the tenfold excellent sound of the five spaces; thus she was described.
May the venerable Kubjikā, whose entire lineage is permeated by the five *ra*s, the five *pa*s, and the *praṇava* (OṂ), protect us.

[The ritual sequence includes: offering flowers into the fire, invocation (*āvāhana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth; the internal placement (*nyāsa*) within one's own self; and *Aiṃ* to the Lord of Mantras.
Adoration to Śrīkaṇṭha; may there be success for us. Furthermore, the oblation of sesame seeds combined with the three sweets is likewise stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Milk, honey, and ghee—these together are known as the 'three sweets' (*trimadhura*)."
Alternatively, [one may offer] the "three sweets" (trimadhura)— clarified butter, honey, and sugar— along with the root-mantra:
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ khaphreṃ hamayārthaṃ bhagavati asvehasakhahraiṃ sa hakhaheṃ śrīkubjike hsāṃ hsīṃ hasarthaṃ jañaṇana*.
Meaghoramukhe-chāṃ-chīṃ-kiṇi (2) viśvehasa-yartham-khaphraṃ-śrīṃ-hrīṃ-aiṃ (108) aiṃ-hrīṃ-śrīṃ-khahreṃ-hamayūṃ-asve-hṛda-hasakha-phem-sahakha-phreṃ-śrī-kubjike-śi.
*Ra hsāṃ hsīṃ*, O you whose form is a lion, *jaṃ ña ṇa me*, for the *śikhā*, *ghora-mukha*, *kavacāṃ chīṃ* for the eyes, *kiṇi (2)*, *vicce astrāya*.
[The deity holds] the full [arrow], the bow, the book, the rosary, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

May she who holds a skull-cup joined with a *khaṭvāṅga* staff and a trident, and who bears the goddess Kubjikā seated upon a lotus, protect us— [the mantra] ending in the root-syllable, followed by *vaṣaṭ* for libation: *aiṃ paraprakāśasānandam oṃ vaṃ li* three times.
One should worship that reality, the Lord of the Kula, which is augmented in six ways,
vastly expansive, pervaded by five and nine, blazing with the imperishable supreme bliss;
one should worship that circle of gurus, the source of that [reality] and the support of that family.
That Aparā-avidyā, which is essentially devoid of inherent form, impure,
and characterized by non-violence (*ahaṃsā*), is the power of Rudra (*raudraśakti*); she consists of thirty-two syllables and is Aparā, who is subtle and the illuminator of the nature of Rudra.
By the mere remembrance of her, the cage of the body trembles;
there is no knowledge equal to hers, no lineage equal to hers,
no illusion equal to hers, and no pride equal to hers.
Just as clarified butter is the essence of food, the moon among the stars,
and Takṣaka among the serpents, so is that Lord the master of the sky-goers. The five-syllabled mantra has been proclaimed, while the thirty-two syllabled mantra is the Goddess.

I bow to that which is called the Guru— consisting of seven syllables, nine vowels, and eight consonants; where the god Manu is the science (vidyā), and this [reality] exists as an unbroken circle, the essence of Śrīdhara,
which has been illuminated by my gurus through this mantra.

By this oblation, may the deities of the Śrī-Kubjikā-Paścima-tantra, together with their retinues and attendants, be pleased; may they be satisfied. Now, regarding the four Pratyaṅgirās, first is Siddhalakṣmī: Oṃ De...
I meditate upon her who is as white as pure crystal, five-faced and three-eyed,
endowed with ten arms and adorned all around with necklaces of jewels;
she holds a sword, a goad, a noose, a trident, and a sharp-edged discus.
Carrying with her right hands the excellent, peerless, and supreme *tsāra* weapon—
a sharp-edged tool that is hard, formidable, and powerful.

I bow to Siddhalakṣmī, who is worshipped by the entire universe, who holds in her auspicious left hands a noose marked with the syllable *Sviṭ*, a book consisting of the essence of the nectar of knowledge, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the wish-granting gem (*kāma*), and whose feet rest upon a lotus and a corpse.
I bow to this Śrī Siddhalakṣmī. [The seer is] Śrī Brahmā, [the meter is] Gāyatrī, [and the deity is] Śrī Siddhalakṣmī. Hrīṃ vī huṃ śa krīṃ kī.
In the fire of the *homa*, [I offer] flowers, the invocation, water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth—*svāhā*.

The Nyāsa of the faces of Tmāga: *Oṃ siddharamāyai vidmahe pratyaṅgirāyaidhīmahi tannaḥ pratyaṅgirā pracodayāt* (3). The oblation of clarified butter and guggulu with the *srūva* ladle: *Ā* (21), *Vā* (7), *Vā* (3), *Oṃ namaḥ sarvasiddhi*.

Homage to the Yoginīs! Homage to the Mothers of all Siddhis! Homage to her who is eternally arisen in bliss, the sovereign of the entire wheel of families (kulacakra), the Blessed One Caṇḍīkapālinī! Thus it is: Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ.

HĀṂ PHEṂ KṢAUṂ KRAUṂ NAMAḤ! Obeisance to the one who bestows the path of supreme liberation, O Goddess who pacifies calamities and misfortunes, who shatters all evils, portents, and afflictions, and who is the boat for crossing the ocean of all adversities.
O Goddess who crushes the enemy host with the *kalaśa* [vessel], come! (2) Laugh! (2) Va lā (2)! O you who consume human blood and fat, subdue all my enemies!
Mand (2) Khāhi (2)! O you with the trident, pierce! (2) Cut! (2) Kha!
Strike! Strike! Cut! Cut!
Accomplish all our desires until they are fulfilled, O most compassionate Blessed One, bearer of the Great Terrifier, best among the thirty gods!
O Mother, you who possess the complete mantra; O Goddess Mahākālī, who are compassionate toward those who bow before you and destroy all afflictions; *huṃ huṃ huṃ*, be gracious!
Make me, who am afflicted by passion, one who possesses the daughters of gods and demons. *Oṃ*.
Hrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ phaṭ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Ā (24) vā (14) vā (7) vā (3).
O Supreme Swan, who points out the path to Nirvāṇa within the heart;
O crest of flame that pacifies all calamities and misfortunes; [O you who destroy] all evils...
O Mother of Mantras, you who destroy the host of afflictions, who are the boat for crossing the ocean of all calamities,
and the weapon that crushes every enemy;
you are like the black crow, the cuckoo, and other such birds.
Resembling a young woman, four-armed and one-faced, radiant with three eyes, mounted upon a white corpse, bearing the *khaṭvāṅga* marked with the letter *Ā*,
holding a noose and a mallet in her hands, and smeared with fat and blood.
[To] the cloth [image], most exalted, greatly formidable, with nine petals, slender-waisted, the shatterer of all machines, the Mother of Mantras: (3) *ā* in the fire [mandala]; flowers;
the invocation, water for the feet, and so forth; the root mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ joṃ huṃ phreṃ mahāmāyāyai*.
Mounted upon a great preta that devours blood, marrow, and flesh, with a khaṭvāṅga,
skull-cup, noose, and mallet in his hands, he shatters the mechanical devices of the enemy.
*matha matha, cūrṇaya cūrṇaya, phutpha phutpha, sphoṭaya sphoṭaya! For the destruction of him who hates us and whom we hate—phaṭ svāhā!* Now follows the *Ḍāmarikā* mantra: *gajacarmatumbavīṇautri*.

She holds a trident, a spear, a banner, and a vulture; in her lotus-like hands she bears a human skull, a knife, a sword, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, while her hair is adorned with a swarm of bees and a garland of *kokila* flowers.

She has the form of a donkey and a pig, with two hands placed upon her breasts; she holds a mantra-chopper and sits upon a very white, great corpse; she possesses eighteen creeper-like arms and is slender.
I bow to Maṃtraḍāmarikā, whose form is fierce with distorted fangs, adorned with serpents, and blazing. [For the fire-oblation: flowers, invocation, water for the feet, and so forth:
Oṃ phaḥ phaḥ hā hā khā (2) kha (2) khā.
Indeed, swallow all mantras! Destroy the rites performed by others—subjugation, attraction, incantation, causing hatred, killing, expulsion, and so forth!
Hrīṃ raḥ phara thaṃ phreṃ phuḥ phuḥ phaṭ phuḥ phaṭ namaḥ svāhā!

Alas! O Mistress of seven hundred million, her unmanifest meditation is seen nowhere; she is intent on devouring the single digit of the crescent-mudrā, seated upon the seventh high throne, and has emerged from the *ādhāra-cakra*.

May that Goddess Ghoracaṇḍā, who is the Mistress of Speech (Vāgīśvarī) in the great void at the end of sound, whose sevenfold tongues of flame flicker like the fire at the end of an aeon, and who dwells within the beginning, the end, and the interval— may she destroy our evil. Seven times over.

To the Mistress of the Seven Crores (Saptakoṭīśvarī), [I offer] fire-flower, invocation, water for the feet, and so forth: Oṃ nīrūpāyai viśaktyatītāyai dhī tanno devī pra oṃ oṃ kaḥ saḥ caṇḍini saḥ kaḥ saptakoṭīśvaryambā pā.

Homage to the pair (dukābhyo namaḥ). (108) Ā. Now, [she is] Pūrṇā, whose hands hold a Khaṭvāṅga, a boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, a ṭaṅka, a noose, a goad, a sword, a manuscript, and a lotus; she has five faces.
For which man on earth could there be fear while meditating upon you, who are mounted upon the bull of Vasubhuja and Giriśa? *Mūla-ante vauṣaṭ*;
the offering of water for restraint: O Supreme Lord, source of the nectar of immortality!
O Maheśvara, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon, who has a blue throat, who is mounted upon a bull,
and who bears the Gaṅgā— speak of the goddess Pratyaṅgirā, the destroyer of fear in the three worlds, and of the yantras, mantras, and magical incantations.

She effortlessly destroys [all obstacles], bestowing peace and nourishment; she is pure, the devourer of possession-demons (*agrahāpasmāra*), the subduer of spirits (*bhūta*) and vampires (*vetāla*), the destroyer of malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*) and the *kharkhoda* demons; she is the universal benefactress, the terrible one who [overcomes] all [evils].

The Plavanāśinī is the most excellent bestower of all prosperity and the producer of every kind of wealth; when she is merely known, one’s power increases greatly. On this earth, no other knowledge more terrible than hers exists.
"O Mahādeva, tell me how to utter that [mantra] by your grace.
The Lord, the Leader of the Universe, said: "The supreme ignorance (avidyā) which bestows sovereignty and liberation consists of two hundred and nine syllables."
This [Vidyā], which consists of thirty-two syllables, is renowned by the names Mahāvidyā and Trailokyamohinī; she is the Goddess Lakṣmī,
known as Mahālakṣmī and Mahākāntā, who bestows a great abundance of enjoyments upon all.
In this Droṇa chapter, she is remembered by the Lord of Gods as the bestower of good fortune; no other like her is known to exist.
She should be understood as the pacifier of misfortune (Alakṣmī), the crusher of sorrow and poverty, and the queller of the evil dreams of the Kali age. Thus [it is said].
She who destroys calamities, who pacifies the afflictions of dust and passion,

who annihilates wicked bandits, and who [protects] in all terrible fears of the forest, in the peril of lions, tigers, and the like, in difficult thickets, in fire, and against spirits, epilepsy, and elephants.
This [teaching], which— by means of constant mindfulness, the purification of impurities, and the non-transmigration [of karma]— once and for all eradicates the flood of evil like a heap of straw,
has destroyed this entire world and been filled by the knowers of Brahman; O Guru!

It shall liberate one from the sin of killing a father, killing a brother, killing a mother, and likewise killing an embryo; it shall liberate one from the sins of uprooting the *liṅga* and so forth, from minor sins (*pāpa*), from mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), and likewise from secondary sins (*upapātaka*). And thus...

When remembered, she liberates one from the kings of sins; the wise man shall always be endowed with prosperity like the lord of elephants. O Goddess, one should worship the Queen of the Gods, the most excellent of all the excellent, even once, [in the waters] of the seven oceans.

O Goddess, by reciting [this] three times, one shall have performed a bath at all the holy fords (tīrthas); through divine, terrestrial, and celestial holy fords, O Goddess, a bath is accomplished—of this there is no doubt. By reciting it seven times, O Goddess...
One who has received initiation from Śānin becomes possessed of sons in every maṇḍala through ten recitations of the mantra to the deity; by twenty-seven recitations,
the practitioner is born in the Mātṛ-maṇḍala as a Vīrarājeśvara.
By reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, the leader Bhairava becomes Bhairava himself; there is nothing where he acts that does not exist, and there is nothing he does not accomplish.
He always destroys fetters, thunderbolts, and blades of grass with ease.
O Goddess, by performing this three times a day for seven days, there is no doubt that a living being is released from bondage, even if [death] occurs at the appointed time.

The land of the practitioner shall always be filled with wealth and grain, never consumed by calamity; just as the god Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Lakṣmī, remains eternally present, so too does the King of Sādhas abide through mere remembrance.
"By this mantra-homa performed daily, may Siddhalakṣmī be a granter of boons. Now, the libation (tarpaṇa) with the Mantra-mātṛkā:
"O Great Goddess, there are seventy-seven crores of mantras belonging to this Kālī..."
Since all [beings] born from the body are its protection, therefore this Mantra-mātṛkā—
by means of the offering of mantras— may this Mantra-Ḍāmarikā become the bestower of boons;
may she [grant] these and other mantras such as those for eradication (uccāṭana) and so forth, even those composed by others.

Then, by the mere recollection of this mantra, the Mantra-Ḍāmarikā slays [the enemy]. By this mantra and its fire-oblation, may the Mantra-Ḍāmarikā become a bestower of boons. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which destroys the deceivers (kuhakas).

By the mere worship of her, one is liberated from all suffering; whoever worships her in a secluded and pleasant abode attains the state of being a locus for all enjoyments, just like the station of the lords of the gods. If...
Whatever he desires, he obtains that without doubt;

he does not become an object of hatred in the world, but is beloved even by his enemies; neither diseases nor famines and other such calamities seek to destroy him—this is for him who [practices this].
He constantly worships the Goddess, the supreme Mistress of seventy million, the seven-syllabled one,
the most terrible Caṇḍakālī of great power, who wears seven skulls, who devours human flesh, and who traverses as many worlds as there are syllables; she is the poet and the knower of fate.

And by the mere worship of the Goddess, one obtains those very great prophecies (*mahāvyākaraṇa*); there is no doubt in this matter. By this mantra-homa, may the Mistress of the seventy million (*saptakoṭīśvarī*) become a granter of boons; likewise for Pratyamgirā.
May her attendants, along with their limbs, faces, Śivās, and the granting of boons, be present; and may Caṇḍikā,
whose left and right [hands] are adorned with the sounds of the trident, skull, sword, *sphurikā*, *khaṭvāṅga*, and severed head, [be victorious].
The Goddess, radiant with nine syllables beginning with the letter *ṇa*, possessing a single face with a brilliance equal to fire, standing upon a *preta* and surrounded by her divine messengers,
should be established by the practitioner within the fire of her own abode.
Flower, invocation, water for the feet, and so forth: *oṃ yamāntakāya vi kālarātryai dhī tannaścaṇḍīpra*. (3) *oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍīkāpālinyai svāhā* (108). *Hrīṃ* is the heart; *caṇḍi* is the head.
*Kāpāśikhā*, *linyaikava*, *svānetre*, *hāstrā*,
and the *mūla* [mantra] for the full libation (*pūrṇā-tarpaṇa*), the *virodhārgha*, and the oblation of grapes and clarified butter (*drākṣājya-homa*).
Now, the *Īśvarīmālinī* according to the previous tradition, the nectar within the self.
I bow to that certain supreme Goddess of Trika,
who is marked by the lotus of the heart, who is innate, whose power is released into the abode of the trident of Citrāṅghri (Śiva), the Lord of the Age, and the Lord of Men.

With the root mantra *oṃ nṛ sṛ sṛ thaca dhargha ūrdhavakakhagagha ṅi avabhaya ḍaḍha ṭhajha ña ṇara ṭapakalāsa*, [one should offer] one's own power (*miśaktiṃ*) as flowers into the fire, along with the invocation, water for the feet (*pādya*), and other offerings.
*Āḥ hasakṣamaśaaṃeaioaudahahrīṃ mālinyai namaḥ svāhā*. This is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) of Mālinī. Now, [the mantra of] Lakṣmī: *Śiṃjṛṃjīra-saṃśobhi-pādāmbhoja-virājita...*.
She was adorned with a girdle resplendent with a multitude of nine kinds of gems;
she shone with a waist-band composed of pearls, rubies,
and diamonds, which was radiant in the middle with the beauty of three folds.
Adorned with a navel beautiful with the whirlpools of the Hlavī river,
her breasts decorated with the paste of pāṭīra-sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, she bore a necklace of pearls as magnificent as a rain-cloud released from its burden of water.
Her upper garment was fashioned from fine silk;
she was adorned with armlets of beryl set in molten gold;
her lotus-like hands were enriched with golden bracelets shimmering with rubies and [set with] rubies...
Adorned with bracelets set with gems, beautified by necklaces and armlets fashioned from refined gold, her neck resembling a water-lily bud of various and wonderful colors, like the rising sun—

Adorned with earrings that were ornaments of exquisite artistry, beautified by shimmering golden ear-ornaments marked with jewels, her sprout-like lower lip was charmingly lovely with the splendor of hibiscus flowers and coral,
resembling the seeds of the pomegranate fruit.
Adorned by a row of venerable ones, her face resembles the autumn moon freed from stains and spots; the playful grace of her creeper-like eyebrows surpasses the ball of the god of love,
and she possesses the splendor of blooming sesame flowers.
Her nose is uplifted in victory; she has surpassed the half-moon with the splendor of her forehead’s radiance; she is marked by the *tilaka* of musk endowed with intense fragrance;
and her locks of hair are graced by the play of swarms of intoxicated bees.
Her lotus-face is adorned with a smile that bears the splendor of *pārijāta* blossoms;
her hair is bound with jasmine flowers, and her head is marked by a crest-jewel set with priceless gems, the very essence of all beauty.

One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should thus meditate upon the Goddess— the source of the splendor of the three worlds, the birthplace of all luminous powers, the Great Fortune (Mahālakṣmī), and the enchanting one.
Her face is graced with a smile resembling the rising sun;
she wears red garments and a lower garment of fine cloth; holding a water-pot, a vessel, a goad, and a noose in her hands, she stands upon a lotus, possessing lotus-like eyes and firm breasts.

This is the venerable Jyeṣṭhalakṣmī, an ocean of beauty who grants the fruit of the desire for all arts mastered by Vyāsa; she is the venerable Mahālakṣmī, the middle [of the three]. The meter is Anuṣṭubh. This is the venerable Mahāla...

KṢMĪRDE ŚRĪṂVĪ HRĪṂŚA OṂKĪ; for the fire-oblation (homa), flowers, invocation (āvāhana), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth: OṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ LAKṢMI MAHĀLAKṢMI, bestower of all desires, giver of all good fortune, [be present].

Grant me [your] favor, O You who are all-pervading, whose nature is omnipresent, and who liberate one from all suffering! Hrīṃ Saḥ Svāhā. (108) Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Lakṣmi, Great Lakṣmi, O Heart! Oṃ, O Bestower of all desires, O Giver of all good fortune!
Yiniśira: Oṃ abhimataṃ prayaccha śikhā: Oṃ sarve sarvagatasvarūpeka vauṣaṭ netre: Oṃ sarvaduḥkhavimocini astrā: Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ svāhā kavaca: Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ.
Mahālakṣmiprasīda (2) Śrīṃ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Svāhā (108). Śrīṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ Sauḥ Mahālakṣmiprasīda (2) Śrīṃ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Svāhā (108). Now, Vittalakṣmī: Oṃ.
HŪṂ! Give me wealth from the hands of all! HŪṂ! To Vittalakṣmī, svāhā! (108) OṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ! To Śrī, the dweller in the lotus, svāhā! (108) OṂ ŚRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ AIṂ KLĪṂ SAUḤ! O Rājalakṣmī!
"Bhīmāya prayaccha svāhā" (108). Then [he saw] all of them holding full water-pots grasped by both hands;
some were mounted upon great elephants, with conch, discus, and lotus in their hands, while others...
In some places, she is the beloved Lakṣmī, her hands busily occupied with chowries;

elsewhere, she wields the goad and the noose. [The mantra is: *mūlānte vauṣaṭ*. Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the obstructive offering (*nirodhārgha*). Now, the portion concerning fortune (*bhāgya*):

The Great Goddess, seated upon a lotus with her pair of feet resting there, possessing four arms and three eyes, holding a noose, a goad, a heart, and a great skull-cup, protects [the world] by the power of fortune.
May she, who is mounted upon a bull, grant prosperity.
Having performed the invocation and other rites with the *agnipuṣpa* mantra from the *Haṇakṛtābhidhākāvatāra*:
*Śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śobhāvati bhāgyabhūte huṃ phaṭ svāhā* (108 times), [one should perform] the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) at the end of the root mantra.
O Goddess, by the mere remembrance of this *tarpaṇa* offering at the riverbank,

even a man who has committed every kind of evil deed, though born into the family of a slave, shall undoubtedly attain sovereignty. Now follows Bhagamālinī, [holding] the noose, the goad, the rosary, and the string.

Even though she holds a book and a sword in her hands, she constantly displays a wondrous power and valor; she possesses the three eyes of the Lord Śiva, and her beautiful left side is occupied by him.
One should offer the goddess Śrī Bhagamālinī into the fire with flowers, beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*).
*Hasaralarīṃ pūrṇagirigahvare bhagamālinyai svāpādukābhyāṃ namaḥ* (108). *Hasarala*.

*Rīṃ hṛpūrṇagirigahvareśira bhagamālinīśi khā ambākava pādunetre kebhyaḥ namaḥ.* [This is] the weapon-mantra (*astra*). At the end of the root-mantra: *pūrṇā*, *nirodha*, *argha*, and *tarpaṇa*. Now, [the worship of] the Goddess Tārā.
She who has serpents for ornaments, whose luster is like the moon and the conch, who possesses the radiance of the cool-rayed moon and the conch,

whose neck and bracelets are encircled by pearls and gems, who wears red garments, who holds the conch, lotus, sword, and mace, and who is attended by hosts of gods headed by Vaikuṇṭha— [I bow to her].
I worship the Blessed Lady Tārā, who is eternally praised, whose mind is intent on the protection of the three worlds, and who has the moon as her eye. Regarding the mantra of the Blessed Lady Tārā:
Akṣobhya is the ṛṣi, the Vṛhatī is the meter, and the deity is the glorious Ekajaṭā; *huṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
For the *homam* of Phaṭśa Strīṃ, perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites in the fire with:

*oṃ hrīṃ strīṃ krīṃ huṃ ugratāre sauḥ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ svāhā* (108 times). Perform the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with *trāṃ trīm* and so forth, and offer the final oblation (*pūrṇā*). [Visualize her] standing upon the chest of a supine corpse.

She has four arms and three eyes, resounds with a terrible, loud laugh, and her lotus-like face is fierce and formidable; she holds a sword, a blue lotus, a spear, and a skull-bowl; she is short of stature and dark-faced.

I bow to Ugratārā, whose tawny single-braided hair is bordered by fierce serpents and who is surrounded by formidable nagas; *mūlānto vaṣaṭ*, *nirodha* [with] the long *argha*; now, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for Bhuvaneśvarī, [who is like] the rising sun...
She has a face resembling the moon, full breasts, and stands upon a lotus;
she holds in her arms the goad, the noose, the book, and the gesture of victory,
and is ever praised with joy by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Indra, and the sages.

With prostrations, hymns, and other forms of praise, I worship here in the lotus of my heart the three-eyed Bhuvaneśvarī. Of this Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī mantra, Śakti is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), and Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī is the deity; Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja).
*Śrīṃ śa klīṃ kī*, [perform] the oblation (*homa*) into the fire; [perform] the invocation (*āvāhana*) with flowers and so forth.

*Oṃ hrīṃ bhuvaneśvaryai namaḥ* (108 times). *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ bhuvaneśvaryai namaḥ* (108 times). The six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) begins with *hrāṃ hrīṃ* and so forth; [this concludes] the full oblation (*pūrṇā*).

I worship Bhuvaneśī, who possesses the splendor of the rising sun, who wears the moon as a crown, whose breasts are lofty, who is endowed with three eyes, whose face is smiling, and who holds in her hands the gestures of granting boons (*vara*), the goad, the noose, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*). At the end of the root mantra, *oṣaṭ* is added for the *nirodha-arghya*.
Then Bhadrakālī appeared, her lotus-face serene,
her eyes misty with playful glances, clad in blue garments,
adorned with the jingling of pearl-bells, and possessing lips as crimson as young shoots.
Wearing a black silk bodice and holding a divine staff adorned with various jewels,
she was radiant with the luster of diverse gems and flowers, resembling a row of autumn clouds, and girt with a golden waistband.

Having meditated upon the deity Bhadrakālī with a focused mind— she who wears tinkling bells, who is beautiful with a creeper-like pearl braid, who resembles the rising sun, and whose eyes are sunken and emaciated from hunger— one should [worship her].
