With my face turned down and my hair disheveled, not yet satiated, I said to her: "I shall make this entire world a single morsel for my mouth.
She held [the world] with both hands, which resembled the blazing crests of fire.

O Bhadrakālī, may you, who burn with fierce nooses and teeth resembling Jāmbūnada gold, protect me from fear! To this Śrī Bhadrakālī—Brahmā is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, the deity is Śrī Bhadrakālī, and *huṃ* is the seed-syllable. *Śa*.
Svāhā! O Agni, in the fire-offering, [offer] flowers. For the invocation and other rites:
*Kṛṃ* (3) *Huṃ* (2) *Hrīṃ* (2). We know Bhairavī Bhadrakālī; we meditate upon Kālī, the wife of Bhairava.
*Bhai* *Hrīṃ* (2) *Huṃ* (2) *Kṛṃ* (3) *Svāhā*. May she protect us. *Tanno Bhai*.
*Drakālī pracodayāt*. (3) *Krīṃ* (3) *Huṃ* (2) *Hrīṃ* (2) *Bhaiṃ Bhadrakāli Bhaiṃ Hrīṃ* (2) *Huṃ* (2) *Krīṃ* (3) *Svāhā* (108).
*Krīṃ* (3) *Hṛ* *Hrīṃ* (2) *Hūṃ* (2) *Śira* *Bhai Bhadrakāli Śikhā* *Hrīṃ* (2) *Bhai Kavaca Huṃ* (2).

For the eyes: Hrīṃ (three times). For the weapon: Pūrṇā. [I worship] Śyāmā, whose face is dark as a dark cloud, whose form is tremulous, whose eyes are like hollows, who is auspicious, who possesses a form exceeding twenty years of age, who dances with the intoxication of wine, and who is clad in red garments.

I worship Bhagavatī Bhadrakālī, who holds Brahmā, Muṇḍa, Śiva, and Viṣṇu in her hands, who is radiant, who stands upon a corpse, and who resides in the lotus of the heart— at the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ*. This is the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the obstructive offering (*nirodhārgha*).

Then, having recited the mantra "O Kālikā of the South, who holds aloft a sword in the left hand and a severed head upon the palm of a lotus, and below that, in the right hand, the gestures of fearlessness and boon, you who take away the three worlds," one should worship Dakṣiṇakālī.
Meditating upon this, which possesses the color of collyrium and the power of the syllable *Tat*,
eight Siddhis, with smiling faces, reside in the hands of those who have attained [this state] through the worship of Aṣṭamukha;
they resemble a mass of crushed collyrium.
Seated upon Śiva, with streams of blood flowing from her throat,
she whose lotus-face is fierce, whose pair of breasts are full and elevated,
whose hips are thick and high, who has disheveled hair, and who delights in being naked as the directions themselves.
She is entered by Mahākāla and Śivā, augmented by the bliss of Smara, and resplendent with yoginīs whose faces and eyes are deep red;
she has two corpses as her crest-ornaments and is radiant with a tilaka of vermilion. Paṃ...
She is adorned with a jeweled crest-ornament fashioned from human skulls,
enriched with various kinds of precious gems, and decorated with diverse ornaments;
she is further embellished with bracelets made of human bones and a conch-shell on her right arm.
In some places, she is mounted upon the chest of a corpse, licking Śiva;
in others, she repeatedly laughs loudly while devouring the flesh of a corpse.
She holds a sword and a severed head in her left [hands], and bestows fearlessness and boons with her right [hands]. May she protect us!
She was exceedingly fierce, with a terrible roar and most fearsome;
she was surrounded by jackals of horrific cries, yet she was the destroyer of fear. She uttered a terrifying sound, crying out to her own devotees, "Do not fear! Do not fear!"
To her who speaks, "What host, what host shall I give?",
belongs this *uṣṇik* meter in the *anuṣṭubh* style for the venerable Dakṣiṇakālikā:
*Śrīdakṣiṇakālikāde hrīṃ vī huṃ śa krīṃ kī*.
OṂ HOMEVI AGNAU PUṢPAM ĀVĀHANĀDI KRĪ (3) HUṂ (2) HRĪṂ (2).
To the right: KĀLIKE KRĪṂ (3) HUṂ (2) HRĪṂ (2) SVĀHĀ (108). OṂ KĀLIKĀYAI VIŚMAŚĀNAVĀSINYAI DHĪ TANNO GHORAḤ.
Pra (3) Krīṃ Hrīṃ (3) Hrīṃ (2) [is] for the head; Hūṃ (2) [is] for the crest-lock; Dakṣiṇekālike Kavakrīṃ (3 3) Huṃ (2) Hrīṃ (2) [is] for the eyes; Svāhā [is] for the weapon.
O Pūrṇā, whose pair of lotus-feet are worshipped by the three worlds, I bow to that Kṛṣṇā.
I meditate on her who possesses a form resembling that of Śiva, who has three eyes, who carries a trident, sword,
and shield in her own arms, who is dark-complexioned, who sits upon the body of the Lord of Smara (Śiva), and whose seed-mantra is *mūla-ante auṣaṭ* with *nirodha*.

O Goddess of terrible form, O Great Fierce One, who causes the destruction of all enemies, grant boons to your devotees; O Goddess, protect me who have come to you for refuge! O Goddess worshipped by gods and asuras, served by siddhas and gandharvas!

O Goddess who removes the sin of dullness, protect me! (2) O Goddess who resembles the flickering tongue amidst the mass of matted hair, O Goddess who increases swift intelligence, protect me! (3) O Goddess who possesses both a gentle form and a fierce form of wrath!

Salutations to you in the form of creation; protect me! (4) O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, you destroy the dullness of the dull-witted; O Goddess, take away my delusion and protect me! (5) O Goddess, you whose nature consists of the sounds "Huṃ" and "Huṃ," the offering...

Obeisance to Māpripriyā; obeisance to Ugratārā—protect me always! (6) Grant me intelligence, grant me glory, and grant me poetic skill forever; O Goddess, take away my foolishness and protect me! (7) O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods beginning with Indra!
O Tārā, whose nature is compassion, O Saviouress, protect me!
(8) Paralyze the speech, mouth, and feet of all evil ones! (2) Pin the tongue! (2) Destroy the intellect! (2) Hlīṃ oṃ svāhā! (108)
Oṃ hlīṃ hṛdaya! O Vagalāmukhi, paralyze the head and the mouth of speech (2). Pin the tongue at the crest-lock (2). Destroy the power of the armor (2).
Hlīṃ oṃ svāhā! [This is] for the weapon; it is the full oblation that binds all various [obstacles].

I bow to Śivā, who is seated upon a lion-throne, whose hips are adorned with a girdle of jewels, who wears yellow garments, who bestows good fortune, whose eyes are like the rays of the sun, fire, and moon,
who resembles the celestial musician Gaṅgānandana, and who shines brilliantly with precious gems.
One should always worship that Goddess Vagalamukhi in the heart—
she who grants all desires and bestows devotion— with the mantra "mūla-ante vaṣaṭ" for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and "nirodha-arghaḥ" for the final offering.
Alternatively, one may worship Vajreshvari, whose eyes are like fire and the sun.

I worship Vajrayoginī, who holds a noose and a goad, who is auspicious, two-armed, and seated upon a lion; [one should offer flowers and other substances] into the fire with: *oṃ hrīṃ vajrayoginyai svāhā* (108 times), *śrīṃ hrīṃ*.
HŪṂ AIM VAJRAVAIROCANĪYE HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ (108). PŪRṆĀ MŪLĀNTAIVAUṢAṬ. This is the *tarpaṇa*. Now, here is the *pūrṇā*:
[I offer] the red one with variegated eyes and a fresh moon as her crest-ornament.

Beholding her who is devoted to bestowing intoxication, bowed by the weight of her breasts, dancing, adorned with the crescent moon, and possessing the luster of the rays of the rising sun— one should worship the Goddess Aṣṭā, the remover of the suffering of worldly existence.
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, and necklaces, her slender ankles glistening;
her lotus-feet bearing serpents as anklets; her hair thick with the radiance of the jewels in her crown; three-eyed, she drinks the sweet honey from my mouth.

I bow to the venerable Annapūrṇā. Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), the Virāṭ meter, the venerable goddess Annapūrṇā is the deity, *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*vīja*), *svāhā* is the exclamation (*śakti*), and *namaḥ* is the salutation (*kīlaka*). [This is for] the purpose of invoking the presence of food during the fire-oblation (*homa*).
The ritual procedure (*niyoga*) is as follows: [one should offer] flowers into the fire, perform the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth;
one should eat the food oneself, reciting "We know [thee], the self-existent (*svayaṃbhu*)," and the self-existent Creator himself should eat.
(3) *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ namo bhagavati māheśvari annapūrṇe*.
Oṃ svāhā (108). Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Great Goddess Annapūrṇā, svāhā (108). Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Great Goddess; grant me this desired food, O Annapūrṇā, svāhā.

Hā (108) Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Great Sovereignty who bestows food, svāhā! (108) Oṃ hṛ—obeisance to the head; Bhagavatī—obeisance to the crest-lock; Māheśvarī—obeisance to the armor; Annapūrṇā—obeisance to the eyes; Svāhā—obeisance to the weapon; Pūrṇā Mandā.

O Girijā, you who possess the crescent moon upon your crest, whose forehead is adorned with a flickering third eye, and who have eyes as large as a bull’s— grant alms for my hunger while I stand amidst the coral trees, yellow sandalwood, and *pārijāta* flowers, within the jeweled pavilion on the altar at the center of the moon.
*Tāpa* to me, *mūla*, *anteva*, *auṣaṭ*; *tarpaṇa*, *nirōdha*, *argha*.
Now, [I salute] the auspicious Goddess Sṛgālavadanā, who is ruddy, three-eyed, single-faced, and eight-armed, holding a sword and a trident.
I bow to the one who dwells in Śiva, who holds in her hands a bell, a goad, a skull-bowl with small bells, a trident, and a book.
[One should offer] a flower into the fire, and perform the invocation, the water for the feet, and so forth, with the mantra "Tatpuruṣāya."

Salutation to the Goddess who is of auspicious form; let that be for us. (3) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the Blessed Śivā, svāhā. (108 times). At the end of the root mantra, perform the *tarpaṇa* (libation) and the *nirodhārgha* (oblation of restraint). Now, Cāmuṇḍā... kha.
She who holds in her hands a discus, mace, arrow, bow, iron club, trident, *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon,
a severed head, and a conch; she who has three eyes and is adorned with ornaments on all her limbs— her he praised while Hari was asleep.
I worship Mahākālī, who has the luster of a blue sapphire, who slew the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and who holds in her ten hands a rosary,
an axe, a mallet, arrows, a thunderbolt, a lotus, a bow, and a sword.
I worship her who has the luster of coral, who crushes the buffalo-demon with her hands as she holds a skull-bowl, a staff, a spear, a sword, a shield,
a lotus, a vessel of wine, a trident, a noose,
and the Sudarśana discus.
I bow to Mahālakṣmī, who rests upon a lotus, holding in her lotus-like hands a bell, trident, plow, conch, mace, discus, bow, and arrow,
resembling the cool-rayed moon shining at the edge of a dark cloud.
I worship here Sarasvatī, who is preceded by Mahā, who is the light arising from the body of Gaurī, who is the support of the three worlds,
and who destroys the Daityas and others— [this being] of this glorious nine-syllable mantra.
The sages are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; the meters are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, and Anuṣṭubh;
the deities are Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī; and [the forms] are Nandā, Śākaṃbharī, Kālarātri, and Bhīmā.
The suffixes are *ktayaḥ*; the seed-syllables (*bījāni*) are Raktadantikā, Durgā, and Bhrāmari;
the principles (*tattvāni*) are Fire, Wind, and Sun; their application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
[One offers] a flower into the fire for the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth: *oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍā*.

With *yaiviśve* (108), *aiṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *klīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *cāmuṇḍāyai kavacāya huṃ*, *ḍākinī netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, and *vicce astrāya phaṭ*, [one performs] the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) at the end of the root mantra with *vauṣaṭ*.
Then follows the libation for restraint (*nirodhārgha*), and thereafter all sixty-four Yoginīs.
Furthermore, there were those fond of blood, meat, and milk;
those fond of strife, clamor, dance, and song; those who were young, mature, or old;
those with the color of bees or fire, or the color of the moon; and those with fierce eyes.
With matted hair, bared teeth, and disheveled locks; with terrifying tongues and sounds that are extremely subtle, sweet, harsh, or loud;
steady yet flickering, peaceful yet fierce; they manifest through the power of both peaceful and wrathful stratagems.
The Viṣṇus and others have four arms and are adorned with divine garments and ornaments, as well as weapons such as the goad, water-pot, chisel, trident, sword, conch, discus, mace, spear, bow,
and thunderbolt. They are headed by Viṣṇubha and the rest.

The twenty-seven yogas; the twenty-eight lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī; the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries; the nine planets beginning with the Sun; Nṛsiṃha, Vīra, Kṣetrapāla, Maṇibhadra, Sahillā, and so forth.
One should meditate on the circle of the attendants (*parivāra*). [Offer] flowers, invocation (*āvāhana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth. *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hsauḥ namaḥ* (108 times).
To Brahmāṇī (1), Kaumārī (2), Vārāhī (3), Śāṅkarī (4), Indrāṇī...
To Ṇyai (5), Kaṅkālyai (6), Karālyai (7), Kālyai (8), Mahākālyai (9), Cāmuṇḍāyai (10), Jvālāmukhyai (11), Kāmākhyāyai (12), Kapālinyai (13),
Bhadrakālyai (14), Durgāyai (15), and Ambikāyai.
To Lalitā (16), to Gaurī (17), to Sumaṅgalā (18), to Rohiṇī (19), to Kapilā (20), to Kulakarā (21),
to Kuṇḍalinī (22), to Tripurā (23), to Kurukullā (24), to Bhairavī (25).

To Vyai (26), Bhadrāyai (27), Candrāvalyai (28), Nārasiṃhāyai (29), Nirañjanāyai (30), Hemakāntyai (31), Pretāsanāyai (32), Īśānyai (33), Vaiśvānaryai (34), Vaiṣṇavyai (35), Vinā... [the remainder of the text is not provided].

To Yakṣī (36), to Yamaghaṇṭā (37), to Harisiddhi (38), to Sarasvatī (39), to Totilā (40), to Vanditā (41), to Śaṅkhinī (42), to Padminī (43), to Citriṇī (44), and to Vāruṇī (45). Nā... [text truncated]
To Rāyaṇī (46), to Vanadevī (47), to Yamabhaginī (48), to Sūryaputrī (49), to Śītalā (50), to Kṛṣṇā (51), to Raktākṣī (52),
to Kālarātri (53), to Ākāśī (54), to Śreṣṭinī (55), to Ja...
To Yāyī (56), Vijayā (57), Dhūmāvatī (58), Vāgīśvarī (59), Kātyāyanī (60), Vajreśvarī (61), Mahāvidyā (62), Agnihotrī (63), Īśvarī (64), and Pūrṇāmūlā.
With *ante vauṣaṭ*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is declared to be sixty-fourfold.
When the Yoginīs of Kāmarūpa have been worshipped and honored in return, they shall always be bestowers of boons. Now follows the *nirodhārgha* (the offering for cessation) of Bhairava.

Chanting this mantra known as Vāgbhava— which contains the syllable *vī*, the letter *ka* from the word *kānta* and so forth, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and the letter situated in the ocean (*jaladhi*) preceded by the teeth (*danta*)—
the best of men on earth [attains] the essence of the nectar of speech.
One attains success by reciting this mantra known as "Kāma," which consists of the word *kāntā* (the beloved) joined with the fifth letter of the preceding *kula* (the consonant group),

followed by the two eyes (*netra*), the end of the staff (*daṇḍa*), and the letter *ta*; this mantra is said to directly agitate the world like a rutting elephant, and when joined with that [mantra], it is indeed powerful.
The Kula known as Daṇḍisakalasaṃkṣobhaṇa belongs to this Siddha;
its eight qualities are the attainment of moving through the sky and constant success through recitation (*japa*).
[The mantra is] *agni-puṣpa-āvāhana-ādi*, *ha-sa-ra-iṃ-ha-sa-kala-rīṃ-ha*.

Salutation to Sarauḥ Mahābhairavī (108). At the end of the root mantra, *pūrṇā* and *vauṣaṭ* are used for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). If the Bhairavī [mantra] is preceded by the Ākulā [mantras] according to the teachers, or if it is preceded by the Kula [mantras], that very [mantra] bestows swift results upon the earth.
This is called "Vidyā," which should be kept secret from the common folk; it is worth its weight in gold.
Now, regarding the Nine Durgās: first among them is Śailaputrī, whose luster resembles the rising sun, and who wears a crown adorned with a crescent moon.
I meditate upon the daughter of the mountain (Śailaputrī), who has three arms, wears red garments, possesses eyes like fire, the sun, and the moon, and bestows boons—
this [mantra] of Śrī Śailaputrī, [accompanied by] Mahākāla and Bhairava.
The Triṣṭubh meter; Śrī.

Hrīṃ vī sauḥ śa, salutation; this is the binding of the directions (digbandhaḥ). Oṃ kī home, this is the application (viniyogaḥ). [Offer] a flower into the fire. [Recite] "To Kāmadhātrī... [and] "To Śailaputrī... [and] "May that Śailapracoda... [be for us].

Oṃ hrīṃ sauḥ śailaputri śrīṃ svāhā (108). Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ sauḥ sauḥ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śailaputryai namaḥ (108). The six-limbed [mantra] beginning with Oṃ hrām and so forth; at the end of the root mantra, *vauṣaṭ* for the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering of the vessel of restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Or else, one should worship in the heart that Brahmācāriṇī, who holds the lotus, sword, boon-granting gesture, and protection gesture as her weapons;
who has a moon-like face and a crescent moon as her crest; who is auspicious, wears reddish ornaments, and possesses three eyes. Of this [mantra]:
To the venerable Brahmācāriṇī, the Bhairava meter is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is the venerable Brahmācāriṇī.
Śrīṃ vī hrīṃ śa klīṃ kīṃ. For the fire-oblation (homa), flowers [are offered] into the fire. Invocation and other rites: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ saḥ brahma.
*Cāriṇī aiṃ phaṭ svāhā* (108). *Pūrṇā*, at the end of the root mantra: *vauṣaṭ*.

The libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering for cessation (*nirodhārgha*). Then [one should meditate on] Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, whose faces are as numerous as ten million moons, who has three eyes, and whose face is smiling.
I meditate upon the heart of Śrī Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, who holds in her six hands a conch, a lotus, a noose, and a jar of nectar.
Of this [mantra] of Śrī Caṇḍaghaṇṭā-Bhairava, the seer is Anuṣṭubh, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Śrī Caṇḍaghaṇṭā. The seed-syllables are Klīṃ, Vī, Sauḥ, Śa, and Śrīṃ.
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the *kīhoma*. For the fire, the flowers, and the invocation (*āvāhana*), etc., [the mantra is]:
*oṃ klīṃ sauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ sauḥ caṇḍaghaṇṭāyai namaḥ* (108 times). The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) begin with *klāṃ*, etc. At the end of the root mantra, [utter] *vauṣaṭ* for the full oblation (*pūrṇā*).

*Tarpaṇa* (libation) and *nirodhārgha* (the offering for restraint). Now, for the *Kūṣmāṇḍa*: there is no introductory praise (*adhyāna*) for this. For this *Śrī-Kūṣmāṇḍī*, the seer is Brahmā, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Śrī-Kūṣmāṇḍī. The seed-syllables are *krīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, and *oṃ*. [This is] for the *homa* (fire sacrifice).

The application (*viniyoga*) is as follows: the offering of flowers, the invocation, the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth; *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ krīṃ kuṣmāṇḍyai namaḥ* (108 times); the six limbs beginning with *krāṃ*;
the full oblation at the end of the root mantra with *auṣaṭ*; the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the obstructing water-offering (*nirodhārgha*).
One should worship the Mother of Skanda, whose face shines with the luster of ten million moons,
who has three eyes, is clad in saffron-colored garments, is seated upon a lion-throne accompanied by elephant-faced beings and others, and is joined by Skanda.

The Vāṇī-mantra of Śrī Skandamātā: Śrī Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), and the deity is Śrī Skandamātā. Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (vīja), Hauḥ is the power (śakti), and Kī is the application (kīlaka).
Its application is in the fire with flowers.
The invocation and subsequent rites: Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hauḥ, [to] Skandamātṛ:
haḥ haḥ phaṭ svāhā. (108 times; the six limbs beginning with *hrām*, etc.; the full oblation at the end of the root mantra: auṣaṭ.)

The libation is the offering for the restraint [of obstacles]. Now, one should worship the auspicious Kātyāyanī, who has a thousand radiant limbs, three eyes, and is resplendent in red garments; she is four-armed, seated upon a corpse, and holds a *nīvi* (lower garment).
Of this [mantra], the Śrī-kā[tyāyanī]...
For the *tyāyanī* [rite], the meter is *anuṣṭubh*; for the worship of Śrī Kātyāyanī, the seed-syllable is *hrīṃ*, the *vīja* is *oṃ*, and the *kīlaka* is *svāhā*.
In the fire during the *homa*, flowers are offered; for the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, recite: *oṃ hrīṃ kātyāyanyai namaḥ* one hundred and eight times.
With *hrām* and so forth for the six limbs, the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ends with *vauṣaṭ* at the root mantra;

this is the libation (*tarpaṇa*), followed by the offering of the vessel of restraint (*nirodhārgha*). Now, [one should meditate on] Kālarātri, who has the luster of a fresh cloud, whose eyes are like the moon and fire, and who holds a sword, a discus, a mace, and a lotus in her hands, bestowing peace.
I meditate in my mind upon Śrī Kālarātrī, who is clad in yellow garments and radiant with a crown.
For this [hymn] to Śrī Kālarātrī, the meter is Anuṣṭubh and the deity is Śrī Kālarātrī. The seed-syllables are *Śrīṃ*, *Vīṃ*, *Hrīṃ*, *Śa*, and *Oṃ*.
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the *kīhoma*. [The procedure begins with] the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth into the fire.

*Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ kālarātri klīṃ aiṃ saḥ phaṭ svāhā* (108 times). The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) begins with *śrāṃ hāṃ* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, the *pūrṇāhuti* is offered.

Six libations, the pouring out of water, and the offering of *argha*; now, I worship Mahāgaurī, who possesses a luster equal to the rising sun, who has a crown of radiant rays, who is auspicious, four-armed, and three-eyed. Of this [mantra]... Śrī...

For the worship of Śrī Mahāgaurī, accompanied by Karālabhairava, the meter is Anuṣṭubh. Oṃ oṃ vī oṃ sauḥ is the Śakti. Oṃ oṃ kīṃ is for the application in the fire sacrifice (homa). [One should offer] flowers into the fire, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).

*Śrīṃ aiṃ aiṃ sauḥ gīṃ gūṃ mahāgaurīyai namaḥ* (108 times). The six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ritual begins with *gāṃ* and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, *pūrṇā* is followed by *mūla-ante vaṣaṭ*. Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the *nirvāṇa-dhārā*, and the *argha* offering. Now, Devadūtī, who is as radiant as the orb of the moon...

I worship the illustrious Devadūtī, who has two arms, three eyes, and has gone to the realm of the pretas; she possesses eyes like blue lotuses, a body-staff of molten gold, and is clad in white garments.
This is the Śrī-Devadūtī-mahābhairava-vṛtti.

The meter is *anuṣṭubh*, the deity is Śrī, the seed-syllables are *klīṃ* and *sauḥ*, and the application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire for the oblation (*homa*). [The mantra for] the offering of flowers and the invocation (*āvāhana*) etc. is: *oṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ devadūti śrīṃ phaṭ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svā*.

Hā (108) Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, etc., [is] the six-limbed [mantra]; the full [offering] at the end of the root [mantra], the six libations, and the *nirodhārgha* [offering]. By this mantra-homa, may the Blessed Navadurgā, together with her retinue, be pleased; may she be pleased. Now...

[One should meditate on] Gaṅgā, who holds a lotus with its stalk in her hand, who bears a lotus in both hands, who has a hand in the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*), who is pure white, and who rides upon a crocodile; [the deity is] Śrī Gaṅgā, for whom Maheśvara is the Ṛṣi and Gāyatrī is the metre, in the *Śrī Gaṅgādevī-homa*.
The ritual application (*niyoga*):
[the offering of] flowers into the fire, the invocation (*āvāhana*), and so forth; *oṃ namaḥ śivāya enārāyaṇyai daśahārāyai svāhā* (108); [and the six limbs beginning with] *gām*, etc.
*Gaḥ*, *pūrṇā*, *mūla*, *ante*, *vauṣaṭ*; this is the libation for the rite of cessation (*nirodhārgha*).
Then, [one should visualize] the goddess Vitastā, holding a rosary, a lotus, a mirror, and a water-pot (*kalaśa*) in her hands, seated upon a broad lotus throne.

I take refuge in Agni; obeisance to the Blessed One, the source of all desires, who flows from the Puṣpa [river] and the Vitastā. (108) [The ritual consists of] the six limbs beginning with *sāmi*, the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ending with the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the respectful offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*). Now, the ten-fold...
There, at the beginning, [one should meditate on] the Lord who is the fire for the skull-heap, resembling ten thousand rising suns,
radiant with the rays of the jewels in his crown, embraced by the goddess Padmāśanikaromā, beautiful with a thousand eyes, and shimmering with a priceless necklace.
One should meditate upon that god whose chest is covered with jewels and whose feet are saluted by the world-protectors; [one should worship] Indra, the lord of the east. His mantra is:
*oṃ śrīṃ indrāya sadaśivāya jagatīchanda indro devaḥ hrīṃ vī śrīṃ śa klīṃ kīṃ hūṃ*.
The application of the mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ*—this is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
*Āgneye puṣpam* (Flower in the southeast). Invocation and so forth: To the King of Gods, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand, may Śakra further that for us. *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ indrā*.

*Obeisance to Yavajrahastā* (108). The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with *hrāṃ śrāṃ ktāṃ* and so forth; the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ending with the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*; the libation (*tarpaṇa*); the offering for the cessation (*nirodhārgha*). Then, for the fire:
the desired power (*śakti*), holding a book and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, with the long [syllables].
I meditate upon him who holds a rosary and performs recitation, who is adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, possessing three eyes, crowned with matted locks like a blazing fire,
and who is the Śrī-Vaiśvānara mantra, Sadāśiva, and the Jagatī meter. Śrī.
Vaiśvānara-oṃ-raṃ-vī-troṃ-śa-hrīṃ-kī; [this is] for the oblation in the fire.
[The mantra for] the flower is: Āvāhanādi rudra-hastāya vi-śakti-hastāya dhī; tan no vahniḥ pra (3); oṃ hrīṃ trauṃ raṃ vaiśvānara ja.

Grant the accomplishment that shines with the splendor of the *ṭābha* [mantra], svāhā (108). The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) begin with *drāṃ drīṃ*, etc. The full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ends with the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*. The libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*). Now, the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of Dharmarāja.

I worship that Lord Dharmarāja in my heart, who is seated upon a lotus throne, who holds a staff, the gesture of fearlessness, a lotus, and the boon-granting mudrā with his four arms, and who is blazing with the brilliance of the sun and fire. [Recite] "asya śrīdharmarāja... [etc. for this Śrī Dharmarāja.
Śrī Kālāgnibhairava; the meter is Triṣṭubh; the deity is Dharmarāja.
Oṃ aiṃ vī juṃ śa hrāṃ kīṃ! [This is] for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa). [The mantra for] invoking [the deity] with flowers into the fire:
"To Vaivasvata, who holds a staff in his hand, we offer our thought—that is Yama."
Pra (3) Oṃ Hrāṃ Jūṃ Aiṃ Saḥ, obeisance to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand.
(108) The six limbs [are assigned] with Hrāṃ and so forth; at the end of the root mantra, "Vauṣaṭ" [is used for] the full oblation, and "Tarpaṇa" [for] the offering of restraint.
Now, for Nirṛti: the supreme hero, holding a spear...

I constantly meditate upon Nirṛti within the lotus of my heart— he who holds a goad and a lotus in his hands, who resembles an autumnal cloud, wears red garments, and has blood-red eyes; for this [mantra] of Śrī-Nirṛti, Brahmā is the seer and Gāyatrī is the meter.

Ṭachaṃ. Obeisance to the venerable Nirṛti. Hrāṃ vī hraiṃ śa hraḥ kī. For the homa, [there is] the invocation of Puṣpa and so forth into the fire. To the night-walker (niśācara), who holds a sword in hand, [I offer] dhī;
may Nirṛti grant us that. (3) Oṃ śrīṃ phrāṃ nirṛ.
Salutation to her who holds a sword in her hand (108). The six limbs [are performed] with "hrām" and so forth.
The full oblation (*pūrṇā*) ends with the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*. The libation (*tarpaṇa*) is the offering for the restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Now, for Varuṇa: [he is] like the wind of universal destruction (*saṃvarta-vāyu*), moving with the speed of a thousand suns, blazing.

I worship Varuṇa, the primordial god praised by the sole creator Brahmā, who holds the goad, the noose, and the gestures of fearlessness and boon-giving with his own arms, who has three eyes, and who is the great crocodile-bannered one worshipped by crocodiles, fish, and aquatic creatures. [The sage of this Śrī Varuṇa-mantra is Brahmā; the meter is Anuṣṭubh.]

Ṣṭupcha Varuṇa, O God! Śūṃ, Viśraiśa, Śraḥkī, in this homa, [perform] the invocation of Puṣpa and so forth into the fire. To the one with pure hands, to the one with the noose in hand, [recite] "That of us, O Varuṇa... (3) Śrīṃ Śūṃ Juṃ Saḥ Varu.

Salutation to the one who holds the noose in his hand (Nāyapāśahasta), [ending with] *namaḥ* (108). The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with *śrāṃ*, the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ending with the root mantra and *vauṣaṭ*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the water-offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*).
Or else, [one should meditate on the deity] of pure form, possessing the luster of the rising sun, [red as] the *japā* flower.

I worship the primordial Vāyu, the life-force of all worlds, who holds a golden jar in his hand, is marked by the weapon of a pair of lotuses, is adorned with white garments and other ornaments, and resides in the heart of all the lords of the gods.
Of this Śrī-Vāyu...

Oma Bhagavan Pulastya Triṣṭap Śrī Vāyude Klīṃ Vī Huṃ Śa Svāhā-kī! Obeisance to the one who is engaged in the fire-sacrifice (homa), who has released all vital breaths through the invocation of flowers and other offerings, whose hand is the source of creation, and who is the wisdom of that [Lord]— to us, [grant] that.

*Yuḥ pra oṃ yaṃ klīṃ huṃ vāyave dhvajahastāya namaḥ* (108). Thus, with *ktāṃ* and so forth, [one performs] the six-limbed worship (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ending with the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the obstructive offering (*nirodhārgha*). Now, for Kuvera: [the form] has the luster of a red lotus and the sun...

I meditate upon the god Kubera in my heart— whose form is that of a *koṭi*, who holds in his lotus-hands a rosary of beads marked by power (*śakti*), who sits upon the throne of Bhadrāsana, whose face is smiling, and who possesses three eyes. This is the *mahādevī* hymn of the illustrious Kubera, composed in the *vṛhatī* meter, [dedicated to] Śrī.
Kuvera, the lord of the Kṣas, is [represented by] *oṃ*, *de*, *klīṃ*, *vī*, *m*, *kluṃ*, *śa*, *hsauḥ*, *kī*, *ho*.
The application (* viniyoga*) is for the offering of flowers and other oblations into the fire. [The mantra is:
"To Yakṣeśvara, who holds a mace in his hand, we meditate; may Kuvera impel us. (3) *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ mkluṃ*.
Hsauḥ, obeisance to Kuvera, who holds a mace in his hand (108). [The six limbs] beginning with "ktām" and so forth; the full oblation at the end of the root mantra with "vauṣaṭ."
The libation is the offering for the rite of restraint; now, one should meditate upon Śiva, the Lord, who holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff,
who has three eyes, whose limbs are radiant with ashes, who wears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
who bears the Gaṅgā, and whose matted locks are bound together.
The Lord is the recipient of the offering; the rite begins with the invocation of the flowers and so forth.
Its Śrī is Īśāna; the Seer is Brahmā; the metre is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is Śrī Mahārudra;
the seed-syllable is Gaṃ; Haḥ Śa Oṃ Kī is the application for the Homa; [the presiding deity is] Sarveśvara.
If Rudra, with trident in hand, is intent upon that [offense], may he protect us. (3) Oṃ Gaṃ Hauṃ, salutation to Śiva.
(108) The six-limbed [nyāsa] beginning with "Gāṃ," the full oblation at the end of the root mantra with "Vauṣaṭ," the libation, and the *nirodhārghya*—then Brahmā.

Having meditated upon Brahmā, the four-faced one, who is said to have four arms, who wears a black antelope skin as an upper garment, who is seated upon a lotus throne, and who likewise holds a water-pot, a staff, a rosary of beads, and a lotus— in the petal.

The destroyer of all sins through proper placement; for this Śrī Brahmā mantra, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Śrī Brahmā, the seed-syllable is Hrāṃ, the power-syllable is Vīṃ, the weapon-syllable is Huṃ, the *śakti* is Śa, and the *kīlaka* is Oṃ. It is employed in the fire sacrifice with flowers.

To the one whose vehicle is the elephant and so forth, who is born from the lotus, whose mouth is the Veda—to that Brahmā, let there be success for us. Oṃ hrāṃ hsauḥ, grant me the supreme accomplishment of the Four-faced One!

Svāhā! (108 times). The six limbs begin with *hrām*, etc.; [this is] the full [offering]. The root [mantra]: *(Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a ritual manual (*paddhati*) for the worship of Brahmā. The final portion "pūrṇā mū" indicates the completion of the full oblation and the recitation of the root mantra.)*
*Lāṃ te vauṣaṭ*: [this is] the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the water-offering for the restraint (*nirodhārgha*). Now, regarding Ananta:
from the feet to the knees he is like excellent gold; from the region of the navel downwards to the region of the neck, he has the luster of a pearl;
and from the region of the neck upwards, he is like the young sun.
I bow to that primordial Varāha, whose forehead is blue from the peak of Mount Bhaṅga, who holds in his hands a chariot,
a discus, a terrible sword, a shield, a mace, a spear, and the gestures of generosity and fearlessness,
and whose tusk shines upon the earth at his feet.

To the venerable Nārāyaṇa, the meter is Triṣṭubh; for the venerable Nārāyaṇa, the seed-syllable is Śrīṃ, the power-syllable is Hrīṃ, and the Praṇava is Oṃ. This is applied to the fire during the oblation (homa).
After the invocation of the deity with flowers and other rites, [the mantra is]: "To Vāsudeva, to Nārāyaṇa, [I offer] dhī..."
To me, Viṣṇu: *oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ hīṃ śrīṃ nārāyaṇāya namaḥ* (108 times).

With the six limbs beginning with *śrāṃ hrāṃ*, etc., [one performs] the full [offering], at the end of the root mantra, the six libations (*tarpaṇa*), and the obstructing water-offering (*nirodhārgha*). By this mantra-homa, ten [times].
May the world-protectors be pleased; may they be satisfied.

Then follow the mantras for the nine planets (navagraha), written previously at the conclusion of the oblation of barley and sesame seeds (yavatilahoma). Now follows the oblation for the eight Bhairavas (aṣṭabhairavahoma).
I bow to the Lord of the Gama-vara-bhairava, who has four arms and three eyes,
holding a skull-cup, a sword, an axe, and a spear in his hands;
whose limbs are adorned with serpents, decorated with ashes, bones, and snake-jewels, and who is seated upon a corpse.

One should meditate upon the Lord Bhairavanāyaka, who is endowed [with all attributes]. Of this *Śrī-aṣṭabhairava-mantra*, the seer is Śrī-Sadāśiva, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Aṣṭabhairava.
The seed-syllable is *Hrāṃ*, the power is *Oṃ Śrīṃ Krīṃ*. It is employed in the fire during the *homa* sacrifice.
[Perform] the invocation with flowers and so forth: *hrīṃ* (3) *devadattaṃ hrīṃ* (3) *svāhā* (108).

[Perform] the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with *hrāṃ*, the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), at the end of the root mantra *auṣaṭ*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the cessation, and the water-offering (*argha*). Now, for Gaṇapati: the citron and the mace...
He should be meditated upon as holding in his lotus-like hands a bow, a trident, a discus, a lotus, a noose,
a blue lotus, a stalk of rice, a sword, a horn, a jewel, and a jar; he is embraced by his beloved, whose hand likewise holds a lotus.
Obeisance to Śrī Mahāgaṇapati, the ornament of the world, who effects the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the universe, who removes obstacles, and who bestows distinguished goals;
[the meter] of this [hymn] is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Śrī Mahāgaṇapati.

Tirde gaṃ vī hrīṃśa kuru (2) kī homevini. In the fire, [perform] the invocation of the flowers and so forth with "Gaṃ tatpuruṣāya vi vaktra tuṇḍāya dhī tanno dantī pra" (3). Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇa.
O Giver of Boons, bring all people under my control; svāhā!
(108) Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glaum gīṃ! O Beloved of Gaṇapati, make the hearts of all people subject to my own self; svāhā! (108)

The six-limbed [mantra] beginning with *gām* is the full offering (*pūrṇā*); at the end of the root mantra is *vauṣaṭ*, followed by the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering for restraint (*nirodhārgha*). Now, the nature of Anandeśvara is his own essential form, situated on his own path, self-perceived, possessing his own splendor, independent, and established in his own state.
I bow to that Bhairava who has ascended, who is as radiant as ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons, the god with eighteen arms,
five faces, and three eyes, stationed in the midst of the ocean of nectar.
Seated upon a lotus of Brahmā, mounted on a bull, blue-throated,
adorned with all ornaments, resembling a heap of vermilion, possessing a luster like a ruby, and appearing like jasmine or cinnabar,
[as bright as] the pomegranate...
The god who resembles Soma, who bears a skull and the staff of Khaṇḍāṅga, who resounds with bells and hand-drums (ḍamaru), who holds a noose and a goad, whose hands carry a mace and a pestle,
and who likewise holds a sword, a shield, a mallet, a trident, and a spear.
The god who wields a jewel-tipped spear, adorned with severed heads and skulls,
the bestower of boons and the destroyer of all diseases; the Great God mounted upon Rudra, adorned with every ornament, [of] red...
That indeed is proclaimed as the meditation upon the God of Gods:
the Goddess Surā is in His lap, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons,
white as the moon and Makaranda, five-faced, and three-eyed.
Possessing eighteen arms, with all weapons raised in her hands,
the large-eyed goddess, laughing, stood facing the God of gods;
or else [she faced] the Lord of the God of gods, the omnipresent Ardhanārīśvara, who was red...
One should meditate upon that Ānandabhairava, together with his consort, who is saluted by Brahmā and Acyuta,
and who is the sole cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Of this Śrī Ānandeśvarabhairava,
[the mantra is] Makālāgnirudrabhairava...

The deity is Ānandeśvarabhairava; the seed-syllables are Śrīṃ, Vī, Hrīṃ, Śa, Klīṃ, Kī; the application is in the fire sacrifice (homa). [The procedure begins with] the invocation of flowers into the fire and so forth: Oṃ juṃ saḥ ha sa kṣa ma la va ra ya rthaṃ saḥ juṃ.

Oṃ ānandeśvarabhairavāya vauṣaṭ. (108) By repeating this twelve-syllable mantra twice, the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is performed; the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ends with *vauṣaṭ* at the conclusion of the root mantra. This is the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering for the cessation (*nirodhārgha*). Alternatively, there is the hand-offering (*karakali*) to Vaṭukabhairava.

Victorious is Vaṭukanātha, skull-bearer and wearer of earrings, staff-in-hand, possessing the hue of dense darkness, with a serpent for his sacred thread, and expert in destroying obstacles during the service of sacrificial rites.
This Śrī Vaṭuka Bhairava is the bestower of success upon practitioners; its source is the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, its meter is Anuṣṭubh,
its deity is Śrī Vaṭuka Bhairava, its seed-syllable is Hrīṃ, and its power is "Vaṭukāya" (Oṃ Kī).

In the domestic fire (*homevini*), perform the invocation of flowers (*puṣpāvāhana*) and so forth with: *Oṃ hrīṃ vaṭukāya āpaduddhāraṇāya kuru* (twice), *vaṭukāya hrīṃ* (one hundred and eight times). Perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with *hrāṃ vām* and so forth. [The mudrās are] the full [mudrā], the noose (*pāśa*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the *ḍamaru*.

Having meditated upon Vaṭuka, who carries a skull-staff marked with the letter *ka*, who is white, single-faced, and beautifully adorned, who is dancing, has the face of a bear, three eyes, and a mass of matted hair bound with crescent moon-crests,
and who is established on the northern pedestal— one should worship him at the end of the root mantra with *auṣaṭ*.

The libation (*tarpaṇa*) is the offering for cessation (*nirodhārgha*). Alternatively, [one should visualize] Tālabhairava, who has flaming hair, three eyes, and is as terrifying as a lord of serpents;
he wears a garland of severed heads, holds a goddess, a sword, a skull-cup, and a *ḍamaru* drum, and is deep blue-black in color.
I bow to the Lord who holds a trident, who is skilled in playing the lute placed against his chest,
who plays it with both arms,
who beats the rhythm like the rising sun, and who is absorbed in the dance.
Now begins the *Śrīvetālabhairavamantroddhāra*: for this *Śrīvetālabhairava-mantra*,

Rudra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śrīvetālabhairava is the deity (*devatā*), Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (*vīja*), Śrīṃ is the power (*śakti*), Oṃ is the crest-syllable (*kīlaka*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
O Agni, whose vehicle is Puṣpa; for that one who has the form of a Vighna, [I offer] this oblation.
May Vetāla grant us [protection]. (3) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ haṃ haṃ haṃsa kṣa ma la va ra ya rthaṃ sarva-siddhiṃ kuru. (2) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ vāṃ vetā...
Salutations to Labhairava (108). With the six limbs beginning with *hrām* and so forth, [one offers] the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

He whose eyes are like blazing fire, who is adorned with serpents, who possesses a fierce form, who is three-eyed, who removes fear, and who bestows both the sword and fear—[I worship him] who enjoys the sound of the lute.
I myself always worship the King of Vetālas, who causes the wheel of yoga to revolve;
*mūlānta vaṣaṭ* for the libation, and *nirodha arghaḥ* for the offering of water.
Then, having offered oblations one by one to Svacchanda together with his retinue...
Having offered the oblation, one should perform the homa for the enclosures as follows: *kṣaṃ svāhā* to the face of Īśāna;
*yaṃ svāhā* to the face of Tatpuruṣa; *raṃ svāhā* to the face of Aghora; *laṃ svāhā* to the face of Sadyojāta; *vaṃ svāhā* to Vāmadeva.
Ktrāya Oṃ-kṣamaraya-rthaṃ-kapāleśa-bhairavāya; Oṃ ha ra r-ūśikhivāhana-bhai; Oṃ-kṣayaryaṃ-krodharāja-bhai; Ra oṃ-jārayaryaṃ-vikarāla-bhai; Oṃ-hrāṃ-manmatha-bhai.
Oṃ haraya-artham meghanāda-bhai | Oṃ hūṃ soma-rāja-bhai | Oṃ ha-sa-kṣa-ma-la-va-ra-ya-artham vidyārāja-bhai | Now,
the armor of weapons: svāhā to the sword, to the shield, and to the noose.
Salutations to the goad, to the arrow, to the Pināka bow, to the excellent one, to the fear-dispelling one, to the shaven-headed one, to the one with matted locks, to the lute, to the hand-drum,
to the bell, to the trident, to the thunderbolt, to the staff, to the battle-axe, and to the mudga-bean.
[The offering] for the covering of the power of sovereignty (rāya-athaśakti) is for Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī,
Balapramathanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī.

Now, the sevenfold enclosure consists of the Vidyeśvaras, Gaṇeśvaras, Lokapālas, Mātṛs, Grahas, Nāgas, and those beginning with Vajra; this is called the sevenfold enclosure. Among these, first are the Vidyeśvaras: Oṃ Hrīṃ.
anaṃtāya svāhā | oṃ glūṃ sūkṣmāya | oṃ śivottamāya | oṃ juṃ ekanetrāya | oṃ kṣuṃ ekarudrāya | oṃ glūṃ trimūrtaye | oṃ śrīkaṇṭhāya | oṃ śrīṃ śikhaṇḍine || a ||
Oṃ rāṃ rīṃ rūṃ nandine svāhā. Oṃ māṃ sīṃ mlūṃ hsauḥ sahā kālāpa hsauḥ bhyaṃ girudrāya. Oṃ ga larthaṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye. Oṃ vrāṃ vṛṣabhāya hsāṃ kuṅkumā.
Rāya oṃ hrīṃ saḥ aṃvikāyai h; for the sake of the offering, to Caṇḍeśvara.
Now the world-protectors (lokeśās): oṃ lūṃ indrāya vajrahastāya; rthaṃ agnaye śaktihastāya; rthaṃ yamāya daṇḍahastāya; yūṃ vā...

Yaṃ to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand; Kūṃ to Kubera, who holds a mace in his hand; Śūṃ to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand; Āṃ to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand; Hlāṃ to Viṣṇu, who holds a discus in his hand.
Now, the *mātrā-āvaraṇa* (syllabic enclosure): Oṃ ja sa rtha jayāyai svāhā;
Oṃ ta ma yūṃ vijayāyai; Raṃ subhagāyai; Yaṃ durgāyai; Jaṃ raṃ jayantyai; Paṃ tha hi nyai; Ha rūṃ aparājitāyai.
To Jaṅkarālī; now the enclosure of the planets: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūryāya svāhā* for the sake of *sa*; *ra* for the sake of the Moon;
*ha* for the sake of Mars; *ra* for the sake of Mercury; *rasa* for the sake of Venus; *kṣama* for the sake of [Saturn].
To Śanaiścara, *huṃ*; to Rāhu, *hrīṃ*; to Ketu, *atha*.
Oṃ, svāhā to the serpent-king Ananta; to Vāsuki the serpent-king, Padma, Mahāpadma, Takṣaka, and Kārkoṭaka.
*Arkoṭanā śaṅkhapālanā kulikanā athavajrā āvaraṇaṃ vajrāya phaṭ svāhā |* To Śakti, to Daṇḍa,
to Khaḍga, to Pāśa, to Dhvaja, to Gadā, to Triśūla, and to Pa...
To Māyā Halāya: Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vrahmai Svāhā! To Māheśvarī: Oṃ! To Kaumārī: Oṃ! To Vaiṣṇavī: Oṃ! To Vārāhī: Oṃ! To Aindrī: Oṃ! To Cāmuṇḍā: Oṃ! To Aparājitā: Oṃ! To Nārasiṃhī: Oṃ Mahā...
To Lakṣmī; Oṃ to Jayā; Oṃ to Vijayā; Oṃ to Jayantī. Now, the enclosure of the Lords of the Field (Kṣetrapālas): Oṃ to Vaṭuka Svāhā; to the Yoginīs;
to the Sthānacaras; to the Bhūtas; to Rājarājeśvara; to Vetāla.
To Bhairava, the great devourer; to Viśvaksena, the royal Rudra; to Maṅkharājānaka, the auspicious royal Maṅgalyarājānaka, and Ānandeśvara, the royal Sātī.
Kāyadhānparā, Rudrarā, and Pāñcālarā become cool.
Hrāṃ hrīṃ kṣīṃ to Heruka; aiṃ hrīṃ lāṃ kṣīṃ to Tripurantaka;
hrīṃ huṃ huṃ to Agnivetāla; rāṃ kṣīṃ to Agni.
To the one called Kāla on the tongue: *jihvāya hrīṃ hūṃ hsauḥ*; to Kapālin: *kṣāṃ yūṃ kṣīṃ*; to Ekapāda: *āśaṃ kṣaṃ*; to Bhīmarūpin: *kṣāṃ hrīṃ kṣāṃ*;
to the one called Tāraka: *hrīṃ hrīṃ*; to Hāṭakeśvara: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ huṃ*.

To the Lord of the Kings of Rāṇas: I shall now proclaim that great mantra, which is pervasive throughout the unmanifest sky, which is both with parts and without parts, which is the mixture of all and non-all, the destroyer of great sins, and the slayer of the bonds of the fettered (paśu). Thus, [I shall speak].
Gāyatrī: Oṃ, to that Maheśa, who pervades the sky, may Śiva impel our intellect.
(3) Oṃ, to Śiva, who pervades the sky, whose form is the sky, who pervades all, who is infinite, and who is the unconditioned, the eternal...
Obeisance to the one who dwells at the eternal seat of yoga, who is eternally nourished by meditation,
Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the source of all; to Śiva whose head is Īśāna,
whose face is Tatpuruṣa, and whose heart is Aghora.
To Vāmadeva, the secret; to Sadyojāta, the head; Oṃ namaḥ!
Oṃ namaḥ to the one who is more secret than the secret, the protector, the refuge, the presiding authority over all yogas, whose form is light, the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, O you who are beyond consciousness, pervasive, formless, primordial, splendorous, luminous, formless, infinite,
smokeless, ashless, without beginning, neither one nor many, *dhū dhū dhū dhū*, *oṃ*.
Bhūḥ oṃ bhuvaḥ oṃ svaḥ! O you who arise from the non-ending, the ending, and the source of endings;
O Śiva, O All, O Soul of All, O Maheśvara, O Mahādeva, O Lord of True Being, O You of Great Splendor, O Sovereign of Yoga—release me! (2)
O Pramatha! O Śarva! O Bhava! O Source of Existence! O Bestower of Happiness upon all beings!
O You who cause the presence of all! O Supreme One beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra!
O Unworshipped! O Unpraised! O You who were present from before! O Witness!
*Taru* (2), *pataṅga* (2), *piṅga* (2), *jñāna* (2), *śabda* (2), *sūkṣma* (2),
*śivaśarvaśarvada* (2), *oṃ namaḥ śivāya namaḥ*,
*oṃ namaḥ śivāya iti*, *oṃ namaḥ*— these belong to Vyomavyāpin.
The root mantra and its limbs are: *oṃ namaḥ sarvātmane parameśvarāya yogāya yogasaṃbhavāya kara kara (2) kuru kuru (2) sadya (2) bhava bhava bhavodbhava vāmadeva sarvakārya*.
*Praśamana namo'stu te svāhā hṛdayāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ śiva śiva namaḥ śirase svāhā*. *Oṃ śiva hṛdayajvālini svāhā śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*. *Oṃ śivā...*
O auspicious one, I invoke the great and most terrible armor, which is of the nature of great splendor, all-knowing, unconquered, and tawny-hued:
O Armor, come by the command of Śiva, O Great Tawny One! HṚM.
Dayaṃbandha (2) ghūrṇa (2) kaki (2) sūkṣma (2). Having entered the bodies of Vajradhara, Vajrapāśa, Vajrāśani, and Ama, devour all the wicked ones! Hūṃ phaṭ! Hum for armor! Prasphu!
RA (2) GHORAGHORATARATANURŪPA (2) CAṬA (2) PRACAṬA (2) KAHA (2) VASA (2) BANDHA (2) CĀTAYA (2) HŪṂ PHAṬ ASTRĀYA PHAṬ | OṂ JUṂ SAḤ NETREBHYO VAUṢAṬ | To the five faces together with the limbs, GĀYA.
Third: Oṃ, all this is of the nature of Śiva;
it proceeds from Śiva, for the sake of Śiva, and may Śiva, the womb of Śiva, impel everything. (3) Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta.

Oṃ, salutations to Sadyojāta; be present in every state of existence, O source of all that arises from existence, be gracious to us. Oṃ, svāhā to the one whose desires are instantly fulfilled—this is for the heart.
Oṃ, repeated salutations to the one who grants the boon of instantly fulfilled desires.
Svāhā to the head; Oṃ to the tuft of hair (śikhā) in the form of a serpent; Sadyojāta to the body (mūrti); Phaṭ to the armor (kavaca); Oṃ Hūṃ to the eyes; Oṃ Phaṭ to the weapon (astra);
Oṃ Vāmadevāya namaḥ, Jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ, Rudrāya namaḥ.
Salutation to Kāla; salutation to Kalavikaraṇa; salutation to Balavikaraṇa; salutation to Balapramathana; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana; salutation to Manomanī; Oṃ Vāma.
Devāya namaḥ, *tat-sad-om-hy-ad-om-vāmadeva-hūṃ phaṭ* for the head;
*sarvapāpapraṇāśana-vāmadeva-śikhine maḥ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *om-vāmācārāya hūṃ phaṭ* for the armor (*kavaca*); *om-tat-sa-* [for the eye].
*Doṃ phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*). Then the *Aghora-mantra*: *Tatsad oṃ hṛdaya bhava caṇḍa huṃ phaṭ* for the heart (*hṛdaya*);
*bhīma-bhīṣaṇi sarva-vidyā-hṛdaya-vidāriṇi huṃ phaṭ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *oṃ aghora huṃ phaṭ*.
Ṭkava oṃ tatsad oṃ haṭ astrāya | oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi | tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt || 3 || oṃ tatpuruṣa oṃ tatsad hṛdayāya namaḥ | oṃ bhūḥ svāhā śirase svāhā | oṃ bhu...
Vaḥ svāhā for the tuft (śikhā); Oṃ svaḥ svāhā for the armor (kavaca); Oṃ tat sat oṃ for the weapon (astra).
Oṃ, Īśāna is the Lord of all sciences, the Lord of all beings, the Sovereign of Brahmā, the Sovereign of Brahman; may He be our blessing.
*Vomeṣṭasadāśiva-ōṃ namaḥ*. *Oṃ amogha svāhā phaṭ ṛ*. *Oṃ pañcamūrtaye namaḥ* (to the head). *Oṃ īśāna svāhā* (to the crest-lock). *Oṃ jvalavit sa huṃ phaṭ* (to the armor). *Oṃ hūṃ tatsadoṃ*.

"Phaṭ astrāya phaṭ"—with this, one performs the *vyomavyāpin* oblation; then one should offer three full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*). One should worship the Lords of the Gates, who are vermilion-colored, adorned with jeweled crowns, and graced with beautiful crescent-moon ornaments.
O Lord, behold this [vision]: the lotus-face of my beloved is graced with a gentle smile, adorned with divine ornaments and celestial pigments;
her hand rests upon her beautiful left thigh, holding a lovely red water-lily, while her gaze is fixed upon the tips of her high, rounded breasts.
Oṃ juṃ saḥ! May there be satisfaction for all mantras and rituals;
svāhā! (1) One should constantly meditate upon Maheśa in the center of the vital breath, resembling a mountain of silver and adorned with the beautiful crescent moon.
I worship Him who is radiant with jewel-ornaments, holding the syllable *Hūṃ*, the axe, the deer, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
who is gracious, seated upon a lotus, surrounded by hosts of deities standing with mantras;
who wears a tiger-skin, the primordial source of the universe, and is worshipped by all the world.
Oṃ huṃ! Salutations to Bhairava, the bestower of fearlessness, five-faced and three-eyed;
may you be nourished, svāhā! (2) On the left, [he holds] a shield;
he possesses the luster of the rising sun, his mass of matted hair is radiant with the crescent moon, and he is adorned by the lords of serpents.
I worship the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha, who is adorned with ornaments, holding a rosary, a trident, a skull, and a Khaṭvāṅga staff in his hands; he has three eyes, a beautiful five-faced countenance,
wears a tiger skin, and resides in a lotus.
Oṃ hūṃ nyūnātirikta-vidhiṃ pūrayāmi vauṣaṭ.
(3) Then, the homa with curd-rice: Oṃ juṃ saḥ amṛteśvara-bhairavaṃ toṣayāmi svāhā. (3) Oṃ juṃ saḥ amṛtalakṣmīṃ to...
*Ṣayāmi svāhā*. (3) With his lotus-like hands, he holds a crystal rosary the color of silver, a string of pearls, a jar of nectar, and the mudrās of vidyā and jñāna; he wears a serpent as a sash.
I praise the southern form of the moon-crested, three-eyed Lord, adorned with various ornaments—
*Oṃ juṃ saḥ Amṛteśvara Bhairava oṃ juṃ saḥ*.
May there be the attainment of immortality (*amṛta-lakṣmī*) for the sacrificer, and worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) for the left-hand Guru.
"May the fruit of liberation be complete, astu vauṣaṭ. Then follows the protection mantra:

an oblation (*homa*) with milk, clarified butter, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and all medicinal herbs [is performed]. *Oṃ juṃ saḥ*, O Amṛteśvara Bhairava, [protect] the disciple named so-and-so from all calamities...

Vibhyorakṣa (2) Oṃ juṃ saḥ svāhā (10). With all herbs, [I offer] the full [oblation]: Oṃ juṃ saḥ, I satisfy Amṛteśvara Bhairava together with the Goddess and his retinue; Vauṣaṭ. With clarified butter: Oṃ hāṃ, to Brahmā, svāhā.

Hā (3) Oṃ vāṃ, svāhā to the Vāstupuruṣa (3). Some say that one should also worship the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and their presiding deities (*devatā*). Oṃ śrīṃ (3) huṃ (3) hrīṃ (3), may there be peace for the reversal [of obstacles], svāhā (1). Oṃ śrīṃ (3).

HŪṂ (3) HRĪṂ (3) may there be peace for transgressions, svāhā! (1) Likewise, may there be peace for the faults of deficiency and excess, svāhā! (1) Likewise, may there be peace for misdeeds committed and not committed, svāhā! (1) Then, having brought fire from another source...

Having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite and offered the naivedya, and having performed the worship of Guru Śiva, one should offer [the food] starting with the Bṛhatparṇa: "Oṃ! To the one whose chest is captivating, whose eyes are wide, who is adorned by the Lord of the Earth, the five-faced..."
(1) To him whose crest is adorned with a beautiful crescent moon that outshines the sun; who, together with his staff and mace, carries the noose, the arrow,
the bow, the goad, the khaṭvāṅga, the lute, the bell, and the drum.

Indeed, one should meditate upon him here as Vāmana, holding in his nine right hands a sword, a goad, a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, a skull-cup, a *ḍamaru* drum, a trident, a thunderbolt, and an axe.
The face of the Blessed One above is white;
the five faces in front are yellow; the right [face] is green;
the left is reddish; and the western face of the God is beautiful with white luster.
One should likewise meditate upon the Goddess Aghoreśvarī, who rests upon his lap and is adorned with all the sacred sites of the Blessed One that have been thus revealed: Oṃ juṃ saḥ, O immortal one,
arisen from nectar, accomplisher of all aims, [O you who are] all...
O subduer of beings, bestower of enjoyments and liberation, destroyer of all suffering,
you who are intent on [protecting] all, O remover of the violation and destruction of all pledges (samaya), O Viśve! [You who remove] the errors of sequence,
inversion, transposition, deficiency, and excess.

"May there be peace for what has been done and what has been ill-done; may there be the fulfillment of the injunctions regarding the performance of penance for actions performed according to rule—Vauṣaṭ!
Having thus completed the Great Full Oblation (bṛhat-pūrṇāhuti), one should pay homage to the Fire from all sides. Sarvataḥpā... [The text ends here].
With feet, heads, eyes, and mouths on every side, the great Agni of universal form has been invoked for all rites; may he grant long life, health, sovereignty, fortitude, goodness,
strength, fame, splendor, luster, cattle, and valor.

O Lord, witness of all, when you are pleased with embodied beings, you grant heroism, imperial sovereignty, good fortune, success in action, preeminence in one's lineage, and the capacity for virtuous deeds— all of this; therefore, worship the blazing fire.

Having recited, "Tāṃ saṃjātavedasaṃ suvarṇavarṇasamalaṃ susiddhiṃ sarvatomukham," one should pay obeisance. Then, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should pray: "O Brahman, [grant] the luster of a Brahmin..."
With the mantra "svojāyatām," he should then release the fire with palms joined in *añjali*, saying: "Oṃ, go to the sacrifice, go to the Lord of the Sacrifice, go to your own source, svāhā!
This is your sacrifice, O Lord of the Sacrifice, the Great Thread."

"O you who have performed all heroic deeds, accept [this], svāhā!"—thus is the dismissal. "O Blessed One, O Blessed One, O Vahni, you are the supreme mouth of the gods; you are the manifest deity in the world, the fulfiller of all rites. [He who dwells] within...
"For you alone have established your presence among the worlds;
when you are pleased, the gods are pleased—so say Sanaka and the others.
O Great Fire, you are now weary from the rites of initiation; [protect] dharma, wife, and..."
"Having given these [offerings], come to your own abode"—thus one should offer salutation.
Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*): "May all sin committed throughout ten million births, whether hidden or manifest, go to destruction; may the darkness [be dispelled] by the sun."
Just as, by the recitation of this Mṛtyujit-bhaṭāraka,
all the lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśas), beginning with Ananteśa and ending with Paramaśiva, together with their retinues and attendants, [become manifest] as a commonality for all.

"May they be pleased and grant boons. Now follows the announcement of the *homa*: "O you who are the protector of the most secret of secrets, may there be auspiciousness; may no deficiency ever arise for the patron (*yajamāna*).
By the grace of the God and the Goddess, protect, protect me, O Bhṛgu!"
"Agni is peace"—this is ash;
"Vāyu"—this is ash; "Ākāśa"—this is ash; "The gross"—this is ash; "All this indeed"—this is ash; these eyes are ash, and [all] this is ash.
Having smeared his forehead with these ashes, he becomes liberated from the state of a bound soul (paśu), obtains the fruit of bathing at all sacred fords (tīrtha),
and all his ritual actions become free from defect. Then, in the fire, according to the rule...

Pūjā: Oṃ juṃ saḥ! To you who are of the nature of nectar, whose radiance is nectar, who arise from nectar, whose essence is the flow of nectar, who possess a flood of nectar, whose eyes are nectar, who wear a necklace of nectar, whose body is nectar, whose exhalations are nectar, and whose ultimate end is nectar.
To the embodiment of nectar, to the Lord of nectar, to the one supreme in all nectars, to the one who wards off the violation of all observances, to the one whose body consists of all mantras,
to the Fortune of Nectar— *Hrīṃ Svāhā Vauṣaṭ Saḥ Oṃ Juṃ Sa*.
One should recite the *melāpa-vidyā* of all the mantras: the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*) is upon the wheel, the lotus upon the wheel, the trident upon the trident,
the mace upon the mace, the banner upon the banner, the noose upon the noose, and the sword upon the sword.
In the Gaṇḍa [direction] he places Ruṇḍa; in Śakti, Śakti; in Vajra, Vajra; in Ananta, Ananta; in Brahmā, Brahmā; in Īśāna, Īśāna;
in Kuvera, Kuvera; in Vāyu, Vāyu; in Varuṇa, Varuṇa; in Nirṛti, Ni... [he places].
To Ṛtiyama, Yamamagrau; to Agni, Indre; to Indra, Vidyārāja;
to Vidyārāja, Somarāja; to Somarāja, Meghanāde; to Meghanāda, Manmathe; to Manmatha, Vikarāle.
One should worship Karāla in Krodharāja, Krodharāja in Śikhivāhana,
Śikhivāhana in Kapāleśa, Kapāleśa in Śakti, Śakti in Astra, Astra in Nairṛta, Netra in Kavaca, and Kavaca [in the heart].

One should contemplate the *śikhā* [mantra] in the *śikhā*, the head in the head, the heart in the heart, the root-mantra in the root-mantra, the fire in the fire, and the arghya-vessel in the arghya-vessel; one should then contemplate the light as dissolved into one's own self. Then...
With the water from the *śāntikalaśa* (peace-pitcher) and the *sruva*-ladle, one should create a continuous stream [of water] in the four directions with the mantra:
*oṃ phaṭ śivāgniṃ vimuñcāsi phaṭ 3 naya me dharmaṃ dehi dhanaṃ dehi putrapautrāṃś ca dehi me*.

O Havyavāhana, grant me long life, health, and sovereignty; O Vahni, you who consume the oblation, carry the *havya*; O Pāvaka, you who consume the *kavya*, having bestowed upon me wealth, long life, and health, depart, O Hutāśana, whose mouth is the sacrificial fire.
Salutations to You, the Self, by whom the gods sustain the entire world and through whom the oblation is first offered; grant me devotion, grant me prosperity,
grant me happiness.
By way of independence.

O Lord, you who are satisfied through devotion by the oblation within the midst of the fire—with the body, enjoyments, and liberation as desired by the mind—take unto yourself all the potency that resides in the sacrificial substances. Saṃ... [end of fragment]

O Lord, whatever expiation was performed by me out of delusion in this essential [teaching] has all gone to destruction, like darkness at the rising of the sun. O Master of Mantras, you who possess eternal bliss, forgive me.

O Lord of Devas, O Universal Form, please accept this which I have offered—whether it be deficient or excessive—for the sake of the path, desire, and liberation, and so that I may return again; be gracious, for salutations unto You! May You depart.
May that which was intended for the expiation of the transgressions committed during the middle of the year lead to my return;
may all that expiation which has passed away go to destruction;
and may the splendor of Maheśvara, through this fire-offering, merge into my own splendor.

Saying "Give [me] yourself," he should offer himself as a sacrifice to the space-goer (*ākāśagāminī*); having performed the libation for the lords of the fields (*kṣetreśatarpaṇa*), he should prepare the inquiry regarding the water-jar (*kalaśapṛcchā*) as before, beginning with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svas tatsavitur... and so forth. Acchi.

"May the drama be complete; so be it. Having taken fragrant water and performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the words "I take [this]," he then offered barley-water with the words "Salutation to the water-libation. Then, he received the command for the food offering (*naivedya*). Command.

O Lord, please accept this offering; O Blessed One, you ought to consume it for the sake of sustaining my body. I am fallen, I am without refuge, and I am in every state of need in every respect. Bha...
O Bull, I have sought refuge in you; protect me, who have come to you for shelter.
Indeed, [I am burdened by] sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, illicit sexual intercourse, drinking liquor, theft, causing an abortion, violating the Guru’s bed, and stealing gold.
The killer of a friend, the slayer of cows, the murderer of a father, the murderer of a mother, the violator of a woman, the killer of a preceptor,
and all other terrible sins committed by others— those threefold sins in their thousands— all vanish through the remembrance of Amṛte.
If there should be even one slayer of a Brahmin, the hundred recitations of these mantras will undoubtedly reduce him to ashes;
O Śivā, all those seventy million mantras have been recited by me.
O Goddess of the gods, by the power of reciting this [mantra] one hundred times, one shall obtain the merit found in the four Vedas,
the fruit of all sacrifices, and the majesty of all sacred fords— indeed,
that same result comes from a hundred recitations.
When worshipped before Śiva on the ground that yields the fruit of Nirvāṇa,
a mortal shall attain that in a single birth; there is no doubt that he becomes equal to me, the reciter of the mantra of one hundred and eight syllables.
O beautiful lady, he in whose heart this [mantra] resides, being ever-disciplined,
uplifts ten generations of his ancestors and ten generations of his descendants; O lady of virtuous vows, death does not afflict him, even when seized by Time.

Whoever constantly remembers the *sandhyā* prayer, wherever they may be situated, shall never fall under the power of death; neither diseases nor thieves shall afflict them. By merely worshipping it once, harmful beings and the like are indeed destroyed. Destroyed.
Just as deer flee in all ten directions upon seeing a lion,
so too is poverty destroyed from one's lineage through the practice of those two.
Wherever and whenever the knower of mantras may dwell, he should always remain joyful.

Diseases, as well as kharkhadas, thieves, and the like; various *śākinīs*, unknown [spirits], *piśācas*, *rākṣasas*, and *grahas*; child-seizing spirits (*bālagrahas*), eruptive boils, and intermediate beings—may all these perish.
All afflictions arising from the six classes of beings, as well as the torments of famine,
do not prevail through the presence of such a knower; for he always honors all living beings and kings with incomparable acts of giving, worship, and respect.
If [this] is performed, by that mere act of worship all mantras become worshipped and bestow happiness; therefore, one should worship those [deities] through its mouth.
In every case, the grahas who cause obstacles harm the practitioner.
Therefore, water and cooked rice should always be offered to the planets;
for when they are satisfied, the malevolent planets are pacified and no longer exert their influence.
Now, the Bhairava-samaya: Oṃ juṃ saḥ, to the embodiment of nectar, Vyoma...

O you whose body is pervasive space, protect me from the violation of all commitments; fulfill all commitments! O you whose mantra-body is common to all, oṃ juṃ saḥ, immortal one, supreme nectar, eternal one!

*Hrīṃ svāhā*. Now, O Blessed One, Lord of Devas, King of the Gods, you have been served by me with flowers of forgiveness from the guardians of the world; accept this worship through my mouth. O Lord of Devas, may it be forgiven, may it be forgiven, O Master! (1) Bhaga...

O Lord Agni, you have been troubled by me; O Lord of Gods, accept this offering and forgive me. O Lord Dharmarāja, you have been troubled by me; having accepted this worship of Śiva, please forgive me.
O Blessed One, protect me from the terrible eyes of Nirṛti and from the ocean of saṃsāra;
O Lord of Gods, come to me, for you are the state consisting of eternal bliss, O Blessed One, who are worshipped as Śrī Śiva by Varuṇa and others at the sacrifice. I am weary.
O Blessed One, O Lord, through Toṣimayādevī, go to your own purifying abode.
O Blessed One, O Vāyu, you have been exhausted in the mouth of Śambhu; having accepted this *arghya* from me, protect me and yourself according to your own will. O Blessed One, O Kubera! (6)

"You have been exhausted during the sacrifice of Śaṅkara; having taken the image bestowed by me, may you be forgiven, O Blessed One, O God of gods! O Lord, take this image of Īśāna into your own mouth and give it back."

O Lord, grant me all human goals! O Blessed One, worshiped by the three worlds, Grandfather of all the worlds, you who have provided protection to Śiva and Īśvara, may this be forgiven! O Blessed One, O Blessed Viṣṇu, you who have performed [this] gift...
"O Destroyer of the Nine, since protection has been established by you against this Śaiva affliction, may that be forgiven, O Lord!
(10) Now, for the planets, the flowers of forgiveness: O Twelve-fold Self, salutations to you; salutations again and again to Mārtāṇḍa! Vyā...
O Sun, grant protection to one bitten by the serpent of the afflictions; O Moon, the lord of the night and the ornament of the sky, salutations to you, the son of Rohiṇī!
O Maker of Night, grant protection to one scorched by the poison of saṃsāra. (2) O Aṅgāraka...
Salutations to you, the remover of all suffering; O Son of the Earth, grant protection to the wretched and the destitute. Salutations to you, born of Soma;
salutations to that King of Planets; salutations to him who is submerged in the mire of worldly existence.

O Savior, O Rohiṇī’s son, grant me protection! O Vācaspati, Teacher of the Gods, salutations to you, the destroyer of fear! Be ever-gracious toward me, a sinner devoid of wisdom. O Enemy of the Demons... (4-5)

Omitra, salutations to you who are supreme in compassion; having destroyed the afflictions caused by the adverse planetary positions within the ten stages of life, protect me, O son of Bhṛgu. (6) Salutations to the one whose body is Kṛṣṇa; salutations to you, the son of the Sun; [protect me from] the fear of saṃsāra.

O Śanaiścara, provide protection for my destruction; O Saiṃhikeya, obeisance to you, ward off the affliction of the planets. O Vidhuntuda, provide protection for me who am consumed by the fire of suffering. [May] the Sun and the others, joined with Ketu, [grant this].

May those devoted to the worship of Śiva protect the wealth, life-span, friends, and sons of the patron (yajamāna). Now, [the offering] of the eight Bhairavas: O Lord Kapāleśa and the others, you have been propitiated with flowers. O Śakra! [End. (9)
O Bhairava, Lord of Indras, salutations to you who have been worshipped by me exceedingly during this sacrifice!
O Blessed One, Śikhivāhana, who are worshipped in the sacrifice of Śaṅkara, you have been propitiated and satisfied by me; now go to your own abode. (1-2)
O Blessed One, King of Wrath, honored by the people for the sake of Dharma,
having performed protection at the mouth [of the rite], O Lord of Śiva, go to your own stainless state.
O Blessed One, you who are most formidable, always worshipped by Nirṛti...

O Conqueror, accept this Śaiva worship; depart, O Blessed One, Lord of Love, you who were worshipped by Varuṇa! You have been distressed during the sacrifice of Śiva; may it be forgiven, may it be forgiven!
O Blessed One Meghanāda, you who are faultless and honored by Vāyu;
O Lord Soma, King of the Moon, you who are worshipped by Kubera; you have been fatigued at this Śaiva sacrifice—may it be forgiven, O Blessed One. You have been made to toil in this Śaiva rite.
O Protectors, please forgive me; O Blessed Ones, Lords of Mantras and so forth, you have been troubled by me in this ritual act—please forgive me.
And those beginning with Ananta who reside within the seven enclosures in the hot springs...

May all of them, being honored and satisfied, attain the state of Śiva. O Śambhu, O All-pervading Lord of the World, O Blessed One, I am weary in the performance of ritual acts; You alone are the God of gods, and You alone are the supreme refuge.
You are the enjoyer, the one said to be the eater, and the cause of all causes;
when you are pleased, all the gods are forever pleased.
I bow to that Supreme Being, who consists of the five Brahmans, along with his limbs, his attendants, and his followers.

I seek refuge in Maheśvara, who possesses power and his retinue; whether it was committed by my hands or my feet, may you forgive me, O Lord of Mantras, eternal bearer of bliss, for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. May there be prosperity once again!
Forgive me for my departure, and whatever I have done that was deficient or excessive; O you whose form is the universe, accept this, be gracious, O Lord of Gods, salutations to you!
Depart satisfied, so that I may welcome you again when you return alone.
The omniscient God is the witness of all action; He who is unapproachable even by Brahmā and the other gods is worshipped at the outset through the *samaya*.
That God, both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), abides in the station at the end of the twelve; that very God is Bhaga.

O God of gods, Śambhu—who is capable of performing the creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe; who possesses three forms and consists of the three *guṇas*; and who is worshipped according to the rules in this sacrifice—has been invoked by me in this ritual procedure. May he be pleased with me.

That Śakti, who is of threefold nature and whose form is the self, having been worshipped according to the rules at the sacrifice by means of the three-fold thread, [declares]: "Today my birth has become fruitful; today my rites have become fruitful. Such is his power.

O Śambhu, I am distressed; O Śivā, protect me today who am without a protector from this peril of sin! Grant me success, prosperity, as well as intelligence and mental purity, and bestow upon me the enjoyment of worldly pleasures.
O Great Lord, grant me liberation as desired by my mind, as well as eternal perfection in all things; O Śambhu, O Supreme Lord, grant me the state that is free from affliction. Now... O Supreme...
O Lord of the Meṣāna constellation, may you forgive, may you forgive;

you have been exerted in this sacrifice, so go contentedly to your own abode. O Gaṇeśa, who is remembered at the beginning, for the task of guarding the door; and the world-protectors, Indra and the others.
And likewise the Ādityas and other planets, those Bhairavas beginning with Kapāleśa who reside within the Bhairavas,
the mantras of the seven enclosures, and the deities of the garments and so forth.
Likewise, the deities of the six paths and the Gāyatrī and others;
Vāstoṣpati and the rest, the presiding deities of the house;
and Vaṭuka, Heruka, and the others, the eternal guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas).
Having granted all those various desires, may they return to their own abode.
I do not know invocation at all, nor do I know worship; I do not know dismissal—may it be forgiven by you both, O Supreme Lord.
With my two knees, two hands, chest, and head, I perform prostration; "Homage!
Homage to Brahman," and so forth—thus [one should recite] in secret.
Regarding the libation (*tarpaṇa*) that was previously introduced as being within that light, it is within that very light.
Various mantras, like sparks,

should be meditated upon as having entered within the mantra-vessel; that mass of splendor contained within the vessel is the Lord Bhairava, who withdraws everything by means of the Saṃhāriṇī [mudrā].
In the system of Pañcniṣkalānātha as well, by the sequence of utterance (*uccāra*),

the bindu is merged into bindu and the nāda into nāda; that too is dissolved into the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and the obstructress (*nirodhinī*) through the method of pacification (*praśama-yukti*), and finally merged into the pervasive form (*vyāpaka-rūpa*)— this is the dissolution of the mantra.
Having sequentially manifested and explained the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) as *oṃ juṃ saḥ*—

the supreme splendor of mantra— and having taken it with the inhalation (*pūraka*) through the twelve-finger limit of the *bhoga* channel while reciting "I offer this into my own self, *saḥ juṃ oṃ namaḥ*," [one should place it] in the heart.
The teachers say that, having performed the *tsthaṃ* [mudrā] according to rule, one should worship there mentally;
then, one should recite the Melāpa-vidyā three times: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ saḥ saḥ sukhasaubhāgyadāyini haṃsavāgīśvari*.
Riehyehihasa (2), establish your presence (2)! O bestower of all prosperity, warder-off of all that is evil, and creator of welfare for the entire world,
effect the union of the divided mantras (2) pra...
Sādobhavatu me hrīṃ śrīṃ saḥ saḥ huṃ huṃ. Now, the Kṣamā-mantra:
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ strīṃ prīṃ jyoparameśvara ṣaṭsadhīpate, [accept this] by means of the pure nectar of all samayas. Prati.
O ṢṬHĀṂ, perform the presence; dry up the sins of body, speech, and mind;
produce the expansion of the heart; shatter the impurity of the heart, O Surā!
Ward off the arrogance of the Ṛcas! (2) Stay, stay!
To the one who dwells in the seven netherworlds, carrying both the gross and the subtle—huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā! Arise, arise, O Lord of Gods, you who are the maṇḍala!
O you who possess the nature of Tatpuruṣa, protect us constantly from the east together with the gods; likewise, O Bhairava whose self is Aghora, protect us from the south;
and similarly, O Śaṅkara, you who are Vāmadeva, protect us from the north.
O Sadyojāta, you are my protection from the west;
O Maheśāna, protect me from above; you are the deity Īśāna. O Lord, in every way, at all times, and everywhere on this path of worldly existence, protect me.

O Lord of Gods, [worship] Himāyāhi; then, reciting "nityānandamayaṃ padaṃ tato bahurūpagarbham," one should consecrate oneself and the ritual participants with the water from the mantra-pitcher, or otherwise with the water from the arghya vessel. Perform the sacrifice.

One should sprinkle [the disciple] along with the retinue of pride: *Oṃ*, may Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara consecrate you; Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Vāyu, Vijaya, Ākhaṇḍala, the lord Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Pāvaka, the lord of wealth (Kubera),
and Śiva, along with Brahmā and Śeṣa, were present in the various directions.
May Peace, Auspiciousness, Fame, Prosperity, Conduct, Intelligence,
Nourishment, Faith, Forbearance, Intellect, Modesty, Body, Tranquility, Praise, and Beauty— these Mothers consecrate you, O Lord of Dharma.
The planets— Āditya, Candra, Bhauma, Budha, Jīva, Śukra, and Arkaja— as well as Rāhu and Ketu, having assembled together, consecrate you; so too do the deities,
the Navagrahas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas.
The Nagas, Rishis, Munis, Ganas, Devas, Mothers,
the wives of the Devas, the Dhruvas, Nagas, Daityas, the hosts of Apsarases,
all weapons, all scriptures, kings, and mounts.
May the medicinal herbs, the jewels, Mount Kailāsa, the winds, the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, the sacred fords, and the clouds—
may these all consecrate you for the attainment of dharma, kama, and artha.
"May the meanings of the mantras be fruitful for us," and so forth. Thus ends the *Laghuparipāṭāgnikāryapaddhati*. Oṃ tatsat.
Now follows the *Āśvarapaddhati* according to the oral instructions of the Guru.
I bow to that Bhairava who is known as one’s own true nature (*svasvarūpa*), established on one’s own path, self-perceived, possessing its own splendor,

consisting of its own bliss, and ascended to its own state. [The mantra] beginning with "I bow to her who is one’s own true nature, established on one’s own path," and so forth, is within the vessel, the excellent lotus.
The Lord, whose eightfold form shines within the eight wheels, is accompanied by four goddesses— red with passion and white as the moon— and by the eight goddesses of the vessel;
above the severed head, he is adorned with the sixteen digits of the moon.
May the eleven-fold Bhairava, with five faces and eighteen arms, be victorious;
Oṃ Phaṭ! To the weapon of infinite power, Phaṭ! Thus [is the mantra] for Madhubhā.
One should consecrate the vessel; having taken a handful of honey from the vessels, one should begin by joining the two hands— which,
through the application of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), take the form of the moon and the sun— and [offer] the drink, which consists of the central radiance, into the fire.

One should bathe the body from the crown of the head to the feet with "Oṃ huṃ, I purify the body, face, and limbs, svāhā. Having thus performed the purification of the face, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra three times. Oṃ hūṃ, to Vāmadeva...

May the divine Surā inspire this for us; may Ānanda impel us. (3) Oṃ, salutation to the eternal Self—thus one should offer a flower upon the seat. One should perform the binding of the directions, the veiling, and the piercing with the Astra-mantra.
Śrīṃ Oṃ, [to] Pātāla and Bhūloka...
To Kāśasvana, Mahojas, Tapa, Satya, Brahma-loka, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Kālāgnirudra, and to all the Mothers who dwell in their radiant worlds— vauṣaṭ; thus [is the offering] to Brahmā.
