For the purpose of warding off injury, one should cast a drop [of liquid] in the ten directions with the mantra: *oṃ vāmadevabhairavāya vauṣaṭ*. Having taken the *gauḍī* liquor from the vessel, one should pour it back into that very same place with the mantra: *vaṃ vāmadevabhairavāya vauṣaṭ*.

One should prepare the *arghya* vessel with *tipānaka*; having sprinkled all the ritual substances (*dravya*) with that, [one recites]: *oṃ blīṃ vīrabhasmane svāhā*, *plīṃ sindūre*, *puṣpebhyo vauṣaṭ*, *jkrīṃ dīpāya vauṣaṭ*, *mtkuṃ*. māṃ.
Sāyavauṣaṭ; kṣūṃ āsavāyavauṣaṭ; vāṃ sīnaca ravevauṣaṭ; kṣarārthaṃ kṛśodaryai vauṣaṭ; kṛṣṇāṃ māṃse oṃ vauṣaṭ; arghye huṃ svāhā; sindūre atha pa.
Stable, resembling a mountain of blue collyrium, with disheveled locks of hair, possessing round and fierce eyes,
holding a mace and a skull-cup, adorned with serpents, having formidable fangs— the field that brings peace and wonder.
I bow down to that god, the bearer of the skull and the khaṭvāṅga staff, adorned with a garland of severed heads; I salute that god Bhairava, who delights in wine and women.
Oṃ huṃ, vauṣaṭ to the traveler! O God, Siddha!

Vauṣaṭ to the Gaṇanātha, Śākinīs, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, and the inhabitants of the earth and the netherworld; to the deities of travelers and their attendants; and to the Kṣetrapāla beginning with Ajarā.
"Vauṣaṭ to those who have arrived;
vauṣaṭ to the deities of travelers! Having thus taken the *gauḍī* liquor from the jar and having made the traveler [offer it], [he places] incense, flowers, and so forth outside.
One should cast [the image] into a vehicle; with an unadorned body, one should offer oblations at the four junctions.
If there is an obstacle, it will be in the *saṃskṛta* [mantra]; if the offering (*bali*) is deficient, it will be fruitless.
For the purpose of filling the five faces of Bhairava, there are the five vehicles (*yāna*), beginning with Vaṭuka, located in the east, south, west, north, and the center.

With what [is] the worship? As follows: Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, O Devīputra Vaṭukanātha, come! (2) O Ucchuṣma-hārin, repeatedly! (2) Kṣaḥ kṣapaṇa vaṭuka, this is the bali offering: Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ pheṃ saḥ saḥ blūṃ vauṣaṭ yogi.

Salutation to the two *nī* syllables. Oṃ kṣprīṃ! To the lord of the eight directions, the stationary and moving *kṣetrapāla*, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ kṣūṃ yūṃ rūṃ! O Kala-dhāva! Stand, stand! Destroy all enemies! All *bhūtas*, kha!

"May those who dwell on the earth and in the netherworld be satisfied; may success be mine forever, Oṃ Vauṣaṭ! Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Saḥ. Thus, at the conclusion of the worship of the Kṣetrapāla, [one should offer] four handfuls of water each into the middle of the ground.
Then, having performed the exhalations (recaka) and so forth, one should perform the mental sacrifice (manoyāga):
[one should visualize] the Lord with eighteen arms and red complexion, seated upon a corpse-throne within his own ocean of nectar, together with her who is situated in union with him.
Having remembered the ten thousand Surādonyā mantras with the mind and performed worship,

one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* (limb-assignment) in the following places: at the heart, the *dvādaśānta*, the *brahmarandhra*, the center of the *brahma* (the palate), the forehead, the navel, the genitals, and the knees.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the order of emanation is as follows: *rthaṃ* on the big toe of the foot;
*ya* on the knee; *ra* on the secret place; *na* on the navel; *la* on the heart;
*ma* on the palate; *kṣa* between the eyebrows; *sa* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*); and *ha* on the head.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhāra-krama) ending at the ten [fingers], one should perform the offering over the support (ādhāra) of the vessel (bhāṇḍa): "To the Support-Energy (ādhāra-śakti), svāhā!
To the Ocean of Nectar (sudhārṇava), vauṣaṭ! To the Throne of the Pretas (pretāsana), vauṣaṭ! To the Red Lotus (raktapadma)..."
Having placed the vessel upon the support with *sanāyavauṣaṭ*,

and having performed the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, one should consecrate [the substance] as nectar using the Amṛteśa mudrā while reciting: *oṃ juṃ saḥ vauṣaṭ kulāmṛteśvarabhairavāya namaḥ*.

Then, one should worship Bhairava and Bhairavī within the vessel: *oṃ ānandeśvarabhairavāya vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ surādevyai vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ siddhāyai vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ śuṣkāyai vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ raktāyai vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ utpā*...
"LĀYAIVAUṢAṬ! Homage, homage to the deities and to the Mothers;
homage, homage to the Śākinīs and the Khecarīs, and to the Yoginīs, homage, homage!"—with these words, he should scatter [the offerings] upward and downward with his left hand. Then, the vessel...

Regarding the consecration (*saṃskāra*): first, with the left hand, one should perform the illumination of the vessel (*pātra-sandīpana*) with the *choṭikā* (finger-snap) while reciting: "Oṃ ślīṃ paśu huṃ phaṭ, to the noose, the lord, and the weapon, phaṭ; I illuminate the vessel, namas. Then: "Oṃ juṃ saḥ vauṣaṭ, may the vessel be well-living (*suṃjīva*)."
"Vayāmi namaḥ | Oṃ huṃ, I veil the vessel, namaḥ"—thus is the consecration of the vessel (*pātra-saṃskāra*).
Then, with the left hand [and] the right hand, [recite]: "Oṃ jhrīṃ huṃ huṃ brahmāṇḍa-ca..."
"Ṣakāyanārikīlāya svāhā"—with this, perform the washing.
"Oṃ vaṃ vāmadevāya vauṣaṭ"—with this, purify the vessel.
Having thoroughly fumigated [the vessel] with incense while reciting "Oṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ," [proceed].

One should place [the vessel] upside down upon the support (dhāra). Then, having poured the liquid from that support into another vessel, one should set it aside. This is the specific consecration (viśeṣa-saṃskāra).
With the left hand, [one recites]: "Oṃ Oṃ! To the Self-principle (ātmatattva), the seed-syllable of the Support-power (dhāra-śakti-bīja)..."
Saying "kurāya vaṣaṭ," one should then place it on the ground with both hands.
Then, saying "juṃ vidyā-tattvāya padmāsanāya vaṣaṭ," one should again place the vessel upon the support (ādhāra) facing upwards. [Then] saying "oṃ saḥ śiva-tattvā..."
With the mantra *yapretāsanāyavauṣaṭ oṃ hrīṃ jrīṃ huṃ saḥ*,
one should make five tilaka marks upon the vessel. With the mantra *oṃ huṃ nārīkelāya svāhā*, even those who are unworthy vessels become worthy vessels.
I bow to that Goddess Nareśvarī, by whose mere remembrance one attains lordship over dogs; Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, Hrīṃ Phreṃ Huṃ, O Great Lakṣmī,
Sovereign, Supreme Abode, who flows through the void above!
O you who consume the moon, sun, and fire, resplendent in the supreme ether!
Come (2), enter (2), seize the vessel (2) HŪṂ PHAṬ!
With this mantra of the Lord of Men, one should worship the vessel. Thus is the secret consecration.
Then, having meditated on the vessel— such as a coconut shell and so forth—

which is in the right hand and has the form of the Sun, and having contemplated the vessel of Śrī Harṣadeva in the left hand which has the form of the Moon, [one should contemplate] the radiance of the *arghya* in the center.

Having visualized the fire as the mantra, one should recite: "Oṃ! Bring forth the great vessel filled with the essence of nectar, produced from the portion of Brahmā and overflowing with all essences," while holding the vessel with the hand of placement (nyāsahasta).
One should fill the vessel; while it is being filled, [one should recite] the *pātravidyā* (vessel-mantra): *hrīṃ śrīṃ caṇḍīkāpālini bhagavati grasa svīṃ svīṃ svāhā*, and *hrīṃ śrīṃ surāsaviśuddhe*.
*O you who cause emaciation, who cut down, who are shameless, O Śrī, take away the sin of killing a Brahmin, Svāhā! O you who repeatedly contract the scent of intoxication!
Having received [this] through the method of the Guru’s mouth, [place it] in the six locations within the bulbous root.*
Having meditated upon the circle of the navel (*nābhi-maṇḍala*) as having a blazing and radiant form, one should contemplate [the breath] arising from its center in the shape of a coil,
having the form of a sleeping serpent— white, motionless,
with its face turned upward, and [controlling] both the *prāṇa* and *apāna* within the vessel (*kumbha*).
By the flow of the middle path through me, pierce the six wheels, the sixteen supports,
the twelve knots,
the three lakhs [of channels], and the five voids by opening the floodgate of the vital breath.
Having meditated on the descending power (*yanti-śakti*) and having restrained the mind at the lower part of the palate,
one should remain for a moment with a focused mind after breaking the bolt and knot [of the vital centers], experiencing a sensation equal to the touch of an ant.

Having experienced a firm state of mind and having crossed through the door of Brahmā to reach the *dvādaśānta*, one should contemplate there, within that ever-shining tranquility, the supreme light of consciousness, which is like the orb of the full moon.

Having meditated upon that nectar, resembling molten silver, falling through the path of the *śakti* in an unbroken stream from the channel of the *dvāra* and emerging through the path of the nose like a torrential downpour, one should drink it.

One should meditate upon that which has fallen into the filled vessel; when the vessel is full, the deities situated in the sky become satisfied and dance. Having placed the vessel upon its support, one should worship it with "Oṃ Śrīṃ Gaṇapataye..."
Oṃ, salutation to the sandals of Gaṇapati’s beloved; Oṃ, salutation to the sandals of Vaṭukanātha’s beloved; Oṃ, salutation to the threshold. Thus is the worship of the door. Oṃ.
Śrī Gurunātha-pādukāṃ, Paramaguru-pādukāṃ, Oṃ Parameṣṭhi-guru-pādukāṃ, Oṃ Paramācārya-guru-pādukāṃ, Oṃ Ādisiddha-guru-pādukāṃ,
Oṃ Svagurunātha-pādukāṃ; thus [is] the left-hand guru.

Having worshipped oneself with scents and flowers using the root mantra, and having meditated upon the Supreme Lord as red as the hue of a lotus, one performs the "unbolting" (utkīlana) with the mantra: *aṅgamadhyabhairavāya vauṣaṭ*.
In the center of the vessel: Oṃ juṃ saḥ | Oṃ saḥ juṃ oṃ | To Ardhānārīśvara Bhairava, vauṣaṭ | To Ānandeśvara Bhairava, vauṣaṭ | To Surādevī, vauṣaṭ | Root mantra: Oṃ | Oṃ kaha (2) vasa (2).

O you with a tongue like lightning, O greatly terrifying one who laughs with loud laughter, *ki li* (2), O you whose face is formidable with fangs, O you whose mouth licks [its corners], O you greedy for devouring the world, O you of great and horrific form, *hana* (2) *huṃ* (2) *phaṭ* (2)!
*Oṃ svāhā*, salutation to the eastern face: *Oṃ oṃ*, to Mahābhairava, slay!

[Slay! You who are filled with the fierce and ghastly *ghur-ghura* roar of distorted majesty, and who possess the divine splendor of a great and terrifying fire like the wrathful sun at the end of time.
Nivarhaṇagulu (2), garja (24), daha (2), paca (2), matha (2), huṃ (2), haḥ phaṭ (3). Homage to the right face!
Oṃ jraṃ, homage to the sovereign of the great heroes, hāsa (2), vihasa (2).
Visphūrjaya (2), console with nectar!
Namaḥ klūṃ vauṣaṭ! Homage to the northern face!
Oṃ oṃ huṃ! O Aghora, O Ghorā, O Sovereign of all desires, O Siddhi-yoginī!

To the one praised by the circle of Niśākinīs, endowed with great blood-red power that is unimpeded, the bestower of happiness and good fortune, huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā; salutation to the western face. Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ sama.
In the Stavidyālaya [temple], the Great Lord of Mantras, the Pure Awakening, the Great Abode, the Supreme Brahman, eternally manifest, the dispeller of great delusion,
the blissful one overflowing with the bliss of the partless Yoga, the Śiva-śā... [is established].

Victory to the one worshipped by the great Mothers and Bhairavas, who is self-existent, eternal in nature, free from conceptual proliferation, and the reality of all that exists and does not exist; O Blessed One, *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, obeisance to the upward-facing mouth— thus is the fivefold set of faces.
Oṃ mahāmadyāya vi ānandeśvarāya dhī tannaḥ somaḥ pracodayāt (3). Oṃ hūṃ namaḥ hasa (2). To the supreme abode, whose nature is Śiva, to Mahābhairava, to the Heart, obeisance. Oṃ huṃ namaḥ (*).
To the supreme Śiva, the sovereign of all, for the head, svāhā!
Oṃ huṃ! O Mahābhairava, flame of fire, you who blaze, reduce the obstacles to ashes! To the one who destroys great darkness, for the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ! Huṃ! (2)

Phaṭ (2) Prasphura (2) Jvālāmālākularakṣa (2) Māṃ Huṃ Haḥ Phaṭ! To the armor, Huṃ! Oṃ Juṃ Saḥ! To the Lord of Divine Splendor, may you become the bestower of all accomplishments, O Wisdom-Self, for the sake of the three eyes, Vauṣaṭ!
The six limbs are: *oṃ hrīṃ prasphura (2) ghora (2) taratara (2) rūpa (2) caṭa (2) pracar̤a (2) kaha (2) vama (2) bandha (2) ghātaya (2) hūṃ phaṭ svāhā astrāya phaṭ*. Then: *oṃ hrīṃ rthaṃ drā*.
Oṃ viṃ vaiḍiṇyāyai vauṣaṭ; Oṃ hrīṃ yaṃ vaidinyāyai vauṣaṭ;
Oṃ oṃ hrīṃ ānandinyāyai vauṣaṭ; Oṃ laṃ bodhinyāyai vauṣaṭ;
Oṃ hrīṃ maṃ unmādinyāyai vauṣaṭ; Oṃ hrīṃ kṣaṃ sammohinyai vauṣaṭ.
Having worshipped the group of eight goddesses in a separate vessel by circling counter-clockwise with the mantras: *Oṃ hrīṃ raṃ grāsiṇyai vauṣaṭ* and *Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ mūrchinyai vauṣaṭ*,
[one should worship] *Oṃ gluṃ mluṃ pluṃ nluṃ lkuṃ Ratneśvaryai amba pādu*.

"Kābhyo namaḥ"—with this, for the sake of averting the confusion of vessels, one should worship Ratneśvarī in the vessel. Oṃ glūṃ slūṃ slūṃ mlūṃ; [I worship] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, who are of the nature of the five jewels, as food.

*yāmiphaṭ svāhā*, *carukāya vauṣaṭ*. Having prepared the sacrificial pap (*caru*) in the vessel, one should offer black meat. Then, taking the black meat between the middle finger and the thumb, one should satisfy the Guru upon the head according to the traditional method: *oṃ hrīṃ*.
Śrīṃ bhairavāya vauṣaṭ; oṃ anāśritaśivāya vauṣaṭ;
oṃ sadāśivāya vauṣaṭ; oṃ īśvarāya vauṣaṭ; oṃ rudrāya vauṣaṭ; oṃ viṣṇave vauṣaṭ; oṃ brahmaṇe vauṣaṭ.
Six: Oṃ durvāsāya vaṣaṭ; Oṃ vyāsāya vaṣaṭ;
likewise to Vyāsa, vaṣaṭ; likewise to Vāsuki, vaṣaṭ;
to Yājñavalkya, Vasiṣṭha, Utuṅga, and Śrīkaṇṭha.
To Ṭhāya, Somānanda, Kṣemagupta, Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, Kṣemarāja, Janakarāja,
Amṛta, Deveśvara, and Prajñālipta— salutations to them.

Having gratified the lineage of gurus at the crown of the head with the *pānaka* (nectar) while reciting, "To Dānanda, to Śarvānanda, to my own guru, vauṣaṭ," one should then satisfy the others between the eyebrows; thereafter, [one should satisfy] the Brahmin within one's own body.

The sprinkling (starpaṇa) is as follows: Oṃ, to the wheel of the big toe, whose presiding deities are Kālāgni Rudra and Bhairava, O Mistress of the Brahmā-ādi Bhūcarī-cakra, to the Śakti of Brahmā, to Gāyatrī, Vauṣaṭ. Oṃ, to the wheel of the knees...

To the goddess Bhairava born from *dyo*, to Ulkāmukhī and the others in the directions, to the mistress of the wheel (*cakra*), to the power of Viṣṇu, and to Mahāmāyā— *oṃ* six times. To the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*), to Vāmadeva-Bhairava as the presiding deity, and to Jayā.
Oṃ, to the mistress of the wheel of deities beginning with Disiddhā and Vāmā, the power of action (kriyā-śakti), Nityaklinnā, svāhā; oṃ,
to the mistress of the wheel of the range of the red [deities] and others, whose deity is Caṇḍeśvara-Bhairava, at the navel-wheel (nābhicakra).

Oṃ, to the one who is the single Kuṇḍalinī power, to Kāmamālinī, Svāhā! Oṃ, to the one whose deity is Aghorabhairava in the heart-cakra, to the leader of the circle of Mothers beginning with Aruṇā, to Rudra-śakti, to the Red One, Svāhā!

Oṃ, to the one whose deity is Mahābhairava in the face-cakra, who belongs to the Kulakaula lineage, who is born from the beginning, who is the leader of the circle of the eight Yoginīs beginning with Akṣobhyā, to the Jyeṣṭhā-śakti Kālarātri, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ, to the center of the eyebrows...
Oṃ, to the sovereign of the wheel of energies (śakticakra), who is both non-terrible and more terrible than the terrible, peaceful, and whose deity is Cakreśvarī-Bhairava;
to Jñānaśakti, the wearer of the garland of points (bindu), Vauṣaṭ! Oṃ, in the Karandhra-cakra, [resides] Anāśrita-bhairava.
"Oṃ, to the mistress of the circle of the *khecarīs*—beginning with Viccā, Ugra, Ghorā, and the rest—who is the lord of the deities, who is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), and who is peaceful;
*aiśāntāyai* *oṣaṭ*. Thus, the eight wheels are to be worshipped on the staff with drops from the drinking vessel. Then, on the skull..."
Oṃ ānandeśvarabhairava-surādevyardhanārīśvarabhairavāya vauṣaṭ; oṃ caṇḍabhairavāya vauṣaṭ; oṃ krodhabhairavāya vauṣaṭ; oṃ śekharabhairavāya vauṣaṭ. Asi.
Oṃ tāṅgabhairavāya vaṣaṭ; oṃ svacchandabhairavāya vaṣaṭ;
oṃ rurubhairavāya vaṣaṭ; oṃ kapāleśabhairavāya vaṣaṭ.

Oṃ unmattabhairavāya vauṣaṭ; Oṃ vāmadevabhairavāya vauṣaṭ. Thus, Bhairava should be worshipped by the twice-born in the skull-bowl (muṇḍapātra). Then: Śrīṃ vāmāyai vauṣaṭ; likewise to Jyeṣṭhā and Raudrī. Kā...
To Lyai Kalavikaraṇyai, Valavikaraṇyai, Valapramathinyai, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanyai, *vauṣaṭ*.
Thus, they should be worshipped with wine, meat, and rice by the Brahmins. Then, [the offering of] wheat...
One should offer the *caru* mixed with clarified butter, saying "May it be nectar," and so forth.
As for that which was stated: "The sinful soul who eats the four [meats] beginning with the *khecarī*, which are devoid of wheat and parched grain—even a hero [goes] to hell."
Then, having first performed the removal of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍotsādana*) with all the ritual materials, he should perform the invocation of the ancestors by name: *Oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍīkāpāle svāhā;
[I invoke] my ancestors, named so-and-so, of the Bhairava lineage, eternally...*

"Make them [the ancestors] consist of eternal bliss"— having spoken thus, one should offer the *piṇḍas* with the end of the *caru*. Then, one should offer [oblations] all around the *piṇḍas* for those who are anywhere in the three worlds— whether in the netherworld (*pātāla*), in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), or in the middle [on earth].

"May all my ancestors be satisfied with the sacrificial porridge and drinks. Then follows the offering (*bali*) to the young students (*vaṭuka*) and others. Next is the recitation (*japa*) of Śrī Ānandeśvara Bhairava, whose [mantra] is that of Kālāgnirudra Bhairava.

Ṛ, Samrāṭ, Ānandeśvarabhairava-ude, Śrīṃ Vīṃ Hrīṃ Śa Klīṃ Kīṃ; this is the viniyoga for the recitation (japa). Oṃ Juṃ Si [and so forth] is the nyāsa. Now, the meditation (dhyāna): [He who is] like ten million suns, like the moon...
One should meditate upon the Lord who is exceedingly cool, possessing eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes; situated in the midst of an ocean of nectar, standing upon a Brahma-lotus,
mounted on a bull, blue-throated, and adorned with all ornaments.
The god who wears a palaka and a khaṇḍāṅga, who resounds with the ringing of bells, who holds a noose and a goad, who bears a mace and a club, who wields a sword, a shield, a spear,
a mallet, a trident, and a lance, and who possesses a variegated shield—
One should meditate upon Ānandabhairava, whose hands grant boons and protection, who has a red body, who is accompanied by his Goddess, and who is saluted by Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
he is the sole cause of worldly enjoyment and liberation, established in his own nature and his own path.
I bow to that Bhairava, who is the object of experience, whose own splendor is his own bliss, and who is established in his own state. Now, the root mantra: Oṃ juṃ saḥ (9) saḥ juṃ oṃ.
To Ānandeśvara Bhairava, vauṣaṭ svāhā (108). This is the *guhmantra*.

Then follows the rite for the preparation of the *caru* offering; may the supreme nectar, the *caru*, which effects the complete fulfillment of all the Mistress-of-the-Body deities moving within the entire wheel, attain perfection for me, O Mother!

Thinking that the cold [nectar] has arrived, the wise one should meditate on the *caru* in the left hand as having the form of the Moon, and contemplate the vessel in the right hand as having the form of the Sun;
having filled it with the five nectars and drunk the nectar from the left, he should raise [the vessel].
Having become nine-fold in age, one should enter the middle digit;
having emitted the resonance of the *piṇḍa*, one should then satisfy Vāmeśī.
Thus, having drunk the beverage from the vessel, one should turn the vessel face down.
One should place [the offering] upon an inverted vessel and scatter [the substances] over it,
while reciting the five-fold *samaya*: *Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ namaḥ te jorāśe sarvatattvāhlādakāriṇi mayūramukhi*.
O bestower of non-terrible accomplishments, O you who are fashioned by great enthusiasm, O Pālinīvarma, O Raṅga, grant me the *samaya* [pledge], O Rudra,
beloved of the fierce gods and asuras, O destroyer of Śukra’s curse!

*Vrahmahatyāhare hrīṃ phrīṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. We praise the Goddess Ānandasamayā, who wears a garment of blood-stained hide, who is mounted upon a corpse, possesses four arms, and holds a skull-bowl (*kādy*) and a sword (*khaḍga*). Oṃ Oṃ.

O Great Bhairavī, who grants forgiveness and liberation; O Raktacāmuṇḍā, who is impassioned with love; O Mistress of Heroes and Skulls, mounted upon a corpse whose waist is covered with human skin and who is surrounded by a multitude of hissing serpents—Viśve Svāhā! (1) Oṃ Hrīṃ Huṃ Ku...

Lakauleśvarī, comfort me! O flood of the nectar of bliss, salutations to you, the bestower of all desires! Hrīṃ Huṃ Svāhā. (2) Oṃ Haṃ Pi Cu, to the one with the face; Haṃ, O attractor of all; Haṃ, [to the one who draws] the entire world without remainder...

I am the one who embraces; I am the one whose nature is supreme bliss; in the Lord Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, who is all-pervading and immeasurable, phaṭ svāhā. Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ, [I bow] to her who arises from the union of Śiva and Śakti, the immortal one.
O Caṇḍa, whose body is made fragrant by the scent of [sacrificial] fat; O Mahākāpālin Caṇḍeśvara, who abidest in the midst of the iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumṇā;
[salutations] to you, O Kulakaulīśvarī, with the flood of the nectar of your own bliss. Saḥ saḥ.
She who grants all desires: viśve hrīṃ huṃ sphreṃ phaṭ (3) svāhā (4).
Oṃ hrīṃ, O source of the six wheels and sixteen supports, vauṣaṭ! O Mother, [residing] in the belly, in the midst of the *suṣumṇā*, and in the equal apertures.
*Viṣamanityoditaprabhave guhyacakreśvari svā / Nandāmṛtaughasaḥ saḥ saḥ saḥ saḥ sarvakāmaprade vi cce svāhā.* (5) Thus is the fivefold pledge (*samaya*). Then [he addressed] the Blessed One.
One should release [the deity] with: *Oṃ hūṃ bhagavan sarvamitra arciṣe vyomavyāpine mahācakreśa śaraṇādhika sarvataḥ kṣamasva me punarāgamanāya prasīda sarvasiddhīḥ prayaccha namo namaḥ*.
Oṃ namaste tu svāhā.
[This is the mantra for dismissal. Thus ends the secret discussion regarding the initiation of the arts (kalādīkṣā). Thus the Ānandeśvara-paddhati is completed.]
Oṃ, salutations to the Guru. Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Oṃ, I bow to that Bhairava Āgama which they declare to be the fruit of the Veda-tree, whose infinite branches are complete. Oṃ, vi...
With the right hand [holding] faith (*bhraddakṣiṇahasta*), one should perform the complete worship with the mantra: *oṃ namo bhagavate vighneśvarāya hrīṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā gāṃ gīṃ guṃ gaiṃ gauṃ gaḥ*,
and having offered honey, ghee, and sugar as the food offering (*naivedya*).

"O Lord Vighneśvara, may whatever has been deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in procedure be forgiven by you; show your grace. Thus is the worship of Gaṇapati on the eight-petaled lotus to one's left. Then...
On a circular and very beautiful auspicious throne one cubit in size,
a lotus made of *iṣṭadala* (eight petals) should be fashioned. [The goddess] should be depicted as seated upon that lotus,
brilliant white, with three eyes, and holding in her four hands a rosary of fire (*jvālākṣamāla*), a lotus, a discus, and a sword.
I bow to Sarasvatī, the bestower of success, who is eternally praised by the Ṛbhus as the Great One.
Oṃ klīṃ sauḥ vada vāg-vādini sarasvatyai namaḥ. Aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ—thus is the worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjana*). Then...
Having offered an oblation of ghee and sugar to the four-armed one, who dwells upon a great lotus, resides in the lotus, abides in the garland of letters,
and is endowed with the trident, garland, and sword— one [purifies] that which is deficient in mantra and deficient in ritual action.
"O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, may whatever has been performed by you without the proper ritual procedure be forgiven out of Your compassion. Thus ends the worship of Pustaka-Vāgīśī.
Now, in the northeast corner, upon a beautiful seat smeared with auspicious unguents...
One should worship the auspicious vessel named Śiva— which is adorned with lotuses, filled with fragrant and pure water, and endowed with fruits, red minerals, and medicinal herbs—
using the Śiva-mantra; and likewise, having poured [the water] out.

One should worship the vessel for the water for the feet (*vārdhānikā*) placed on the left with flowers, fragrant substances, and sandalwood, by means of the application of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). Thereafter, one should recite the hymn containing many forms (*bahurūpagarbha-stotra*). Then, in the southwest (*naiṛtya*), one should prepare the vessel for the weapon-offering (*astrārghyapātra*) with the weapon-mantra.

Sprinkling all substances with *tvāta*: *oṃ phaṭ*, may there be purification of all ritual offerings, *phaṭ svāhā*. *Ādhūmra* (2), *jīva* (2), *saḥ* (2). *Sarvāsāṃ puṣpajātīnāṃ jīvā āgacchantu svāhā*. *Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ*.

*Plīnamaḥ puṣpeṣu*—thus, for the flowers: *Oṃ, to the one whose form is the fire of time (Kālāgni), who possesses the fragrance of the universe, the bearer of all scents, salutations to the incense.* For the lamp: *To the one whose form is the light of the universe, the lamp, salutations.* For the scent: *Gandhamā...* [The text ends here].
May all living beings partake of the fragrance of the day, svāhā! To the sandalwood, hrīṃ svāhā! To the saffron, oṃ lāṃ, obeisance to the Earth, O Dharitrī, the Power!
For the arghya: oṃ blīṃ, to King Varuṇa.
*Oṃ namo to the body in water; Oṃ Nluṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhasman in the vermilion; Jrīṃ, obeisance to Sāvitrī, the devourer of sins, on the *darbha* grasses.
Thus is the purification of the substances. [One should contemplate] the messenger, gentle, four-armed, and sweet-sounding, with the mantra...

One should worship her with the mantra: "Obeisance to Ghoṣiṇī, who holds a rosary, a book, a garland, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; Oṃ Huṃ, obeisance to Śuddhavidyā, the Mother of Mantras, the Messenger. While sounding the tabor, [one worships] Amṛteśā.
"May He whose body is the sky, whose intellect is the ether, and whose eyes are the sun, impel us. (3) "Salutation to the one who possesses a halo within the circle of planets; salutation to Vṛṣabha;
salutation to Bhṛṅgīśa; salutation to the quarters of space"—thus [one should worship] in the sky.

Then, the worship of the door: *Gaṅganeśāya namaḥ*, *Kumārarāya namaḥ*, *Śrīṃ Śriyai namaḥ*, *Saṃ Sarasvatyai namaḥ*, *Vaṃ Viśvakarmaṇe namaḥ*. [One should offer] a handful of flowers facing [the deity].

One should cause the All-pervading Lord, together with his retinue, to enter, and utter "Welcome! Welcome to Śiva, together with his retinue! Then, one should offer a seat with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Self. Thus, [one prepares] the seat.
One should offer [oblations with]: "To Umā, Durgā, Bhadrakālī, Svasti, Svāhā, Śubhaṅkarī, Gaurī, Śrī, Lokadhātrī, and Vāgīśvarī—salutations to you!
Salutations to Umā! Salutations to Durgā! Salutations to Bhadrakālī!"

Then follows the worship of the door: on the left branch of one's own [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*; on the right branch of one's own [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the left branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ diṇḍine namaḥ*. On the right branch of the opposite [side], *Oṃ naṃdine namaḥ*, *Oṃ meṣāsyāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*, *O
To the one [marked] with *Oṃ mahākālāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ yamunāyai namaḥ*,
*Oṃ chāgalāmyāyai namaḥ*, and *Oṃ mahodarāya namaḥ* above the door; and *Oṃ gaṇeśāya namaḥ*.

*Maḥ* at the door; *Namaḥ* at the threshold. *Oṃ vāstupuruṣāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*. *Namaḥ sarvebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ*. "May those beings depart, O beings!"—thus [one should recite] over the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Having performed the *yāma* [offering] with the mantra "O God, svadhā," and having meditated upon Śiva, one should offer salutations:

"Salutation to the principle of Sadāśiva (*sadāśivatattva*) in the aperture of the crown (*karandhra*); salutation to the principle of Īśvara (*īśvaratattva*) on the forehead; salutation to the principle of Vi[ṣṇu] between the eyebrows."
Salutation to the principle of *dyā* (the sky) in the palate; salutation to the principle of *māyā* in the palate;
salutation to the principle of *kāla* (time) in the throat; salutation to the principle of *niyati* (destiny) in the heart; salutation to the principle of *puruṣa* (the person) in the navel.
Oṃ! Salutation to the principle of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva) at the genitals; salutation at the feet. Oṃ.
Oṃ juṃ, obeisance to the Śivatattva at the crown of the head; Oṃ juṃ, obeisance to the Vidyātattva between the eyebrows; Oṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Ātmatattva in the heart;
Oṃ juṃ saḥ, obeisance to the embodiment of nectar (Amṛtamūrti) throughout the entire body. Then:

The ritual placement of the six limbs on the hands (*kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*): *hūṃ phaṭ oṃ juṃ saḥ oṃ juṃ saḥ*. With "I bow to my own self," one sprinkles oneself (*ātma-prokṣaṇa*). One should apply a tilaka mark on one's own forehead seven times with the root mantra. [One should perform] the water-offering (*argha*) with the six limbs.
One should place flowers upon the heads [of the deities]. Then, for the worship of the seat within the two jars at the *svastika* and lotus: "Obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to the stalk;
obeisance to Dharma; obeisance to Jñāna; obeisance to Vairāgya..."
Salutations to Sovereignty; salutations to the Ṛgveda; salutations to the Yajurveda; salutations to the Sāmaveda; salutations to the Atharvaveda;
salutations to the Kṛta Age; salutations to the Tretā Age; salutations to the Dvāpara Age.

Salutations to the one who embodies the Dvāpara Yuga; salutations to the one who embodies the Kali Yuga; salutations to the one seated upon the thousand-petaled lotus throne; salutations to the one seated upon the eight-petaled lotus throne;
salutations to the sword of knowledge whose form consists of the thirty-six principles (tattvas).

The Guru, taking the mantra-vessel and the weapon-water vessel, should place them in the hands of the disciple and cause a continuous stream [of water] to fall in the directions starting from the east, saying:
"O Indra! Come! (2) Stay! (2) Be present! (2)"

One should not perform the *vārdhānī* (water-offering) while reciting "Bho-bho Brahman" or "Bho Ananta.
Then, one should place the *śivakalaśa* upon a lotus;
the *astravārdhānī* is placed upon a *svastika* in the northeast (*īśāna*).

One should worship her holding in her left hands a shield, a noose, a bow, a boon-granting gesture, and a triple-pointed trident, while in her right hands she holds a lute, a flag, a mallet, a conch, a goad, a kandalī flower, and a ḍamaru drum.
We praise the Lord who is moon-white, whose face is like an arrow, and who stands amidst a trident, a lotus, and gestures of fearlessness and granting boons;
with the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," one should worship the God residing in the pitcher, together with his limbs and his retinue. Oṃ.

One should worship the six limbs with "namaḥ śivāya" and so forth. Then follows the worship of the seven enclosures (āvaraṇas): "Oṃ, obeisance to the path of mantras"; likewise for the paths of words, letters, worlds, principles (tattvas), and kalās. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the kalā of Nivṛtti. Oṃ hāṃ ni... [and so on].
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the *vṛtti-kalā*. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*.
Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the *vidyā-kalā*. Oṃ hūṃ, [salutation] to the lord of the *vidyā-kalā*.
Salutation to Rudra.
Oṃ haiṃ śāṃtākalāyai namaḥ. Oṃ haiṃ śāntyatītākalādhipataye īśvarāya namaḥ. Oṃ phāṃ śāntyatītā...
*Oṃ hāṃ śāntyatītā-kalādhipataye sadāśivāya namaḥ*.

Salutations to Sadāśiva, the lord of the Śāntyatītā Kalā. He is marked by white [arms] on the right, equipped with a conch, mace, lotus, and discus, and by [arms] on the left, bearing a book and a mirror.

I now bow to the all-pervading Lord Śrī Vāsudeva, who shines eternally in close proximity to the jar of the primordial lotus-lake, who is mounted upon Garuḍa, who is the supreme object of compassion for his devotees, who is marked by the digit of Lakṣmī, and who today grants boons.

To Vāsudeva, to Lakṣmī, may that Viṣṇu [grant] us [protection]. (3) Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva. Oṃ hṛṃ, obeisance to the head; to the Blessed One, obeisance to the crest-lock; vāsuka, obeisance to the eyes; devān, obeisance to the weapons.
Oṃ! [I bow to the Lord] whose face is as radiant as ten million fires at the end of an aeon,
who has the color of vermilion powder and the *japā* flower, who wears a jeweled crown, who is two-eyed,
who sits upon the center of a white lotus, who is adorned with various ornaments, and who possesses a smiling countenance.

I worship the Sun, who is clad in red garments, whose nature is consciousness, and who holds a golden lotus and a jeweled pitcher in his two arms; O Bhāskara, [grant] that wisdom to us for the sake of the thousand-rayed Sun. Om hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sū.
Oṃ, salutations to the vehicle! Oṃ hrāṃ [heart], oṃ hrīṃ [head], oṃ hūṃ [crown-lock], oṃ hraiṃ [armor], oṃ hauṃ [eyes], oṃ hraḥ [weapon]. Oṃ, salutations to the elephant-faced one!
One should meditate upon him who has sharp tusks, three eyes, a large belly, and is infinite.
I bow to Śrī Gaṇeśa, who holds a rosary, an axe, and a pair of lotuses in his hands, and who is seated upon the pair of lions.
Oṃ gaṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ. (108) Oṃ gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ.

*Gaigauṃgaḥ*—these are the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgāni*). Oṃ! To her who holds in her left hands a trident, a sword, a great arrow, a discus, a conch, a shield, a bow, and a threatening gesture, and who stands upon the back of the great buffalo-demon, [I offer salutations]. Her thighs are like stalks of *dūrvā* grass.
May she, the beloved Durgā, who is the source of all desired attainments, be present. Oṃ duṃ, obeisance to Durgā.
(108) Oṃ hṛ, hrīṃ śi, duṃ śikhā, duḥka gā netre, yai namaḥ astrā, subhamāyai vikāmamalinīyai dhī, tat no durgā.

The visualization is with the seven seed-syllables: *pra*. "Oṃ, that wisdom which [is attained] by the seven-syllabled mantra of Śārikā, may that Śārikā inspire us. (3) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ phrāṃ āṃ śāṃ, obeisance to Śārikā. (108) repetitions)
Śāṃ, śīṃ, śūṃ, śai, śauṃ, śaḥ—these are the six seed-syllables. Oṃ! [I bow to her] who has six arms and three eyes, whose smiling face is praised by the sage Śāṇḍilya, and who stands upon a mountain.
O you who possess splendor, fortitude, and power!
I meditate upon the blessed Goddess Śāradā in my heart: Oṃ śmīṃ, obeisance to the blessed Goddess Śāradā.
Śmāṃ for the heart, śmīṃ for the head, śi for the crest-lock, śmūṃ for the armor, śmai for the eyes, śmauṃ for the neck, śmaḥ for the weapon. Oṃ, like the rising sun...
With the fifteen-syllable mantra for the bestowal of sovereignty, beginning with *sahasra*, [the prayer is]:
"Obeisance to that Queen. (3) *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rāṃ klīṃ sauḥ bhagavatyai rājñyai hrīṃ svāhā* (108). *Oṃ hrīṃ hṛ śrīṃ śi rāṃ śikhā*.
*Klīṃ kava sauḥ netre bhagavatyai rājñe hrīṃ svāhā trāya phaṭ*. Oṃ, she whose face and limbs are surrounded by flames,
who holds a lotus, a conch, a sword, and a mace, and who is seated upon a lion-throne.
I meditate with devotion upon the lotus feet of Jvālāmukhī.
*Oṃ*, to the Mother, to the Great Illusion, *dhī*; may that Mother inspire us.
(3) *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ jvālāmukhi*, destroy all my enemies!
*Kṣaya* (2) *huṃ phaṭ svāhā* (108). Then the six-limbed [nyāsa] beginning with *hrāṃ hrīm* and so forth.
Thereafter, the worship of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī:
[I bow to] the primordial deity, whose crown is adorned with the crescent moon, who is exceedingly beautiful, and who possesses a face like the orb of the full moon.
I take refuge in the three-eyed Lord Amṛteśvara, who is seated upon a lotus-throne,
who holds a vessel of nectar, a lotus, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and whose body is the void.
We know Amṛteśa, whose body is the void.

*Dhī tanno netraḥ pra* (3) *Oṃ juṃ saḥ amṛteśvara-bhairavāya namaḥ* (108). *Oṃ hṛ juṃ śivyoṃ śikhā īka jyauṃ ne phaṭ a*. Having thus worshipped the Śiva-vessel (*śivakalaśa*), [perform] the invocation of the weapon (*astrāvāhana*).

One should worship the *Rdhānī* [the seat of accomplishment] with: *oṃ haḥ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*, *oṃ haḥ phaṭ jñānāstrāya phaṭ*. Likewise, [one worships] the *Brahmāstra*, the *Brahmaśirostra*, the *Agnyastra*, the *Lokapālāstra*, the *Pāśupatāstra*, the *Aghorāstra*, and the *Divyāstra* with: *oṃ haḥ phaṭ sa*.
Oṃ, salutation to the sword; Oṃ, salutation to the shield; Oṃ, salutation to the noose; Oṃ, salutation to the goad; Oṃ, salutation to the arrow;
Oṃ, salutation to the Pināka bow; Oṃ, salutation to the boon-granting gesture; Oṃ, salutation to the gesture of fearlessness.
Oṃ, homage to Muṇḍa; oṃ, homage to Khaṭvāṅga; oṃ, homage to Vīṇā; oṃ, homage to Ḍamaru; oṃ, homage to Ghaṇṭā;
oṃ, homage to Triśūla; oṃ, homage to Vajra; oṃ, homage to Daṇḍa.
Oṃ, obeisance to Paramaśava; Oṃ, obeisance to Mudgara; Oṃ, obeisance to Vajra. Thus, ghee, milk, sugar, honey, and likewise grapes—these five nectars (pañcāmṛta) should indeed be offered.
Having given [the gift], one should inform the Lord.
O Blessed One, you who come to partake of stored offerings, who protect the sacrifice, who fill the voids, and who remove impurity;
O Supreme Lord, whose power pervades the universe, by your grace may the sacrifice be completed. O Destroyer of Evil, you are the universal power of all.
By your grace, may the sacrifice be accomplished.

"I shall always remain present for you; may there be no deficiency. Śaṃkara Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ. To the one whose nature is the sacrificial substance Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ. O Immortal One, accept [this]; obeisance. Thus is the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa). Now, furthermore—
Having performed the worship of the *la-śa* [syllables] and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's own self with "Oṃ nau," one venerates the Great Lord (*Maheśa*),
who is the light of one's own self and who has pacified the mass of uneven afflictions; she then conceives that goddess of speech.

I take refuge in the excellent Guru who first bestowed initiation and later granted knowledge— the king of obstacles, whose vast belly is like the sky for the continuous devouring of impediments, and who is the root of the creeper of speech that lies dormant.

I bow to Maheśa, the Lord of the Universe; I bow to the supreme Goddess of Speech; I bow to the god Lambodara; I bow to the sandals of my Guru. Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ, I offer this sacred thread (pavitraka) with obeisance to the Self.
To the one whose nature is Śiva, obeisance to the unguent of fragrance;
obeisance to the water-offering (arghya); obeisance to the flower. I bind this bracelet upon you, O steadfast one skilled in devotion, for the severing of the fear of worldly existence.

May Lord Śiva protect that which is impure, that which leads to non-existence here, and the eternal state; may He protect the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the eyes, ears, nose, mind, head, and hands—whatever has been acquired even in its primordial nature. (2)
May the Blessed Lord Śiva, the remover of evil, grant you auspiciousness;
may the hosts of spirits be intent on peace; and may Nārāyaṇa protect you with effort from the great delusion in the desert wilderness of saṃsāra. (3)
O Śiva, please accept this nectar-like eye;
O Śiva, please accept this lamp which has the form of Kālāgnirudra and destroys all sins.
O Śiva, please accept this incense which generates all auspicious fortune and possesses two arms.
One should meditate upon the Sun in this manner— as having a gentle face, holding a lotus in his hand, being circular, clothed in red garments, and situated in the center of the orb of light—
bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, and identical in nature to Śiva himself.
Incense, obeisance; Lamp, obeisance. The life-force of the Aśvins, the taking of life:
Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Krau Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Vaṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ Haṃ Haṃsaḥ So'haṃ. The vital breaths of Paramaśiva are here, his vital breaths.
Thus,
all the senses of Paramaśiva are situated here; thus, the speech, mind, skin, eyes, ears, vital breath, and so forth of Paramaśiva are situated here within the individual self (jīvātman).
It does not come from a bodyless source.

"May this [mantra] remain for a long time in happiness, svāhā. One should perform the ritual of placement (nyāsa) upon the body exactly as it is on the deity; the Rākṣasas seize half of that rite which is devoid of nyāsa. "Anābhau," etc., Oṃ bhūḥ.
I invoke the Puruṣa, obeisance! Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa, obeisance! Oṃ svaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa, obeisance!
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ;
may he inspire our intellects. Oṃ (3). To the one who lies in immortality, whose body is the ether—[we meditate upon him]; may he, the leader, inspire us. (3). That Pu...

Oṃ, salutation to the one with the curved trunk; may that Dantī inspire us. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose form is the sun; may that Sūrya inspire us. Oṃ, salutation to Kārttikeya; may he, the commander of the army, inspire us.

May that Kumāra inspire our intellects. (3) May that Maheśa, whose body is the sky, inspire our intellects. (0) May that Netra inspire our intellects. (3) May that Puruṣa, the Great God, inspire our intellects. (0) May that Rudra, whose nature is Śiva, inspire our intellects. (3) Śivātmakam.
[And so forth: "Obeisance to Vāsudeva; may that Viṣṇu, who is the consort of Lakṣmī, inspire us. Obeisance to Subhaga; may that Durgā, who is the consort of Kāma and Mālya, impel us.
Today, [at this time], of the Blessed Nandirudra... gaṃ.
[The hymns] of Mahākāla, Yamunā, Meṣāsya, Chāgalāsya,
Caṇḍa, Upacaṇḍa, Śaṅkhanidhi, Padmanidhi, Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, and so forth.
[This is] for the sake of the eight Bhavas, of Dyuti with her retinue,
of the maker of causes, of the eleven Ādityas,
of the deities of the mantra-vessel, of the deities of the weapon-vessel, and of Vāsudeva.
[The seed-syllables] *syā* (3), *hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūryasya* (6), *vināyakasya* (13),
*amāyā* and so forth [are for] the ten world-protectors beginning with Indra, and the eight Bhairavas beginning with Kapāleśa; this is situated in the center of this maṇḍala.
Of that glorious Svacchandabhairava, there are the deities of the seven enclosures,
the five faces, the six limbs, and the nine powers beginning with Vāmā, [along with] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva.
Of which six paths [is this the purification]: of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī and her retinues, of the Pratyaṅgirā deities, of the twelve Aṃhas, of Heruka, of Tripurāntaka,
of Agnivetāla, of Agnijihva, and of Kara...

On the thirteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], [one should worship] Lasya, known as Kāla, the one-footed one of terrifying form; Tāraka, Hāṭakeśvara, and Rājarājeśvara; and all the deities who are guardians of the fields (kṣetrapāla), beginning with Aja.
To the south of Devīputra Vaṭukanātha.

To the north of the Vaṭuka-bali is the place of the Yoginīs; to the west is that of the Kṣetrapāla; to the east of the Bhūta-bali is the center for the Rājarājeśvara; in the northeast is that of the Vahukhādaka; and in the northwest is [the place] of Sava.
To Labhasya Gaṇapati, to Nairṛti, to Āhu, to the deities of the fourfold tradition, to Vetāla Bhairava, to Turuṣkarājānaka,
to Maṅgalyarājānaka, and to Kulavāgīśvara.
Of Ryyāḥśuṣkeśvara, Pathikeśvara, Puṇyarājānaka,
Loṣṭarājānaka, Kuḍārarājānaka, Ānandarājānaka, and Pañcālarājānaka.
For the purpose of warding off the sins accumulated through speech, mind, and body by myself and by the lords of Kaṇṭhaka, Heruka, and the others,
and for the sake of attaining the aforementioned results, [this is performed] on account of the Śivarātri vow.

"I shall perform the worship of the Laśas, the worship of Śrī Śiva, and the worship of the Kṣetrapālas; Oṃ, do so! Having scattered sesame and mustard seeds, [one performs] the worship of the deities of the door beginning with Mahāgaṇapati.
This is the seat for them; obeisance. This is the seat for the deities of the mantra-vase and the deities of the weapon-vase; obeisance.
To the Lord Nandirudra and to the other deities, [I offer] you...
I worship you: *Oṃ pūjaya bhagavantaṃ nandirudram*. Thus, I shall invoke the deities. *Oṃ āvāhaya*.
Having scattered barley grains, I invoke Gaṇanātha.

I invoke the God, whose pair of arms bears a goad, a rosary of beads, and a bracelet, who has a lion as his seat, and who shines with an axe and a vessel in his two left hands for the sake of protecting the world.

"May Śiva, the lord of Pārvatī, mounted upon his bull-throne, adorned with serpent-ornaments, be pleased; may the Lord of the Universe be satisfied for the sake of the sacrificer. [Recite] "O white-colored one," and so forth, ending with "I invoke."
I indeed [saw] that Lord Viṣṇu, who possesses universal forms, having four faces and four arms,
bearing the conch, discus, and mace, seated upon the lord of birds (Garuḍa),
ever united with Kamalā, resembling the *atasī* flower, and yellowish-white.
Those who worship Govinda, whose garment is the sky and who is imperishable—for them no fear exists. I invoke here the god Bāli, the flower;
I invoke the god Bhānu, the teacher of the entire world; Aruṇa...
O Lord of the World, mass of splendor, whose chariot is drawn by seven horses and whose charioteer is he [Aruṇa]— O you who possess the brilliance of a thousand suns!
Out of compassion for me, O Bhakti, please remove my suffering like the sun dispelling darkness;
O Bali, I invoke the god Gaṇeśa,
who is well-worshipped, the eternal remover of obstacles, and the granter of all desires.

I invoke the goddess Pārvatī, the bestower of boons, who grants fruits [of action], who possesses the color of jewels, who is endowed with great splendor, adorned with garlands of gems and ornaments, and who is the beloved wife of Hara.
O you of beautiful limbs, who increase prosperity, come, O Goddess, Sovereign of the World,
who delight the heart of Menā; O pure one, giver of boons, gentle one, ever dear to your devotees— I invoke you with this offering of flowers.
I bow to that great lord, the protector of the field (Kṣetrapāla), who dwells within all embodied beings— from worms and insects to humans— as well as in houses, fields, and forests,
and who is the Yakṣa, Bhūta, and Piśāca of dwellings, and who is the Gaṇas, Gandharvas, and Devas.

One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) with offerings (bali) and flowers. "I shall invoke these deities. Oṃ, invoke! Breath control (prāṇāyāma). Water for the feet (pādya), obeisance (namaḥ) phaṭ, to the weapon-mantra (astra).
*Phaṭ*. Fried grain, saffron, along with all medicinal herbs, sprouts of *darbha* grass, and water—this five-fold offering is the characteristic of the *pādya*.
"O Blessed Ones, this *pādya* for the Blessed Nandirudra. Thus [he offers].
"Obeisance to the deities; [I offer] water for the feet. One should set aside the remainder of the water for the feet.
Again: *phaṭ*, "to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, clarified butter, curd, rice, and barley—these are the six substances.
The eightfold *arghya* is proclaimed as consisting of these [eight] items. O Blessed One,
this *arghya* for the deities beginning with Bhagavān Nandirudra—
*namas* to the Blessed One Nandirudra, and so forth.

Having completed the rites beginning with the anointing from the *vātās* (wind-objects), saying "Obeisance to the fragrance," "Obeisance to the water-offering (*argha*)," "Obeisance to the flower," "Obeisance to the incense," "Obeisance to the lamp," and so forth, up to the final sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), [he should offer] a full vessel filled with rock-salt balls (*saindhava-vaṭaka*) and other such items.
Setting aside non-informative action (*avijñapti*), one should perform it as follows:
"O, Lord of Wealth! Make this place free from obstacles now; I shall perform the *Harārccana* for the sake of protecting others. O Blessed Planets!"
May all those who are considered subordinate deities grant me their presence for the pacification of obstacles. O Indra,
you must remain vigilant in your own quarter until the completion of the rite for the pacification of obstacles.
"By the command of Śiva: O Agni! O Yama! O Nairṛta! O Varuṇa! O Vāyu! O Kuvera! O Īśāna! O Brahmā!
O Ananta!"—thus the world-protectors (Lokapālas) were made to hear the command of Śiva.

"Salutations to all yogis; salutations again and again to the perfected ones (siddhas). Obeisance to the host of powers that perceive the Lord in both manifest and unmanifest forms. Having spoken thus, he performed the half-circumambulation.

Having performed the worship of the five deities (pañcāyatana-pūjā) specifically at the Śivaliṅga Mṛteśvara, one should perform its worship; that [procedure] has been written elsewhere. Then, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), one should worship Heruka and the others.
One should meditate on Heruka as tawny-black in color, with a distorted face, three faces, six arms, and three eyes; he wears red garments. [The mantra is:
*Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Kṣīṃ Herukāya Vauṣaṭ*. To the east, [one should meditate on him] with three faces and six arms.

And one should contemplate the hand [of the deity] holding a scissor (kartarī), a hand-drum (ḍamaru), a skull-bowl (kāpāla), an iron arrow (nārāca), and a bow; [the hand] with a fierce mouth, possessing fierce valor, the Bhairava who is the destroyer of Tripura.
[The mantra: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Lāṃ Kṣīṃ, obeisance to Tripurāntaka.
In the southeast and the south, there is the one-faced Agnivetāla,
black in color, with fangs like a mass of lightning, resembling the flaming fire of universal destruction; [his mantra is] Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ kṣuṃ agnivetālāya.
With the syllable *yavauṣaṭ*, [one should worship] the four-faced one of great splendor on the right, who has eight arms, whose seat is the corpse (*śava*),
who holds a skull-bowl (*muṇḍa*) and a battle-axe (*paṭṭisa*),
a bow, a noose of *kuśa* grass, a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), a *suraja* drum, and a lute (*tantrī*), and who dances upon a corpse.
In the center, accompanied by the eight guardians of the field (kṣetrapāla), with eyes gazing upward and a long neck,
[is the deity] Oṃ Rāṃ Kṣeṃ Agnijihva Yauṣaṭ; in the southwest is the one called Kāla,
and in the western seat (pīṭha) is the four-faced, three-eyed [deity].

One should meditate upon him who has four arms and a massive body, who wears a shaven head and a skull-staff, who holds a sword and a shield in his hands, who stands upon a tortoise-seat, who is adorned with a mass of matted hair and a crescent moon, and who bestows the eight supernatural powers: Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ hlāṃ.
"Kālākhyāya vaṣaṭ" [is for] the west; and I shall now describe the sixth [deity] in the northwest:
Kapālin, who has long arms, is of great stature, adorned with a snake-bracelet, and holds a skull-bowl, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a mace.
One should worship [the deity] seated upon a peacock-throne, adorned with tinkling bells, with offerings. [The mantra is: *KṢĀṂ KṢŪṂ* to Kapālīna, *VAUṢAṬ*.
In the northwest is Ekapāda; likewise, in the north is the four-faced one of auspicious countenance, *LAṂ*.
O Śīlinī, become one with a massive body, possessing eight arms and a corpse for a seat;
you who are bold, adorned with necklaces of jewels,
whose limbs are richly beautified by charming chowries, who delight in song, dance, and passion— drink the liquor!
Vāmana, the destroyer of all obstacles: ĀṂ YŪṂ KṢŪṂ Ekapādāya Vauṣaṭ. In the north, I shall describe the eightfold mantra;
in the northeast is Bhīmarūpin, who has eight arms, three eyes, and five faces.
In the northeast (Īśāna) is the ninth [deity], white in color, holding a sword and a shield in his hands, bearing weapons and a noose, seated upon a *preta*,
adorned with a garland of skulls, possessing a terrifying form, with the mantra *kṣāṃ hrīṃ kṣāṃ vauṣaṭ*. This is the ninth [deity] in the northeast.
I shall describe the supreme *Tāraka* [mantra] situated above, which has five faces, large eyes, and a terrible, fearsome form; it holds a shield,
a spear, a bow, arrows, a severed head, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a skull-cup, and is accompanied by the *Kṣetrapālas*.

Endowed with wrath, blazing brightly, and beloved by the people; *oṃ kṣāṃ hrīṃ kṣāṃ tārakāya vauṣaṭ*. Above, I shall now proclaim the tenth [deity], Pātālehāṭakeśvara, who has four arms, a massive body, and is long-limbed.

[He has] a face like that of a mute goat, holds a vajra and a khaṭvāṅga in his hands, is adorned with boisterous laughter, and holds a trident and a sword in his hands; he has a beautiful face and is the remover of fear. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Hāṭakeśvara in the netherworld (pātāla).

One should meditate upon the Lord of the King of Kings (Rājarājeśvara), who has three eyes and four arms, adorned with a garland of tinkling bells, and who delights in the sound of the lute. [The mantra is:
"Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Huṃ, Vauṣaṭ to the Lord of the King of Kings," in the center; thus [is the twelve-syllable mantra].
One should worship Śyāmā. Now, on the thirteenth day, the worship of Vaṭuka and others is as follows:
Oṃ! To that pervasive Lord Vaṭuka, who resides in the state beyond both Kula and Akula, whose form is consciousness, and who is filled with the essence of bliss—him I salute.

I bow to the god Ṭukabhairava, who is surrounded by the eight goddesses with their retinues seated upon lotus-thrones and corpses; he has five faces, is accompanied by his consort, dances while keeping time with a pair of arms, possesses five mouths, and is like a firefly in the midst of a conflagration.

I take refuge in Vaṭuka, the Lord of Heroes, who has a tawny luster, holds in his hands an excellent vessel, a banner, a sword, and a shield, grants all desires, carries a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff,
wields a sword and a shield, and dances with two hands.
Four-armed and bestowing prosperity, holding a skull-cup in his hand,
with earrings and a staff in his grasp, possessing the color of thick darkness,
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, he is the destroyer of obstacles during the worship at the time of sacrifice.
May Vaṭukanātha, the bestower of success upon practitioners,
who holds a noose, a goad, and a ḍamaru drum, who possesses a single face with a tawny beard, who is dancing, who has a bear-like countenance and three eyes, grant us joy.
I bow to the all-pervading Vaṭuka, whose crown is adorned with the mass of matted locks of Śiva; I bow to the Lord who resides upon the Northern Seat (Uttara-pīṭha),
whose face is radiant like crystal,
whose hair is dark, and who is adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh jewels and tinkling bells.

Where is the sky, where the wind, where the fire, and where the water— [compared to] Vaṭuka, who is richly adorned with anklets, radiant in form, praised by the three worlds, clad in red garments, possessing three eyes, and constantly holding a trident and a staff in his lotus-like hands?
Where are the gods and asuras, where is Brahmā, and where is Janārdana?

Victorious is the Lord Mahābhairava, the hero of the drama of divine play, who rejoices in the armies of the warriors of the dissolution at the end of the aeon— the earth, the waters, and the world-sustainer— He, the illustrious Siddhayogīśvara.

O Brahmā, fill the ocean with the mountain-like heads of the black lord of the Rākṣasas, which fall from their hot and cold uṣṇīṣas— heads thick with blood and fat, and dark with the dense smoke of the burning fragments of the cosmic egg. O Queen of Pātāla!

"O Tārā, O Mountain of Kurukṣetra Gold, stay! O Śambhu, the Goddess herself desires to form a circle. Thus addressed and commanded by Vaṭuka, may he purify [us]. Now, the door-keepers: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ viśvarakṣā*.
Oṃ, salutation to Karakiṃkara; Oṃ, salutation to Viśvarakṣākarakiṃkarī; Oṃ, salutation to Viśvasaṃmohanakiṃkara; Oṃ, salutation to Viśvasaṃmohanīkiṃkarī; Oṃ, salutation to Puṣpahāsā.
*Oṃ namaḥ adṛṣṭavigrahāya namaḥ*—thus [to] the door-keepers. *Oṃ gurupādukābhyāṃ namaḥ*—thus on the left. *Oṃ ādhāraśaktyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ dhātryai namaḥ*, *Oṃ payorṇavāya*.
Homage! Oṃ, homage to the Ocean of Nectar; oṃ, homage to the Lotus;
oṃ, homage to the Sprout of the Seed; oṃ, homage to the Lunar Disk; oṃ, homage to the Seat of the Thousand-Petaled Lotus; oṃ, homage to the Eight-Petaled [Lotus].
"Oṃ āsanāya namaḥ"— thus is the worship of the seat. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ phaṭ kṣaḥ kṣaḥ kṣaḥ hrīṃ aiṃ ha sa ya rthaṃ devīputra hrīṃ vaṭukanātha hraḥ kapila-jaṭā-bhāra-bhāsura-trinetra.

Jvālāmukha, Huṃkāra, Alipa, Piśitāda, take [this offering]! Jachā, Mudga, Kha, Kha! O Madonmattaka, Kāyavaṭuka, Ulkāmukha, Agnimukha—may the grace of your command be bestowed upon me! Oṃ ha sa kṣa ma.
Lava-ra-ya-rthaṃ-vaṭukāya namaḥ. Root mantra: Oṃ hrīṃ vaṭukāya āpaduddhāraṇāya kuru (2). Vaṭukāya hrīṃ (108).
Oṃ oṃ namaḥ to the eastern face; oṃ oṃ namaḥ to the southern face; oṃ.
Oṃ, obeisance to the upward-facing face. Oṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Sadyojāta face.
Oṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Vāmadeva face. Oṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Aghora face.
Oṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Tatpuruṣa face. Oṃ, obeisance to the Īśāna face.

Next is the mantra of the Goddess: *Oṃ hsaiṃ, may the grace of the command from the feet of the Goddess Sarvamaṅgalā be mine; hrīṃ svāhā* (108 times). This is the mantra of the Goddess in her lap. Now, on the right:
Thus concludes the worship of the *vaṭuka*. Now follows the worship of the *kṣetrapāla*:
Oṃ, [I salute] the one-footed, great-faced, five-faced, three-eyed one.
I bow to that son of the Goddess, Vaṭuka, who is exceedingly fierce,
who carries a noose, a goad, a hand-drum, and other weapons,
who performs a single, pure, and supreme dance, and whose face is like a bear.

Having meditated upon Vaṭuka, who has eyes like the moon and a mass of matted hair, and who is seated upon the northern pedestal, one should worship him with: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ devīputra vaṭukanātha kapila-jaṭābhāra-bhāsura trinetra jvālā*.
From [your] mouths (2), destroy all obstacles (2);
O you who have drawn up the heat, repeatedly (2); KṢUḤ (2); O protector of the field, accept the offering! SVĀHĀ.
Then, in the north, there is the movement of the wind from the earth, the netherworld, and the sky.
Those who bear the faces of a peacock, a lion, and a tiger, possessing four, ten,

and six arms respectively, and are endowed with various weapons; and the fierce female messengers (Dūtīs) with the faces of a horse, a deer, a cat, and a crow, are stationed in the direction of Kubera (the north).
The yogi, whose mind is firmly fixed on the seat (pīṭha) and who has meditated [upon it], should offer oblations with:
*oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ pheṃ pheṃ pheṃ khecarībhyo bhūcarībhyo dikcarībhyo sarvābhyo yoginībhyo vauṣaṭ*.

Liṅgṛhṇa (2) Haṃsaḥ saḥ pluṃ vauṣaṭ. Certain yoginīs, such as Raudrī and others—Oṃ, salutation to the Khecarīs; Oṃ, salutation to the Bhūcarīs; Oṃ, salutation to the Dikcarīs; Oṃ, [salutation] to the Ākāśa...
Salutation to those who go [there]. Now, in the western station,
there is the Lord Śaśa, possessing six arms and a most terrifying form,
holding in his hands an axe, a human skull, a khaṭvāṅga, a goad, and so forth.
May he who holds the mudrās, the svastika, and the tāṇḍava,
who is black in color, who daily bestows grain, and whose abode is in the western direction of the Lord of Asuras,
and who carries the khaṭvāṅga, the skull, the axe, and the staff— may he be victorious forever.
I bow to the fierce Kṣetrapāla, who is red in color, holds a vessel and a goad, and resides in his station—
[he] who dwells in this field, and so forth. Oṃ kṣeṃ, obeisance to the local Kṣetrapāla, the lord of your own kingdom.

O follower of Lāyasā, together with all beings, accept this worship, svāhā! Come, come! Curu, curu! Muru, muru! Break, break! Destroy, destroy! the obstacles! In the form of Mahābhairava, accept the offering, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ kṣāṃ!

To those beings who reside in the field-site, the Kṣetrapālas along with their attendants—to them I offer this bali; may they grant me auspiciousness. Now, in the east, [one should worship] those with one, two, three, or four arms, and those with ten, sixty-four, or one hundred arms.

In some places, we bow to those who possess various fierce and excellent weapons, who are the ornaments of all the worlds, who are endowed with the Tandava dance, who are either enraged or accompanied by their consorts,
who always face the east, and who dwell in the abode of Varuna— those most formidable ones.
I bow down to those spirits who have six, one, two, three, or four arms, whose hands blaze with various weapons, and who stand in the dramatic poses of frowning and joyful mirth.
Haṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! To all beings who follow the Blessed One, together with their wives and attendants, accept this offering and worship—Vauṣaṭ! Bhlūṃ Kṣlūṃ Nlūṃ Glūṃ! Kala (2)! Dhāva (2)! Tiṣṭha (2)!
Destroy all enemies! May all beings dwelling in the sky, on earth, and in the netherworld accept this offering;
may you be satisfied, and may success always be ours, *oṣaṭ*! Those who are the sustainers of the universe...
May those who have become separated from them, their followers, bring offerings;
being satisfied, may they destroy my misfortune.
Now, in the center, [is] the Lord of the Realm, with five faces and eleven arms, great—
I bow to the Lord of Siddhas, who dwells among the *pretas*, who has eleven eyes, and who resides in cities, sacred fields, and other holy places;
whose beautiful body is of various colors and golden hue,
and who shines with the sword, the goad, the noose, the blade, the severed head, and the trident.
One should meditate on Rāṣṭrapāla seated upon a corpse,
holding a *ḍamaru* drum and a jar in his hands; he has eleven faces in the center, five mouths, and is endowed with a bell, a noose, a sword, a radiant staff, a goad, and a *khaṭvāṅga*.
I bow to the Trident, the Vajra, and Kṣetrapāla. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ kṣuṃ! O Sovereign King of the Lords of Kṣetrapālas, ruler of this kingdom, descend! Drive away the obstacles! Drive them away! Kapi!
With a terrifying form possessing three eyes blazing with the brilliance of a mass of matted locks,
[uttering] *turu (2) muru (2) kha (2) la (2) ha (2) hā (2) he (2)*,
[offer] perfumes, incense, and so forth to the Great Lord of the Ḍāmaras.
*Liṅgṛhṇa* (2) *Vauṣaṭ*. Now, in the southeast, we praise the two-armed attendant of Viṣṇu with a dark-blue face;
I bow to Viśvaksena, the bestower of victory, who wears the sacred thread and possesses a single face with great fangs. *Viśva...*
O Bhūmnīśvatomukha, O Viśvaksena, bestower of all splendor and boons, you who accept the offering; with one hand raised in a fist with the nails touching the tip of the nose,
and the other right hand doubled over it, held uplifted in a fist.

Oṃ! I bow to the unborn Viṣvaksena, who holds his thumb-tip against his forefinger, carries the conch and mace, has tawny eyes, eyebrows, beard, and yellow garments, and is adorned with four fangs and faces. Oṃ.

*Hrīṃ śrīṃ rīṃ kṣmāṃ kṣāṃ yūṃ kṣāṃ*, obeisance to Viśvaksena, the protector of the field (*kṣetrapāla*). Now, in the northeast (*īśāna*), [one should meditate on] the white-bodied one, with a protruding nose, three eyes, and eyebrows and hair as tawny as a flame.
With disheveled hair and formidable fangs.
Śrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ, to those who are more terrible than the terrible, oṃ śrīṃ bhrāṃ saḥ, to all, from all, to all, huṃ (4). Homage to you whose forms are Rudra, huṃ (3).
Homage to the Great Lord, the Eater of Many; [homage] to the one named Bhrūkuṭa.
Nīlabhadra, Vīrabhadra, Bhayāpaha, Kaṅkāla,
Bhūrīrāva, and Bhūridhāra as the seventh; likewise Bhūrīrāva,
and in their midst the leader of the circle named Bahukhādaka.
One should worship them with diligence: Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc;
Oṃ, obeisance to the deformed skull; Oṃ, obeisance to the ḍamaru drum;
Oṃ, obeisance to the great sword; Oṃ, obeisance to the great shield.

Oṃ, descend! O you who shine with a mass of tawny matted hair, three-eyed one, with a flaming mouth, accept this offering of perfumes, incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as the sacrificial cake and flesh!
Svāhā! Likewise, there are yakṣiṇīs of various forms.
May all those Yakṣa maidens, with joyful minds, accept this offering; may they grant us constant success and ward off all fears. Or, in the northwest: Oṃ Vibhra...
To the South: Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ gāṃ, to Gaṇapati together with Vallabhā, accept this offering and worship, svāhā! (2) Then, to the Southwest: Oṃ siṃ, to Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā, the fierce one...
(pṛṣṭhasaṃkhyā 121 followed by 123, then 122 follows) With "rūpāya vaṣaṭ," perform the worship of Vaṭuka and others;
then the four traditional mantras: in the east, oṃ hsīṃ kulakṣetrapāla.
Bhairavarūpavaṭukanātha, accept this bali! Svāhā! Svāhā!
To the south: Oṃ hrīṃ vyauḥ, to all the Yoginīs, accept this bali! Phaṭ svāhā! To the west: Oṃ hrīṃ kṣāṃ, Kṣetrapāla, [accept this] bali...

*gṛhṇa (2) svāhā (2)*; in the north: *oṃ hrīṃ sarvabhūtebhyo huṃ ca tuṣpathavāsinībhyo baliṃ gṛhṇa (2) svāhā*. Thus is the worship of the weapons (*āyudha-pūjana*). Alternatively, perform the worship of the Vetālas and others in the northwest (*vāyavya*).
I bow down to that Vetāla, the destroyer of obstacles, who has two arms, stainless eyes, and a body as flickering as lightning.
May Kṛṣṇa protect us— he whose face is uplifted,
whose neck is thick and formidable, and who [tramples] the buffalo.
The goddess is most terrifying, with eyes like those of a vulture and an owl, ears like those of a donkey, and hair of flames;
she wears a garland of skulls, holds a skull-cup, a hand-drum, and a great dark-blue trident. She is the mistress of serpents.
I salute Vetāla, who holds a lute expert in playing upon his chest,
sounding it with both arms,
resembling the rising sun, engaged in dance, laughing, and [terrifying] the cruel ones.
Seated upon his throne, accompanied by these terrifying rākṣasīs known as Carakī and others, as well as the Bhairavas of the cremation ground, he—
whose skull-bowl and khaṭvāṅga staff are ever-present— conquers while simultaneously satisfying his great hunger and thirst.

May that Lord Śaṅkara, who assumes the form of the waters, be victorious—he who resounds the quarters with the ringing of bells and the sound of tridents amidst garlands of human skulls; who is ablaze with tawny matted locks and beard;
who is three-eyed; and who is mounted upon a corpse.
Delighting in blood, holding a sword, a skull-topped staff, and so forth, as well as a severed head, a bell, a trident, a ḍamaru drum, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness in his hands;
wearing a lion’s skin as an upper garment and bearing a great garland of skulls and a vessel.
Victorious is he who rises at dawn, known as Bhīma-bhāskheśvara;
he is many-eated, a bestower of success, and one-faced.
He is joined with four arms—bearing a shield, a banner, a sword, and a club—and possesses an equal number of faces.
I bow to Him who is eternally surrounded by mandalas as pure as the moon, who is encircled by fifty-two great divisions (mahāpadas), who always bears the mantra, who consumes many [offerings],
and who dwells in the field as the Lord of the World.
I bow to that one-faced, stainless, and captivating Lord, who has four arms, is saluted by the lords of the immortals,
is compassionate toward his devotees, is born of the Unborn, is intent on mercy, is the all-pervading consumer of many offerings, and possesses a single countenance.
The fierce Kṣetrapati, who enjoys the well-cooled Vedas,
holds a trident in his hand and a skull-staff (khaṭvāṅga) that causes the destruction of Naraka and others;
he resides upon a corpse, is joined by the lords of the eight seats (pīṭhas), and is known as Bahukhādaka.

I bow to the one with a flat nose, who is very white, four-armed, the bestower of siddhi, the consumer of many [offerings], whose food is many arms, and who dwells in the cremation ground— Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, to Mahābhairava, the Lord who consumes many, possessed of fierce wrath!

Yavikṛtānanāya hūṃ (2) kṣuṃ (2) hūṃ (2), O you who have arisen from nectar, whose form is nectar, quickly provide me with all nectar! O Lord of all the fields, in the form of Bhairava, accept the offering! Vauṣaṭ!

Svāhā! Namaḥ! Oṃ! To the Lord of Many-Eaters, who dwells in the cremation ground, the sovereign of the yakṣa army, whose form is presided over by trees, the lord of the eight siddhis—accept this offering and worship! Vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ, obeisance to Valisiṃha Kṣetrapāla, the lord of the Mahāḍāmara, the devourer of many; Oṃ namaḥ, huṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ,
obeisance to Mahābhairava, the devourer of many, the deformed one.

To the one who has conquered fierce anger, who arose from the nectar, who was born from the womb of nectar— quickly bestow all prosperity! To the Lord of all fields, [offer] this oblation and worship.
"Gr̥hṇa (2) vauṣaṭ! Oṃ bhrāṃsaḥ aghorebhyaḥ huṃ (4) tha ghorebhyaḥ hrīṃ (3).
By means of these designations and those four [mantras] beginning with *karma*, [one worships] those with well-distorted faces who are established in all directions and stationed in the corners.

May the Lord, who is the support of all, who devours the flesh of Nārāyaṇa, who is accompanied by Vetālas clapping their hands, who removes all fear, who stands in the midst of the dance, whose hair is like flames, who is adorned with serpents, and who is fierce— may he protect us.
I perpetually bow to the King of Vetālas, who has three eyes, who removes fear yet bestows fear upon enemies, who holds a lute with his two arms,
who is white in complexion, and who bears a sword and a noose.

May Vetālabhairava, who is permeated by the Supreme Lord, endowed with the Khecarīmudrā, and possessed of great power and valor, be victorious. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ! O Vetālabhairava, descend! O Kṣetrapāla of great strength and prowess, Kapila!
O you who shine with a mass of matted hair, whose face is ablaze with three eyes, accept this offering of perfumes,
flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth; in the form of Bhairava, *turu* (2), *muru* (2), *kha* (2),
*ha* (2), *hā* (2), *he* (2), *jacchrāṃ* (2), *muhuḥ* (2), be gracious!
Oṃ namo bhagavate mahāvetāla-bhairava-ḍāmarādhipataye svāhā. Oṃ oṃ, O Vetāla, Lord of the eight Vṛddhis, manifest your presence before me! Vauṣaṭ. Oṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One...
To the Lord of the seven islands of copper, the Lord of all wings, the Lord of the eight prosperities: come, come, Blessed One! Enter this body!
Show your own mudrā! Release the sound! Release the sound!

Look toward the four directions; reveal the past, the future, and the present time. Speak what is beneficial for the king, beneficial for the subjects, and beneficial for the virtuous. Come, come, O Blessed One Vetāla, who has gone to the earth!

Reveal to me the treasure located in the quarters and the intermediate space! Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Place your heart upon the supreme practitioner above the corpse! Come from your own abode! Come here for the sake of success!

*Dhyāṃkuru (2) hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—thus is the worship of the Vetāla. Now, the offering (*bali*) to Turuṣka: In the southwest (*nairṛta*), he holds a vessel in his left hand and laughs with a loud laugh; he is of a clear white-blue complexion, and in his right hand he holds a staff (*daṇḍa*) upon the earth.
I bow to the one who removes all fears of the womb, who is established in the root of the virtuous,
who wears blue garments or black clothing,
who possesses beautiful hair, and who observes excellent vows.

I take refuge in Kharāja, who is joined by the river Sitā, who dwells within the altar of Vetasī, and who is eternally devoted to stringed instruments; I bow to that Kharāja. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ māṃ makhāmbhi.
*Dhaturuṣka-kṣetrapāla-avatara (2), nāśaya vighnān (2), vighnāṇa (2), alivalipiśita-saṃyuktaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa (2) vauṣaṭ.* Thus is the *bali* offering for the King of Turuṣka. Now, the limb (*aṅga*).

We pay homage to the King of Auspiciousness, the Lord of the Field, the all-pervading Sovereign, who is adorned with auspiciousness, whose presiding deity is the glorious Maṅgalā, and who bears a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff; he who is the three-eyed one... [lyarājānakapūjā śrīmaṅgalādhidaivatyanāma maṅgalabhūṣitaṃ vandemaṅgalyarājānaṃ kṣetreśādhīśvaraṃ vibhuṃ kapālakhaṭvāṅgadharastrilocana].
May this King Maṅgalārāja— who possesses four arms, a red body, a smiling face, and is radiant with a goad, a lordly serpent, and hair like the bristles of a boar— be ever victorious!
[And may] he who has four arms, three eyes, and wears a garland of jewels...
One should salute Maṅgaleśvara, who is adorned, seated upon a *preta*, and has a smiling face. Oṃ, descend, O King of Auspiciousness, Kṣetrapāla!
[He] is radiant with a mass of tawny matted hair and possesses three flaming eyes.
Accept this face-to-face offering as part of the worship, Vauṣaṭ! O you who possess the form of Bhairava! Turu (2) Muru (2) Kha (2) La (2) Hā (2) He (2) Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Huṃ Saḥ!
Svāhā to the Great Lord of the Ḍāmaras! To the Great Roar, Rāva!
To the one who is to be proclaimed, the auspicious one, together with his retinue of royal attendants, accept this offering (*bali*); *vauṣaṭ*. Homage to Śuṃśuṣkeśvara!
Homage to Kṣāṃ Pathikeśvara! [He is] two-armed and single-faced.

I bow to the King of Merit (Puṇyarāja), who is filled with nectar and resembles the clouds at the end of an eon. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the King of Merit together with his retinue. Thus is the bali offering to the King of Merit.

I bow to the fierce Loṣṭeśvara, whose body is adorned with eight arms, who possesses five faces with blooming human skulls, and who is equipped with weapons such as a sword; Oṃ hrīṃ śrī, salutation to the body of King Loṣṭha together with his retinue.
This is the offering of Loṣṭharāja: [he visualizes] the god Śvetavaktra, who has four arms,
is adorned with a garland of skulls, holds a sword and a *kādyaka* (shield), destroys the fear of his devotees, and carries a lute and a *ḍamaru* drum in his hands— [that is] Kuḍāra.

I pay homage! Oṃ hrīṃ hukuḍāra-nātha-kṣetrapāla-ali, accept this offering (vali)! Kha (2) khāda (2) sphoṭa (2) garja (2) śāntiṃ kuru (2) puṣṭiṃ kuru (2) phaṭ svāhā! Thus [ends the mantra] of Kuḍāra-kṣetrapāla.

Lavalī [worships] him who is adorned with a garland of skulls, filled with the essence of bliss, the granter of boons and the remover of fear, holding a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) marked by the letter Kā and other symbols,
wearing a lion’s skin as an upper garment, and bearing a skull-topped staff marked by the letters Kā and others.

To the one who upholds [the world], whose great roar dispels fear, who is impelled by desire, who is most fierce, and adorned with all ornaments: Oṃ Hrīṃ Āṃ Saḥ! O King of Bliss, descend, descend! (2) Kapi!

Accept this worship, mixed with parched grain, matted locks, radiant three-eyed fire-flames, fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, beautiful sandalwood, water for the guest-offering, honey, meat, and blood. (2)

Vauṣaṭ! This is the offering of the King of Bliss (Ānandarājānaka). I, the King of Pañcāla, bow to Him who has two arms, one face, and three eyes; who is clad in red garments; who removes the fear of His devotees; who is the letter Raṃ; who dwells eternally on the mountain.

To the all-pervading lord of the Naṃkṣetra protector, Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, to the King of Pañcāla, Nakāya, together with his retinue, who eternally dwells on the mountain and bestows fearlessness upon travelers: accept this offering and worship! (2)
"Protect the path! (2) Destroy the thieves! (2) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ pluṃ phaṭ (2) namaḥ.
This is the bali offering for the King of Pañcāla.
[He holds] a skull-cup, a sword, a dagger, a shield, and a beautiful *suhyadvara* weapon; he is the Lord of Pretas, possessing three eyes.

I bow to the tiger-skin-clad one, who is dark and of black form, the presiding deity of the Kaṇṭakarāja. Oṃ huṃ, O Kaṇṭakarāja, accept this offering and worship! Vauṣaṭ. Thus [ends] the section on Kaṇṭaka.

The offering of *argha* to these deities is as follows: "Salutation to [the deity], salutation with flowers, salutation with incense," and so forth. Then, the worship of Ānandeśvara in the *pānaka* [offering] has been written elsewhere; after that, the *vaiśvadeva*.
