The proponent should perform the daily rites: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I dismiss the Puruṣa;
obeisance," and so forth, as before, for the purpose of warding off sins acquired through speech, mind, and body by oneself, and for the attainment of the aforementioned fruit.

For the sake of [attaining] the desired goal, on account of Śivarātri, may the worship of the water-pot (kalaśa-pūjana) and the worship of Kṣetreśa be free from defects; may it be complete; may it be so.
Salutations to You who are the water; salutations to the libation of water; grant me Your command.

"O Lord, for the sake of accomplishing the maintenance of my body, you ought to forgive me for eating this offering intended for You; I am in distress and I have no other refuge. Thus [he spoke] to that most terrible one, whose nature is even more terrible than the terrible.

We praise the Great Lord, the supreme deity who consists of the five Brahmans, together with his limbs, his attendants, his veil, and his power— the cause of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, dissolution, and grace. Kar...

He who has conquered the transformations of nature, who has fashioned the welfare of the world, who has warded off calamities and injuries, who has stilled the darkness of delusion, whose human effort is incomparable, and who has attained universal sovereignty— him [I praise].
Fie upon me! I am a sinner who has brought disgrace through the passion of love, yet I am devoted to flattering Pārvatī; I am skilled at destroying sin, yet I have become Śaṅkara;
I am afraid, yet I am intent on granting fearlessness to you who are terrified.
O Lord, you are solely intent on the method of removing the distress of the distressed;
you do not know how to speak anything else here. O Lotus-seated One, O Lotus-like One, bestow your boundless compassion upon us who have entered the ocean of worldly existence.
I take refuge in the Mother who destroys all sins, known as Śivā, who is the Night of Brahmā (Brahmāṇī), whose face is like an elephant's, and who is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahmaṇī).

O Maheśvara, whatever was omitted, whatever was done deficiently or excessively during the year, and whatever was devoid of ritual procedure— may all that be made complete for me by this Śivarātri vow, which delivers one from the ocean of hell and sustains the world.
Whatever was deficient or lacking in mantras has been reported by me as a servant;
O Supreme Lord, may it be forgiven. Gaṇeśa and the others have been remembered here for the duty of guarding the gates, as well as Indra and the other guardians of the worlds.
May the Ādityas and other such planets, the Vaṭukas and others, the Herukas and others,
and the eternal Kṣetrapālas— may they all, having granted various desires,
return to their own abodes. O Lords of the Field, forgive me!
May the lords of the fields (Kṣetrapālas) residing in heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, and in the cardinal directions,
having been propitiated, return to their own abodes; and those lords of the fields who have departed from the sacred site of Śiva by the command of Śiva, may they return to that sacred site of Śiva.
"May they be pleased by the command of Śiva. "I do not know how to perform the invocation," [he says].

Then, with both knees, both hands, and his head, he performs a prostration from the front of the body, saying "Namaḥ" (Salutation). With "Oṃ namo brahmaṇe" (Oṃ, salutation to Brahman), [he offers it] at the secret place.
Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa) and the ritual raising of the water-pot (kalaśotthāpana).
Arise, O Lord of Devas, together with the deities of the maṇḍala! You who are named Tatpuruṣa, protect us eternally from the east; likewise from the south.

O Bhairava, you are Aghora, protecting the western quarter; likewise, O Śaṅkara, you are Vāmadeva, protecting the northern quarter. You are Sadyojāta, constantly protecting the rakṣasas in the direction of Varuṇa (the west); O Maheśāna, protect [us] from above.
O Lord, you are the deity of all; O God, protect me in every way and at all times in this entire world. Come, O Lord of Gods, to that state which consists of eternal bliss.
Then, reciting the hymn containing many forms, one attains knowledge.

One should consecrate oneself and one's companions with water from a vessel that has not been defiled by nails, saying: "May the meanings of the mantras be fruitful; may our desires be fulfilled; may there be the destruction of the intellect of enemies; [may there be the increase of friends]."
[Thus ends the worship of Kṣetreśa in the Śivarātri vow; may there be prosperity for both of us. May it be auspicious!
Oṃ, salutations to the Guru, who is the embodiment of the illustrious Sarasvatī. Therein,

first having briefly worshipped the mantra-vase and the scripture-vase, one should perform the rites of incense, lamps, and so forth with the words "I bow to my own Self," and then [proceed] at the door with Oṃ.

The Lord of the Gaṇas resides in the heart, which is the dwelling place for the senses; the mind, speech, and the other [organs] are the gurus; the ten vital breaths consist of the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti);
and the Consciousness-God is accompanied by the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti), possessing the sixfold attributes.
Having meditated upon the Lord known as Sudhākalaśa— the one whose limbs are the guardians of the world (Lokeśas) and whose senses are the lords of the directions— we praise Him.
Then, having performed his ablutions and washed his hands and feet, [he should stand] at the edge of the altar.

Seated upon the throne of the Jina and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then begin the worship. Facing [the deity], one should meditate on the Lord with his retinue by means of a handful of flowers, for the sake of the seat of the Self.
Saying "Namaḥ," one should offer a flower upon the seat. Then, with the Astra mantra, "Phaṭ astrāya phaṭ," one should worship the vessel for the *arghya* water of the weapon-mantra.
[It is] blazing, devouring the multitude of obstacles, and bringing about the destruction of all sins. Tri...

One should meditate on the two-armed Eye weapon facing the deity: *phaṭ*, may there be purification through all ritual services, *svāhā*. Again, one should consecrate the flowers and other offerings with their respective mantras, such as: *ādhūmra* (2), *jīva* (2), *saḥ sa*.

Oṃ, may the life-force of all varieties of flowers come; svāhā! To the flower, which has the form of Kālāgnirudra, which is the ornament of the universe, which possesses a sweet fragrance, and which carries all scents—homage! To the incense, which has the form of the light of the universe—Oṃ!... [to the lamp]... homage! To the food offering, which has the form of the essence of the universe—Oṃ!... [to the naivedya]... homage! To the water for sipping, which has the form of the nectar of immortality—Oṃ!... [to the ācamana]... homage! To the betel leaf, which has the form of the supreme bliss—Oṃ!... [to the tāmbūla]... homage! To the flower garland, which has the form of the supreme splendor—Oṃ!... [to the mālya]... homage! To the parasol, which has the form of the supreme sovereignty—Oṃ!... [to the chatra]... homage! To the fly-whisk, which has the form of the supreme service—Oṃ!... [to the cāmara]... homage! To the throne, which has the form of the supreme majesty—Oṃ!... [to the āsana]... homage! To the bell, which has the form of the supreme sound—Oṃ!... [to the ghaṇṭā]... homage! To the mirror, which has the form of the supreme knowledge—Oṃ!... [to the darpaṇa]... homage! To the conch, which has the form of the supreme purity—Oṃ!... [to the śaṅkha]... homage! To the flag, which has the form of the supreme victory—Oṃ!... [to the dhvaja]... homage! To the drum, which has the form of the supreme proclamation—Oṃ!... [to the mṛdaṅga]... homage! To the musical instruments, which have the form of the supreme joy—Oṃ!... [to the vāditra]... homage! To the dance, which has the form of the supreme play—Oṃ!... [to the nṛtya]... homage! To the song, which has the form of the supreme praise—Oṃ!... [to the gīta]... homage! To the hymn, which has the form of the supreme devotion—Oṃ!... [to the stotra]... homage! To the prostration, which has the form of the supreme surrender—Oṃ!... [to the praṇāma]... homage! To the fire-offering, which has the form of the supreme satisfaction—Oṃ!... [to the homa]... homage! To the mantra, which has the form of the supreme power—Oṃ!... [to the mantra]... homage! To the mudrā, which has the form of the supreme seal—Oṃ!... [to the mudrā]... homage! To the yoga, which has the form of the supreme union—Oṃ!... [to the yoga]... homage! To the dhyāna, which has the form of the supreme meditation—Oṃ!... [to the dhyāna]... homage! To the samādhi, which has the form of the supreme absorption—Oṃ!... [to the samādhi]... homage! To the liberation, which has the form of the supreme freedom—Oṃ!... [to the mokṣa]... homage! To the teacher, who is the embodiment of the supreme grace—Oṃ!... [to the guru]... homage! To the disciple, who is the vessel of the supreme truth—Oṃ!... [to the śiṣya]... homage! To the lineage, which is the source of the supreme transmission—Oṃ!... [to the paramparā]... homage! To the scripture, which is the treasury of the supreme wisdom—Oṃ!... [to the śāstra]... homage! To the deity, who is the manifestation of the supreme reality—Oṃ!... [to the devatā]... homage! To the preceptor, who is the bestower of the supreme initiation—Oṃ!... [to the ācārya]... homage! To the initiate, who is the recipient of the supreme blessing—Oṃ!... [to the dīkṣita]... homage! To the ritual, which is the means of the supreme attainment—Oṃ!... [to the vidhi]... homage! To the result, which is the fulfillment of the supreme purpose—Oṃ!... [to the phala]... homage! To the universe, which is the field of the supreme manifestation—Oṃ!... [to the viśva]... homage! To the soul, which is the witness of the supreme consciousness—Oṃ!... [to the jīva]... homage! To the Supreme Lord, who is the essence of all that exists—Oṃ!... [to the Parameśvara]... homage! To the All-pervading One, who is the support of all beings—Oṃ!... [to the Vyāpin]... homage! To the Infinite, who is beyond all limitations—Oṃ!... [to the Ananta]... homage! To the Unmanifest, who is the source of all creation—Oṃ!... [to the Avyakta]... homage! To the Manifest, who is the display of divine power—Oṃ!... [to the Vyakta]... homage! To the Formless, who is the ground of all forms—Oṃ!... [to the Amūrta]... homage! To the Embodied, who is the sustainer of all bodies—Oṃ!... [to the Mūrta]... homage! To the Silent, who is the speaker of all truths—Oṃ!... [to the Mauna]... homage! To the Vocal, who is the revealer of all sounds—Oṃ!... [to the Vācāla]... homage! To the Motionless, who is the mover of all things—Oṃ!... [to the Niścala]... homage! To the Moving, who is the impeller of all actions—Oṃ!... [to the Cala]... homage! To the Still, who is the abode of all peace—Oṃ!... [to the Śānta]... homage! To the Active, who is the agent of all deeds—Oṃ!... [to the Pravṛtta]... homage! To the Withdrawn, who is the master of all dissolution—Oṃ!... [to the Nivṛtta]... homage! To the Expanding, who is the cause of all growth—Oṃ!... [to the Vikāsin]... homage! To the Contracting, who is the source of all reduction—Oṃ!... [to the Saṃkocin]... homage! To the Radiant, who is the light of all worlds—Oṃ!... [to the Tejasvin]... homage! To the Obscured, who is the veil of all ignorance—Oṃ!... [to the Tirobhūta]... homage! To the Revealed, who is the dawn of all knowledge—Oṃ!... [to the Prakaṭita]... homage! To the Hidden, who is the secret of all mysteries—Oṃ!... [to the Guhya]... homage! To the Manifested, who is the revelation of all secrets—Oṃ!... [to the Prakaṭa]... homage! To the Unknown, who is the limit of all inquiry—Oṃ!... [to the Ajñāta]... homage! To the Known, who is the fruit of all realization—Oṃ!... [to the Jñāta]... homage! To the Unborn, who is the beginning of all births—Oṃ!... [to the Ajāta]... homage! To the Born, who is the end of all existences—Oṃ!... [to the Jāta]... homage! To the Deathless, who is the life of all beings—Oṃ!... [to the Amṛta]... homage! To the Mortal, who is the cycle of all transmigration—Oṃ!... [to the Mṛtyu]... homage! To the Eternal, who is the changeless reality—Oṃ!... [to the Nitya]... homage! To the Transient, who is the flux of all time—Oṃ!... [to the Anitya]... homage! To the Fixed, who is the pole of all stability—Oṃ!... [to the Dh

*Maḥdīpe gandhamādinigandhaṃ sarve jīvāpayantu svāhā.* (In the lamp: O you who possess the fragrance of incense and the like, may all living beings be made to live; svāhā! *Caṃdane hrīṃ svāhā.* (In the sandalwood: hrīṃ svāhā! *Kuṃkume lāṃ pṛthivyai dhari triśaktaye namaḥ.* (In the saffron: obeisance to Lāṃ, to the Earth, to the bearer, to the triple power. *Arghye oṃ nlīṃ varuṇa vājānakā.* (In the water-offering: oṃ nlīṃ, O Varuṇa, O source of strength!)
Thus is the purification of substances with water. Now, the worship of the messenger (dūtī):
We praise the gentle messenger, who has four arms, possesses a beautiful voice, and proclaims the mantra;
she holds a rosary, a book, and a garland, and displays the gesture of fearlessness. Oṃ.

Oṃ *Huṃ*, salutations to the Mother of Mantras, the Pure Knowledge (*Śuddhavidyā*). Again, one should wave the bell over the left hand; there, for the sake of removing impurities, one should offer incense.
Oṃ, we know the Lord of Nectar (*Amṛteśa*), whose body is the void (*Vyomadeha*).
*Dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt.* Now, for the worship of the light-maṇḍala before the deity:

the meditation on the Bull (*Vṛṣabha*). White, three-eyed, the Bull is radiant, bearing a trident, and likewise holding the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), he is the remover of all sins.

One should meditate upon the bull, the destroyer of all obstacles, who has one face and four arms, who is radiant within a circle of light, and who is brilliant; [one should offer salutations] to the circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*),
to the bull (*vṛṣabha*), to Bhṛṅgīśa, to Kumāra, and to Ambikā.
To Dvāraśrī, to Lakṣmī, to Gaṇapati, and to Oṃ Sarasvatī; [and to] the Trident: [these goddesses] are beautiful, holding in their hands nectar-jars, fine flower-garlands, and [the trident].
Facing the deity Ākāśamātṛ-Ekavaktra: *oṃ māyāyai namaḥ*, *durgāyai*, *bhadrakālyai*, *svastaye svāhāyai*,
*śubhaṃkāryai*, *goryai*, *śriyai*, *lokadhātryai*, *vāgīśvaryai*.
Then, for the worship of the elements (bhūta-pūjā) in the sequence starting from the eastern direction:

*lāṃ* to Earth (*pṛthivī*), *raṃ* to Fire (*agni*), *śoṃ* to the Sacrificer (*yajamāna*), *ṣoṃ* to Āditya, *vāṃ* to Water (*jala*), *yāṃ* to Wind (*vāyu*), *saṃ* to the Moon (*candramas*), *haṃ* to Sovereignty (*aiśvaryā*).
To Ākāśa, on his own left branch: *namaḥ* to Nandī;
to Gaṅgā, on his own right-left branch: *namaḥ* to Meṣāsya and Diṇḍi; to Mahākāla, *namaḥ* to Yamunā.

Salutations to Chāgalāsya (the Goat-faced), to Mahodara (the Large-bellied), to Dehalī (the Threshold) at the bottom of the door, to Vāstupuruṣa (the Architectural Spirit), and to Brahmā in the western quarter; salutations to all beings. Then follows the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma); first, the Nārāca [mantra].
Taking the *arghya* water with the union of the two index fingers and the thumbs, consecrating it seven times with the Astra-mantra, and visualizing it as having a blazing, radiant form,
one should cast it into the center of the altar for the purpose of driving away obstacles: *phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*.

Having expelled the three kinds of obstructors with the mantra beginning "O beings, depart from here," and having displayed the trident mudrā (*triśūlamudrā*), one should veil [the site] with the armor-mantra "Oṃ huṃ kavacāya huṃ" and pay homage to the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) with "Namaḥ."
"Salutation to Padmāsana," etc.— having thus addressed one's own seat such as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and so forth,
one should perform *recaka*, *pūraka*, *kuṃbhaka*, and *ūrdhvarecaka* by means of the application of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*),
reciting "I perform *recaka*, salutation" according to the capacity [of the breath].
Thus, one should expel the impure air through the right nostril for the duration of twelve recitations of the *praṇava*. Then, with "Vaṃ pūrakaṃ karomi namaḥ," one should draw in the pure,
white prāṇa-vāyu for twenty-four [recitations].

At the time of uttering the *praṇava* three times, one should fill the body [with breath] while reciting "OṂ RAṂ KTAṂ BHA KAṂ KAROMI NAMAḤ," remaining as motionless as a water-filled jar for as long as it takes to utter the *praṇava* thirty-six times.

One should remain motionless; then, one should exhale that very [air] held in the *kumbhaka* (retention) through the sequence of piercing the heart, throat, palate, and the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*)—this is the upward exhalation (*ūrdhvarecaka*). Then, by that same sequence...

One should place oneself, shining like a star, in the state of Śiva at the dvādaśānta. Then, through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās), one should perform the purification of the gross body with the mantra: "Oṃ, for the sake of destruction, I dry up the body; namas"—thus reciting the Praṇava in the form of the Sun pervading the entire body.

One should contemplate the body as being like a withered tree, having reflected upon its perishable nature; this is the *pārthivī* [mudrā]. With the mantra "Oṃ kṣala yūṃ, I burn the body," one places [the hand] on the big toe of the right foot.

Having meditated on the fire, one should contemplate the body—both external and internal—as reduced to ashes by its flames; this is the Agnāyī [rite]. With the mantra "Oṃ yalūṃ, I make the body mind-transcending (unmanī), namaḥ," one applies the bodily ash.
One should contemplate the wind pervading the ten directions; this is the Vāyavī [mudrā].
With "Oṃ vaṃ, I purify the body, namaḥ," one should contemplate that place as washed by streams of consciousness-drops; this is the [Vāruṇī mudrā].
"Ruṇī oṃyaṃ tanuṃ amṛtīkaromi namaḥ" (I make this body immortal, obeisance);
"Tanuṃ saṃjīvayāmi namaḥ" (I restore the body to life, obeisance)—thus [it is said].
Just as the poisonous nature of poison is warded off by the power of a mantra, but not its own [nature].
In this manner, the physical form is dissolved by means of the sustenance of the ego-sense within the body;
then, having meditated upon the divine form, one should contemplate the seat beginning from the *kanda*, [reciting]: "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti" and "to Dhātrī."

Then, having brought oneself down onto the seat within the heart— from the *dvādaśānta* by means of the sequence of piercing the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*)— one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) mentally upon that seat which is the ocean of milk, the lunar disc, and the lotus throne.

One should perform [the ritual] as follows: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva" at the base of the throat; "Oṃ, obeisance to the Sadāśiva-tattva" on the forehead; "Oṃ, obeisance to the Īśvara-tattva" between the eyebrows; and "Oṃ, obeisance to the Vidya-tattva" on the palate by me.

"Oṃ, obeisance to the principle of *tattva* at the throat; obeisance to the principle of *kāla* (time) at the heart; obeisance to the principle of *niyati* (destiny) at the navel; obeisance to the principle of *puruṣa* (the individual soul) at the genitals; obeisance to the principle of *prakṛti* (primordial nature) at the feet. Thus [are the nine].

Furthermore, the Nyāsa of the three principles (*tritattva-nyāsa*) is as follows: having meditated upon the white form with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Form" (*mūrtaye namaḥ*), one performs the placement: "Oṃ saḥ, obeisance to the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*)," on the head;
"Oṃ juṃ, obeisance to the Knowledge-principle (*vidyātattva*)," between the eyebrows; "Oṃ... [and so forth].

Oṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ at the heart; Oṃ juṃ saḥ amṛteśamūrtaye namaḥ on the entire body. Then, one should perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) mentally: Oṃ juṃ to the heart... [and so forth].

*Vyoṃ* to the head, *svāhā*, on the two thumbs; *ī* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*, on the two index fingers; *huṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*, on the two middle fingers; *oṃ juṃ* to the eyes, *vauṣaṭ*, on the two ring fingers; [on the two little fingers... *kani*.

Having performed the *karanyāsa* (finger-assignment) with "Oṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ" for the thumbs and little fingers, and "i ti" for the nails, one should begin the *dehanyāsa* (body-assignment): [place] the Heart in the heart, the Head in the head,
the Crest-lock in the crest-lock, and the Armor on the shoulder.

Having performed the placement on the body (*dehanyāsa*) thus—"The *yoḥ* [syllable] is the eye; the *netra* [syllable] is in the two eyes; the *astra* [syllable] is in the nails"—one should again place the root mantra (*mūla*) over the entire body, from the head down to the soles of the feet, as the pervasion of the root.

One should touch the root [mantra] with "Oṃ, salutation to the pure body and abode; salutation to the form," and so forth, in the case of one who has not received initiation. However, in the case of one who has received initiation, there is the performance of the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) on the hands using the *Niṣkala* mantra of Aghorāghoreśvarī.
One should place [the syllables] by way of pervasion throughout the body; then, having again formed the mudrās,

one should perform the meditation as previously described, visualizing the deity with the "Vessel of Nectar" (sudhākalaśa) mantra, and mentally offering water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), the respectful offering (argha), and flowers.
[He is endowed with] gains, the sacred thread, necklaces, earrings, anklets, and other such ornaments;
increasingly fine flower garlands, betel leaves, food, and mouth-perfumes;
and [the offerings of] excellent canopies, umbrellas, chowries, dance, song, and recitation.
One should contemplate the deity as being fully satisfied by means of the *mādhi-homa* and other rites;

then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's own body as before, for the sake of the external sacrifice, one should perform the worship of the *argha* vessel with the root mantra and its limbs to the left of oneself at the Ocean of Milk.
Or, by means of the upper portion, one should make it eight-limbed, left-limbed, or three-limbed; then,
having formed the Amṛta-mudrā and sprinkled all the offerings with those drops of water, one should sprinkle oneself as being of the nature of Śiva.

Then, a vertical-line tilaka should be made on one's own forehead, consecrated with the root mantra seven times. One should place the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the water for libation (argha) and the flowers on the head.
Then, on one's left [side], in the order of an upward row, [one should place] the Guru...
Salutation to the Guru for the performance of the form-worship; salutation to the Paramaguru;
salutation to the Parameṣṭhiguru; salutation to the Paramācārya;
salutation to the primordial Siddhas; salutation to Kṣetrapāla; salutation to Vāgīśvara.
*Oṃ namaḥ*. Thus is the worship of the Guru. Then, on one's left side, is the worship of Gaṇapati:
"O Bhobho! O Lord of the Gaṇas, now make my place free from obstacles. I shall perform the worship of Hara for the sake of protecting others. *Oṃ*.

Oṃ, salutation to Ghoradaṃṣṭra; Oṃ, salutation to Virūpākṣa; Oṃ, salutation to Kākatuṇḍa; Oṃ, salutation to Cillavaktra. Thus is the worship of the four guardians of the Gaṇas. Oṃ Vibhra... [text truncated]
Regarding "with the right hand": *Oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe vakratuṇḍāya dhīmahi, tanno dantiḥ pracodayāt* (3). *Oṃ namo 'nantāya, namo mahāpadmāsanāya, namaḥ siṃhāsanāya, mū...*
Laṃ Oṃ Glūṃ Gaṃ Gaṇapataye Namaḥ; Gāṃ Gīṃ, etc., for the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). Gaṃ Laṃ Vodarāya Namaḥ; Gaṃ Gaṇeśāya Namaḥ;
Gaṃ Virūpākṣāya; Gaṃ Vibhī...
Gaṃ to Gaṇāya, Gaṃ to Vighneśāya, Gaṃ to Dīrghanāsikāya, Gaṃ to Gaṇarājāya, Gaṃ to Ibhānanāya—
thus is the eightfold hymn to Gaṇeśa. Oṃ Plīṃ, salutations to the one who holds a pestle in his hand.
*Oṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ gāṃ gīṃ guṃ gaiṃ gauṃ gaḥ gaṇeśāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ gūṃ saḥ gaṇapativallabhāyai namaḥ*. Thus is the worship of Gaṇeśvara. In the center is the worship of Kumāra. Kārtti...

The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows: "Who is this one who has the best of gods [as his vehicle], who has six faces, who destroys the wicked and the wicked-behaved, who holds a bell and a spear, who is radiant, whose hand holds a rosary, who has two eyes, who is mounted upon a *cātaka* bird, who has the form of a child, and who possesses the luster of the moon. This is the visualization.

Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ huṃ hai hauṃ haḥ, obeisance to Kumāra, whose vehicle is a peacock—this is the root mantra. Hāṃ and so forth constitute the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Oṃ, obeisance to Kumāra, who holds a spear and a *kukūṭa* in his hands and has a peacock as his vehicle.
"Obeisance to you, the Lord of Yama, who possesses six faces and is accompanied by the Yoginīs; obeisance to the Lord of the South, Svāhā! Then, to the right of oneself, is the worship of the Sun:
the God who has assumed the lotus posture, who is affectionate toward those who have sought refuge in him.
The Sun-god, who has seven horses, holds a lotus in his hand, and possesses two arms; he is the one who causes [the world] to fall [into the cycle of rebirth].

He is mounted upon a white lotus, has the luster of a pomegranate flower, is surrounded by a halo of great brilliance from shimmering jewels, and stands amidst a circle of light. Upon his shoulders...
One should meditate upon the Sun as having one face and two arms, with two hands holding a pure, radiant lotus stalk, clothed in jeweled garments—this is the visualization.
Then follows the Gāyatrī: *Oṃ sūryarūpāya vi* [sūryajñānāya].
May Sūrya inspire our intellect (3). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lotus Throne;
oṃ aṃ, salutation to the Sun Throne; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Sūrya, the Firebrand of the Sky. Thus, having worshipped the throne, [one recites] the root mantra: oṃ hrāṃ.
Hrīṃ Saḥ, salutation to the Sun; Aṃ, salutation to the Heart; Arka, Svāhā to the Head; Oṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, Vaṣaṭ to the Flaming Crest;
Huṃ, Huṃ, to the Armor; Oṃ Bhāṃ, Vauṣaṭ to the Eyes; Oṃ Raḥ.
*Astrāya phaṭ.* Then, in the sequence of ascending rows above that, the worship of the planets:
*Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ agnyādityābhyāṃ namaḥ*; *Oṃ syuṃ varuṇacaṃdramobhyāṃ namaḥ*; *Oṃ hūṃ kumārabhaumābhyāṃ namaḥ*; *Oṃ...*
Oṃ Ṣaḍharthaṃ Viṣṇu-Budhābhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ Rsthaṃ Indra-Bṛhaspatibhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ Hrīṃ Sarasvatī-Śukrābhyāṃ namaḥ.
Oṃ Kṣa Sarayarthaṃ Prajāpati-Śanaiścarābhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ Yūṃ.

Salutation to Gaṇapati and Rāhu. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Rudra and Ketu. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Brahmā and Dhruva. Oṃ huṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Ananta and Agastya. Then, [the ritual] for the great bathing of the Blessed One...
One should cause him to receive the command for the sake of the goal, as follows: "O Lord of the Mistress of Gaṇanātha,
O Sandalwood-footed One, Teacher of the World, know that men shall worship this [image] so that it may become a source of prosperity."

"O Blessed One, having requested permission from you, the all-pervading Lord who remains in embodied form, I shall today remove the previous [seat] and offer a new one. Having received this command, one should worship the auspicious seat with: *oṃ bhadrāsanāya*.
*Yanamaḥ*. *Oṃ ādhāraśaktyai namaḥ*. Likewise: to Ananta, to Dharma, to Jñāna, to Vairāgya, to Aiśvarya, to Adharma, to Ajñāna, to Avairāgya, and to Anaiśvarya.

To the Kṛta Yuga, to the Tretā Yuga, to the Dvāpara Yuga, to the Kali Yuga; to the Ṛgveda, to the Yajurveda, to the Sāmaveda, to the Atharvaveda; to the quality of goodness (sattva), to the quality of passion (rajas).

Having worshipped the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) with the mantra: "Obeisance to the one who is in that darkness, to the lower covering, to the middle covering, to the upper covering, to the thousand-petaled lotus seat, and to the eight-petaled lotus seat."
Having offered a flower upon the head of the deity with the mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya* and having established [the deity] upon the auspicious seat (*bhadrapiṭha*), one should worship.
First, one should offer a single *gaṇḍūṣa* (mouthful of water) upon the head of the deity with the Astra-mantra, as follows: *pha*.

With the mantra *ṭ asrāyaphaṭ*, one should again cast the weapon-offering vessel (*astrārghyapātra*) onto the head of the deity. Then: *oṃ oṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ* (Oṃ Oṃ, salutation to the principle of the Self);
*oṃ juṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ* (Oṃ Juṃ, salutation to the principle of Knowledge); *oṃ saḥ śivatattvāya* (Oṃ Saḥ, [salutation] to the principle of Śiva).
Having honored the seat upon the petals,

filaments, pericarp, and excellent pedestal with the mantra "Oṃ juṃ saḥ, obeisance to the form of Amṛteśa," and having thus arranged the seat, one should then [proceed] from one's own heart with the mudrā of invocation.

One should invoke the deity; taking flowers in cupped hands, one should then invoke the deity with "Oṃ Bhagavan, come" (twice). This is the invocation. Then, with "Bhagavan, be seated, svāhā," this is the installation.

"O Bhagavan, be present! Having caused [the deity] to be present by means of the *atisannidhi-mudrā*, and having established [the offering] with 'O Bhagavan, this oblation is offered; *svāhā*!', one should say:
*oṃ huṃ bhagavan avaguṇṭhanaṃ karomi namaḥ*."

Having thus veiled [the deity], [one says]: "O Blessed One, I make you immortal; *namaḥ*. Then, from the *argha* vessel: "O Blessed One, accept the *pādya*; *namaḥ*. O Blessed One, accept the *arghya*; *svāhā*. O Blessed One, [accept] the *ācamana*..."
O Blessed One, accept the food offering, svadhā!
O Blessed One, accept the flower, svāhā! O Blessed One, accept the incense, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ! O Blessed One, accept the lamp, vauṣaṭ! i.
Then, having offered three incenses and lamps,

and having worshipped the deity on the head with the root-mantra and its ancillaries, one should [offer] the conch with one hundred and eight, or fifty-four, or thirteen, or seven, or three recitations of the root-mantra, or with the *gaṇas*.
One should worship the deity with mudrās on special days, using water, milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugarcane, medicinal herbs, grains, flowers, and water.
With water from fruits, with water from white mustard seeds and parched grain, with scented water,
and with auspicious water containing gold and jewels— one should thus always perform the great ablutions for Śambhu in sequence, using these five excellent waters together.
One should offer the baths for Śiva with their respective mantras. Then, above the deity, libations (tarpaṇa) should be performed using the lineage of Śiva (śivagotra) beneath the pedestal (pīṭha).
Again, having consecrated the water-pitcher (gaṇḍuka) with the root mantra and its ancillaries, [one should perform] the offering of the mantra-water (argha) in the vessel.
Having offered a little water with the syllable *trāt* and brought it to the location of the bulb (*kanda*),
one should meditate there upon a triangular mandala at that bulbous site, blazing and radiant in form;
then, from the center of that, one should bring forth the flame of fire to the location of the wheel (*cakra*).
Then, having visualized the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) at the tip of the nose,

and having meditated upon the second syllable of Amṛteśa in its center, one should contemplate the solar disc being pierced and the crest of fire rising upward, and thus open the aperture of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having led this flame of fire along the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the end of the *brahmarandhra*,
one experiences for a moment a sensation equal to the touch of an ant; having brought it to the *dvādaśānta*, one remains there eternally and perpetually.
One should contemplate that nectar, resembling molten silver, flowing through the nostrils from the nature of the full orb of the cool-rayed moon and falling into the center of the vessel;
thus, the vessel is filled with nectar.

Having meditated upon *traṃ*, *vi*, *bhā*, *yoṃ*, *juṃ*, *saḥ*, [one should say]: "O Amṛteśa-mūrti, O Amṛteśa, who are the inner self of all beings, who pervade the void, whose body is the void—enter this image! O Gaḍuka, manifest your presence! (2) (2)

"Salutation to the one whose self is the five Brahmans"—with these words, one should perform the pouring of the stream very slowly and with great care upon the Lord. The heart of Bhaga is the Liṅga, and the heart of the Liṅga is Bhaga; salutation to that Bhaga-Liṅga.

One should touch the eyes with the *liṅgamudrā* while reciting "mā rudrāya vainamaḥ. Then, having whirled the *ārātrikā* three times above the deity while reciting the *astramantra*, one should say: "May the devotees of the Blessed One and the spirits accept [this]."
"May those five elements that dwell outside the palace,

and those who are their followers, go away— svāhā! With these words, one should discard the night-blooming flowers, cast off the floral remains (*nirmālya*), remove the forehead mark (*tilaka*), and meditate upon the sword.

Incense burns away fear and destroys sins; by offering lamps, one’s debts are extinguished; through worship, there is abundant gain; food offerings are the means to liberation; and flowers are the pacifiers of misfortune.
This bathing [rite] destroys evil dreams, pacifies poverty,
and brings about the cessation of disease; when the worship of the deity is performed, ten defects perish, and the ten transgressions are washed away by the water like milk.
O man, he who bathes a Liṅga with curd, ghee, or even ten thousand pots of sweet water intended for the ancestors,

his ancestors, being satisfied, shall go to heaven. Furthermore, he who bathes it with cool water intended for the ancestors, a hundred, a thousand, or even ten thousand ancestors shall likewise attain satisfaction.
The bell-mantra is: "kārṇavāt maṃtramātredyatya enam iti.

The bell should be sounded at the door, during the offering of the arghya vessel, in the worship of the Guru, likewise at the time of invocation, worship, and the offering of food (naivedya), as well as at the time of dismissal (visarjana).

O beloved, without the messenger (dūtī), the sound [of the ritual] would be fruitless; O Goddess, without the messenger, the worship would undoubtedly be fruitless. Having sipped water again, he sat down.

One should worship those who are not on one's own side: *oṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*; likewise to the Earth, to the Ocean of Milk, to the Lunar Maṇḍala, to the Lotus Throne (*padmāsana*), to the Embodiment of Nectar (*amṛtamūrti*), to the *akāra* principle, and to the *ukāra* principle.
The end of the Veda is thus: "To the reality of the letter *ma*, to the Ṛgveda, to the Yajurveda,
to the Sāmaveda, to the Atharvaveda, to the Kṛtayuga, to the Tretāyuga,
to the Dvāparayuga, and to the Kaliyuga."

Having worshipped the seat with the mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*, and having established Śiva—who has been honored with water for the guest-offering (*argha*) and flowers—one should worship Him [with the following]:
"Salutation to the lower covering; salutation to the upper covering."

*Maḥ* for the principle of *Saṃsatva*, *raṃ* for *Rajasa*, *taṃ* for *Tamasa*, *oṃ* for the principle of *Ātmatattva*, *juṃ* for the principle of *Vidyātattva*, and *saḥ* for the principle of *Śivatattva*.
Then, one should worship the God with the root mantra and its limbs: *Oṃ juṃ saḥ Amṛteśvara Bhairava*.

*Oṃ juṃ saḥ*, salutation to Amṛtalakṣmī; *oṃ juṃ*, salutation to the Heart in the southeast; *vyoḥ*, salutation to the Head in the southwest; *ī*, salutation to the Crest in the northwest; *oṃ huṃ*, salutation to the Armor in the northeast; *oṃ hūṃ*, salutation to the Eyes in the center; *phaṭ*, salutation to the Weapon in the four [corners].

One should know that the Heart is in the east, the Head in the south, the Topknot (Śikhā) in the north, and one should place the Armor (Kavaca) in the west. The Eye of the Deity is in front, and the Weapon (Astra) is in the four corners. Oṃ juṃ.

HṚ at the east, VYOŚIRA at the south, ĪŚIKHĀ at the north, HUṂKAVAPA at the west, HUṂNETRA in front, PHAṬ ASTRĀ in the four corners; then follows the worship of the seven enclosures (āvaraṇas) in due order, beginning with the Vidyeśvaras.

Rāgaṇeśa and the others, the Ālokeśas, the Mothers, and the Planets; the Nāgas, Vajra and the others—this is called the sevenfold enclosure (*saptāvaraṇa*). Within the lotuses, starting from the center and proceeding in order from the west, are the Vidyēśvaras: Oṃ Hrīṃ Anantāya Na... [etc.]
*Maḥ* to the subtle one; *Oṃ* to Śivottama; *Jrūṃ* to Ekanetra;
*Kṣrūṃ* to Ekarudra; *Glūṃ* to Trimūrti; *Huṃ* to Śrīkaṇṭha;
*Śrīṃ* to Śikhaṇḍin, salutations! Now follows the *Gaṇeśāṣṭaka*: [Paścimā...]

In clockwise order: *rāṃ rīṃ rūṃ* obeisance to Nandin; *māṃ sīṃ mlūṃ hsrrīṃ* obeisance to Mahākāla; *hsauḥ bhṛṃ* obeisance to Bhṛṅgirudra; *galarthaṃ gaṃ* obeisance to Gaṇapati; *vrāṃ* obeisance to Vṛṣabha; *hsauṃḥ kuṃ* obeisance to Kumāra.
Maḥ Oṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ to Ambikā; Oṃ Hsuṃ to Caṇḍīśvara.
Now, the eight lamps and the world-protectors (lokapālas): Lūṃ, obeisance to Indra, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand;
Rūṃ, [obeisance] to Agni, who holds a spear in his hand; Rūṃ, [obeisance] to Yama.
Salutation to Daṇḍahasta (Staff-in-hand), KṢŪṂ to Nirṛti with sword in hand,
NLUṂ to Varuṇa with noose in hand, YŪṂ to Vāyu with banner in hand,
KUṂ to Kuvera with mace in hand, and ŚŪṂ to Īśāna with trident.
To Lahaṣṭā, who holds a lotus in her hand, *āṃ*; to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand, *hlāṃ*; to Ananta, who holds a plow in his hand, *yah*.
Now, the Mothers: *jamarayūṃ* salutation to Jayā;
*tamarayūṃ* to Vijayā; *rāṃ* to Subhagā; *yaṃ* to Durbhagā.
To Yamamāra-yūñjayantī, Paṃūhinī, Hasayartha, Aparājitā, and Jaṅkarālī; now the planetary deities (grahas): Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, salutation to Agni and Āditya;
sayarthaṃ, salutation to Varuṇa and Candramas.
Hūṃ to Kumāra and Bhauma; Hsthūṃ to Viṣṇu and Budha;
Rasthaṃ to Indra and Bṛhaspati; Hrīṃ to Sarasvatī and Śukra; Kṣamayūṃ to Prajāpati and Śanaiścara; Nlūṃ to Aum Gaṇapati and Rāhu.
Hrīṃ to Rudra and Ketu; hrīṃ kṣīṃ to Brahmā and Dhruva; hrīṃ huṃ to Ananta and Agastya. Now the Nāgas: the Nāga king Ananta, Vāsuki, Padma, Mahāpadma, and Takṣaka.
To Kārkoṭaka, to Śaṅkhapāla, to Kulika, or [the mantra for] the first enclosure:
*vajrāya phaṭ*, *śaktaye phaṭ*, *daṇḍāya*,
*khaḍgāya*, *pāśāya*, *dhvajāya*, *gadāyai*, *triśūlāya* pa...
*Hūṃ* *māyā-cakrāya phaṭ*. Or else, the five faces:
*namaḥ* to the face of Īśāna; *yaṃ* to Tatpuruṣa; *va* to Aghora; *luṃ* to Sadyojāta; *vaṃ* to Vāmadeva; *oṃ* to Sarvajñatā at the heart; *tṛptiḥ* at the head.
The *nādi* is awakening, the *śikhā* is self-sovereignty, the armor (*kavaca*) is the unobstructed eye, the weapon (*astra*) is infinite power; *Oṃ*, salutation to Svacchandabhairava,
to Kapāleśabhairava, to Śikhivāhanabhairava, and to Krodharājabhairava.

Karālabhaī, Manmathabhaī, Meghanādabhaī, Somarājabhaī, Vidyārājabhaī—thus is the *Bhairavāṣṭaka*. Now, the *Mūrtyaṣṭaka*: obeisance to Lord Bhava in the form of Earth; obeisance to Rudra in the form of Water; obeisance to Paśupati in the form of Fire.

Salutations to those who are Vāyu, Ugra, Ākāśa, Mahādeva, Sūrya, Bhīma, Soma, and Īśāna; salutations to the power of will (icchā-śakti), the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and the power of action (kriyā-śakti); salutations to the path of mantra (mantrādhvan). Pa.
Oṃ! To the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhva), the path of the letters (varṇādhva), and there, the path of the kalās:
to Nivṛttikalā, Pratiṣṭhākalā, Vidyākalā, Śāntākalā, Śāntyatītakalā, and to Brahmā, the lord of Nivṛttikalā.
To Viṣṇu, the lord of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā; to Rudra, the lord of the *vidyā* kalā; to Īśvara, the lord of the *śāntā* kalā; to Sadāśiva, the lord of the *śāntyatītā* kalā; Kha.
To the mace, to the shield, to the noose, to the goad, to the arrow, to the lotus, to the boon-granting gesture, to the gesture of fearlessness, to the shaven head, to the sword,
to the lute, to the drum, to the bell, to the trident, to the thunderbolt, and to the staff.
For Paraśu and Mudgara—thus according to one's own mental inclination—the worship should be performed for Śiva together with his retinue: "Obeisance, fragrance;
obeisance, water-offering (argha); obeisance, flower; obeisance, incense; obeisance, lamp."

Having performed the worship ending with the *maḥ* [syllable] and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should take up the rosary and perform the recitation (*japa*). Then, having performed the secret libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the daily rites such as the *vaiśvadeva*, one should recite the *samayā* at the time of dismissal (*visarjana*).

Oṃ juṃ saḥ! To the form of Amṛteśvara, the inner self of all beings, who pervades the sky and possesses an ethereal body, ward off the violation of all commitments; fulfill all commitments; [fulfill] all... [sā...]

To the one whose body is the *dhāraṇā-mantra*, *hrīṃ svāhā*. *Oṃ juṃ saḥ*, O Immortal One, O Supreme Nectar, O Eternal Bliss, *saḥ*, O Lord of Immortality, O You who dwell within all beings, O You whose nature is Brahman, O You whose body is the Great Void, [Salutations] to You, the All!
Restrain [me] from violating the samaya; fulfill all samayas. To the Fortune of Immortality, svāhā! [Thus ends the Amṛteśvara-patrikā.
May it be auspicious! Oṃ, may there be well-being!
Oṃ. Salutations to the Guru; salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Oṃ.
Now, when the night has turned to dawn, having risen and performed the necessary duties, having discarded the night-garment and put on another garment, [he should sit] upon soft grass...
Having sat down, one should meditate upon one’s own Guru in the form of Śiva, seated upon a white lotus on one’s own head, adorned with camphor,
holding the gestures of boon and fearlessness, and marked by the Śakti on his left lap; having thus visualized him, one should worship him with mental offerings.
Vītayathā: Oṃ, salutations to you, O Blessed One, Śiva, who possesses the form of the Guru;
to the lion of the descent of knowledge (*vidyāvatāra*), who has assumed manifold forms;
to the one whose nature is ever-new, whose singular form is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Sa...

Salutations to the Sun who shatters the darkness of ignorance; to Him who is the dense mass of consciousness; to the Independent One whose form is fashioned by compassion; to the Self of Śiva who appears dependent for the sake of those devoted to Him; to Him who possesses a beautiful form for the fortunate ones, and who is the embodiment of knowledge for the wise.
Before those who illuminate form, before those who discern that which is not illuminated,
and before those who reflect upon that which is not reflected, I shall always bow— with my mind as my form— before, on both sides, behind, above, and below.

Then, having meditated upon the Kundalini consisting of the Root-mantra— which is seated within the *bhava* (the source), which shines forth from the base (*mūla*) up to the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), which is thinner than a lotus fiber, and which is as radiant as the rising sun— one should contemplate its splendor.
One should contemplate the universe as having a body reddened by saffron;
then, having arisen, [one recites] "Oṃ Klīṃ, to Kāmadeva, beloved of all people."
Having performed the cleansing of the teeth with this mantra: *yanamaḥ*, [one should recite:
(1) *oṃ śrīṃ | oṃ oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ kamale kamalālaye prasīda prasīda śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ* | (2) *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ* | (3)

Oṃ śrīṃ sa ha ka la hrīṃ śrīṃ (4). With these four types of mantras, one should wash the face. Then, having arrived at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) or similar location and bathed according to the sequence of one’s own *sūtra*, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) beginning with "Today... for the propitiation of the Supreme Deity.
Having recalled, "I shall perform my ablutions," [one should recite]: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, take up your residence in these waters!
Thus [ends] the Sūrya-mantra.
Having invoked the sacred sites of Ḍāla, Aṅkuśa, and Netra, one should visualize the Śrīcakra or a triangle there; then,
recollecting the Goddess therein and imagining her foot-water to be crimson with lac, one should immerse oneself three times with the root mantra and touch the head three times with it.

One should sprinkle [the site] with the *caguhyamudrā*; then, having saluted the assembly (*saṃdhā*), sipped water for purification (*ācamana*) with the root mantra, tied the topknot (*śikhā*), and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*),
one who is adorned with the *tilaka* made from the root mantra and decorated with the vomit and other substances produced by its recitation should perform the *mantra-saṃdhā*.
Having sipped water with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), having rendered the water nectar-like by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*,

having consecrated it three times with the root mantra, and having sprinkled his head three times with that same [mantra], he should draw that [water] up to the tip of the nose by means of the same [mantra],
and [wash away] the sins with the waters drawn into the interior of the body.
Having washed away the accumulation [of impurities] and having discarded that black water, one should strike it against a vajra-stone prepared beforehand. Then,
having offered arghya three times to the Goddess who resides within the sword-maṇḍala, one should perform worship with the root mantra.
One should recite the Gāyatrī according to one's capacity:
*sakala hrīṃ vāgbhaveśvari vidmahe, haṃsa kahala hrīṃ kāmeśvari dhīmahi, sakala hrīṃ tannaḥ*.
"May [the Goddess] Śakti impel [us]. (3) Having offered arghya to Sūrya with the mantra "hrāṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ," one should satisfy him three times, pay obeisance, and then dismiss him.
In this regard, for one performing Vedic rites, the Tantric rite is not prescribed.
Some say that because of the statement, "For one performing Tantric rites, Vedic karma is not prescribed," there is a sublation of Vedic acts such as ritual bathing (*snāna*) and so forth;
others say [it applies] to sexual intercourse with a stranger (*mitho'vyavāya*), while yet others say it applies specifically to Vedic [rites].
The meaning is that only that which is tantric should be performed here according to the tantric method, and not the other by means of the other, lest there be a deficiency in either; otherwise,
due to falling away from one's own tradition, it would result in harm— so says the tradition.

Then, having arrived at the entrance of the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should worship [the door] with the mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the pavilion for the worship of Tripurā. Then, having sprinkled the door with pure water while reciting the *praṇava* (Oṃ), [he should proceed].
One should begin the worship with: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Dvāṃ Dvāraśriyai Namaḥ* (Salutation to the Goddess of the Door) in the center of the upper archway;
*Oṃ Gaṃ Gaṇeśāya Namaḥ* (Salutation to Gaṇeśa); and *Oṃ Saṃ Sarasvatyai Namaḥ* (Salutation to Sarasvatī).
In the two corners thereof: *Oṃ Gaṃ Gaṇapataye Namaḥ* (Salutation to Gaṇapati). *Oṃ...* [The text continues].
Kṣeṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla; Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā; Oṃ Yaṃ, obeisance to Yamunā; Oṃ Dhāṃ, obeisance to Dhātrī; Oṃ Viṃ, obeisance to Vidhātrī;
Oṃ Śaṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi; Oṃ Paṃ, obeisance to Padmanidhi.

With "Maḥ" [and the respective mantras], [one worships] the two door-posts; with "Deṃ dehalyai namaḥ," [one worships] the threshold; having opened the door preceded by "Astrāya phaṭ namaḥ" three times for the palate, [one says] "Vāṃ vāstupuruṣāya."
Having thus worshipped the doors within the mandala of the gateway, contracting the left leg, one should touch the threshold-bough;
having entered within with the left foot, [one recites] *hrīṃ ādhā*.

Having worshipped one's own seat with "Oṃ, salutation to the lotus-seated one who possesses power" (oṃ śaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ), [one should know that] for this seat-mantra, Meru is the ṛṣi, Sutala is the meter,
and Kūrma is the deity; its application is in sitting upon the seat.
Gaḥ (2). Prīṃ. Salutation to the Earth. O Earth, you are supported by the worlds; you are supported by Viṣṇu; and may you, in turn, support me.

"O Goddess, make the seat pure. Having sat down with these words, [he recites] three times: "May those beings depart who are established upon the earth; may those beings who are creators of obstacles perish by the command of Śiva."
Having dispelled all obstacles with "huṃ astrāya phaṭ," one should bind the ten directions.
To the left: (2) *guṃ* obeisance to the Gurus; to the right: (2) *gaṃ* obeisance to Gaṇapati; in front: (2) *kṣaṃ* obeisance to Kṣetrapāla. (2) *i*.

Having prostrated with "Oṃ [Name of the Deity] Devatāyai Namaḥ," and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the fulfillment of the qualification, saying "I shall perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi)," one should raise the Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra by means of the syllable *Huṃ* and unite her with the individual soul (*jīvātman*).
Having joined [the breath] with the *haṃsa* mantra, one should dissolve it into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Then, having dissolved the earth element situated from the feet up to the knees into the water element situated from the knees up to the navel, [one should dissolve] that [water]...
[One dissolves] fire, which resides from the navel to the heart, into air, which resides from the heart to the space between the eyebrows;

that [air], which resides from the space between the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), into ether; and that [ether] into the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra); and that into the Great Principle (mahat-tattva).

Then one should dissolve that [mind] into Brahman within its own primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Thereafter, having visualized the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) within the belly, and having filled it with the syllable *Yam* repeated sixteen times, one should dry up that body along with its sins.
With the syllable *ram* (24), recited with the right and left [hands] through the practice of *kumbhaka*,
one burns the body together with its sins until it is reduced to ashes; then, with the syllable *yam* (32), recited with the right and left [hands], the ashes of the personified sin—

Then, one should recite "Oṃ vaṃ" and, causing a rain of nectar consisting of the letters of the Mātṛkā originating from the moon on the forehead to descend, one should dissolve the ashes and manifest the limbs [of the body] through the sequence of placement (nyāsa), ending with "Laṃ."
Having firmly meditated upon the nature of the Supreme Self, he established the Great Principle (mahat-tattva),
then the ego (ahaṃkāra), and from that, in the sequence beginning with ether (ākāśa) and so forth, the elements and the rest in their proper places.

Having drawn the self with the *ham* mantra, one should cause Kuṇḍalinī to reach her abode and contemplate one's own self as transcending the phenomenal world; this is the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Then, in the heart...

Having placed it [the image or object] there, one should recite the *āṃhaṃsita* mantra three times; this is the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kro yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ mama prāṇā iha prāṇāḥ, evaṃ mama jīvaḥ.*

"O you who abide in the wind, even so do all the senses abide here—speech, mind, skin, eye, ear, tongue, and nose; having come right here, may they remain for a long time in their own mouths, svāhā! Thus is the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*.
Of this Śrīmātṛkā-nyāsa:
Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā), *aṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *aḥ* is the power (śakti); it is employed for the purpose of nyāsa.

Having assigned the syllables *gaḥ*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, and *aṃ* to the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet [of the deity], one should assign *ṭaṃ*, *ṭhaṃ*, *ṛṃ*, *ṝṃ*, and *ḷṃ* to the two hands; then *aṃ* to the palm of the right hand, *āṃ* to the palm of the left hand, *iṃ* to the back of the right hand, and *īṃ* to the back of the left hand.

Having placed the syllables *uṃ* on the palm of the right hand and *ūṃ* on the palm of the left hand, and having assigned the syllables *ṛṃ*, *ṝṃ*, *ḷṃ*, *ḹṃ*, *eṃ*, *aiṃ*, *oṃ*, *auṃ*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ* starting from the right thumb and ending with the left thumb,
one should [then assign] the consonants from *ka* to *sa*.
Beginning from the left index finger and ending with the right index finger,
having placed four [syllables] in each finger-joint in the sequence of root, near-root, middle, and tip, one should place *haṃ* and *laṃ* on the two thumbs, and the syllable *kṣa* on all the limbs.

One should properly place [the mantras]: *Aṃ* (5), *Aṃ-aṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ* (2); *Iṃ Caṃ Pīṃ* to the two index fingers, *namaḥ* (2); *Uṃ Ṭaṃ* (5), *Rthaṃ* to the two middle fingers, *namaḥ* (2); *Eṃ Taṃ* (5), *Aiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *namaḥ*; *Oṃ Paṃ* (5).
Salutation to the thumbs and little fingers (2).
*Aṃ yaṃ ṭhaḥ aḥ*—salutation to the palms and backs of the hands. Likewise for the heart and other limbs (2): *Aṃ kaṃ* (5); *Āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* (2); *Iṃ caṃ paṃ īśirase svāhā* (2); *Uṃ ṭaṃ* (5).

*Rthaṃ-śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (2); *aiṃ-taṃ* (5); *aiṃ-kavacāya hūṃ* (2); *oṃ-paṃ* (5); *auṃ-netrebhyo vauṣaṭ* (2); *aṃ-yaṃ-ṭhaṃ-aḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Thus is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). Then one should meditate as follows: *pañcāśat...*

I bow to Varṇeśvarī, who is as white as a jasmine flower or snow, whose slender body was fashioned by Dakṣa, whose eyes are like the moon, who is beautiful with the digits of the cool-rayed moon she bears, and whose hands are adorned with a seal, a rosary, gems, and a book.
[The letters] Śa, Gaura, Ka, Na, Na, Va, Rta, Dvi, Akṣi, Śru, Ti, Naga, Ṇḍa, Oṣṭha, Danta,

Mūrdha, Asye, Doḥ, Yat, Sandhi, Agra, Iṣu, Ca, Pārśva, Dvaya, Pṛṣṭha, Nābhi, Jaṭhare, Ṣu, Hi, Adoḥ, Mūla, Apa, Ra; [are placed] upon the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the two temples, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, the head, the mouth, the two arms, the joints, the tips, the arrows, the two sides, the back, the navel, the belly, the base of the lower arms, and the other [parts].

One should then sequentially assign the syllables, together with the *bindu*, to the eyes, the pair of hands and feet, the belly, and the two [shoulders], starting from the beginning and ending with the pervasive designation (*vyāpaka-saṃjñā*),
first in the forward order and then in reverse.

Having arranged [the letters] according to the sequence of the necklace (hārakrama), and then having performed the *utpatti-nyāsa* in its proper order, one should place [the letters] in their respective locations from *ka kha* etc.
up to *taṃ*, and then from *aṃ āṃ* etc. up to *aḥ*.
Having placed [the letters] from *tha* to *ma* in their respective positions, one should place them up to *kṣa*; this is the *sthitinyāsa*.

Then, having performed the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) beginning with *vālā*, beginning with *mūla*, beginning with *vrīḍā*, beginning with *kāma*, and beginning with *ramā*, one should perform the placement (*nyaset*).
The practice is as follows: (2) Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ.
*Oṃ namaḥ keśānti*, etc., the root mantra *oṃ namaḥ keśānti*,
etc., *hrīṃ oṃ namaḥ*, *klīṃ oṃ namaḥ*, *śrīṃ oṃ namaḥ*, etc.— thus [ends] the *Subhagā* [mantra] engraved by Āgami Rāmacandra.
The First Ray in the Jewel of Hymns (Rcāratna). Now, the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa):
"Oṃ, salutation to Ānandabhairava, the seer (ṛṣi)," at the head; "Salutation to the Paṅkti meter," at the mouth; "To the goddess Śrī Mahātripurasundarī... [at the heart].
*Tāyai namaḥ* on the heart; *Vāgbhava-bījāya namaḥ* on the secret place;
*Tāyai Tṛtīya-śaktaye namaḥ* on the feet; *Kāmarāja-kīlakāya namaḥ* on all limbs. This is the Nyāsa of the Seers and other [limbs]. Now, the hands...
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is as follows: *aṃ namaḥ* on the two middle fingers;
*āṃ namaḥ* on the two ring fingers; *sauḥ namaḥ* on the two little fingers;
*aṃ namaḥ* on the two thumbs; *āṃ namaḥ* on the two index fingers; and *sauḥ namaḥ* on the palms and backs of the hands.
Now, the placement of the seats (2): (2) *hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ*, salutation to the seat of the self of the Goddess Tripurasundarī, on the feet;
(2) *hai hlīṃ hsauḥ*, salutation to the seat of all the wheels (*cakras*) of Tripuravāsinī, on the shanks.
*Hsaiṃ hasakalīṃ hsauḥ tripurāśrī sarvamantrāsanāya namaḥ* at the knees. (2) *Hrīṃ klīṃ nle tripuramālinī sādhyasiddhāsanāya namaḥ* at the *mūlādhāra*. Thus, the four [seats].

Rāsananyāsa (2): *Aiṃ Āṃ Sauḥ*, obeisance to Tripurā, whose seat is the ocean of nectar, to the feet. (2) *Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ*, obeisance to Tripurīśvarī, whose seat is the lotus of the boat, to the knees. (2) *Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ*.

*Oṃ hraiṃ hrlīṃ hsauḥ Tripurasundarī-devy-ātma-āsanāya namaḥ* on the two thighs. (2) *Hraiṃ hrlīṃ hsauḥ Tripuravāsinī sarva-cakra-āsanāya namaḥ* on the two buttocks. (2) *Hsaiṃ hasakalīṃ hsauḥ Tripurāśrī...* [on the anus].

*Oṃ* *Rvamaṃtrāsana-āya namaḥ* at the anus. (2) *Hrīṃ klīṃ nleṃ tripuramālinī-sādhyasiddhāsana-āya namaḥ* at the *mūlādhāra*. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six seats. (2) *Aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ namaḥ śrīma-*
Hā! Protect this Tripurasundarī! (2) *Namaḥ* to the heart, *svāhā*. *Oṃ namaḥ* to the head of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, *svāhā*.
*Oṃ namaḥ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*) of Śrī Mahātripura, *vaṣaṭ*. *Oṃ namaḥ* to Śrīma...

Hā tri(0) kavacāya huṃ. Oṃ namaḥ śrīmahātri(0) netrebhyo vauṣaṭ. Oṃ namaḥ śrīmahātri astrāya phaṭ. Thus is the protective six-limbed assignment (*rakṣā-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*). Oṃ aiṃ, obeisance to the heart of the All-Knowing One (2).
*klīṃ nityatṛptāyai śirase svāhā* (2) *sauḥ anādivodhāyai śikhāyai* *oṃ aiṃ svatantrāyai kavacāya* (2) *klīṃ nityamaluptāyai netrebhyo vaṣaṭ* (2) *sauḥ anantaśaktaye astrāya phaṭ* (0)

Thus ends the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). (2) Ka (4) To the abode of the power of omniscience, the venerable Mahātripurasundarī; to the heart (0 2) Ha Sa Ka La Hrīṃ, the abode of the power of eternal contentment, the venerable Mahā (0) Śi.

Rase (0 2) sakalahrīṃ śrīmahā-anādivodhaśaktidhāmne śikhāyai vaṣaṭ (2) Ka (5) śrīmahā-svatantratāśaktidhāmne kavacāya hūṃ (2) Ha (6) śrīmāhā-nityamalupta-śaktidhāmne netratrayāya vauṣaṭ (2) La (10) śrīmahā-nityānandaśaktidhāmne astrāya phaṭ (2) Sa (14) śrīmahā-sarvaśaktidhāmne sarvātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā (2).

To the abode of power, O Eye; to the venerable Mahānanta, the abode of power, [the weapon]. Thus is the Nyāsa of the six limbs and the young maidens. Aṃ Āṃ (16) Kluṃ, obeisance to Vaśinī, the goddess of speech, on the head. Kaṃ (5).
*klīṃ kāmeśvarīvāgdevatāyai namaḥ* on the forehead; (2) *caṃ* (5) *nlīṃ modinīvā* between the eyebrows; (2) *ṭaṃ* (5) *yluṃ vimalāvā* at the throat;
(2) *taṃ* (5) *jasrīṃ aruṇāvā* at the heart; (2) *paṃ* (5) *hasalavaya*.
Arthajayinī at the navel (yaṃ);
