178a) Oṃ, salutations to Tripurasundarī. The Blessed One said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is auspicious, more secret than the secret. Kava...

O Caṇḍaparameśānī, O Greatly Auspicious One, O Tripurā, O Nārāyaṇī, O Abode of the Universe, O Beloved of my heart, O Supreme Refuge— this has been told by you, O Great Goddess, though it was concealed even from your own sons throughout all the Tantras.

O auspicious one, that which has not been stated in the *Yāmalas* and that which has not been stated even in the *Ḍāmaras*—let all of this be accepted. Desiring the perfection of your own *vidyā*, you must protect this with effort; it is the knowledge consisting of the nine *vidyās*.

O Goddess, O Auspicious One, this which grants the fruit of all desires is the most secret [teaching]; one should not reveal it to just anyone. O Maheśvarī, in this Vaiśeṣika-jñāna-tantra, which is to be honored by the Vīras, [it concerns] Aruṇeśa, Modinīśa, and Viśu.
O Goddess, I have said this repeatedly— truly, truly— that nowhere else has this been spoken by me. O Mistress of the Gods, having recited this which destroys old age and death,
and having worshipped the Śrīcakra and chanted the Vidyā, [one attains] auspiciousness.
O Hero, saluted by all, I am capable of bestowing, protecting, and withdrawing [this knowledge];

therefore, having acquired the lore, one should perform everything according to the armor-mantra (*kavaca*). Otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment, except when the supreme armor-mantra is present.
For this armor, the Ṛṣis are remembered as the three gods;
its meter is known to be Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is the Sovereign of the Moon (Candreśvarī).
Its application, O Great Goddess, is for the accomplishment of the fruits of the three aims of life. May she protect [me].

May the eternal Mahātripurasundarī protect me day and night; may Kāmeśvarī protect me, and may Bhagamālinī protect me; may the eternal Kkinā protect me, and may Bhīruṇḍā always protect me, as well as Vahnivāsini.
May Sinīpāta, Mahāvidyeśvarī, and Caṇḍā protect me;
may Śivadūtī protect me, and Tvaritā always protect me;
may Kulasundarī protect me, and Nityā Nīlapatākinī [protect me].
May Vijayā protect me always; may Sarvamaṅgalā protect me;
may Jvālāmālinī protect me; and may Vicitrā protect me at all times.
Having worshipped the Śrīcakra, which bestows happiness and liberation— [may she protect me].
May Kuleśī, the beloved of the Kula, who always descends into the Kulakuṇḍa, protect me;
may the Goddess, whose nature is Brahman, who descends during the thousand-spoked [breath], protect me;
may Tripurasundarī, the Mistress of the Four Seats, protect me from within.
May the hosts of deities beginning with Indra always protect me;
may Vālā protect me at all times; may Sṛṣṭi protect me always;
and may she who is the eleven-fold [form] of the eternal invocation always guard me.
May Ekakūṭā protect me always; may Trikuṭā protect me always.
May she whose nature consists of five peaks protect me; may Pañcamī protect me always. May Vidyāpañcadaśī protect me; may Gopyā protect me as the sixteenth. Six.

May she who is the eternal Kūṭāvatī, who is always the single-syllabled one, who dwells eternally within the nine wombs as the triple peak (kūṭatraya), and who is the dream-like Madhumatī consisting of the seed of Śakti— may she protect me.

May Kāmeśvarīdevī protect me at the Ādhāra on Mount Kāma; may Pūrṇeśvarī, the Supreme Goddess, protect me at Jālandhara in the middle of the eyebrows; and may Bhagamālinī always protect me at Oḍḍiyāna.

May Mahātripurasundarī protect my head; may Saṃkṣobhaṇī, Drāvaṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśīkarī, Unmādinī, Mahāṅkuśā, Khecarī, Vījayonī, and Khā protect me from all fears on every side; [and may] Vāgīśvarī protect my knowledge.
May the Śakti who is Vāgbhavī always protect me; may the Kāmarūpiṇī Śakti, who consists of the digits of desire (kāmakalā) and is the Kāmarāja-bīja, always protect me;
and may the Śakti who is the very form of Śakti protect me within the Śakti-bīja, [beginning with] the letters a, ka, ca, ṭa, and ta.
May the goddesses, who abide in the groups of syllables consisting of *nnaddha-paya-śākṣara*,

protect me incessantly for the sake of the accomplishment of the conduct (*ācāra*) of the *Kula*; and may she who is the source of *Lakṣmī* in the *allekhā* of the three peaks (*trikūṭā*), accompanied by the *sara*, protect me from all evil.
Whatever deficiency has occurred in the family tradition through the transgression of the lineage succession, whatever in worship, recitation, and meditations,
whatever in the purification of the *kula-kuṇḍa*, and whatever [defect] regarding the *kula* and *akula*...
May the five arrows, encased within the *prāṇavidyā* mantra, always protect during the worship of the Goddess;
may the sugarcane bow, which brings all under control, always protect from sin; and may the noose protect.
May Vimocanī, along with Jambha, Moha, Vaśa, Stambha, and Mahākuśa, protect me from all disturbances, from the fear of disease, grief, and worldly existence;
and may the goddesses known as Prakaṭā, situated in the center of the Śrīcakra, [grant their protection].
May the Mothers, who are both concealed and most concealed, born of the oral tradition (sāṃpradāya), who abide in the Kula, Kaula, and Nigarbha, who dwell in the secret and the ultra-secret,
and who are the supreme and non-supreme secrets— the Yoginīs— protect me always.
May Tripureśvarī, the beautiful one who bestows the flesh of the cities, protect me;
may Tripurādyā, the sovereign of the Asuras who bestows the flesh of the cities, protect me; may Vāsinī, together with the glorious Tripurā, along with the garlanded Tripurā, protect me.
May the Goddess Tripurā herself, whose nature is the *nīpāta-siddhi* preceded by the three cities (*tripura*),
who is the knowledge of destruction (*niśam-vidyā*), and who is worshipped by the goddesses who are the mistresses of the four wheels (*catuścakra-īśvarī*), protect me.
Even from the multitude of malevolent and non-malevolent planetary influences, she is the Mistress of the Bindu, whose glorious feet are the great primordial refuge; she is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.

Near whose footstool dwell the three gods, filled with joy, their hands joined in the *saṃpuṭaka* gesture; yet they do not know the true description of her form— this secret armor (*kavaca*) is to be kept hidden.
Whoever, being pure and with a mind fixed upon her, should daily recite this armor of the Goddess with effort, he shall be invulnerable among all living beings.
And whoever should diligently wear it when facing a difficult battle, [he shall be victorious].
Those who have turned their backs in battle and fled without fighting, or those who, having recited [the mantra], enter the royal palace— having recited it again—
I declare the truth, the absolute truth: the king shall treat them like slaves for ten years during the period of worship.
Even one who is incapable of performing recitation, meditation, libations, or offerings— by merely remembering this *kavaca*, he too shall become a bestower of success.
O King of kings, one should protect this *kavaca* and the mantra itself from one's own guru in every way.

Whether one is in a prison, or even if bound by shackles, or scorched by the fires of various miseries, or fallen upon a path of hardship— if such a person desires their own welfare, they should, with effort, remember this armor-mantra.
"May one be liberated from distress"—thus it is stated in the *Kumārabodhakatantra*.
The *Saubhāgyakavaca* is complete.
The Śrī Devī said: O Blessed One, ocean of compassion who has satisfied every single being without exception, I shall speak the name of the Goddess Tripurasundarī.
"O Lord, having heard this *Sahasraka*, I am now unable even to retain it; therefore, out of mere compassion, you ought to explain it to me.
Śrī Bhairava said: "The Thousand Names of the Mantra..."

O fair-faced one, O Maheśvarī, having heard this which must always be guarded with great effort, [know that] for this *Śrī Tripurasundarī-sahasranāma-mantra*, Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*) and Paṅkti is the meter (*chanda*).
The application (viniyoga) is for the worship of the deity Mahātripurasundarī:
Oṃ, Subhagā, Sundarī, Śobhyā, Suṣamā, Sukhāvatī, Manojñā, Surasā, Ramyā, Śobhanā, Lalitā, and Śivā.

She is Kānti (Beauty), Kāntimatī (the Radiant One), Kīrti (Fame), Agādha (the Unfathomable), Mānamanoramā (Delightful to the Mind), Kalyāṇī (Auspiciousness), Śubhadā (Bestower of Good), Hṛdyā (Charming), Peśalā (Elegant), Hṛdayaṅgamā (Heart-Captivating),
Bhadrā (Blessed), Abhikhyā (Renowned), Suramaṇī (Divine Jewel), Sādhvī (Virtuous), Cārvī (Exquisite), and Sumaṅgalā (Most Auspicious).
Possessing a beautiful left side, she is desirable, exceedingly tender, radiant with supreme beauty, sweet, charming, beloved by Rati,
delightful to the gods, and as cool as the moonlight through her affection.
She is the mind-born Great Illusion, the Elephant-faced One, and the nature of wine;
she is Mahālakṣmī, the Great Power, whose very form is that of Mahādeva;
she is Maheśvarī, the Great Bliss, who bestows great bliss. Mā.
She who is intoxicated by the honey of the *mādhvī* wine of the *linī*, fierce with passion; the source of bliss, the victorious, the Mistress of Knowledge (*vidyeśī*), whose form is the universe;
she who is the radiant *kaumudī*, the peaceful, and whose nature is the *nāda* of the crescent moon—she is Kā.
Meśī, Kāmakalī, Kāmadā, Kāmavardhinī, Bhīruṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍī, Cāmuṇḍā, Muṇḍamālinī,
Aṇurūpā, Mahārūpā, Bhūteśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Citrā.

She whose limbs are variegated and non-variegated, who contains the seed-syllables within her, the Mistress of the Kula, whose form is consciousness, eternal, imperishable, and primordial; she who is the utterance *klīṃ*, the coiled energy (*kuṇḍalinī*),
the sustainer, the earth, the source of all beings, and the one who intoxicates.
The Great Messenger, well-pleased, worshipped by the gods, the outflow of supreme bliss,
whose nature is the ultimate reality, dwelling in the hollow of the heart, subtle, residing in the abode of space— Jvā.
She who wears a garland of rays, the most excellent among illusory powers, the bestower of boons; she who has the hue of coral, the large-eyed one, the preeminent one, the leader of the universe;
she who is the primordial source of the universe, the one to be venerated by the universe, the one whose face is the universe, and the protector of the universe.

She who transcends all, who is auspicious to all, the support of all, the most excellent; she who is intoxicated with bliss yet free from intoxication, who pierces through the ego, who increases the pride of the non-egoistic, who is the delighter, the gladdener, the venerable one, whose abode is the wine of passion, and who is the destruction of that very passion.

She who causes slow trickling, who is the intoxication of the wine of illusion, languid with the pride of passion, whose nature is intoxication, who is free from the blindness of passion, whose eyes flow with the nectar of love,
who is the fundamental source, the great root, and dwells in the *mūlādhāra*.
She who binds, she who is red-eyed and non-red-eyed, the giver of fortune, the Fortune herself, whose nature consists of the three qualities;
she who is Vaśinī, Vāgminī, Vāṇī, Vāruṇī, and the beloved Aruṇī; she who is Aruṇā, Taruṇī, she who reclines on ashes, and she who dwells in fire.
She is Siddhāsiddheśvarīsiddhi, Siddhāmbā, Siddhamātṛkā, Siddhacintā, Siddhanityā, Siddhādyā, and Siddhasaṃmatā; she is Vāgbhavī, Pramadāvidyā, Vāṅmayī, and likewise Vādinī.

She who is swift, yet free from haste, beyond all ailments, the impeller of speed, and whose very essence is velocity; she who dwells in the stainless lotus, who is the embodiment of all auspiciousness,
whose belly is the abode of the Lord, who is bowed down by devotion, who is the sister, and who is garlanded with the *bhaga*.
She who bestows fortune, she who is the bliss of fortune, she whose face is fortune, the mistress of fortune, whose very self is fortune, whose abode is fortune, she who dwells in fortune,
she who brings forth fortune, she who is worshipped by fortune, she who is the source of fortune, and she who carries fortune.
Bhagavimvāsadāklinnā, Nityaklinnā, Madadravā,
Sakalā, Niṣkalā, Kālī, Karālī, Kālarūpiṇī, Kaulinī, Kamalā, Vāmā, Karuṇā, and Karuṇāvatī.
She is Bhāsvatī, Bhairavī, Bhīmā, and Bhadrakālī; she is the consort of the Kula, Nirvāṇī, Gīr, and Rati; she is Gaurī, the most venerable, the mountain, and the ocean;
she is the essence of the aesthetic flavors (rasa), the abundance of those flavors, the flow of those flavors, and the bearer of those flavors.
She is radiant splendor, flowing with grace, desirable, free from desire, and the sustainer of all desires;
she is the destroyer of obstacles, the knower of all, the primordial source of the universe, and the wearer of diverse garments;
she is beautiful in every limb, an ocean of the river of all loveliness.
She who possesses four limbs and four arms, who smiles with a fourfold beautiful smile; she who consists of the Mahāmāyā mantra, who resides in the Maṇipūra cakra;
she whose essence is mantra, the mother of mantra, who is accessible through mantra, and the possessor of excellent mantras.
She who has flowers as arrows, she who is a rain of flowers, she who is flowering, she who increases the flowers;
the Mistress of the Wheel, holding a wheel in her hand, the Ancient One, the Dweller in the City;
Tārā, Sutārā, the Savior, the Deliverer, she whose form is the syllable *Tāra*.

She who holds the sugarcane bow and the great bow, the bestower of auspiciousness and the giver of what is dear; she who is the first of all, the mother of all, the consumer of all, and the one who gladdens all;
she who is the prosperity of all, the great means, and the accomplisher of all yoga.

She is of great majesty, the consort of Mahendra, omniscient, the purifier of all; she is the knowledge of the Self, the Great Knowledge, the Knowledge of Brahman, and the Radiant One; she is the auspicious Sovereign, worshipped by Śiva, the Mistress of Śiva, and whose very essence is Śiva.

She whose abode is the unstruck lotus, she who is full of intense bliss, she who is the earth, she whose form is liberation, she whose method is discipline, she whose radiance is fruitful, she who bears the fruit of fortune,
she who grants the blessings of Śiva, she who is the illustrious one, she whose form is Śiva, the Supreme Kuṇḍa.
She whose locks of hair are as curved as the *linī* plant, who possesses a great belly, who is of magnificent form,
who is vast, honored, and the earth itself; she who bestows auspiciousness, whose nature is reality (*tattva*),
who is the mistress of the Vedas and the various lords, and who dwells in the center of the solar orb.
She who is steadfast, beloved of Śaṅkara, fragrant, the mother of the gods, the mother of Sūrya, adorned by the moon, overflowing with nectar, whose form is the stream of nectar,
whose nature is the consciousness of the void, immortal, and whose resolve is truth— she is Satya.

She who pierces the six knots, the power of will, the power of knowledge, and the power of action; she who acts for the beloved, who is both with and without abode, whose bliss is beyond all resting places, whose nature is subtle knowledge, who is full of flavor, the essence of the nectar of immortality, and who is reachable through the flow of that essence.
Sarasvatī, the supreme refuge, the ultimate goal of Padmā, the supreme goal of Parā,
the bestower of prosperity, the consort of Śaṅkara, the dark-hued one, the source of Śiva, the eye of Śiva, beyond bliss, beyond the object of meditation, free from duality, and devoid of attributes.

She whose nature is the Self, the Great One, the Nourisher, the Brahmin-like, the Brāhmaṇī, the Speaker of Brahman, Fortitude, Memory, Intelligence, Wisdom, Faith, Contentment, Revelation, the Path, Faith, and the Source of Bliss— she who is all-auspiciousness.
Gyavardhinī, Nirālambā, Nirādhārā, Jṛmbhiṇī, Stambhinī, Dhṛti, Bhogadā, Kamalā, Raudrī, Drāviṇī, praised by Īśa and Hari,
Kuleśī who dwells in the center of the *kula*, and she whose movement is in the fierce channel (*ugranāḍī*).

The beloved one who has transcended the family, the ornament of the noble lineage, she who is to be known through speech, the virtuous Umā, she whose vows are dear, Lakṣmī, she who is not of a family yet illuminates all families,
the soul of the universe, the source of the universe, and the one inseparable from the essence of the universe.

She is Yakī, Vyāpinī, Vādinī, Tīrthā, Śākinī, Mātṛśākinī, she whose form is pure existence (sanmātra), Brāhmī, Śāṅkarī, the bringer of auspiciousness to Śiva, she of beautiful limbs, the abode of the gods, and the sovereign of the hosts of Asuras.

She who is golden-hued, she of abundant splendor, she whose form is beyond description, she of graceful limbs, she who is most beautiful, she whose very nature is the flow of bliss; she who is the paralyzer, the delighter, the joy itself, whose essential form is great bliss, and who is the state of Nirvāṇa.

Victorious is she who crushes the demon Mahiṣa, the sister of Viṣṇu, who possesses the forms of Viṣṇu, who manifests various meanings, the mother of the universe, who delights in the foundation of all things,
and whose abode is between the eyebrows.

She who is the ultimate, devoid of qualities yet increasing all virtues; she who is a streak of light, the non-existent, and the very soul of the world; she who is prosperity, majesty, manifestation, and the splendor of heaven—the one who brings about well-being.
She is the sovereign, eternal, devoted to Śiva, the one who lies within, the bestower of tranquility, Bhavānī, the future,
the beautiful, the perpetual, the destroyer of darkness,
residing in the center of the heart-lotus, the cessation of the state of being a demon, and whose essence is the divine.
She whose form is beautiful and who possesses the moon, who is adorned with the moon and the bindu, who is primordial wisdom,

possessed of wisdom, meritorious, established in the Self, and whose nature is consciousness; she from whom the rise of full bliss flows, her eyes rolling from the intoxication of fullness, the one who dwells in the throat.
She who is beyond the senses, whose form is neither red nor white nor dark, who is infinite, whose majesty is boundless, who is eternally unsatiated, and who is stainless; she who is inconceivable,
the supreme power beyond thought, whose nature is both conceivable and inconceivable, and who is identical with the universe.
The Mother of the World, the Essence of the World, the Origin of the World, the Nourisher, the Night, Bliss, the Immutable One, whose form is the Sun,
attainable through knowledge, whose body is knowledge, whose nature is both ignorance and non-ignorance, the Sky-walker, the Mother of the Sky-walkers.
She whose form is the yoga of the *khecari* movement; the protector of the protectorless, she who is beyond all protectors;

the terrible one, whose form is most terrible; the flow of the stream of nectar, whose nature is nectar, who consists of nectar; she whose form is both burning and non-burning, situated in the center.
Dwelling in the midst of the village, she who possesses both auspicious and inauspicious forms,
the great goddess of auspiciousness, the bestower of auspiciousness, the venerable one whose form is perfect auspiciousness, she who is brilliantly luminous, eternally radiant, and ever-present.
She is the one whose form is yet to come, who dwells in Kātyāyanī, Kalā, Vāsā, and Pūrṇikā;
she is possessed of illusory power, the abode at the end of Nandā, the one who captivates the mind of Nārāyaṇa,
the knower of the method for the path to liberation, and the ground of origin for Viriñci.
She who is unsurpassed, difficult to propitiate, hard to attain, and difficult to transcend;
she who bestows intelligence, fulfills desires, and grants peace; she who bestows knowledge and wisdom;
she who is Svadhā, Svāhā, and the delight of the gods; she who is joy itself and the abode of bliss.

She who bestows nirvāṇa, whose ultimate state is Śaradā, who relies upon Śaradā, who is worshipped by the gods, who is to be propitiated by the asuras, who is the refuge for pure beings, who is auspicious, who consists of praise,
who is worthy of praise, whose form is praise, and who is fond of praise.

She who destroys desire, form, and the death-bringing goddess Kāmamārī; she who slays Time and possesses the form of Time; whose womb is the syllable Oṃ; she who is beyond all forms; Kālakālī; the beautiful one of Time; the consort of Viṣṇu; she who is praised for her awakened purpose; the daughter of Vīra.

She who is worshipped by dogs, who has the form of a flute-player, who destroys all, who possesses universal forms, who is the garden, whose limbs are six times six, who is the Ḍākinī, who has the luster of a pomegranate,
who is the ordainer, who possesses the quality of binding, who is the conqueror of enemies, who possesses her own innate form, who is Jālandharī, and who is born...
She who is the mother of the world, the blazing one, the progenitress, the ascetic lady, the essence, the twilight,
and the source of manifestation; she is Sadāśivā, ever-shining, whose form is throbbing with light, and whose nature is the radiance of the primordial fire.

She who delights the beloveds of the Rākṣasīs, who brings about enchantment, who sustains the universe, who is the eldest according to the sacred ordinances, the beloved of Sāvitrī and the ritual rules, whose purpose is most wonderfully radiant, who is trusted by all, and who bestows the prosperity of worldly existence upon the entire world.
She is the one skilled in the knowledge of cranes, courtesans, and all things; she is the source of Brahman, the Great Source, the source of desire, and the sweet-spoken one;
she is Hākinī, the remover of frost, the golden one, the Yoginī, the destroyer of disease, and Śrī.
She who is the glory of elixirs, the consort of Śrīdhara, the refuge of Śrīdhara, the bestower of fortune, the illustrious one,
the abode of all auspiciousness, the Goddess of Śiva and Śrī, the resort of desire, the messenger of desire, and she who dwells within the womb of desire, whose essence is Rudra.
She who is compassionate, gentle, eternal, accessible to Rudra, free from passion, the syllable Oṃ,
the sacrificial fire, the sixteenth digit, the Truth, the Terrifying One, the Enchantress, the Destroyer, she whose body follows that of Rudra,
the Mistress endowed with the drop of nectar, Kākinī, the lotus.
Lāvāsā, Pārvatī, Pārarūpiṇī, Mālāvatī, Ghoramukhī, Tāpinī, Dīpinī, Indirā, Mākārā, the Mistress of the Circle of Mothers (Mātṛcakra),
Mahāsenā, Vimocinī, and Utsukāntotsukā.
She who causes joy, the leader of the wheel of the letter *Ī*, the one who utters *Phreṃ*, the fierce Rudrā,
the one with a severed head, the one who utters *Hūṭ*, the traveler on the path of the Sugata, the one belonging to Garuḍa, the eldest of Garuḍas,
she who has ascended to heaven, the celibate student, she who bears a dark body.
Verīkamalapriyā, Caṇḍeśvarī,
Caṇḍaśiras, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍamātṛkā, Kālapatnī, Kalandhī, Kaumārī, Kālavallabhā, she who is devoted to Yama, she who dwells upon Yama, and she of terrifying form.
She who removes fear, whose throat is red, who delights the Asuras, who is triangular, who is intoxicated by the downward breath (apāna),
who possesses great splendor, who is pleased with the Vasus, who is the earth, who is the supporter of the earth,
who possesses the luster of all colors yet is colorless, who is beyond death, and who is the great ocean.
The womb is ninefold, consisting of intellect, heroes, and the Mother of Heroes;
it is ninefold in nature, situated within the ten [directions], abiding in the lotus, and bestowing the fruit of liberation.
Arising at the beginning and the middle for men, she is the auspicious Kaṇṭhā, the carrier of her own nine [streams].
Parāghorā, Ākarālākṣī, Sumātā, Merunāyikā, born from the Liṅga of Space, whose essence consists of the nectar of the five ambrosias,
Śrīsabhā, Rudrasiddhārthā, and she who is gratified by the lineage of Ākekarṇa.
Gīśvarī, who is praised by the Siddhas through the Yonimudrā and the Trikhaṇḍā; she whose abode is the Śṛṅgāṭa-pīṭha, the maiden of the Kaula path;
she who resides within the Saṃvarta-maṇḍala and dwells in the garden of the world—[to her] the sandals [belong].
The goddess Aparājitā, whose face is terrifying and never satiated with devouring, who is filled with the bliss of the multitude of spirits, who revels in the nectar of the divine voice,
who is eager, a great hero, and scorched by the rays from her crown, [is present here].
She who delights in the play of intoxication, who satisfies hundreds of yoginīs, who gladdens the lineage, who effects the union of the seed-syllable wheel,
who manifests as the leader of the sky-wheel, and who deludes those with false knowledge.
She who originates from Śākambharī, who is offered by Skanda and Nanda’s son, who grants protection and consolation, who takes the form of a drop on the body of a woman,
whose feet are worshipped by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who holds a lute and a khaṭvāṅga staff— she is Aghorā.

She who manifests through the words of mantra, whose nature is existence, the attractor of the dawn, the smoke-colored one, the female serpent, the auspicious one, the easily attained, the difficult to attain,
the teacher of the scriptures, the expert in the great scriptures, the Great Yogic Lakṣmī.
Lakṣmī, Bhogalakṣmī, Kapālinī, Devayoni, Bhagavatī, Lelihānā, Maheśvarī, Kṣetrātmikā, Mahārātri, Mālinī, Ketumālinī, Sadānandā, and Sadā.
Bhadrā, Kalkinī, Raktarohiṇī, Saṃgrāmamandīnī, Tīvrā, Grāmikā, Sarvabhāṣiṇī, Agnijihvā,
Śayādhīrā, Sthalinī, Madirāmadā, and Sarvajanmākāladūtī.
Tīrdevakāryā, Supūjinī, Jṛmbhiṇī,
Sphoṭinī, Śoṣiṇī, Poṣiṇī, Śravākāriṇī, Vāmadevī, Khaḍginī, Caṇḍadaṇḍinī, Klīṃkārī, Vatsalā, and Hṛṣṭā.
Kārī, Malahaṃsinī, Cakriṇī, Daṃṣṭriṇī, Gomukhī, Gomatī, Dhruvā, Paratejomayī, Saṃvit, Pūrṇā,
Pīṭhanivāsinī, Śṛṅgiṇī, Bhīṣaṇā, Cāndrī, and Pretā.
Sthānamatā, Aṅginī, Ghaṇṭinī, Ceṭinī, Tuṣṭi, Yākinī, Nāṭinī, Naṭī, Kāṭāriṇī, Kālarātri, Meghamālā, Rasātmikā, Bhāpīṭhasthā, and Tadrūpā— these are the Mahābhiḍhūmnas.
Locanā, whose luster is like that of a clear stream, residing at the seat of bliss (Ānandapīṭha),
the kinswoman who binds those bound by fragrant ties,
the liberator from bondage, the embodiment of Sāvitrī, the true goal, and the form of fame and security.
Mahodayā, Guṇeśvarī, Guṇākārā, Sadguṇā, Guṇapūjitā, Gīrmātā, Girijā, Māyī, Śarvāṇī,
Sarvamaṅgalā, Ekākinī, Siddhakanyā, and Kāṣṭhaputrapurī.
Śiṇī, she of unmanifest form, she who is manifest, she whose form is the seat (pīṭha) of the Yoginīs;
Dakṣā, Dākṣāyaṇī, Dākṣī, Madanā, she who is distressed by passion (madanāturā);
Dhiṣṇā, Hiraṇyadharīṇī, Dhāriṇī, Vasuḍākinī.
She who bestows wealth, who maintains the earth, the streets, and heaven;
she who is protected by Narmadā, who grants happiness, who is the essence of the three-syllabled mantra;
she who satisfies, who consumes, who is skillful, who purifies, and who is ever-present.
She is the stream, the mother of streams, the radiant one, the daughter of Kapila, the spark-emitting,
the blazing, the flowing, the lotus-lake, the clearly flowing, the essence of mantra,
she who is worshipped by the universe, the mental one, she whose vehicle is the swan— the Vidyā.

She whose nature is the support of the world, the sustainer, and auspicious liberation; the destroyer of bonds; she who is auspicious in every way; the power of the three Vedas; whose essence is the triad;
whose abode is the three worlds; who is triangular; whose self is the three Vedas; and whose body is the three Vedas; she who is the knowledge of the three Vedas.

The Mother Tripura is the essence of the three Vedas, the form of the three Vedas, possessing three lotuses, residing in the triangle, threefold, consisting of the three vowels, the three-syllabled mantra, the three letters, the three steps, the embodiment of the three forms of the Vedas,
the sovereign of the three cities, the triple goddess, and the queen of the three heavens.

The beautiful lady of the three cities (Tripurasundarī) is threefold; she is the mother of the three worlds (Tridhātṛ), the goddess of the thirty-three (Tridaśā), the three-eyed one (Tryakṣā), and the destroyer of the three (Trighnī).
She is the garlanded one of the three cities (Tripuramālinī), the triad of goals (Trivargā), the threefold path (Trivṛtā), the triangle (Tryasrā), and the destroyer of the three (Trighnī).
She goes to the three cities (Tripuragāminī), she is the glory of the three cities (Tripurāśrī), the mother of the three births (Trijananī), and the great three (Mahātri).

Thus, O Lord of Gods, the thousand names of the mantra of Tripurasundarī, known as *Purasundarī*, have been told to you; it is a secret that grants all desires, pacifies all sins, and bestows the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites.

O Goddess of beautiful waist, by whoever praises the Goddess after worshipping Her with this [hymn], all perfections are attained; it brings about all prosperity, destroys all poverty, removes all diseases, is meritorious, and destroys all calamities.
He who, at the conclusion of worship, should offer this hymn consisting of mantras to the Goddess, which fulfills all desires and bestows perfection, his life shall increase,
and his knowledge and fortune shall flourish. (Thus ends the [chapter] in the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra.)
The *Tresrītripurasundarīnāmasahasram* (The Thousand Names of the Auspicious Tripurasundarī) is completed.
Oṃ Śrī Bhairava said: Now listen, O Goddess of Gods, to the hymn of praise that defines the ultimate reality of Mahātripurasundarī;
it is the supreme essence of all her being, which must never be spoken of nor shown to anyone whatsoever.
This [text] is not to be given to anyone whatsoever except to a wise disciple.
Of this *Stavarāja*, which constitutes the fifth limb of the venerable *Śrī Tripurasundarī*, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Paṅkti is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Śrī Mahā... [is the deity].

The deity is Tripurasundarī; the Vāgbhava-kūṭa is the seed-syllable (bīja); the Kāmaraāja-kūṭa is the power (śakti); the Śakti-kūṭa is the pin (kīlaka). The application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of pleasing Śrīvidyā during recitation. [The syllable] *śu* is mounted upon fire (*vahni*).

O Śivā, if a dull-witted person recites even a single drop of your seed-mantra (*bīja*), which bestows the fruit of all desired goals, then he shall become the sole conqueror of the circle of the earth, his feet worshipped by the lords of the immortals, having defeated the sons of kings.

He who meditates in his mind upon that moon— devoid of its crest-jewel, mounted upon the fire of the void, joined with the stainless left eye, beautiful with the dot of the crescent, and inlaid with the orb of the Bindu— even he, though mute, [attains success].
O Lord of Gods, from the hollow of the lotus-face of the Goddess of Speech, Bhāratī, there immediately issues forth the syllable *ka*, which is like the water of the ocean of the Lord of Suras—
dark as the letter of darkness, endowed with the supreme *mātrā*, and unborn. (2)

The Lord of Mantras, marking the bindu with the half-moon and consisting of the nectar of the stainless moon, recites [this] in the abode of his heart; O Hero-born One, that lord of the earth attains your fearless state. (3) Vāgbha...
If one whose mind is unsteady does not meditate upon the seed-syllable *vaṃ* which bestows auspiciousness,
then by the mere worship of Your feet, O Sovereign Power (*rasā*), he attains servitude in Your abode.
The seed-syllable of power (*śakti*) is stainless and like the moon.
If a practitioner recites [the mantra] with devotion, he becomes like a god;
they delight him with their lotus-feet and with crowns adorned with jewels.
That practitioner who meditates upon a single syllable situated in the middle of the mantra—

A universal monarch who indulges in the playful pleasures of women in this world becomes liberated in the next for hundreds of millions of kalpas. He who chants the seed-syllable of Māyā, being a mantra-practitioner, devoted, and desiring liberation, [attains] your state of Great Lordship. Your...

O Mother of the Universe, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon you, the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, who are composed of all the letters of the mantras; you whose beautiful abode is beheld by the celestial women fanning you with their hands clapped like cymbals, and who are the enjoyer of all that is to be enjoyed.

Having made the sovereignty over the three worlds his own, the Lord of Sadhakas established his abode; he who is known in the world as the Lord of Splendor, beginning with the letter *ka*, dwells within the womb of the three goddesses born of the gods.
In the abode of that wise man,
may the three-eyed Śiva, Viṣṇu, the lotus-eyed one, and the lotus-born Brahmā quickly break their pride.

He who knows this secret peak-syllable beginning with the letter *ha*, which is most guarded, supreme in qualities, yet transcending all qualities, composed of two syllables as its seed-mantra, and joined with the *mānusa* (human) breath—
should constantly recite and meditate upon it; he will suddenly attain great prosperity.
He wanders in this world together with celestial women in the Nandana grove.
That supreme practitioner who would worship the Kārādyakūṭa, which is to be accomplished through the four classes [of mantras],
is within his mind Śiva, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Brahmā.
One should worship that practitioner who possesses a beloved son born of the Śitva lineage.
Whoever chants the seed-mantra of the practitioner, beginning with the syllable of power (*śakti*) and ending with *ḍhāṃsa*, which increases splendor and is endowed with great radiance—
that practitioner, having conquered all hosts of enemies, shall establish his kingdom.

If one constantly meditates upon Him who is adorned with the lunar disc—the ocean of latent impressions from birth after birth—one becomes free from the distress of insurmountability; having abandoned those enemies who are like the lands of the heroes, he enjoys this earth. (12-13)
O Goddess, he who daily joins the Kāmarāja, the sole treasury of nectar,
with the Māyā-bīja at the end of the mantra, shall by his devotion suddenly sustain the earth protected by a universal monarch for the sake of worldly prosperity. (14)
The practitioner who meditates upon you, whether by day or by night,

repeatedly honors the pair of your lotus feet with the clusters of rays from the jewels in his own crown. (15) [Your mantra] contains the syllable 'Ra', which is the essence, immovable, and like nectar.

O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, may he who is unwearied in truth and knows the reality of the clouds— the seed of your auspiciousness— be victorious; for him, O Sovereign Daughter of the Mountain,
the God of the Left-Eyed Goddesses (Kāma) is submissive, and he is honored by the lords of sages.

He who reads or chants this excellent hymn to Śrīsundarī— the abode of the king of glorious mantras, the sole cause of the Lord’s manifestation, and a great wish-fulfilling tree at the time of granting desired boons— is worthy of praise by the gods and should be served by kings. (16)
He who is not distinct from the sun quickly goes to the third heaven.
(17) Thus, this supreme reality is indeed the fifth limb, the King of Hymns, the most excellent praise of Mahātripurasundarī. (18) This [is] the five...

This is the supreme essence of Cāgamaniśaṃ Sundarī; it is to be guarded, more guarded, and most secretly hidden with great effort. It must always be protected, always concealed, and must be shielded even amidst the throngs of the ignorant. A kingdom may be given away, but this [teaching] must not.
This sixteen-syllable mantra of Rodeyanadeyā is secret, extremely secret, and must be guarded like one's own womb; by giving it even to non-devotees or unworthy persons, one shall attain hell.
It must not be given to one who is not a disciple.
One should not reveal it before those who are not practitioners; it must always be hidden from the wicked.
It was kept secret by the one born of the reeds (Kārttikeya). In every way, one should guard it with effort; such is the command of the Supreme Lord. [Thus ends the Śrīrudriya.]
[The King of Praises to the Blessed Mahātripurasundarī from the Mālātantra is complete and finished.]
Joined together and adorned with *nāda* and *bindu*, all [the letters] combined into one become the five-syllabled mantra of the five peaks (*pañcakuṭātmikā*).

O Goddess, this ignorance (avidyā) is hidden in all tantras; it is the crest-jewel of knowledge (vidyā-cūḍāmaṇi), proclaimed by the Lord as the most supreme among the supreme. Out of affection for you, I have explained it;
it must not be told to just anyone. O Goddess, this...

I bow to the Śrīcakra of the Goddess, which must always be guarded with great effort below the Kalpavṛkṣa in the jewel-palace of Bhavānī, situated upon the jeweled throne within the Earth-mansion (Bhūgṛha) consisting of lines of qualities and triangles.

Adorned with the gates of the Vedas, it is threefold, possessing sixteen petals and likewise an eight-petaled pericarp; it has corners facing Indra, corners at the intermediate directions, corners of the Vasus, and a lunar corner— such is this great wheel, eternally [the seat of] Śrī Tri...
Formerly, he beheld the goddess who resembles a lotus, reddened like the rays of the rising sun, similar to the *japā* flower, comparable to the *dāḍima* flower,
resembling a ruby (*padmarāga*), and like saffron.

Resembling liquid mercury, adorned with a shimmering crown and a network of tinkling gems, she sports a diadem that overflows with the radiance of great jewels and delights the moon; [she is] sweet with the fragrance of pure incense...
Adorned with a beautiful mass of hair.
Her sprout-like, curling locks of hair resemble a swarm of black bees;
her lotus-face is like a freshly blossomed red lotus;
and her soft forehead-ribbon is curved like a slender crescent moon.

The Supreme Goddess, whose creeper-like eyebrows are shaped like a drawn bow, whose eyes are playfully swinging to and fro, overflowing with bliss, and whose beautiful cheeks are adorned with shimmering golden earrings that gleam like a cluster of peacocks; her cheeks are perfectly rounded.
Her nose was perfectly defined by the measuring-line of Viśvakarman and others; her lips, possessing the luster of copper, coral, and the bimba fruit, were red like nectar;
and she surpassed the sweetness of a smile even with her mere presence.

She whose ocean of the heroic sentiment was profound, who was adorned with rows of teeth as beautiful as pomegranate seeds and a seed-vessel, whose region of the chin was graced by incomparable qualities,
who possessed a neck like a conch shell, and who had large eyes like lotus stalks.

Adorned with graceful arms graced by jeweled bracelets, armlets, and necklaces, her lotus-like hands— tender as the petals of a red lotus— spread a canopy of moonlight from the radiance of her fingernails.

Her broad chest was adorned with strings of pearl necklaces, her high breasts were prominent, and her waist was beautifully graced by the curvature of the three folds; she shone with a navel that resembled an eddy in the river of loveliness.

The Mistress, whose hips were adorned with a girdle fashioned from priceless gems, whose line of body hair was like a beautiful goad on the orb of her waist, and whose thighs were as delicate as the graceful pillars of a plantain tree— her loveliness...
Adorned with a pair of shanks like those of an antelope,
her two feet with hidden ankles and foreparts surpassing a tortoise; her slender, long toes were resplendent with moon-like nails, [reaching] to the heads of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Her lotus feet were unblemished by any rubbing; she was radiant with a continuous stream of luster resembling hundreds of moons;
her feet possessed the crimson hue of pomegranate blossoms that surpassed the redness of vermilion; and she was clothed in red garments.
[Visualize her] with noose and goad raised in her hands, seated upon a red lotus,
adorned with red ornaments, four-armed, and three-eyed;
holding five arrows and a bow, [and like] a fragment of camphor...

Her face was filled with mixed betel, her body was crimson with the intense saffron of great musk, she was enriched by the grace of every erotic sentiment and adorned with all ornaments— she who brings delight to the world.
I bow to the Mother who brings delight to the world,
who attracts the universe, whose form is the cause of the world, who consists of all Lakṣmīs, who is eternal, and who is gladdened by supreme bliss.

Having recollected the Mahātripuramudrā, the lord of practitioners, having invoked Mahātripurasundarī with the invocation-mudrā and the auspicious vidyā accompanied by the salutation as previously described, [should worship her] in the cakra.
Then, having reflected upon this in the middle, one should perform the worship:
"May Indra protect me in the east; in the southeast, the deity Agni; may Yama always protect [me] in that [direction]; in the southwest, Nirṛti always; in the west, Varuṇa..."
May Vāyu, the deity of the northwest, protect us; may Dhanada protect in the north; may Īśvara protect in the northeast; may Prajāpati protect above;
and may the deity Ananta protect below—thus let there be protection in the ten directions.
May the hosts of deities beginning with the Rudras protect [me]; may Gaṇeśa always protect the field; may Bhairava Vaṭuka protect it;
may Upālī also protect the field; and may Kāmadeva, together with his wife Rati, protect it.

May Śaṅkha and Padma, the two treasures (nidhis), who always dwell together with delight even in the Nandana grove, protect me for the sake of my success at the western gate of Cakrapura in the jeweled palace of Bhavānī. Pā.
O Bhavānī, you who possess a jeweled staircase adorned with supreme sovereignty, protect the western gate in this jewel-palace; Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī,
Māyā, Durgā, Vibhūti, and Bhadrakālī.
Līlā, Cāmuṇḍā, Svāhā, Śubhaṅkarī, Gaurī, Śrī,
Lokadhātrī, Vāgīśvarī, and the others— may all these, remaining here, always grant me protection against those who act as heretics.

May those who dwell on the elements, those who move in the intermediate space, and those who reside in the heavenly world—may they all vanish by the command of Śiva; may they all bring about auspiciousness for the five deities in their seats. Brahmā is the sovereign lord of the site (vāstu).
May the Creator and Protector always protect at the southern gate of the wheel;
may the glorious vessel (pātra) within its mandala always protect the five jewels for the sake of the success of the worshippers;
and there, upon the seat of the vessel, may the fire-mandala (vahni-maṇḍala) be ever full.
May the fire-maṇḍala protect [me], as well as the worship of the Kula-deity;
[and may] Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Muśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhā, and Kavyavāhā likewise [protect me].
The ten kalās of fire should be known as bestowing the fruits of the ten dharmas;
together with these, may Vaiśvānara grant me protection. There, in that excellent, divine vessel, within the glorious orb of the sun, in the mandala of Sūrya...

May she who is to be worshipped for the sake of accomplishing all my goals— she whose luster is like that of smokeless, radiant, and blazing rays of light, who is exceedingly cool, the bestower of enjoyment, the awakener of the universe, the sustainer, and the patient one— protect me.
These digits (kalās) of the Sun are situated within the solar orb;
together with them, may Āditya grant me protection.
Therein is the orb of Savitṛ, and within that, the nectar-orb of Soma.
First, she who is always the cause of the bliss of Bhairava; Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Vṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā,
Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, and Pūrṇā.
May the digits born of Svaraja, who bestow full nectar and the fulfillment of desires, residing in the center of the lunar orb, grant protection at all times.
O Lord of the constellations, in this orb filled with nectar and complete with the twelve digits of the Sun...

May the gods in the solar and fiery mandalas grant me protection for my prosperity; may the Lord of Fullness (Pūrṇeśa) and Ānandabhairava always grant me protection there in the meritorious and full nectar (pūrṇāmṛta).
May Śakti, who is the portion of Vāruṇī and whose form is bliss,
grant protection for my success; may she who is known as Yātrā, Adhomaṇḍūkā, Ādhārī, Rudrā, and Kālānalā, grant me constant protection.
May that primordial nature (Prakṛti), who is the foundational power (Ādhāra-śakti) from whom the immortal one [Viṣṇu] protects the earth, always grant protection;
may that Tortoise (Kūrma) protect us constantly, and may Ananta protect us at all times;
and may the Discus-bearer (Cakrī), the Boar (Varāha), who is stationed upon his head, protect us.
May the Earth, whose teeth are the mountains, protect me constantly;
may the oceans always protect me with their jewels and nectar-like waters;
may Ratnadvīpa grant me protection, and may the Golden Mountain protect me.
May the wish-fulfilling trees protect me in the Nandana grove;
beneath them, may the variegated jeweled grounds always protect me; may the glorious jewel-palace protect me, and may the altar and the white parasol protect me constantly.
May Dharma and Jñāna, seated at the sides of the lion-throne, always protect you; may Vairāgya always protect you, and may Aiśvarya, situated in the middle of the lion-throne, always protect you.

May Māyā protect me; may Vidyā protect me right there; may the lotus stalk always protect me; may the upper and lower petals protect me; may the pericarp in the form of the syllable *tat* protect me; may the orb of the Sun protect me; may the Moon protect me.

May the mandala of fire protect me; may the mandala of wind protect me always; may the quality of rajas protect me always, and may the quality of tamas protect me constantly. Likewise, may the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), the principle of Power (śaktitattva), the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva), and Śiva protect me.

May that which is the reality of Sadāśiva protect everything at all times; may Jñāna, Māyā, Kalā, Vidyā, and the self-nature of the Tattvas grant prosperity; and may the Goddesses always provide protection upon the jeweled lion-throne.

May he who sits upon the ocean of nectar protect me; may he who always sits upon the lotus of the boat protect me; may he who always sits upon the discus protect me; may he who sits upon all mantras protect me, as well as he who sits upon the seat of the Sādhya and Siddha, established right there.
May those two goddesses always grant protection; may Īśvarī, Sundarī, Vāsinī, Śrī, and Sālinī, as well as all [the goddesses] beginning with Siddheśvarī and Tripurā, protect me.
May the assembly of gurus, the divine Siddhas...
Likewise, may the sages of the stream of silence, the gods, the nāgas, and others, always provide protection;
may all the traditions— whether manifest, secret, more secret, or supreme— as well as the Kula, Kaula, and Garbha lineages, do the same.

O Goddess who dwells in the secret of the heart, O Mistress of the Wheel that Enchants the Three Worlds, O You who are the Destroyer of All Enemies, O Bestower of All Siddhis within the Wheel that Agitates All,
O Supreme One who is the Maker of All Protection within the Wheel that Accomplishes All Aims.

In this ninth wheel of the Supreme Lord, which removes all diseases, bestows all accomplishments, and consists of universal bliss— this most secret of secrets, containing the supreme and the non-supreme,
as well as the exceedingly ancient secrets— these [mantras] are always present.
May the hosts of Yoginīs protect me: Aṇimā in the west, Laghimā likewise in the north, Sahimā at the eastern gate, and Īśitā in the south;
may Vaśitā protect [me] in the northwest, and Prākāmya in the east.
In the northeast, there is the accomplishment of enjoyment; likewise, in the southeast, the accomplishment of instruction; in the southwest, the constant attainment of falling downward;
and from the downward direction, the bestower of all desires, [extends] upward as well.
May Bhairava Asitāṅga,
who destroys from above, together with Brahmāṇī at the seat of Ekāmra in the eastern direction,
protect me; and may Urubhaī, stationed in the southeast at Malaya, protect me.

May Rava, together with Maheshi, protect for the sake of the accomplishment of the Kulachara; and may this Chanda, together with Kaumari, provide protection on Mount Kola; and may Bhairava always grant success to the practitioners (sadhakas).
May Krodha, accompanied by Śuṣṇā, always protect the King of the Pīṭhas at Kulānta in the southwest for the sake of attaining enjoyment, desire, and wealth;
and likewise may he, together with Vārāhī, protect the western gate of Unmanā.
In the great sacred seat (pīṭha) of Jālandhara, may Kapālī Bhairava, together with Indrāṇī, always provide protection for me in the northwestern direction for the sake of my spiritual accomplishment.
In Uḍḍiyāna...
May Bhairava Bhiṣaṇa, together with Cāmuṇḍā, always provide protection for me in the northern pīṭha; and may Saṃhāra,
along with the goddess Caṇḍikā, protect me in the Koṭa pīṭha.

May Sarvadāpātukulācāra protect [me] in the northeast for the sake of accomplishment; may Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇīmudrā always protect [me] in the west; may Drāviṇī protect [me] in the north; and likewise, may Ākarṣiṇī protect [me] in the east and in the south.
May Vaśyā protect me from the lower realms (apāya), Unmādā from wind,
Īśā from the fall of the goad, and Trikhaṇḍā from fire; may Vījarūpā protect me from the southwest, Khecarī from above, and Mahāmudrā from below.

The one whose form is the womb of the adept yoginī— may these deities, who reside eternally within the wheel and grant all desires, always provide protection within the three-lined square; she whose form is the attraction of desire.
She who draws away the intellect, she who attracts the ego,
she whose form is the attraction of sound, she whose form is the attraction of touch, she whose form is the attraction of form,
she whose form is the attraction of the variegated, and she who attracts steadfastness.
She is formless, yet she takes the form of attracting mindfulness; she takes the form of attracting names, the form of attracting seed-syllables, and the form of attracting the self;
she is the Goddess who attracts nectar and who takes the form of attracting the body.
May these sixteen self-reigning goddesses, eternally situated upon the petals of the wheel, who grant all desired fruits, always provide protection for you, O Goddess.
[They are] Anaṅgakusumā in the east, Anaṅgamekhalā in the south, and Anaṅgamadanā in the west...

Anangalekha, afflicted with passion, is in the north of Mathana; Anangavegini is in the southeast; Anangamkusā is in the southwest; and Anangamālinī is in the northwest. These eight [deities] begin with the letters of the *ka*-group.
May all those eight powers of the bodiless one (Anaṅga), stationed in their respective groups, provide protection;
may those goddesses situated on the eight petals— namely the power Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī,
Sarvavidrāviṇī, and likewise Sarvākarṣaṇī— [grant protection].
The power that causes all delight, the power that deludes all, the power that causes all paralysis, the one whose form is universal yawning, the one who brings everything under control,
and the power that enchants all.
She whose nature is universal intoxication, the power that accomplishes all aims,
the fulfiller of all hopes, the power consisting of all mantras,
the destroyer of all duality, residing in the fourteen-spoked wheel.
May she who bestows all perfections, the goddess who likewise grants all prosperity, who does what is dear to all,
who effects all auspiciousness, and who grants all desires, always grant forgiveness.
She who liberates from all suffering, she who pacifies all death, she who destroys all obstacles, she whose every limb is beautiful,
the goddess who bestows all good fortune.
May she who dwells upon the outer ten-spoked wheel always provide protection—
she who is omniscient, all-powerful, the bestower of the fruit of all sovereignty,
the goddess consisting of all knowledge, and the destroyer of all diseases.
The Goddess is the nature of the support of all, likewise the remover of all sins;
she is composed of all bliss and is the very embodiment of universal protection. Likewise, the Great Goddess bestows the fruits of all desires; such is the Antardaśā.

May Vāgdevī protect those standing in the southeast; may Vaśinī protect them always; may Kāmeśvarī protect them; may Sāmodinī protect them; may Vimalā protect them; likewise, may Aruṇā protect them; and may Sarveśvarī protect those reciting mantras. May Merā protect me.
May the Kaulinīs, the goddesses stationed in the eight corners, always provide me with protection.
May the weapons-deities—the goad, the hook, the arrow, and the bow—constantly protect me. May the goddesses situated in the center of the Śrīcakra grant me protection.
May the women of the six limbs, who reside upon the body of the Goddess and whose forms are her very limbs, always perform protection; and may those situated within the wheel of the Great Goddess,
in the center of the glorious triangle and therein at its corners, always provide protection.
Among the three [groups] and always within them, may the three deities of the Śrīpīṭhas protect me: Kāmeśvarī in Kāmarūpa, Vajreśvarī in Pūrṇagiri,
and Bhagamālinī in the great pīṭha of Jālandhara.
May the venerable Tripurasundarī, who dwells in the Bindu-cakra upon the seat of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, and whose nature is Brahman,
protect me in the beautiful four-cornered Cakra that fascinates the three worlds.

May the Goddess Tripurā Parameśvarī, who fulfills all desires, protect me incessantly in the beautiful sixteen-spoked wheel; may Tripureśvarī, the eternal Mistress of that wheel, protect me there; and then [in] the eight...

In that wheel which causes the agitation of all the *lacakra*s, may the eternal Mistress of that wheel, Tripurasundarī, be pleased. And in the fourteen-spoked wheel which bestows all good fortune, [may] the Mistress of that wheel [be pleased].
May Tripuravāsinī, who dwells in that [wheel], protect me always for the sake of auspiciousness in the external ten-spoked wheel,
the Sarvārthasādhaka; and may Tripurāśrī protect me always for the sake of auspiciousness in the internal ten-spoked wheel.

May Tripuramālinī, the eternal Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī) within that supreme Sarvarakṣākara [maṇḍala], protect me; then, may the goddess Tripurāsiddhā protect me within the center of that supreme Sarvarogahara [maṇḍala] consisting of eight triangles.

Likewise, may Cakreśvarī, the bestower of all siddhis within the triangular cakra, and likewise Tripurāmbikā, protect me; may the venerable Matrikoṇa, the Cakreśvarī within the cakra consisting of universal bliss, [protect me].
In the middle [of the heart], may Cakreśvarī protect me; may Nityā Tripurasundarī protect me; may Kāmeśvarī protect me; may Bhagamālinī protect me.
May Klinnā protect me always; may Māṃsā protect me always; may Vahnavāsinī protect me, and likewise Mahāvidyeśvarī; may Śivadūtī protect me, and Tvaritā protect me always, O Kula.

May Sundarī protect me; may Nityānityā protect me; may Nityānīlapatākā protect me always; may Vijayā protect me forever; may Śrī Maṅgalā protect me eternally; and may Jvālāsumālinī protect me constantly.

May Citrā protect me always; may Ṣoḍaśī, who is beautiful, protect me; may Mahāvidyā, the fourth, protect me; may Bahurūpiṇī protect me; may the eternal Saptadaśī, who constantly bestows bliss, protect me; and may the four [others] as well.
O Goddesses and Yoginīs, protect me always— in the east, south, west,
north, above, below, and in between; may all the Siddhis and the deities of the Āmnāyas, including the Cārvākas, Sauras, and Śaktas, eternally protect me.
May the earth, belonging to Viṣṇu, which is the unnameable source of creation, maintenance, and dissolution,
protect me at all times; may Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Pākulā, Kākinī,
as well as Śākinī and Hākinī, protect me.

May the hosts of Yoginīs residing in the Cakra, and all the Mātṛkās residing in the phonemes, grant protection at all times. May Budha protect me within the great lotus of the square; may the Lord Ṣoḍaśā protect me day and night.
May Prajāpati likewise protect me in the eight-petaled wheel; may Śiva and Umā always protect me in the fourteen-spoked wheel;
and may the Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, always protect me in the twenty-two-spoked wheel.

May the Supreme Goddess protect me in the center of the eight-spoked wheel; may Śiva and Umā protect me in the central triangle of the middle wheel; may the eternal Mistress of the nine wheels, the Nityā who is the supreme digit (kalā), protect me.

O Maṇiśaṃdevī, O Śrī Tripurasundarī! May that supreme goddess, the fifth [vowel], whose nature is Brahman, who is the one to be meditated upon by the illustrious Tripurasundarī, and who consists of five times five, protect us.
Whatever is remembered as a pentad is known through mantras of five times five syllables; the fifth [state] consists of five peaks, likewise the five principles (pañcatattva),
and whatever is remembered as a pentad is eternally endowed with five qualities.
May the supreme deity Pañcamī protect us constantly and eternally; may that supreme deity Pañcamī always grant peace;
may she always protect us in the northeast.
She who dwells in that stainless realm.
May Śeṣikāsundarī, who dwells in the Binducakra, always protect me;
may Khecarī, the Mudrā of the Kākamalā, protect me; and may the Śakti who dwells in the Mūlādhāra protect me at all times. This [is] the Tripura...
The protective mantra of Rasundarī, which bestows merit and brings happiness to practitioners, has been taught according to the sequence of the lineage. By this sequential procedure,
the most excellent of practitioners, having fully worshipped the venerable Tripurasundarī—
One should always recite this Kṣāma mantra at dawn after becoming pure,

or at nightfall, or at midnight; or when encountering difficulty, or in a place where clarified butter is unavailable, or in an inaccessible region, or in water, or even in fire, or in a cremation ground, or in a fortress.
A person should recite this hymn everywhere whenever fear arises;
having worshipped the Goddess through the presence of all her limbs, the practitioner should diligently perform protection, which destroys all calamities. The Hymn.

This is indeed marvelous and difficult to find even in the three worlds; it must be guarded with effort by one who desires their own welfare. It should never be given to just anyone, nor should it ever be spoken [to them], except to a disciple possessed of devotion.
One should reveal [this] to a disciplined practitioner; otherwise, it will perish once given—such is the supreme command of the Lord.
One should not show it to fallen practitioners or even to kinsmen; if it is given [to them], there is a loss of accomplishment.
The mantras taught by Śaṅkara as "it may be so" (syāt) become averse [to the practitioner];
when he becomes angry, Bhavānīsundarī [becomes hostile], and misfortune shall befall him.
Therefore, one should protect with effort the book that exists in one's house.
Having become steady, Cañcalā remained there;
therefore, Kamalā stays in that place. Consequently, one should worship this text with effort using perfumes and flowers; thus one obtains the fruit of worship.
O best of practitioners, listen to the fruit that one obtains from this meritorious king of hymns, which becomes beautiful through its presence;
hear what result the wise man attains by reciting it with a well-concentrated mind even once.
Having understood the fruit of worshiping the circle of Mothers (*mātṛcakra*),
the practitioner becomes victorious; devoted to faith, he should recite [the mantra] in due order for one month,
and he shall become renowned even in heaven as the son of the Goddess on this earth.
He who, with devotion, wears this supreme hymn after having it written on his crest,
or on his neck, or on his left or right hand,
shall become the best of practitioners and always dear to the Mothers; he attains everything.

This is the supreme, great blessing for those with desire; therefore, one should always maintain this with effort according to the prescribed rite. Having recited it and having worshipped it, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control. To whichever devotee this mantra is given...
The supreme three-syllable mantra,
situated within the *suvarṇa*, grants all desires;
whatever one wishes for, even those exceeding desire, it bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
One obtains heaven here on earth without a doubt, even in the netherworld (Rasātala).
Having seen the practitioner, all the planets, Rākṣasas, and harmful spirits flee from afar; they are not capable of causing harm. Poison becomes neutralized...

Hundreds of sins go to their destruction; becoming like a god, a person experiences abundant happiness and attains all perfections, being liberated from all evils. Therefore, one should recite it constantly with a focused mind.
For the sake of attaining the goals of liberation, worldly enjoyment, and wealth, one should worship the Goddess with devotion and always practice self-protection;
he who knows his previous births throughout thousands of lifetimes shall not be born again, O Yamunā.

Indeed, there is nothing else; having assumed the form of a Gandharva and worshipped the Supreme Goddess, and having recited the protective mantra, one certainly attains divinity. One without a son obtains a son, and the poor man obtains wealth.
One shall accomplish all that is difficult to accomplish and attain all that is hard to obtain with certainty;
even while situated anywhere— whether in a terrible abode of extreme suffering, in a fearsome state of shackles and bonds, or whether one is pure or impure.
By reciting this hymn to the Goddess, one will certainly be released from bondage.
Even if one is afflicted by a very severe illness, if they worship the Goddess— even if it be only a single complete verse— they shall be instantly liberated from that disease.
Speech such as deluding, attracting, killing, and expelling arises from the mere visualization [of this mantra];
one shall obtain all accomplishments (*siddhi*). This is the protective mantra of Tripurasundarī, which bestows merit when recited in the sequence of the lineage.

This enchanting King of Hymns (Stavarāja) of Tripurasundarī, which brings happiness to practitioners, has been proclaimed by Śiva as a protective mantra that bestows auspiciousness; it is like an umbrella held over one's head.

One should always meditate upon oneself as the Goddess Supūtanā, red in color, seated upon a lotus with a hundred petals, raining down nectar, and being incessantly fanned by celestial women— thus within the mental lotus.
He who, through the destruction of all latent impressions (vāsanās), quickly attains sovereignty over the entire earth,
beholds in the well-illuminated sky— filled with all auspicious qualities— the beautiful woman with red eyes, eternally seated upon a lotus.
Meditating with his whole being upon that beautiful lady, who resembles the rising sun and possesses the luster of ten million moons, and who is endowed with every virtue—
he who beholds her directly is indeed the god Maheśa, the burner of Madana.
He becomes a master traveler through the sky.
[Thus ends the Fifth King of Hymns from the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra. Auspiciousness!
